Chapter 1 — History,
Specifications, and Architecture
of the Mega Drive
Whathardwareliesbeneaththecode: processors,memory,andthedivisionoflaborthatwill
shape every programming decision in this manual
Before writing a single line of C, it’s worth understanding, even if only in broad strokes, the
machine you’re programming for. This isn’t a trivia chapter: almost every design decision
you’ll make throughout this manual —why 8- or 16-bit data types are used instead of int out
of habit, why there’s no floating point, why sound is programmed separately from the rest of
the game, why you have to manually keep track of how much video memory is being used—
has a concrete reason rooted in the architecture described here. Come back to this chapter
whenever a limitation feels arbitrary: it almost certainly isn’t.
1. A bit of history
SegalaunchedtheMegaDriveinJapanin1988, asthesuccessortothe8-bitMasterSystem.
The console arrived in the United States in 1989 under the name Genesis (a name it kept in
that market for its entire commercial life) and in Europe in 1990, already under the Mega
Drive name. It was the main competitor to the Super Nintendo during the so-called “16-bit
war” of the early 1990s, and it went on to sell more than 30 million units worldwide, with a
catalogthatincludesserieslikeSonictheHedgehog,StreetsofRage,PhantasyStar,Shining
Force, and Golden Axe, plus a huge catalog of arcade conversions.
Over the course of its commercial life, three hardware revisions were manufactured (Mega
Drive 1 in 1988, Mega Drive 2 in 1993, and Mega Drive 3 in 1998), with external and
manufacturing-cost differences but full compatibility with the same game catalog. The
console also had a series of expansions and peripherals: the Mega-CD (a CD reader with
additional graphics and sound hardware) and the 32X (a cartridge with extra processors
aimed at 3D graphics). Neither is within the scope of this manual, which focuses on the
original cartridge-based Mega Drive/Genesis; if you ever move on to developing for those
platforms, much of what you’ll learn here —the VDP, memory organization, the SGDK
workflow— remains the necessary foundation, with additional hardware layered on top.
Before the appearance of modern, free development kits like SGDK, programming for the
Mega Drive required direct knowledge of the main processor’s assembly language and ac-
cess to official, Sega-licensed development kits, which were expensive and restricted. SGDK
—created by Stéphane Dallongeville and still actively maintained today— changed that com-
pletely: it’s free, open source, lets you program in C, and includes both the function library
you’llusethroughoutthismanualandthetoolsneededtoconvertgraphics,maps,music,and
3

=== PAGE 10 ===
sound effects into data the console can use.
2. The three protagonists of the hardware
TheMegaDrivesplitsitsworkamongthreemainpiecesofsilicon,eachwithaclearlydefined
job. Thatdivisionexplainsmuchofthedesigndecisionsyou’llencounterthroughouttherest
of the manual.
The main processor: Motorola 68000. This is the console’s brain, a 16/32-bit micropro-
cessor running at approximately 7.67 MHz on NTSC consoles (Japan/America) and 7.6 MHz
on PAL (Europe). All the C code you write with SGDK ends up compiled into instructions for
this processor. The 68000 has no floating-point unit (FPU): there’s no native, hardware-level
waytoworkwithdecimalnumbers,whichiswhySGDKoffersfixed-pointtypes(fix16,fix32)
instead of float or double — a topic revisited in detail later in this same foundational block.
The sound coprocessor: Zilog Z80. The Z80 is a second processor, simpler than the
68000, dedicated almost entirely to handling sound: it controls the FM synthesizer and the
programmablesoundgenerator(bothdescribedbelow). It’salsothesameprocessorusedby
theMasterSystem,whichletstheMegaDriverungamesfromthatearlierconsoleinaspecial
compatibility mode. For the 68000 to talk to the sound chips, it first has to “ask permission”
from the Z80 by temporarily handing it control of the data bus; that bus-handoff mechanism
is why, in SGDK, playing music and sound effects goes through specific functions (covered
in the part of this manual dedicated to sound) instead of being written directly as if it were
ordinary memory.
The video processor: VDP (Video Display Processor). The VDP draws everything that
appears on screen: backgrounds, sprites, any graphic visible on the television. It has its
own video memory, separate from main RAM, and is programmed through a set of control
registers. GivenhowcentralitistoeverythingvisualinaMegaDrivegame,thenextchapter
is devoted entirely to explaining it in depth.
3. The sound chips
Within the audio subsystem, controlled by the Z80, two sound chips coexist with very differ-
ent characteristics, and their combination is one of the console’s most recognizable sonic
trademarks:
• Yamaha YM2612: a 6-channel stereo FM (frequency modulation) synthesizer. It’s re-
sponsible for the more “metallic” and orchestral sound characteristic of Mega Drive
music, and it can also play back digitized audio samples (PCM), sacrificing one of its six
channels to do so.
• PSG (Programmable Sound Generator, an SN76489 or equivalent): a simpler, 4-
channel sound generator (three tone channels and one noise channel), inherited from
the previous generation of Sega hardware. It’s typically used for sound effects and to
reinforce the YM2612’s music with additional lines.
The part of this manual dedicated to sound explains in detail how SGDK exposes both chips
through its XGM and XGM2 drivers, as well as the workflow for creating and playing music
and sound effects.
4. Memory: a map of scarce resources
Oneofthemostimportanthabitsyou’lldevelopthroughoutthismanualisthinkingofmemory
asafiniteresourcethathastobeactivelymanaged,notsomethingthat’ssimply“there.” The
4

=== PAGE 11 ===
MegaDrivesplitsitsmemoryintoseveralindependentblocks,eachwithitsownpurposeand
fixed size:
Memory Size Use
Main RAM 64 KB Variables, data stacks, and
structures for the C program
VRAM (video memory) 64 KB Graphic tiles, plane name
tables, sprite table
CRAM (palette memory) 128 bytes 4 palettes of 16 colors each
VSRAM (vertical scroll 80 bytes Per-column vertical scroll
memory) offset values
Z80 RAM 8 KB Internal working memory for
the sound subsystem
Cartridge ROM Variable (up to several MB) The compiled program and
all its assets (graphics, maps,
music)
The first four rows of this table are internal console memory: they exist in a fixed amount
regardless of how large the inserted cartridge is, and they run out easily if not managed
carefully. Thelastrow,ROM,isthecartridge’sownmemory: that’swherethecompiledcode
lives,alongwithallthegame’sassets(images,maps,music,soundeffects)convertedintothe
format the console can read. ROM is much larger than RAM, but it has a different limitation:
everything in ROM is read-only during execution, so any data the game needs to modify at
runtime first has to be copied into one of the working memories (RAM, VRAM, CRAM).
Thisscarcityofinternalmemory—64KBofmainRAMis,togiveapointofreference,several
thousandtimeslessthanthememoryofamodernphone—isbehindmuchoftheprogramming
practices you’ll see throughout the manual: choosing the smallest data type that will do for
each variable, reusing graphic tiles instead of duplicating them, manually keeping track of
which portion of VRAM is occupied at any given time, and preferring constant data in ROM
over unnecessary copies in RAM.
Review exercises

2. Explain, in your own words, why playing sound on the Mega Drive isn’t as straightfor-

3. What’s the difference between the console’s main RAM and the cartridge’s ROM, in
terms of what you can do with each during a game’s execution?
4. A 4 MB cartridge has, in that sense, much more capacity than the console’s 64 KB of
main RAM. Why doesn’t this eliminate the need to be careful with memory while pro-
gramming?

Chapter 2 — The VDP in Depth -
VRAM, CRAM, VSRAM, Planes,
Tiles, and Palettes
Thegraphicsvocabularythatwillbeused,withoutre-explainingit,throughouttherestofthe
manual
This chapter has no code: it is purely conceptual, and its sole purpose is to establish the
VDP (Video Display Processor) vocabulary that every following chapter will take for granted.
EverythingvisualinaMegaDrivegame(backgrounds,sprites,text,scrolling,transparencies)
passes through this chip, and it’s worth understanding how it organizes its work before you
start asking it to do things from C.
1. Tiles: the smallest unit of graphics
The VDP doesn’t draw loose images of arbitrary size: everything that appears on screen,
whether background or sprite, is built out of tiles, small 8×8 pixel square blocks. Each tile
takes up 32 bytes of video memory, because each of its 64 pixels is represented with 4 bits
(halfabyte): those4bitsaren’tacolordirectly,butratheranindexfrom0to15intoapalette
of16colors. Thisindexed-colorscheme—colorindexinthetile,actualcolorinthepalette—is
thereasonwhy,lateron,you’llseethatchangingthepaletteassignedtoagraphiccompletely
changes its appearance without touching a single bit of the tile itself.
VRAM has 64 KB in total, which would allow up to 2048 distinct tiles to be stored (64 KB
÷ 32 bytes per tile) if all of VRAM were used exclusively for that, which doesn’t happen in
practice: partofthatmemoryisreservedfortheplanes’nametablesandforthespritetable,
both explained below.
2. Palettes and CRAM: from index to actual color
The 128 bytes of CRAM (Color RAM) hold four palettes of 16 colors each (identified in SGDK
as PAL0 through PAL3), and each color takes up 2 bytes with a resolution of 9 bits: 3 bits for
theredcomponent,3forgreen,and3forblue,giving8intensitylevelsperchannelandupto
512possiblecolorsintotal. Atanygiveninstant,however,onlythe64colorscontainedinthe
four active palettes can be on screen (4 palettes × 16 colors), and of those 64, the first color
of each palette acts as the transparent color for sprites and for tiles with normal priority: in
practice, thisleaves60usablecolorsonscreenplusthebackgroundcolor(index0ofpalette
0), a total traditionally cited as 61 simultaneous colors.
Changing a palette’s values at runtime, without touching any tile, is a common technique
6

=== PAGE 13 ===
for achieving fade-ins and fade-outs or color-cycling animations; both are revisited in later
chapters.
3. The planes: A, B, and Window
The VDP organizes the screen background into independent planes, each formed by a grid
of tiles called a name table, stored in VRAM. There are three planes:
• Plane B (BG_B): by default, the one furthest back in the drawing order.
• Plane A (BG_A): by default, drawn in front of plane B.
• Window: aspecialplane,usuallyusedforuserinterfaceelements(scoredisplays,fixed
text)thatdon’tneedtoscrollalongwiththerestofthebackground;it’stypicallyoverlaid
on top of plane A.
Each position in a plane’s name table doesn’t store the graphic itself, but rather a compact
referencetoatilealreadyloadedintoVRAM,togetherwithahandfulofadditionalattributes:
which palette to use to paint it (one of the four, PAL0 through PAL3), whether it has high or
low priority relative to other graphical elements, and whether it should be displayed flipped
horizontally or vertically. This bundle of information —palette, priority, flip, tile index— is
exactly what the TILE_ATTR_FULL() macro assembles in SGDK, which you’ll use for the first
time in the chapter devoted to displaying a background on screen.
By default, the drawing order from back to front is: plane B, plane A, sprites. That order can
be altered by marking a particular plane or sprite with high priority, which brings it in front
of the rest of the elements that don’t have that flag; this tool is the basis for depth effects
such as making a character pass behind a foreground element.
Each plane also has a configurable size in tiles (for example, 64×32 or 128×64 tiles) that
usuallyexceedsthesizeofthevisiblescreen: thenon-visiblepartoftheplaneremainsstored
in VRAM, ready to be shown as the screen scrolls over it. That movement, scrolling, is con-
trolledindependentlyforeachplaneandisthemechanismbehindparallaxscrolling,covered
later on.
4. Sprites: graphics independent of the background plane
Unlike the tiles of a plane, a sprite is an independent graphical element that can be posi-
tioned at any pixel coordinate on the screen, without being tied to a plane’s grid. Sprites
havetheirown controltablein VRAM(theSprite AttributeTable, orSAT)andareassembled
by combining one or more tiles: a sprite can be as large as 32×32 pixels (4×4 tiles) as a sin-
gle hardware unit, although for larger characters it’s common to combine several hardware
sprites to form what looks like a single one from the game’s point of view.
The VDP hardware imposes strict limits on the number of sprites, which depend on the hor-
izontal resolution mode (see below): in H40 mode (320 pixels wide), up to 80 simultaneous
sprites are allowed on screen, with a maximum of 20 per horizontal line; in H32 mode (256
pixels),thelimitsdropto64spritestotaland16perline. Exceedingtheper-linelimitdoesn’t
produce an error, but rather a visible flicker of the excess sprites, a very characteristic (and
often unavoidable) effect of games from this console generation.
5. VSRAM and scroll modes
The 80 bytes of VSRAM (Vertical Scroll RAM) store the vertical scroll offset values for the
planes. The VDP supports different scroll modes, which determine the granularity at which
7

=== PAGE 14 ===
each plane can be scrolled: by whole plane (the entire plane moves as a unit), by pixel line
(eachhorizontallineofthescreencanscrollindependently,thebasisofmanyparallaxeffects),
or by 16-pixel column. This combination of modes is what allows, for example, a per-line
horizontal scroll that creates a sense of depth while the vertical scroll moves by whole plane.
The chapter devoted to scrolling and parallax scrolling returns to this with concrete code.
6. Resolution modes: H40 and H32
The VDP can operate in two horizontal resolution modes: H40, with 320 pixels of width (40
tiles),andH32,with256pixels(32tiles),largelyinheritedfromcompatibilitywiththeMaster
System. The standard vertical resolution is 224 visible lines in V28 mode (the most common,
available on both NTSC and PAL consoles), although PAL consoles also support a V30 mode
of 240 lines, not available on NTSC. The choice of horizontal mode isn’t purely cosmetic: as
mentioned above, it also changes the limits on the number of available sprites.
Review exercises
1. Explain what it means for a tile’s color to be “indexed,” and why that makes it possible

palettes at any given instant? How many of those colors are actually visible on screen,
and why?
3. What’sthedifferencebetweenatileinabackgroundplaneandasprite,intermsofhow
they’re positioned on screen?
4. Why isn’t switching from H40 resolution mode to H32 a purely cosmetic decision?

Chapter 3 — Installing and
Configuring the SGDK 2.11
Environment
How to get your machine ready to build your first project, on Windows, Linux, and macOS
1. What SGDK Is
SGDK(SegaGenesisDevelopmentKit)isafree,open-sourcesetoftoolsandlibrariesthatlets
youprogramMegaDrive/GenesisgamesinC.Itconsistsofthreepieces: aCfunctionlibrary
(theoneusedthroughoutthismanual,includedvia#include <genesis.h>),asetofresource-
conversiontools(forimages,maps,music,andsound)knownasrescomp,andaversionofthe
GCC compiler adapted to generate code for the Motorola 68000 processor. The library and
thetools are MIT-licensed; the GCCcompiler itself, being a third-partyproject, is distributed
under the GPL3 license. The project is actively maintained by Stéphane Dallongeville, and
this manual is based on its latest stable release, SGDK 2.11 (April 2025).
2. Installing on Windows
Windows is the platform with the best direct support, because the project itself distributes
precompiled toolchain binaries (including GCC 13.2) ready to use.
1. Java: rescomp, the resource-conversion tool, needs Java to run. Install a recent version
ofaJavadistribution(OracleJDKorOpenJDK)andmakesureit’savailableonthesystem
PATH.
2. Download: grab the latest SGDK release from the official repository’s releases page
(github.com/Stephane-D/SGDK/releases) and unzip it into a folder whose path contains
no spaces, for example C:\sgdk.
3. Environmentvariable(optionalbutrecommended): createanenvironmentvariable
named GDK pointing to that folder. Several tools and editor extensions (like the one
covered in the next chapter) use it to automatically locate the toolchain.
4. Verification: open a terminal in that folder and run:
bin\make -f makelib.gen
If everything is installed correctly, the command finishes by generating the file
lib\libmd.a, SGDK’s already-compiled library. If that file appears, the environment is
ready.
9

=== PAGE 16 ===
3. Installing on Linux and macOS
Unlike Windows, SGDK does not distribute precompiled binaries for Linux or macOS, and as
of version 2.10 the project stopped maintaining its own Docker image, recommending
instead two alternative paths:
• MarsDev (github.com/andwn/marsdev): a cross-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS) de-
velopment environment that installs and keeps up to date both SGDK and the rest of
the required toolchain, including support for the 32X if you ever need it. It’s generally
the recommended option for anyone not on Windows: you download the project, set an
environment variable pointing to the desired installation folder, and run make sgdk to
complete the installation.
• Third-partyDockerimages: thecommunitymaintainsupdated,testedDockerimages,
the most recommended one currently being Doragasu’s (gitlab.com/doragasu/docker-
sgdk), designed specifically to replace the discontinued official image. This alternative
is useful if you already work with containers in your usual workflow, or if you’d rather
not install the toolchain directly on your operating system.
In either case, Java remains a requirement for rescomp, just as on Windows.
A detail that’s changed since older tutorials |
It’s common to find, in tutorials and documentation from a few | years back, references to
an official Docker image maintained by | the SGDK project itself. That image is no longer
maintained: if | you’re following a guide that mentions it, replace it with MarsDev | or with
the Doragasu image mentioned above. |
4. Verifying the Installation
OnWindows,Linux,ormacOS,theenvironmentisreadyoncetheGCCcompilerforthe68000
responds (natively, via MarsDev, or inside a Docker container), Java is available for rescomp,
and SGDK’s libmd.a library finishes compiling without errors. The next chapter installs the
editor and extension used throughout the rest of the manual to create projects, build them,
and test the result in an emulator, without having to type out every build command by hand.
Review exercises

3. If you’re following a tutorial that mentions an official SGDK Docker image, what should

Chapter 4 — Editor, Extension,
and Emulators
The everyday working tools: a code editor, assisted compilation, and how to test the result
With the SGDK toolchain installed (previous chapter), two more things need to be sorted out
beforewritingthefirstprogram: acomfortableeditorforworkingwiththecodeandresource
files, and a way to run the result without having to pull a real console out of the closet every
time you compile.
1. Visual Studio Code and the Genesis Code extension
ThismanualusesVisualStudioCodeasthereferenceeditor,togetherwiththeGenesisCode
extension, available on the VS Code extension marketplace. The extension doesn’t replace
SGDK: it automates tasks that would otherwise have to be done by hand from a terminal
(creating the structure of a new project, compiling, running it on the configured emulator)

Chapter 5 — First Program -
SGDK Project Structure and
Compilation
From an empty folder to a “Hello World” running in the emulator
With the environment installed and the editor configured, this chapter walks through the
completepathtoseeingsomethingonscreen: creatinganewproject, understandingwhatit
contains, writing the first program, and compiling it.
1. Creating a new project
From Visual Studio Code, with the Genesis Code extension installed, the command palette
(Ctrl+Shift+P) command Genesis Code: Create Project creates the minimal structure of
an SGDK project in the specified folder. That structure consists of three main folders:
• src/: the project’s C source code. This is where the main file, main.c, lives.
• inc/: the project’s own header files (.h), distinct from the ones SGDK generates auto-
maticallyfromresources(atopicrevisitedinthepartofthismanualdedicatedtoproject
organization).
• res/: theresourcefiles—images,maps,sounds,music—alongwiththeresources.res
file that tells SGDK how to convert them.
2. The minimal skeleton of a program
Every SGDK program starts from a minimal structure like this:
#include <genesis.h>
int main()
{
while (1)
{
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return (0);
}
#include <genesis.h> brings in the entire SGDK library: it’s the only inclusion needed to
13

=== PAGE 20 ===
access the functions used throughout this manual (later on, once the project has its own
resources,#include <resources.h>isaddedaswell—thefileSGDKgeneratesautomatically
at compile time).
The body of main() is an infinite loop (while (1)) that never ends as long as the console
is powered on: unlike a desktop program, a game doesn’t “finish” execution in the tradi-
tional sense — instead, it keeps running indefinitely, drawing frame after frame. Inside that
loop,SYS_doVBlankProcess()tellsSGDKtosynchronizependingwork(updatingsprites, pro-
cessing the queued DMA, waiting for the next video frame) with the VDP’s vertical blanking
interval, the brief span between one drawn frame and the next during which it’s safe to mod-
ify certain graphical data. Practically every main loop you’ll write from here on contains, at
minimum, a call to this function on every pass.
In older code or documentation it’s common to find VDP_waitVSync() fulfilling a
similar role. That function was replaced by SYS_doVBlankProcess() as of SGDK
1.60;ifyoucomeacrossVDP_waitVSync()inanoldtutorial,it’stheequivalentfrom
an earlier version of the library.
3. A first visible result: text on screen
To confirm that the project compiles and runs, it’s enough to draw a string of text on one of
the background planes, using VDP_drawText():
#include <genesis.h>
int main()
{
VDP_drawText("Hola Mundo", 10, 12);
while (1)
{
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return (0);
}
VDP_drawText() takes three parameters: the text string to display, and the horizontal and
vertical position in tiles (not pixels) where it should appear, relative to the default text font
that comes with SGDK. There’s no need to declare any resource in resources.res for this
particular example: the default text font is already included in the library.
4. Compiling and running
WiththeGenesisCode: Compile&Runcommand(ortheequivalentbuttoninthestatusbar,
ifenabledintheextension’ssettings)theprojectiscompiledand,ifanemulatorisconfigured,
it’s run automatically to show the result. Manually, without going through the extension,
compilation is triggered with make from the project folder, using the Makefile that comes
with the template.
Theresultofasuccessfulcompilationisarom.binfileinsideanout/subfolderoftheproject:
that binary file is, ultimately, the complete program, ready to run both in an emulator and,
via a flash cart, on real hardware.

Chapter 6 — C Applied to Retro
Development - Data Types,
Limited Memory, and Pointers
When to use u8, u16, int, and the fixed-point types fix16/fix32; how to think about 64 KB of
memory; and what changes about pointers in this environment
This chapter assumes basic knowledge of C (variable declaration, functions, introductory-
level pointers) and focuses on the part that is not the same as programming for a modern
computer: which data types are worth choosing and why, how to think about a memory of
barely 64 KB, and what nuances pointers have when much of the data you work with lives in
the cartridge’s read-only ROM.
1. Integer types: u8, s8, u16, s16, and int
In addition to C’s standard types, SGDK defines a set of aliases with names that make their
size and sign explicit: u8/s8 (8 bits), u16/s16 (16 bits), and, for 32 bits, simply int (signed)
without needing a special alias. The initial letter indicates whether the type is signed (s,
signed) or not (u, unsigned); the number indicates how many bits it occupies in memory.
• u8: 8 bits (1 byte), unsigned. Since 8 bits allow for 2⁸ = 256 distinct combinations, a u8
represents integers from 0 to 255.
• s8: the same 8 bits, the same 256 combinations, the same size in memory, but split
between negative and positive values: from -128 to 127.
• u16: 16 bits (2 bytes), unsigned, with 2¹⁶ = 65,536 possible combinations: from 0 to
65,535. It’snocoincidencethatthisfigurematchesthesizeinbytesofboththeconsole’s
main RAM and its VRAM.
• s16: the same 16 bits, signed, from -32,768 to 32,767.
• int: 32 bits, signed, from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. This range is so large that,
inpractice,it’salmostneveroverflowedbyaccidentwithinthereasonabledurationofa
play session.
When any of these types exceeds its upper limit (or lower limit, for signed types), no error
occurs: thevalueoverflowsandkeepscountingfromtheotherendofitsrange. Thisbehavior
ispredictable,andonceunderstoodinadvance,itcanbeusedtoyouradvantage(forexample,
for cyclic counters); without understanding it, it’s a frequent source of hard-to-track bugs.
Apracticaldetailworthkeepinginmindwhendisplayingthesevaluesastext(withsprintf()
andthenVDP_drawText()orVDP_drawTextBG(),asisdoneinseveralchaptersofthismanual):
the negative sign takes up a character of its own within the destination string. A string
declared with just enough size for a u8 (char texto[3], for “255”) falls short as soon as
that same variable becomes an s8 and takes on a negative value like “-128” (4 characters);
16

=== PAGE 23 ===
the result, if the string and the sprintf() format aren’t enlarged accordingly, gets visibly
corrupted. The same precaution — one extra character for the sign — applies to any signed
type displayed on screen.
When to use each type
Thegeneralruleistoalwaysusethesmallesttypethatsufficesfortheintendedpurpose: each
int takes up 4 bytes out of a total memory of 64 KB, each u16/s16 takes up 2, and each u8/s8
just 1. For values with a naturally bounded range — number of lives, number of continues,
the current level, or a frame counter for invincibility after taking damage (255 frames equal
more than four seconds at 60 frames per second, more than enough in most cases) — a u8 is
usuallymorethansufficient;infact,thisisacommonpatternincommercialgamesfromthat
era: the rupee counter in The Legend of Zelda, for example, caps at exactly 255.
2. Numbers with decimals: there is no float
As explained in the architecture chapter, the Motorola 68000 processor has no floating-point
unit. Using float or double in SGDK is possible at the language level, but every operation
with those types ends up resolved in software, at a very high performance cost for hardware
of this era; in practice, they’re virtually never used. Instead, SGDK offers fixed-point types:
numbersthatreserveafixednumberofbitsfortheintegerpartandanotherfixednumberfor
the decimal part, and that are represented internally as ordinary integers (and are therefore
just as fast to operate on as any int).
• fix16: 16 bits total, split into 10 bits for the integer part and 6 for the decimal part. It’s
declared and initialized with the FIX16() macro:
fix16 posicion = FIX16(0);
posicion += FIX16(1); // add 1 whole integer
With 6 decimal bits, the smallest representable increment is 1/64 ≈ 0.0156, and with
only10integerbits,afix16overflowsfarsoonerthananordinarys16(alittlepast500).
That combination — small integer range, but very fine decimal steps — makes it ideal
for slow, bounded movement, such as a background layer in a parallax scroll.
• fix32: 32 bits total, with 22 bits for the integer part and 10 for the decimal part, ini-
tialized with FIX32(). Its integer range is enormous compared to fix16, at the cost of
takinguptwicethememory. It’stherecommendedtypeforrepresentingthepositionof
acharacteroranenemyonamapseveralthousandpixelswide,whereafix16’sinteger
range would fall short.
Toconvertafixed-pointvaluetoaregularinteger(forexample,todisplayitwithsprintf(),or
touseitasapixelcoordinateinafunctionthatexpectsaninteger),SGDKprovidesdedicated
conversion functions: F16_toInt() for fix16 and F32_toInt() for fix32.
Code or tutorials written before April 2025 (SGDK 2.10) use the names
fix16ToInt() and fix32ToInt() instead of F16_toInt() and F32_toInt(). Start-
ing with that version, the entire fixed-point math library switched to using the
F16_/F32_/FF16_/FF32_ prefix consistently; the functions’ behavior didn’t change,
only the name.
Adding a value smaller than 1 with an ordinary integer type doesn’t make sense (entero +=
0.1 simply doesn’t compile to represent the intended meaning), but it does with fixed point:
it’s the standard technique for movement slower than one whole pixel per frame. That said,
it’s worth keeping the screen resolution in mind when choosing an increment: in H40 mode,
an element can only visually move by one whole pixel at a time, so a very small fractional
17

=== PAGE 24 ===
increment takes several frames to translate into visible movement, which can feel choppy if
the chosen step is too small for the desired speed.
3. Thinking in 64 KB: memory as an active resource
The console’s main RAM has 64 KB in total, a fixed limit regardless of the cartridge’s size.
That total has to be enough for all of the program’s global variables, the function call stack,
anydynamicdatastructures,andtheinternalworkthattheSGDKlibraryitselfneedsinorder
to function. This leads to a few habits that may not be necessary when programming for a
modern computer:
• Prefer constant data in ROM over copies in RAM. An array declared as const (for
example,atableoffixedvalues,orthedataofaresourcealreadyconvertedbyrescomp)
is stored in the cartridge’s ROM and read directly from there, without taking up any of
the 64 KB of RAM. Reserving that memory for what actually needs to be able to change
at runtime is one of the most important design decisions in this whole manual.
• Bewaryofdynamicmemoryallocation. SGDKprovidesMEM_alloc()andMEM_free()
(and,forcompatibility,malloc()/free()redirecttothesamefunctions)toallocatemem-
ory at runtime, but careless use — allocating and freeing blocks of very different sizes
throughout an entire playthrough — can quickly fragment such a small memory space,
leaving free blocks too small and scattered to satisfy a new allocation, even when the
total amount of free space would be sufficient. Declaring fixed-size arrays whose size
is known in advance (for example, an array for up to 16 active enemies instead of a
variable-sized list) is usually preferable whenever the maximum limit can be estimated
with some margin.
• Choosethesmallesttypethatsuffices,asalreadycoveredinsection1: thedifference
between a 50-element array declared as int (200 bytes) and the same array as u8 (50
bytes) may seem small in the abstract, but it becomes significant once it’s repeated
across dozens of structures throughout a complete game.
4. Pointers in an environment with read-only memory
Pointers in SGDK work exactly the same as in any other C program: a variable that stores a
memory address instead of a direct value. What’s particular about this environment is that a
gooddealofthedataapointercanpointto—resourcesgeneratedbyrescomp(images,maps,
sound tables), any array declared const — lives in the cartridge’s ROM, which is read-only
at runtime. A pointer can perfectly well read that data, but any attempt to write through it
to a ROM address has no useful effect (in the best case) or corrupts the program’s behavior
unpredictably (in the worst case). For this reason, it’s good practice to declare as const any
pointerintendedpurelyforreadingaresource’sdata,lettingthecompileritselfflagitifsome
part of the code mistakenly tries to write to that memory.
For cartridges exceeding 4 MB of ROM, SGDK also includes a bank switching mechanism
thatallowsaddressingmorememorythanthe68000canaccessdirectlyatanygiveninstant;
this topic is beyond the scope of this introductory chapter and is revisited, along with the
FAR()/FAR_SAFE() functions that manage it, in the part of this manual dedicated to optimiza-
tion.

Chapter 7 — How to Display
Backgrounds on the Mega Drive
TheBG_AandBG_Bplanes,theSGDKresourcepipeline,andtheVDP_drawImageExfunction
Every Mega Drive game needs, at the very least, to put an image on screen. This chapter
covers that first step in the most direct way possible: how to take a PNG image made on a
computerandturnitintovisibledataononeofthetwobackgroundplanesofferedbytheVDP.
Thejourneypassesthroughfourstagesthatwillreappear,withvariations,inpracticallyevery
graphic displayed on screen from here on: declaring the resource so the compiler includes
it in the ROM, reserving a spot for it in VRAM, assigning it a color palette, and finally asking
the VDP to draw it on a plane.
Chapter 2 developed the hardware behind this operation in depth: the VDP, the VRAM, the
BG_A/BG_B/Window planes, tiles, and the PAL0-PAL3 palettes. That vocabulary is assumed
to be familiar here; this chapter’s focus is on the code: which function to use, with which
parameters, and why.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• AworkingSGDK2.11environmentinstalled,capableofcompilingandrunningaproject
in an emulator, as covered in chapters 3 and 4.
• BasicnotionsofC:declaringvariables,types,functions,andstructures(revisitedinmore
detail in chapter 6).
• A general understanding of what VRAM, a tile, and a color palette are on the Mega
Drive’s VDP (chapter 2).
• An SGDK project with a minimal main.c, following the structure shown in chapter 5.
Thecentralfunctionsinthischapter(PAL_setPalette(),VDP_drawImageEx(),theTILE_ATTR_FULL()
macro, the TILE_USERINDEX constant, and the syntax of the IMAGE resource in a .res file)
keep,inSGDK2.11,exactlythesamename,thesamesignature,andthesamebehaviorasin
fairly old versions of the kit. All the code in this chapter can be written and compiled exactly
as it appears here, with no further adaptation. If you come across older code or forum posts,
onenamingdetailmaycatchyoureye: beforeSGDK1.50, theplaneswerecalledPLAN_Aand
PLAN_B instead of BG_A and BG_B — the same concept under a different name.
1. The resource pipeline: from a PNG file to the ROM
An image created on a computer is not automatically available inside a Mega Drive program.
Before it can be drawn, SGDK needs to be told to include it in the ROM (the final binary file
20

=== PAGE 27 ===
that runs on the console or in an emulator) and under what name the C code will be able to
refer to it. That step is handled with a resource file.
Inside the project’s res folder, a file called resources.res is created. Each line in this file
describesadistinctresourcetobeincludedintheROM:laterontherewillbelinesforsound
effects, music, and sprites, but for now a single image is enough:
IMAGE bg1 "background1.png" BEST ALL
This line declares an image-type resource called bg1, taken from the file background1.png,
with BEST compression and ALL map optimization. Each field plays a specific role, and SGDK
is strict about uppercase, lowercase, and spacing:
• IMAGE(uppercase)indicatestheresourcetype: inthiscase, afullimage(tilesetplustile
map plus palette), meant for a simple static background.
• bg1 is the name the C code will use to refer to this resource. It can be called whatever
you like, as long as it’s a single word with no spaces and reasonably short.
• "background1.png" is the path to the image file in quotes, relative to the res folder.
• BEST (uppercase) indicates the compression mode. The most common alternatives are
NONE(uncompressed),FAST(analgorithmthat’squickertodecompressbutlesscompact),
and BEST (which produces the smallest file, though it takes a bit longer to decompress
atruntime). Forabackgroundimageloadedonlyonce,BESTisusuallythemostsensible
choice.
• ALL, at the end, is the tile map optimization: it tells the compiler to reuse identical tiles
(includingtilesflippedhorizontallyorvertically)insteadofrepeatingthem,savingspace
in the ROM and, later, in VRAM.
The name bg1 isn’t available for autocomplete or for the main.c compiler until the
project is saved and compiled at least once: only then does SGDK generate the
corresponding resources.h file, from which the rest of the code can recognize and
include that resource. If you type bg1 in main.c immediately after creating the line
in resources.res, it’s normal for the editor not to recognize it yet.
The IMAGE resource type bundles the tileset, the tile map, and the palette of a full image into
a single declaration, which is convenient for a static background like the one in this chapter.
For backgrounds larger than one screen, for levels with scrolling, or for sharing the same
set of tiles across several images, SGDK lets you declare the TILESET, MAP (or TILEMAP), and
PALETTEresourcesseparately,givingmorecontroloverhowthey’reorganizedintheROMand
in VRAM. This chapter doesn’t need that yet; the topic comes back in the chapter devoted to
scroll and parallax scrolling, later in this same part of the manual.
With the resource declared and the project compiled at least once, main.c can now include
thefilegeneratedbySGDKandstartsettingthestagefordrawingtheimage. Sincenotextis
goingtobeshownyet,it’sworthremovinganysamplecalltoVDP_drawText()thattheproject
template might include:
#include <genesis.h>
#include <resources.h>
int main()
{
while(1)
{
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return (0);
}

The file included from main.c is resources.h (with a .h extension), generated auto-
matically when compiling from resources.res. The .res file is the source you edit
byhand;the.hfileistheCinterfacethatresultsfromprocessingit,andit’stheone
the rest of the program consumes. There’s no need to include the .res file directly,
and in fact it isn’t possible.
2. Reserving a spot in VRAM: TILE_USERINDEX
The VDP’s VRAM isn’t free space from start to finish: its first positions are reserved for
the system and, if the project uses SGDK’s default text font, also for that font’s tiles. Before
uploadingthetilesofyourownimage,youneedtostartfromapositionthatdoesn’toverwrite
any of that. SGDK exposes exactly that position through a constant:
u16 ind = TILE_USERINDEX;
TILE_USERINDEXisthefirstVRAMtileindexleftfreefortheprogrammeraftersubtractingthe
tiles reserved by the system. The variable ind, declared as u16 (an unsigned 16-bit integer,
more than enough since the VDP’s VRAM has 2048 tile positions in total), keeps track of the
VRAM position at which each new graphic is uploaded as the program needs it. A variable
that advances as chunks of VRAM are reserved — the same idea reappears, with much more
detailandwiththecomplicationsitcanbring,inthechapteronsavingVRAMthroughmanual
sprite loading, in the part of this manual devoted to optimization.
3. Assigning a palette: PAL_setPalette
The Mega Drive can display up to 64 colors on screen, split across four palettes of 16 colors
each (PAL0 through PAL3). Before drawing an image, the VDP needs to be told which colors
to paint it with, and those colors have to come from one of those four palettes. The function
that does this is PAL_setPalette():
void PAL_setPalette(u16 numPal, const u16 *pal, TransferMethod tm);
The three parameters are: numPal, the palette number this color information should be as-
signedto(PAL0,PAL1,PAL2,orPAL3);pal,apointertothecolordataitself;andtm,thetransfer
method. The full call, in this case, is:
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, bg1.palette->data, DMA);
bg1.palette->data takes the color information directly from the Image structure generated
frombackground1.png: there’snoneedtowritethecolorsbyhand,sincethey’realreadypack-
aged together with the image from the moment the resource was declared in resources.res.
The last parameter, DMA, indicates that the transfer of that color data is done via direct mem-
ory access (Direct Memory Access), a copying mechanism that doesn’t use up CPU time; the
alternativeisCPU,whichcopiesthedatausingtheprocessor. Foraone-offoperationlikethis,
either one works fine; DMA is, generally speaking, the recommended option since it costs
less CPU time.
Ifoneofthebackgroundorforegroundimagesisn’tassignedtoPAL0, it’scommon
for it to lose its first color (the color at index 0 of the palette, which on the Mega
Drive’s VDP is always the background/transparency color). For that reason, as a
general rule, it’s a good idea to reserve PAL0 for the farthest-back background
graphic — usually the background itself on BG_B — and use PAL1, PAL2, or PAL3
for the rest.

4. Drawing the image: VDP_drawImageEx and TILE_ATTR_FULL
With the resource declared, the VRAM space reserved, and the palette assigned, the last
step is to ask the VDP to actually draw the image on one of the two background planes. The
function for this is VDP_drawImageEx():
bool VDP_drawImageEx(VDPPlane plane, const Image *image, u16 basetile,
u16 x, u16 y, bool loadpal, bool dma);
Theparameters, inorder,are: plane,thebackgroundplanetodrawon(BG_AorBG_B;there’s
alsoWINDOW,whichisn’tusedinthischapter);image,apointertotheImagestructuregenerated
fromtheresource;basetile,theVRAMpositionfromwhichthisimage’stileswillbewritten;
xandy,thepositiononscreen; loadpal,whetherthepaletteshouldalsobeloadedaspartof
this same call; and dma, whether the tile transfer should be done via DMA.
The basetile parameter isn’t passed as a plain number, but through a macro that packs
severalpiecesofinformationintoasinglevalue: TILE_ATTR_FULL(pal, prio, flipV, flipH,
index).
VDP_drawImageEx(BG_B, &bg1, TILE_ATTR_FULL(PAL0, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, ind), 0, 0,
↪ FALSE, TRUE);
Each tile in the Mega Drive’s VRAM doesn’t just store its pixel pattern: it also carries, in
the plane’s name table, attribute bits that indicate which palette to paint it with, whether
it has high or low priority, and whether it should be shown flipped vertically or horizontally.
TILE_ATTR_FULL() packs those attributes into a single value:
• pal — which of the four palettes (PAL0 through PAL3) to use for this tile.
• prio (priority) — whether this plane is drawn in front of (TRUE) or behind (FALSE, the
default value) the other graphic elements it shares the screen with.
• flipV — whether the tile is shown flipped vertically.
• flipH — whether the tile is shown flipped horizontally.
• index—theVRAMposition(thesamevaluetrackedintheindvariable)fromwhichthis
image’s tiles start.
Withallthisinplace,saving,compiling,andrunningtheprojectalreadyshowsthefirstback-
ground on screen.
Firstresultintheemulator: thenighttimecafescenewiththeneonsign,nowdrawnonBG_B.
5. Experimenting with the parameters
Before adding a second plane, it’s worth pausing to modify, one at a time, the parameters
just used. This isn’t an idle exercise: clearly understanding what each one does saves a lot
of debugging time later on, when these same parameters show up combined with scrolling,
sprites, and several layers at once.
5.1 Switching palettes without having loaded one
If you change the pal in TILE_ATTR_FULL() from PAL0 to PAL1 without having first called
PAL_setPalette(PAL1, ...), the result is not subtle: the image comes out drawn almost
entirely in red.
Thesamebackground,specifyingPAL1withouthavinginitializedit: theVDPdrawsitjustthe
same, but with the default color of an empty palette.
23

=== PAGE 30 ===
Figure 1: The background1.png background drawn on the BG_B plane
Figure2: ThebackgrounddrawnwithPAL1withouthavingloadedcolordataintothatpalette

=== PAGE 31 ===
The red you see isn’t an effect or an error in the image data: it’s simply the default content
of a palette that was never loaded with color information. The VDP draws the tiles just the
same, with the correct geometry, but looks up colors in an empty palette. Switching back to
PAL0, the palette that was actually initialized with PAL_setPalette(), the background looks
normal again.
5.2 Flipping tiles: flipV and flipH
ChangingflipVtoTRUEmakeseverytileontheplaneshowupflippedvertically: theneonsign
and the building’s facade appear upside down. The result with flipH is analogous, flipping
horizontally.
In this specific context — a static background — flipping the whole plane doesn’t have much
practical use, but the same mechanism is the basis for a significant memory saving: if a tile
and its flipped version are visually identical, there’s no need to store both in VRAM or in the
ROM. It’s enough to keep just one and, when drawing it, indicate that you want it shown
flipped. In practice there’s no need to manage this by hand tile by tile: when converting
graphics with the right tools, SGDK automatically recognizes which tiles are flips of others
andavoidsduplicatingtheminVRAM,somethingthat’srevisitedinmoredetailinthechapter
devoted to creating graphics.
Although flipping an entire plane rarely serves a purpose for a static background,
thesameparameterisveryusefulforsprites: it’sthestandardmechanismformak-
ingacharacterfaceleftorrightwithoutneedingdoublethegraphicsordoublethe
VRAMspace,byflippingthesamespritehorizontallydependingonwhichdirection
it’s moving.
5.3 Priority: what gets drawn in front of what
By default, the Mega Drive’s drawing order runs from the background plane (BG_B) at the
back, the foreground plane (BG_A) in the middle, and the sprites in front of everything. The
prio parameter lets you alter that order for a particular plane. Changing BG_B’s priority to
TRUE, for example, makes that plane get drawn in front of BG_A.
WithBG_Bsettohighpriority,thecheckeredfloorofthebackgroundcoversalmosttheentire
car and lamppost in the foreground, which are left barely peeking through.
Inthisparticularexampletheresultisn’tespeciallyuseful(theforegroundendsuppractically
hidden), but the tool itself is very useful in other situations. Streets of Rage is a frequently
citedcase: inseveralscenes,thecharacterspritesneedtoappearbehindcertainforeground
elements (a streetlamp or a sign, for example), even though sprites are drawn in front of
everything by default. The solution is the same tool just shown: give the foreground (BG_A)
high priority and leave both the background and the sprites at normal priority, so the final
order ends up being background, then sprites, and finally the foreground with high priority.
5.4 Coordinates: x and y are measured in tiles, not pixels
The x and y parameters of VDP_drawImageEx() aren’t pixel coordinates but tile coordinates.
Since each Mega Drive tile measures 8×8 pixels, a value of x = 10 shifts the image 80 pixels
to the right (10 tiles × 8 pixels), not 10 pixels.
It’sa common mistake, especially when startingout, topass a value of x or y think-
ing in pixels and end up with a shift eight times larger than expected. It’s worth
keeping this in mind especially later on, when calculating positions from other el-
ements’ coordinates (a sprite’s position in pixels, for instance) which, if combined
without converting, can produce results very different from what was intended.

2. The Mega Drive palette in the editor
The Mega Drive can display up to 64 simultaneous colors on screen, organized into four
palettes of 16 colors each (PAL0 through PAL3, already covered when describing the VDP).

That limit isn’t a retro-style suggestion: it’s just as structural as the multiple-of-8 rule, and
any graphic being drawn has to respect it from the outset, not adjust to it afterward.
Aseprite—likemostpixel-arteditorsaimedatretroconsoles—shipswithpredefinedpalettes
for several classic systems: Atari 2600, Commodore 64, Game Boy, Game Boy Color, Master
System, among others. The Mega Drive, however, usually isn’t among them by default. That
means you need to import a Mega Drive palette from an external file: several circulate on
homebrew community forums and repositories, and any one that faithfully reproduces the
hardware’s 512 possible colors — 9 bits of color, split across 3 bits per channel — will do the
job. Thismanualdoesn’tshipanyparticularpalettefile;it’senoughtoobtainorgenerateone
that’s faithful to that bit distribution.
Once imported and applied to the canvas, the editor’s palette panel is ready to work with.

3. The 8×8 grid and the discipline of drawing tile by tile
Since the VDP organizes everything into 8×8-pixel blocks, it’s worth making that organiza-
tion visible while drawing, not just at export time. Most pixel-art editors let you overlay a
configurable grid on the canvas; for Mega Drive graphics it makes sense to set it exactly to
8-pixel steps, so each cell corresponds to an actual VRAM tile.
This isn’t an aesthetic preference. Seeing each tile’s boundaries while drawing helps antici-
patehowwellSGDK’sautomatictilededuplication(coveredinsection8.3)willbeabletokick
in, and it avoids surprises when a shape ends up split awkwardly between two neighboring
tiles. Thegridcanbeadjustedtoothersizesdependingonwhat’sbeingdrawn—forexample,
16×16tovisuallygroupsetsoffourtiles,asseeninsection7—buttheunderlyingreference
should always be thinkable in multiples of 8.
4. Keeping the 16-color limit in check: the tally column
Each individual graphic — each image that ends up converted into an SGDK IMAGE resource
—is limitedto asingle 16-color palette, even thoughthe hardware hasfour availablein total.
While drawing a scene with several elements (sky, clouds, ground, and eventually sprites),
it’s easy to lose track of how many distinct colors have been added, especially if the editor
doesn’t display that count prominently.
Apracticaltrickforkeepingcountistosetasideastripoftilesoutsidetheareathatwilllater
be exported, and use it as a visual log: every time a new color is introduced into the scene, a
swatch of that color gets added to the strip too. A glance at that column is enough to know,
at any moment, how many distinct colors the graphic has used so far, without opening any
additionalpanel. Thiscolumnispurelyaworkingtool: itgetscroppedoutbeforeexportand
isn’t part of the final graphic.
The habit of counting colors matters much more in complex graphics than in a simple sky-

5. From RGB to indexed: trimming the palette and export-

that’s worth understanding, not just executing.
The first step removes from the file’s palette any color that wasn’t actually used in the draw-
ing: what’s left, for example, are the three or four colors actually painted, instead of the
hundreds carried by the full palette imported in section 2. Most editors — Aseprite included

Thesecondstepchangesthefile’scolormodefromRGBtoindexed,viathecanvasproperties

in indexed mode from the very start, but doing so before trimming the palette can produce
unexpected results if the starting palette is very large. The palette imported in section 2 can
cover all 512 possible hardware colors, and pixel-art editors usually impose a practical limit
well below that on the number of entries an indexed palette can hold — in Aseprite a figure
around 256 slots is often cited, though it’s worth checking the exact value for the version
you’reusing,sinceitcanvary. Ifyouswitchtoindexedmodewithapalettethatexceedsthat
limit, the entries above the cutoff aren’t silently discarded: they get reassigned to already-
occupied slots, and the visible color at those slots changes abruptly and unpredictably.

7. A second graphic: transparency and depth
The same procedure repeats identically for a second graphic meant for a different plane —
forexample,oneclosertotheviewerthanthebackgroundalreadydrawn,withtreesorother
elements that will later in this manual be combined via independent per-plane scrolling —

Thefirstshowsuprightinthecanvascreationdialog: insteadofawhiteorblackbackground,
it’s best to choose the transparent background option, so that the areas of the graphic left
undrawn show, in the editor’s preview, whatever is behind them.
The actual mechanism behind that transparency has a quirk specific to indexed color worth
spelling out: there’s no special transparency color reserved by the format. What actually
happens is that, by convention, both the editor and later SGDK treat the palette’s first entry
— index 0 — as transparent, whatever the actual color assigned to it happens to be. It could
bepink,green,oranythingelse;sinceit’sneverdrawnonscreen,thecoloritselfisirrelevant.
What does matter is that no other element of the drawing uses that first palette slot, even by
accident, because it would end up invisible without the editor warning about the problem.
Thetransparent-backgroundoptioninthecreationdialogissimplyaneditorconveniencefor
previewing how that convention will look in practice.
Theseconddifferenceisoneofscale: ifthissecondgraphiccontainslarger,morespaced-out
elements than a continuous texture like a sky, it can help to set the grid to a larger multiple
of 8 — 16×16, for example — to visually group sets of four tiles without losing track of the

same. The rest of the process — generating the canvas palette, switching to indexed mode,

8. The Mega Drive’s color model: palettes, VRAM, and
their real limits
With at least one graphic already working, this section pauses to look at how the indexed
color used since section 5 actually works under the hood, and at two hardware aspects left
out of the previous examples.
8.1 Indexed color as a paint-by-numbers book
Indexed color mode can be thought of with the same logic as one of those paint-by-numbers
books that put a number inside each area to indicate which color to use: the image data
doesn’t directly store “this pixel is light blue,” but rather “this pixel uses color number 6,”
and it’s the palette, kept separately, that defines which actual color corresponds to number
6 at any given moment. The Mega Drive numbers its 64 possible on-screen colors from 0 to
63, and works under exactly that same numbering logic.
Thepracticalconsequenceisthatchangingwhichactualcoloroccupiesapaletteslotinstantly
changesthecolorofeverypixelusingthatslot,withoutneedingtotouchasinglepixelofthe
image. Swapping two entries in an already-indexed graphic’s palette — light blue and white,
say—makeseverythingthatusedtobelightblueturnwhiteandviceversa,acrosstheentire
image at once.
Figure 7: Background with two palette entries swapped
Thesamebackgroundfromsection4withtwoentriesofitsalready-indexedpaletteswapped:
the light blue sky with green clouds appears inverted without a single pixel of the drawing
having been touched.
34

=== PAGE 41 ===
Far from being a mere curiosity, this property is the basis of a technique widely used in
commercial games of the era: palette cycling, which consists of reassigning, frame by frame
in real time, which actual colors occupy certain palette slots, without redrawing or moving a
single tile. The visual result is a smooth animation — flowing water, blinking lights, pulsing
logos — achieved at a fraction of the processing cost that redrawing the scene would take.
The opening logo and the neon sign in the introduction to Streets of Rage, for example, use
exactly this mechanism.
8.2 A limitation of the tool used so far, not of the hardware: per-tile
palettes
All the code seen up to this point assigns a single palette to an entire background plane,
via the pal parameter of TILE_ATTR_FULL() in the call to VDP_drawImageEx() from Chapter 7.
It’s worth keeping in mind that this is a limitation of how the function has been used so far,
not a limitation of the hardware: the Mega Drive’s VDP actually allows a different palette to
be assigned to each individual tile within the same plane, not just to the plane as a whole. A
singlebackgroundcouldcombinetilesusingPAL0,PAL1,PAL2,andPAL3simultaneously,which
enables,forinstance,sceneswithfarmorethan16colorsvisibleatonce,sensiblydistributed
across different areas.
Takingadvantageofthattile-by-tileflexibilitywiththetoolsuseduptothispoint—apixel-art
editor plus VDP_drawImageEx() — is cumbersome, since it would require manually chopping
uptheimageandassigningeachfragmenttoabasetilewithitsownpalparameter. Thereare
third-partytools, outsideAsepriteitself, aimed specificallyat assigningpalette andtileprior-
ity visually over an already-drawn graphic; it’s worth looking into them if a project needs to
takeadvantageofthisflexibilitysystematically,thoughtheyaren’tpartofthebasicworkflow
covered in this chapter.
8.3 VRAM and automatic tile deduplication
The Mega Drive’s VRAM stores tiles, not a continuous grid of pixels, and its capacity — al-
though considerably larger than that of 8-bit systems like the NES or the Master System —
isn’t infinite: it has to be split between the background, the foreground, and the sprites for
everything on screen. The most effective strategy for not running it dry is, simply, reusing
tiles: a background made of a handful of tiles repeated in a pattern (a tileset) takes up much
less space than the same scene drawn as a single image with no repetition.
SGDKhelpswiththisautomatically: whenconvertinganimageintoatileset,itdetectswhich
tilesare,infact,thesametileflippedhorizontallyorverticallyrelativetoonealreadypresent,
andinsteadofduplicatingthedatainVRAMitstoresasingletileandmarkstherestwiththe
correspondingflipflag(thesameflipH/flipVfromTILE_ATTR_FULL()alreadyusedinChapter
7). An emulator with VRAM debugging tools lets you inspect this savings directly.
The emulator’s VRAM debugging tool shows the CRAM with all four palettes loaded and, be-
lowit,theindividualtiles: asinglemarkedtilereappearsflippedinseveralpositionswithout
having been duplicated in memory.
The practical takeaway is that, when designing a graphic — especially a background meant
for a full level and not just a test screen — it’s worth thinking of it from the start as a tileset:
arelativelysmallsetofdistincttiles, combinedandrepeated(flipsincluded)tobuildascene
muchlargerthantheunique-tilecountwouldsuggest. There’snoneedtomanagetileflipping
byhand: SGDKdetectsitonitsown. Whatdoesdependontheartistisdrawinginawaythat
gives it tiles to detect in the first place.

Chapter 9 — Scroll and Parallax
Scrolling
Chapter 7 left a static image on each of the VDP’s two background planes. This chapter sets
those same images in motion: it’s the first step toward scrolling and, in particular, toward
parallax scrolling, the technique so characteristic of 16-bit games in which the background
and foreground move at different speeds to suggest depth. Without parallax, a game world
looks oddly flat; with it, even in its simplest form, it starts to feel three-dimensional.
Chapter 2 already introduced, at a conceptual level, the three scroll granularities offered
by the VDP: whole-plane, per-tile (or per-column, on the vertical axis), and per-line. Here
theygetcodeforthefirsttime,startingwiththesimplestofthethree: whole-planescrolling,
whichmovestheentirescreenatonce. Theothertwovariants—per-tile/columnandper-line,
whichallowmovingstripsofthescreenatdifferentspeedswithinthesameplane,theclassic
effectusedinracinggamesorcertainbossfights—arementionedbutnotdevelopedindepth
yet: theyrequiremorecodeandadeeperunderstandingofhowVRAMisorganized,andthey
are territory for a dedicated chapter on levels with scrolling that follows the player, later in
this manual.
Implementing plane scrolling requires only a couple more lines of code beyond what was
already written in Chapter 7. What it does demand, and in depth, is understanding several
underlying ideas: what the difference is between specifying a position in tiles versus pixels,
whatthreedistinctsectionsatypicalSGDKprogramhasandwhathappensifcodeiswritten
in the wrong section, and why the VDP stores each plane at a fixed size of 512×256 pixels
even though the visible screen is much smaller.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Completed Chapter 7, “Displaying Backgrounds: BG_A/BG_B and VDP_drawImageEx”:
this chapter builds on the same project, with the same two planes (bg1 on BG_B and fg1
on BG_A) already declared, palettized, and drawn on screen.
• An understanding of the concepts of tile, VRAM, and palette covered in Chapter 2, as
well as the distinction between BG_A (foreground) and BG_B (distant background).
• The fix16/fix32 fixed-point types introduced in Chapter 6, which reappear toward the
end of this chapter.
• Basic knowledge of C: global versus local variables, and the structure of a while loop.

1. Configuring the scroll mode: VDP_setScrollingMode
The VDP doesn’t move a plane simply because the programmer changes an x or y coordinate
everyframe: firstitmustbeexplicitlytoldwhatmodethatplane’sscrollwilloperatein. That
configuration is done once, with the function VDP_setScrollingMode():
void VDP_setScrollingMode(u16 hscroll, u16 vscroll);
The two parameters configure, separately, the horizontal and vertical scroll modes. As pre-
viewed in Chapter 2, the horizontal mode offers three possible granularities:
• HSCROLL_PLANE — the offset is applied to the whole plane: the entire screen moves uni-
formly. It’s the simplest mode and the only one used in this chapter.
• HSCROLL_TILE—theoffsetcanbedefinedindependentlyforeach8-pixel-tallblock(atile).
This allows, for example, different horizontal strips of the screen to move at different
speeds.
• HSCROLL_LINE — the offset can be defined line by line (each 1-pixel-tall line), the finest
granularity possible and the one used by the more elaborate scroll effects, such as the
curves of a racetrack.
The vertical mode offers two granularities: VSCROLL_PLANE, analogous to HSCROLL_PLANE (the
whole plane moves as a unit), and VSCROLL_COLUMN, which allows an independent offset per
16-pixel-widecolumn. Unlikehorizontalscrolling,theMegaDrivedoesnotofferaline-by-line
vertical scroll mode; the hardware itself gives preference to fine horizontal scrolling, on the
logic that the vast majority of games scroll mainly in that direction.
If old sample code ever turns up using a constant called VSCROLL_2TILE for vertical scrolling,
keepinmindthatit’sdeprecated: SGDKreplaceditwithVSCROLL_COLUMN,whichfillsthesame
role (independent offset per vertical strip) with a more precise name. Using VSCROLL_2TILE
directly in SGDK 2.11 no longer compiles.
Since this chapter deals with the simplest case, it uses whole-plane scrolling in both direc-
tions:
VDP_setScrollingMode(HSCROLL_PLANE, VSCROLL_PLANE);
Don’t forget the semicolon. A common typo when writing this line for the first
time is forgetting the trailing semicolon, which produces a compilation error. This
isn’t specific to this function — it applies to any statement in C — but it’s worth
keepinginmindbecausethecompiler’serrormessageinthesecasesdoesn’talways
point to the exact line of the omission, but to the following line.
2. Moving the plane: VDP_setHorizontalScroll and
VDP_setVerticalScroll
Withthescrollmodeconfigured,what’sstillmissingisthepartthatactuallymovestheplane
frame by frame: telling the VDP, on every pass of the main loop, what the current offset is.
Two functions handle that, one per axis:
void VDP_setHorizontalScroll(VDPPlane plane, s16 value);
void VDP_setVerticalScroll(VDPPlane plane, s16 value);
The first parameter is, again, the plane the offset is applied to (BG_A or BG_B). The second,
value, is the offset value, with one important detail that sets these two functions apart from
VDP_drawImageEx(): here value is measured in pixels, not tiles. A value of 8 shifts the plane
8 pixels — that is, exactly one tile — not 8 tiles (64 pixels).

3. Where to put each line of code: the three sections of

Beforewritingtheframe-by-frameoffsetcode,it’sworthpausingonapointthatisn’texclusive

every SGDK main() is organized into three clearly distinct sections:
1. Global section: everything declared before int main(), outside any function. These
are variables that need to exist for the entire life of the program and be visible from
differentfunctions(or,asinthischapter,tokeeptheirvaluefromoneframetothenext).
2. Initial setup section: thestretchofcodebetweentheopeningbraceof main()andthe

starts: loading palettes, drawing the backgrounds, configuring the scroll mode.
3. Main loop section: the contents of while(1) { ... }. Everything here runs over and
over, once per frame, for as long as the program is running.

The variable hscroll_offset is declared globally, together with ind, because it needs to pre-
serve its value from one frame to the next: if it were declared inside the while loop, it would
reset to 0 on every pass and the plane would never advance. Inside the loop, each pass does
three things: it tells the VDP the current scroll position with VDP_setHorizontalScroll(),
increments that position by 1 for the next pass, and calls SYS_doVBlankProcess().
SYS_doVBlankProcess() synchronizes the program with the VDP’s vertical blanking interval
(VBlank), the brief span between frames during which the screen isn’t being drawn and
it’s safe to update VRAM without producing visual artifacts. For application-level program-
ming, it’s enough to know that this call must be present once per loop pass, typically at the
end. In SGDK versions prior to 1.60 the equivalent function was called VDP_waitVSync();
if that name shows up in old projects, it fills the same role and should be replaced with
SYS_doVBlankProcess() when porting to SGDK 2.11.
With this code, the intended effect is already achieved: the background scrolls continuously
to the right, at a rate of 1 pixel per frame (which on the Mega Drive amounts to roughly 60
pixels per second, given that the system runs at 60 frames per second in the NTSC variant).
Reversing the scroll direction or changing its speed doesn’t require any new function: it’s
enoughtochangetheincrementaddedtohscroll_offsetoneachpass. Subtractinginstead
of adding reverses the direction; adding or subtracting a number greater than 1 speeds up
the movement.
hscroll_offset -= 2; // moves to the left, twice as fast
The scroll can look a bit choppier in an emulator than on a physical console con-
nected to a period-accurate TV: different emulators handle timing and video filter-
ing differently. If it’s possible to test the same rom.bin on real hardware, the final
result looks better there.

The cause is exactly the VRAM bookkeeping discipline mentioned in Chapter 7. The vari-

by something else (or, simply, until the available VRAM space runs out and the count wraps
around). The visual result is the mix of incorrect tile data described above.
Thegeneralrule: configureonce,updateeveryframe. Thisexperimentserves
to fix a rule that’s worth applying from here on to any SGDK program: everything
that prepares an initial state — loading a palette, uploading tiles to VRAM, config-

thatneedstobereevaluatedeveryframe—readingthecontroller,movingasprite,
updating the scroll position — belongs in the main loop. Mixing the two doesn’t al-
ways produce a result as visually dramatic as this experiment, but it almost always
produces some kind of error that’s hard to diagnose if you don’t know what to look
for.
Revertingthechange—movingthoselinesbacktotheinitialsetupsection,beforethewhile
— restores the correct behavior.
5. The real size of a plane: 512×256 pixels
With horizontal scrolling working, a problem shows up that no code error explains: once the
scroll moves far enough, the plane starts showing areas with no graphics, like black gaps.
The cause is a hardware characteristic, not a program defect. The VDP doesn’t store each
plane at exactly the size of the visible screen (320×224 pixels in standard mode); instead it
reserves a much larger tile board in VRAM: 512×256 pixels, that is, 64×32 tiles. The reason
isthatthisextraspaceletstheVDPalwayshavetilesalreadyloadedabove,below,totheleft,
and to the right of the visible area, so that scrolling can show new content instantly at the
edgesofthescreeninsteadofhavingtoloaditonthefly,framebyframe,whichwouldbetoo
slow to sustain 60 frames per second.
The problem arises when the image drawn on the plane is smaller than that 512×256 board:
theVDPhasextratilesreserved,butthosetileswereneverfilledwithcontent,sotheyappear
empty (black gaps) as soon as the scroll advances far enough to reveal them. To make the
problem more visible, it’s enough to also enable vertical scrolling on the same plane, using
the same offset variable:

The VDP also doesn’t reserve the same amount of extra space on both axes: it keeps propor-

7. Two speeds: parallax proper
Uptonow,boththebackground(BG_B)andtheforeground(BG_A)moved—whentheymoved
at all — at the same speed, controlled by the same variable hscroll_offset. That’s not par-
allax scrolling in the strict sense: it’s just a single plane in motion. The depth effect that
gives the technique its name only appears once each plane moves at a different speed, typi-
cally with the foreground moving faster than the distant background, mimicking how nearby
objects appear to move faster than distant ones when you move in real life.
Implementingitrequiresnonewfunction: it’senoughtodeclareasecond,independentglobal
offset variable and use it to move BG_A:
u16 ind = TILE_USERINDEX;
int hscroll_offset = 0;
int hscroll_offset_fore = 0;

{

{

hscroll_offset -= 1;
VDP_setHorizontalScroll(BG_A, hscroll_offset_fore);

SYS_doVBlankProcess();

Withthebackgroundadvancingat1pixelperframeandtheforegroundat2pixelsperframe
— twice the speed — the result is already recognizable parallax scrolling: the foreground
visibly glides faster than the background, suggesting it’s closer to the camera.
A visible limitation: the repeat seam. When a plane’s image is narrower than
the full scroll range it’s meant to cover, at some point the pattern starts repeating
and a “seam” or edge can be noticed where one copy of the image ends and the
next begins. This is a natural limitation of working with a fixed-width image rather
than a procedurally generated level or one of arbitrary width, and it becomes less
noticeable the wider and more varied the source image is. Long levels that follow
theplayer,withsectionsmuchwiderthanasinglescreen,arerevisitedlaterinthis
manual.

8. The limit of integers: why int isn’t enough
With parallax working at speeds of 1 and 2 pixels per frame, a natural question comes up:
what happens if a slower speed is needed, for example half a screen’s worth of scroll every
two frames, that is, 0.5 pixels per frame? Trying that value directly doesn’t work:
hscroll_offset -= 0.5; // produces no visible movement
Theplanestayscompletelystill. ThereasonhasnothingtodowiththeVDPoranyofthescroll
functions: it’s a limitation of the very data type used for hscroll_offset. It was declared
as int, an integer, which by definition cannot represent fractions. When 0.5 is subtracted
from an int, the C compiler truncates that result to the nearest integer before storing it; the
practicaleffectisthatthestoredintegervalueneverchangesfromoneframetothenext,and
therefore neither does the scroll position. The same problem shows up with any increment
smaller than 1 in absolute value, not just 0.5: 0.8 subtracted repeatedly from an int still
rounds to 0 at every step, so the visual result is identical to not moving the plane at all.
Thesolution,alreadyfamiliarfromChapter6,istouseafixed-pointtypeinsteadofaninteger.
fix32 (or its lighter variant fix16) reserves part of its bits to represent a fraction, instead of
using all its bits for the integer part. Declaring the offset as fix32 and using the FIX32()
macro to express the fractional increment, subtracting half a pixel per frame does produce a
real accumulated offset:
fix32 hscroll_offset_f = FIX32(0);
// inside the loop:
hscroll_offset_f -= FIX32(0.5);
VDP_setHorizontalScroll(BG_B, F32_toInt(hscroll_offset_f));
The key is in the last line: VDP_setHorizontalScroll() still expects an s16 in whole pixels,
so the fixed-point value accumulates with its fraction intact in hscroll_offset_f, and is only
converted to an integer with F32_toInt() at the moment it’s passed to the VDP. Even though
you’llneverseeless-than-one-pixelmovementinasingleframe(thepixelitselfisthesmallest
unit that can be shown on screen), the accumulated fraction means that, every two frames,
the resulting integer value does advance by one pixel, achieving the targeted average speed
of 0.5 pixels per frame. This same technique — accumulating in fixed point and converting
to an integer only at the end — is what SGDK uses internally for sprite coordinates, and it
comes up again in any situation that requires a fractional speed, such as a character’s jump.
Integers (int, u16, s16, etc.) are enough for speeds of 1 pixel per frame or more, but any
speed slower than that requires a fixed-point type such as fix32 or fix16.

Chapter 10 — H40 and H32
Resolution Modes
How to switch horizontal resolution with a single line of code, and what practical criteria
come into play when choosing between H40 and H32
The chapter on the VDP already introduced, at a conceptual level, the Mega Drive’s two
horizontal resolution modes and their associated sprite limits. This chapter picks that idea
backupfromthepracticalside: whatcodeisneededtoactivateeachmode,whatsideeffects
that change brings, and why much of the industry ended up using one mode or the other
depending on the situation.
1. Quick recap: H40 and H32
As a reminder, the Mega Drive supports two horizontal resolutions:
• H40: 320×224pixels(40tiles,8pixelswideeach). Thisisthedefaultmodeandtheone
used by the vast majority of commercial games. It allows up to 80 simultaneous sprites
on screen, with a maximum of 20 per horizontal line.
• H32: 256×224 pixels (32 tiles wide). Sprite limits drop to 64 on screen and 16 per line.
The reduction in sprites under H32 isn’t arbitrary: by displaying fewer pixels of width, the
VDP also lowers its internal clock speed to match, and that limits how many sprites it can
process in the time available per line. Vertical resolution, on the other hand, doesn’t depend
onthishorizontalmode: thestandardis224visiblelines(V28mode),availableonbothNTSC
and PAL consoles. PAL consoles additionally support a V30 mode of 240 lines, exclusive to
that region; this chapter doesn’t go into it in depth, so it’s enough to know it exists and adds
16 extra vertical lines only on PAL systems.
2. How to activate it in SGDK
If a program doesn’t explicitly specify which mode to use, SGDK starts up in H40 by default.
Switching to H32 (256 pixels wide) takes a single line of code, placed anywhere before the
screen is drawn:
VDP_setScreenWidth256();
This function takes no parameters: it changes the horizontal resolution to 256 pixels the
moment it’s called. Symmetrically, there’s VDP_setScreenWidth320() to go back to (or stay
in) the 320-pixel H40 mode:
VDP_setScreenWidth320();
47

=== PAGE 54 ===
Neither function takes any arguments: each one directly sets its own width. This also means
a program can switch modes at different points during execution — for example, using H32
onatitlescreenandH40duringgameplay—aslongasthecorrespondingcallismadebefore
each screen is displayed.
3. The visual result: a speed effect that isn’t really one
Ifthesameprojectiscompiledinbothmodes—say,awidelevelmapthatscrollsautomatically
at a rate of one pixel per frame, using MAP_scrollTo() as covered in the previous chapter —
and the two results are run side by side, the width difference is obvious: one window shows
320 pixels and the other 256. What’s most striking, however, isn’t the width itself, but that
themapinH32givestheimpressionofscrollingfaster thantheoneinH40,eventhoughthe
scrolling code is exactly the same in both cases.
Figure 11: The same map in H40 and H32, a few seconds after the scroll starts
TheH32window(right)appearstohaveadvancedfurtherthantheH40one(left),eventhough
both scroll at the same rate of one pixel per frame.
That sense of different speed is a perceptual effect, not an actual difference in speed: since
the H32 screen has fewer pixels of width to cross, the same number of pixels scrolled per
second represents a larger fraction of that screen’s total width, which is why it’s perceived
as faster movement. It’s worth keeping this in mind when tuning a game’s scroll speed: a
value that feels right in H40 may feel too fast if the same project is switched to H32 without
revisiting that constant.
4. Why choose H32: examples from the industry
Although most Mega Drive games use H40, a fair number of commercial titles choose H32
undervariouscircumstances. AcommunityresearcherknownasFirebrandXcompiled,years

ago, an extensive and fairly well-cited list of games that use the 256×224 mode during dif-
ferentpartsofthegame(includingbothtitlescreensandgameplayitself),andreviewingthe

in a project of your own.
A common pattern is low-resolution title screens followed by a game that runs in H40, as
happens in Golden Axe. A reasonable explanation is that it reduces the number of unique

5. H32 to reduce CPU load: software-rendered 3D engines
AnotherreasontochooseH32showsupingamesthatrenderpseudo-3Dgraphicsinsoftware

Noteverygamewithanambitiouspseudo-3DengineresortstoH32,though: ZeroTolerance,

full resolution. This is an option worth considering when trying to ease the load of expensive
rendering without dropping out of H40: reduce the effective computation area and leave the
rest of the screen for the HUD.
6. H40 for more simultaneous sprites
Thedecisioncanalsogotheotherway,prioritizingH40overH32evenwhenportingcontent

the Night (originally from PlayStation, whose resolution doesn’t exactly match either of the
Mega Drive’s two modes), the standard H40 mode was chosen instead of trying to replicate
the original resolution. The usual reasons for such a choice are, on one hand, being able to
showmoresimultaneousspritesonscreen,andontheother,anaestheticpreferenceforhow
the final result looks at that resolution.
When working with art originally designed for a higher-resolution console, H40 also has an
added advantage when displaying the result on a widescreen display (on an emulator or a
widescreen CRT television): when the final image is stretched to fill that width, the result
comes closer to the look of the original game than if it were based on an image generated in
H32 mode.
