7. The challenge of porting from other consoles
Choosing a resolution gets even trickier when the source system doesn’t match either of the
Mega Drive’s two modes. The Game Boy Advance, for example, has a resolution of 240×160
pixels,quitedifferentfromtheMegaDrive’sonbothaxes. Therearefanprojectsthatexplore
exactly this scenario, such as a technical demo of Aria of Sorrow (originally from Game Boy
Advance) running on the Mega Drive.
The difference in vertical resolution tends to be the most visible problem in this kind of con-
version: the Game Boy Advance’s original 160 pixels of height are considerably smaller than
the Mega Drive’s 224 lines in V28 mode, which forces a choice between showing black bars
above and below, stretching the image, or redesigning the level outright to make use of the
extraverticalspace(themostlabor-intensiveofthethreeoptions,butalsotheonethattends
to give the best results). On top of that resolution difference, there’s also the need to adapt
the original color palette to the Mega Drive’s limit of colors per palette.
8. Why stretching sprites or levels is a bad idea
Stretching the image to compensate for a resolution difference is rarely a good idea. When
a sprite is stretched vertically without first correcting the horizontal proportion, the result
looks distorted and no longer aligns with the 8×8 pixel tile grid that all of the Mega Drive’s
hardware works on.
Figure 12: The same sprite, stretched vertically
Stretching distorts the art and throws it out of alignment with the 8×8 pixel tile grid.
Thatmisalignmentwiththetilegridisthemoreseriousproblem,beyondthepurelyaesthetic
one: the same 8×8 grid is used both to load graphics into VRAM and to calculate collisions
at the map level, so once the art stops matching it, both the VRAM loading and the level and
collision design become considerably harder to get right. In cases like Aria of Sorrow, it’s
50

=== PAGE 57 ===
usually more practical to redesign a level on a case-by-case basis or add extra tiles than to
accept that kind of distortion.

and sprite limits per frame and per line.

Chapter 11 — Large Level Maps
with MAP_create
Chapter7introducedtheIMAGEresource: asinglegraphic,upto512×256pixels,loadedin
full onto one of the two background planes with VDP_drawImageEx(). That method is enough
for many screens, such as a menu, a static background, or a title screen, but not for a large
platformer level, in the style of a zone from Sonic the Hedgehog, which extends well beyond
those dimensions. This chapter presents the solution SGDK offers for that case: splitting the
map into two separate resources, a TILESET with the unique tiles that make it up and a MAP
with the arrangement of those tiles across the whole level, and scrolling the visible portion
of a map that, as a whole, is much larger than the screen.
The example used is a simplified version of the Green Hill Zone from Sonic the Hedgehog,
reducedto16colorstorespectthelimitofaMegaDrivepalette(theoriginalusesmorethan
one palette in the foreground, a resource revisited in Chapter 14, dedicated to combining
several palettes in the same background). Before writing any code, it’s worth taking a close
look at the tiles that make up that map: the checkered pattern of the ground, the repeated
foliageofthetrees,andmuchofthelandscapearebuiltfromveryfewdistincttiles,repeated
over and over. That repetition is precisely what makes it possible to represent such a large
map with a reasonable amount of memory.
The full Green Hill Zone map open in the editor: the checkered pattern of the ground and
much of the landscape are built by repeating very few distinct tiles.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have fresh in mind:
• Chapters 7 (“Displaying backgrounds: BG_A/BG_B and VDP_drawImageEx”) and 9
(“Scroll and parallax scrolling”): the idea of an 8×8-pixel tile, of background planes
(BG_A and BG_B), of PAL_setPalette() to load a palette into CRAM, and the technique
of scrolling a background by modifying a variable inside the main loop.
• The data types covered in Chapter 6, in particular u16, since they appear in several of
this chapter’s functions.
1. Two resources from a single file: TILESET and MAP
The first step is, as always, to copy the graphic file into the res folder and declare the corre-
sponding resources in resources.res. The first line declares a TILESET resource, which tells
rescomp to examine the image and extract from it the set of unique tiles that make it up:
TILESET our_tileset "large green hill map.png" BEST ALL
52

=== PAGE 59 ===
Figure 13: The full Green Hill Zone map in the editor
The first two parameters are already familiar from other graphic resources: the source file
andthecompressionlevel(BEST,whichletsrescompautomaticallychoosethemostconvenient
method). The last parameter, ALL, is specific to a TILESET: it tells rescomp to discard both
duplicate tiles and their mirrored variants when building the unique tile set. It’s the default
modeandthemostconvenientforamaplikethisone,sinceaplatformerleveltendstoreuse
the same ground, foliage, or sky tile many, many times, sometimes mirrored horizontally or
vertically to vary the landscape without drawing a new tile.
The second line declares the MAP resource itself, which describes which tile goes in each
position of the full map:
MAP our_level_map "large green hill map.png" our_tileset BEST 0
An important detail is that the MAP resource references the TILESET just declared by name
(our_tileset), since a map on its own is just a grid of indices: it needs an associated tileset
to know which tile corresponds to each index.
Both resources use the same image file as their source, and that’s neither a mistake nor a
coincidence. rescomp scans that single image from left to right and top to bottom, identifies
each8×8-pixeltile,andbuildstheTILESETbyaddingonlythetilesithasn’tseenyet(thanksto
theALLmode,bothanexactrepeatandamirroredversionofatilealreadyseenarerecognized
and discarded). The MAP, on the other hand, preserves the complete layout of the level, but
expressed as a reference to each tile’s position within the already-reduced TILESET, instead
of repeating the full graphic of each tile everywhere it appears.
This separation is exactly what allows a visually enormous map, like the one in this chapter,
totakeuprelativelylittlespaceinROMandVRAM:repeatedinformationisstoredonlyonce,
and the map only records “tile number 12, mirrored, goes here” instead of repeating the full
graphic of tile 12 every time it appears.
53

=== PAGE 60 ===
2. Loading the tileset into VRAM and creating the map
With the resources already compiled and #include "resources.h" added to main.c, two vari-
ables are needed before main(): an index indicating where in VRAM the map’s tiles will be
loaded, and a pointer to the map itself, analogous to the Sprite* pointer already used for
sprites.
For the index, SGDK provides a constant marking the first VRAM slot free for programmer-
defined tiles (the tiles before that point are reserved for SGDK’s internal use, such as the
default text font):
u16 ind = TILE_USER_INDEX;
Withindalreadydeclared,thefirststepinsidemain()istoloadtheTILESET’stilesintoVRAM
with VDP_loadTileSet(), giving it the tileset to load, the VRAM index to start loading it at,
andthetransfermethod(DMA,thesamedirectmemoryaccessalreadyusedtoloadsprites):
VDP_loadTileSet(&our_tileset, ind, DMA);
With the tiles already in VRAM, the next step is to create the map structure itself with
MAP_create(), which needs three pieces of data: the MAP resource defined in resources.res,
the background plane where it will be displayed (BG_A or BG_B), and the base attributes with
which its tiles will be drawn:
Map* level_1_map;
level_1_map = MAP_create(&our_level_map, BG_B,
TILE_ATTR_FULL(PAL0, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, ind));
That third argument is built with TILE_ATTR_FULL(pal, prio, flipV, flipH, index), the
same macro already used to combine palette, priority, flips, and VRAM index into a single
value, only here it’s applied to an entire map instead of a single sprite. The exact signature
of MAP_create() is:
Map* MAP_create(const MapDefinition *mapDef, VDPPlane plane, u16 baseTile);
In this example, the map is displayed on BG_B instead of BG_A simply because the chapter
workswithasingleplaneanddoesn’tneedtousebothatonceyet;it’sapracticaldecisionfor
thisspecificexample,notarestrictionofSGDK.Inarealgame,aplatformermaplikethisone
would normally go on the foreground plane (BG_A), reserving BG_B for a distant background
with parallax, like the one seen in Chapter 9. PAL0 is used because the map was prepared to
fill the full 16 colors of a single palette, and no flip or special priority is applied (the three
FALSE parameters), closing the call with the ind index already used when loading the tileset,
so the map knows where, within VRAM, the tiles it references are located.
3. A separate PALETTE resource
One last step remains before compiling: loading the map’s colors into the PAL0 hardware
palette,alreadyindicatedinMAP_create(). Inpreviouschapters,anIMAGEorSPRITEresource
includes a pointer to its own palette as part of its structure (image.palette->data), which
allows the colors to be extracted directly from the same already-loaded graphic resource,
without declaring anything additional.
A MAP, however, doesn’t work the same way: its structure includes no palette field of its own,
so there’s never an our_level_map.palette to fall back on. Trying to write something like
54

=== PAGE 61 ===
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, our_level_map.palette->data, DMA);,copyingthepatternusedwith
an IMAGE, doesn’t compile, because that field simply doesn’t exist in the Map structure.
A MAPresourcedescribesonlythelevel’stilelayout;itdoesn’tcarryitsownpalette.
The colors have to be obtained from elsewhere.
The solution is to declare an independent PALETTE resource in resources.res, telling it to
extract the colors from that same image file already used for the tileset and the map. A
PALETTE resource is, in itself, very simple: a name and a source file, nothing more.
PALETTE our_palette "large green hill map.png"
With this resource already compiled, loading the palette uses the .data field of the new
PALETTE resource, instead of the .palette->data chain that isn’t available for a map:
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, our_palette.data, DMA);
Withallthreepiecesnowinplace(tilesetloadedintoVRAM,mapcreatedonBG_B,andpalette
loaded into PAL0), the program should now compile without errors.
4. The first result: an entirely sky-blue screen
Compiling and running at this point, however, the result isn’t the expected Green Hill Zone
landscape, but an entirely sky-blue screen, with no landscape element visible at all.
There’s no error in the code: the map loaded and is being displayed correctly, it’s just that
MAP_create()startsshowingthemapfromexactlyitstop-leftcorner,coordinate(0,0). Since
the full map is much taller than the screen’s 224-pixel vertical resolution (see Chapter 10 on
the H40 and H32 resolution modes), that top-left corner corresponds solely to the sky, well
above where the ground, trees, and the rest of the recognizable landscape begin. The sky-
blue screen is, in that sense, the correct result of displaying exactly that portion of the map:
it simply isn’t the portion of interest to show first.
5. Finding where to scroll the map, and MAP_scrollTo()
To display a more useful portion of the map, it needs to be scrolled vertically, and to know
by how much, it helps to go back to the original image file in a pixel-art editor and locate,
with the cursor, the Y coordinate where the recognizable landscape begins (just above the
treeline,forinstance). Inthisparticularmap,thatcoordinateturnsouttobe768pixelsfrom
the top. That figure isn’t universal in any way: it’s specific to this particular file, an artistic
decisionaboutwherethelandscapewasdrawnwithinthefullimage. Anyothermaprequires
repeating the same visual-inspection process to find its own starting coordinate.
With that coordinate already identified, MAP_scrollTo() takes care of scrolling the map. The
function needs the map to scroll and the destination X and Y coordinates; in a first attempt,
withnohorizontalscrollingyet,it’senoughtoscrollverticallytothecoordinatealreadyfound:
MAP_scrollTo(level_1_map, 0, 768);
Compiling again with this adjustment, the sky-blue screen gives way to the expected land-
scape: the trees, the flowers, the ground, and Green Hill Zone’s characteristic checkered
pattern, exactly as they appear in the original file, with no sign of tile corruption or visual
artifacts.

6. Continuous scrolling: reusing the parallax scrolling
idea
Withthemapnowshowingthecorrectportion,it’snaturaltoextendtheexamplesoitscrolls
continuously to the right, reusing exactly the same idea already explained in Chapter 9: re-
placingthefixedXcoordinatevaluewithavariable,andincrementingitoneverypassthrough
the main loop.
The variable is declared alongside the rest of the global variables, before main():
int x = 0;
AndthecalltoMAP_scrollTo()movesinsidewhile (TRUE),sinceitnowdependsonavariable
thatchangesovertimeanditmakesnosensetocallitonlyonce,followedbyincrementingx
on every pass:
while (TRUE)
{
MAP_scrollTo(level_1_map, x, 768);
x += 1;
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
Theresult is anautomatic, continuous scroll tothe right, traversing theentire map fromend
to end with no player input at all. The landscape looks the same as in the original file, with
no artifacts, only now in constant motion.
Thisautomaticscrollingismerelyademonstrationdevice,nottheusualwaytodisplayalevel
ofthiskindinafinishedgame. Aplatformerinsteadneedsacamerathatfollowstheplayable
character’s position, scrolling the map according to where the player is moving instead of
doing so automatically and independently. Building that camera logic is left for Chapter 24;
fornow,it’senoughtounderstandhowamaplargerthanthescreenisassembledandscrolled,
which is the foundation that camera will build on.

Chapter 12 — Level Maps with
Tiled and TMX Files
Designing levels with an external graphical tool instead of drawing the map by hand, and
bringing that design into the SGDK project
The previous chapter showed how to declare the TILESET, PALETTE, and MAP resources sepa-
rately,loadthemwithVDP_loadTileSet,andusethemtobuildaMapstructureviaMAP_create,
capable of scrolling with MAP_scrollTo. That workflow assumes the map already exists in
some format rescomp knows how to read, but it says nothing about how that map is designed
inthefirstplace. Drawinganentireleveltilebytile,byhand,ontopofanimageordirectlyas
alistofnumbers, isworkablefora smallscreen, but itquicklybecomesimpracticalonce the
level grows to several screens wide, has several overlapping layers (background, platforms,
decoration), or the design needs to be iterated on many times during development.
This is exactly what dedicated map editors are for. This chapter covers the workflow with
Tiled,ageneral-purposeexternaleditorfortile-based2Dgames,anditsexportformat,TMX.
ThenextchapterpresentsanalternativebuiltspecificallyforSGDK,the16Tiletool,inmore
depth; the goal here is to understand the Tiled workflow well enough to use it comfortably,
and to be able to compare it critically once you’ve read chapter 13.
Prerequisites
• Have SGDK 2.11 installed and a working base project, as explained in chapter 3.
• Know the difference between the TILESET, PALETTE, and MAP resources, and the use of
MAP_create/MAP_scrollTo covered in chapter 11.
• A tileset of your own in image format (PNG), respecting the same palette restrictions
already covered in previous chapters: at most 16 colors per palette and 8×8-pixel tiles,
the smallest unit the VDP can handle.
1. What a tileset is and why an external tool helps
Asmentionedinchapter11,generatingalargebackgroundbydrawingitentirelyasasingle
imagecaneatupanunreasonableamountofROM.Thealternativeisatileset: asmallsetof
8×8-pixelgraphicpiecesthatarecombinedandrepeatedtobuildmapsmuchlargerthanthe
sum of their parts. A handful of “grass,” “dirt,” and “rock” tiles is enough to build an entire
level, as long as there’s also a map: the list of which tile goes in each position of the grid.
Drawingthatlistbyhand—amatrixofnumbers,eachonetheindexofatilewithinthetileset
— is tedious and error-prone even for a modest level. A map-editing tool solves exactly that
problem: it presents the tileset as a palette of brushes and lets you “paint” the map visually,
tile by tile, instead of writing numeric indices by hand.
57

=== PAGE 64 ===
2. Tiled (mapeditor.org)
Tiledisanopen-source,cross-platform(Windows,Linux,andmacOS)tilemapeditorreleased
under the GPL license, available at mapeditor.org. It’s not a Mega Drive– or SGDK–specific
tool: it’s a generic editor used in 2D game development in general, which brings a concrete
advantage — abundant documentation and a community of its own, independent of this man-
ual—andanequallyconcretelimitation: itknowsnothingabouttheMegaDrive’sparticular
hardware restrictions (16-color palettes, a maximum of four palettes, 8×8 tiles), so those re-
strictions remain the responsibility of whoever designs the source tileset, before bringing it
into Tiled.
The typical workflow within Tiled is as follows:
1. Createanewmap,specifyingthegridsizeintilesandthesizeofeachtileinpixels(8×8,
so that each cell of the map corresponds to exactly one VDP tile).
2. Import, as a tileset, the image already prepared with the level’s graphic pieces.
3. Create one or more tile-map–type layers, and paint on each one using the tileset as a
palette of brushes. It’s common to use one layer for the walkable background and a
separateoneforelementsthatbelongonadifferentplane(forexample,decorationthat
appears in front of the sprites), since on the Mega Drive each Tiled layer can later be
mapped to a different hardware plane (BG_A or BG_B).
4. Save the finished map, exporting it in TMX format (an XML format native to Tiled) or,
alternatively, in JSON. SGDK, through rescomp, works with the TMX format.
Tiled’s interface while editing a map typically shows the layers panel on the right — with the
list of layers created so far and controls to show or hide them — and, at the bottom, the tile
palette of the imported tileset, ready for picking the tile to paint onto the map grid.
When saving the tile layer, it’s worth checking that the layer’s encoding format is
CSV (a list of comma-separated numbers) rather than a compressed binary encod-
ing. With layers in CSV, the resulting TMX file is readable plain text, which also
acts as a safety net: if something goes wrong during automatic import, it’s always
possible to open the TMX with a text editor and check at a glance what numbers
were saved.
3. Importing the TMX into the project with rescomp
SinceSGDKversion1.80,rescomp—theresourcecompilerthatalreadyconvertsimagesand
palettesinpreviouschapters—canreadaTMXfileexportedbyTileddirectly,withnomanual
intermediate step. The corresponding resource in the resources.res file generally has the
form:
TILEMAP resource_name "level1.tmx" [options]
This resource generates, in resources.h/resources.c, a structure of type TileMap (different
fromtheMapstructurethatMAP_createbuilds)whichessentiallycontainsthewidthandheight
ofthemapintilesandthelistoftileindicesfromoneofitslayers,exactlyastheyweresaved
in the TMX’s <data> tag. That structure can be used in two ways, depending on what the
game needs:
• Combined with what was already covered in chapter 11: by also separately
declaring the TILESET and PALETTE resources corresponding to the same tileset used in
Tiled, and using MAP_create to build the final Map structure that is then scrolled with
MAP_scrollTo. This is the most direct path when the goal is a large level with scrolling
— exactly the same scenario that motivated the previous chapter.
58

=== PAGE 65 ===
• More directly, when the map is small or static and the scrolling machinery of the MAP
unit isn’t needed: by reading the index list from the TileMap structure and dumping it,
tilebytile,ontoaplanealreadysetupwiththecorrespondingtilesetloadedintoVRAM.
The .tmx file itself doesn’t need to be copied by hand anywhere else: it’s enough to leave it
insidetheproject’sresourcesfolder(alongsidetheimagesandotherfilesalreadyreferenced
by resources.res) and declare the TILEMAP resource line pointing to that file, the same way
it’s done with IMAGE, TILESET, or PALETTE.
The manual technique, prior to direct import
Before rescomp couldread aTMX directly, theonly way tobring amap designed inTiled into
an SGDK project was a more artisanal technique. Today it’s unnecessary in the normal case,
but it’s worth knowing: it helps explain what the TILEMAP resource does behind the scenes,
and it’s useful for specific debugging cases.
1. Save the map in Tiled with the tile layer encoded as CSV, and confirm that each tile is
8×8 pixels.
2. Opentheresulting.tmxfilewithaplaintexteditor. BeingXML,insidethe<data>tagof
each layer appears the full list of the map’s tile indices, comma-separated, in the same
order the grid is traversed (row by row).
3. Copythatlistofnumbersandpasteitintoanarrayinacustomheaderfile(forexample,
map.h, inside the project’s inc folder).
4. Include that map.h from the source code, declare the tileset as a resource the usual way
(TILESETandPALETTEinthe.resfile),loaditwithVDP_loadTileSetandPAL_setPalette,
andfinallytraversethescreendrawingeachtilefromthecopiedarray,onebyone,using
the VDP’s low-level functions.
This is, in essence, the same result the TILEMAP resource achieves today in a single step, but
donebyhandandwithoutthevalidationorcompressionthatrescompapplies. Understanding
this manual path helps clarify what the <data> tag of a TMX actually contains, and what the
automatic import is doing behind the scenes.
4. A complete example workflow
A level designed in Tiled and brought into an SGDK 2.11 project follows these steps, end to
end:
1. Prepare the tileset as a PNG image, respecting the limit of 16 colors per palette.
2. Design the map in Tiled: create the grid with 8×8-pixel tiles, import the tileset, paint
the level’s layer (or layers), and save the layer in CSV format.
3. Export the file as .tmx and copy it into the project’s resources folder.
4. Declare the resource in resources.res:
TILESET tileset_level1 "tileset.png" NONE
PALETTE palette_level1 "tileset.png"
TILEMAP map_level1 "level1.tmx"
5. Inthecode,loadthetilesetandpalettewiththefunctionsalreadycoveredinchapter11
(VDP_loadTileSet, PAL_setPalette), and use the data from map_level1 to build the Map
structurewithMAP_create,ortodrawthemapdirectlyiftheleveldoesn’tneedscrolling.
6. If the level uses scrolling, scroll it with MAP_scrollTo exactly as with a map declared
without going through Tiled.
59

=== PAGE 66 ===
The important point is that, regardless of the map’s origin — drawn tile by tile in a custom
array, as in chapter 11, or visually designed in Tiled and brought in as TMX — the rest of
the loading and scrolling code doesn’t change: MAP_create and MAP_scrollTo work the same
regardless of where the map data comes from. Tiled solves exclusively the problem of de-
signing the level, not the problem of how the Mega Drive ultimately displays it on screen.
5. Tiled versus 16Tile
Chapter 13 introduces 16Tile, a tool built specifically for the SGDK workflow, with more
direct integration with the Mega Drive’s own restrictions (palettes, unique-tile limits, export
tailored to this particular hardware). Without getting into how it works just yet, it’s worth
outlining how the two compare as alternatives:
• Tiled is a generic tool, far more widely used and documented outside the Mega Drive
scene, with active support and features useful for any tile-based game (multiple layers,
objects,customproperties). Inexchange,itknowsnothingaboutthishardware’spartic-
ulars: you have to manually account for palette and unique-tile-count restrictions when
preparing the source tileset.
• 16Tile,beingbuiltspecificallyforSGDK,cantailoritsexporttothoserestrictionsmore
directly, at the cost of being a niche tool, with a community and documentation much
smaller than Tiled’s.
Neither one fully replaces the other: they’re two valid paths to solving the same problem,
and the choice depends largely on how comfortable each person is with a general-purpose
interfaceversusonebuilttomeasure. Chapter13returnstothistopicwiththedetailneeded
to decide with better judgment.

Chapter 13 — Creating Maps with
16Tile
A tool built specifically for SGDK: VDP palette and priority assigned tile by tile, rather than
uniformly across the whole background
The previous chapter showed how to design a level map in Tiled, a generic tile map editor,
and bring it into an SGDK project through the TILEMAP resource from rescomp. Before that,
we had already seen the even more basic possibility of building a background with a conven-
tional image editor —a plain pixel canvas, with no knowledge whatsoever of the console’s
hardware—andimportingtheresultasanIMAGEorMAPresource. Bothapproacheswork,and
both share the same limitation: the entire image ends up tied to a single color palette and a
single VDP priority value for the whole background, with no per-tile distinction.
Thischapterintroduces16Tile,afreeexternaltoolcreatedspecificallyforMegaDrivedevel-
opment with SGDK, distributed by its author under the username Allone-Works on itch.io.
Unlike Tiled, 16Tile is not a general-purpose map editor: it comes with built-in knowledge
of the VDP’s constraints and capabilities, and it lets you assign palette and priority indepen-
dently to each individual tile of a map, while also exporting the files SGDK needs directly.
Together with Tiled from chapter 12, it is one of the two usual alternatives for solving the
same level-design problem: one generic and well documented, the other purpose-built for
this particular hardware.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Completed chapter 11 (“Large level maps with MAP_create”), in particular the TILESET
and MAP resources, and the MAP_create() function.
• A clear understanding of the concept of a palette for a Mega Drive graphics resource
(PAL0–PAL3, 16 colors each, with the first color of any palette other than PAL0 always
transparent).
• Animageeditorcapableofworkingwithindexedpalettes—suchasAseprite,coveredin
chapter 8— to prepare the source tileset before importing it into 16Tile.
1. The Mega Drive palette: why not just any RGB value will
do
The Mega Drive palette works in 9-bit RGB: 3 bits for each of the three channels (red, green,
and blue). With 3 bits it’s possible to represent 8 distinct combinations of zeros and ones, so
each channel supports 8 possible tones, and combining all three channels (8 × 8 × 8) yields
61

=== PAGE 68 ===
a total of 512 distinct colors available. For comparison, other machines from the same era
—the 32X and the Super Nintendo— use 15-bit RGB: 5 bits per channel, 32 possible tones
per channel, and 32 × 32 × 32 = 32,768 colors in total, sixty-four times more than the Mega
Drive.
Thepracticalproblemisthataconventionalimageeditordoesn’tworkwith8tonesperchan-
nel, but with 256 (0 to 255, the standard 8 bits per channel). For a color defined in an image
editor to translate faithfully into one of the 8 actual tones the Mega Drive can reproduce, its
red, green, and blue values must fall exactly on the 8 values the hardware supports between
0 and 255; any intermediate value gets rounded to the nearest tone when displayed on real
hardwareorinanaccurateemulator,whichcansubtlyalterthecolorsofatilesetthatwasn’t
prepared with those exact values in mind.
2. A practical reference for verifying valid colors
The question that remains open is exactly which 8 values per channel, between 0 and 255,
faithfullyreproducetheMegaDrive’shardware. Morethanonereferencetablecirculatesin
the homebrew development community for this console for that purpose: some advance in
approximate steps of 36 (0, 36, 72, 108, 144, 180, 216, 255), others follow a more irregular
curve intended to approximate real measurements of the VDP’s video output (0, 52, 87, 116,
144,172,206,255),andothersuseregularstepsof32(0,32,64,96,128,160,192,224,255,
with a small adjustment to the last value). There is no publicly available official documenta-
tionfromSegaconfirmingwhichofthesetablesmostaccuratelyreflectsthehardware’sreal
behavior;it’sbesttotreatanyofthemasapracticalcommunityconvention,usefulforcheck-
ing at a glance whether a color falls within valid tones, rather than as an officially verified
fact.
For a background meant to be displayed through a generic IMAGE resource, any of these ref-
erences works reasonably well. When working specifically with 16Tile, however, it’s best
to adopt the steps-of-32 table, since that’s the one the tool itself expects and with which it
produces the most consistent results: the rest of this chapter assumes that convention.
3. Getting 16Tile
16Tile is a free tool, distributed on itch.io under the username Allone-Works, that requires
no installation: just download the compressed file, unzip it into any folder, and run the .exe
directly. It’s best to always use the most recent version available on the project’s page.
Theitch.iopageitselfconfirmsthatthetoolwasdesignedspecificallytoworkalongsideSGDK,
and it includes a sample project with the source code needed to import its resources.
The16Tileinterfacejustafteropening,withtheLayerandTilesetpanelsontherightandthe
main canvas still empty.
4. Preparing the source tileset
Before opening 16Tile you need a tileset already prepared in a conventional image editor.
Two rules matter when preparing it:
1. The image’s height must always be a multiple of 8, the base size of a Mega Drive tile.
2. It’s a good idea to reserve the first 16×16 tile as blank, using the background color as
its only color, and the second 16×16 tile for drawing the full palette in order, one pixel
per color. This ensures that, when the image is imported into 16Tile, the order of the
62

=== PAGE 69 ===
Figure 14: 16Tile interface freshly opened
palette indices is preserved exactly as defined, without the tool reordering them on its
own.
5. First steps in 16Tile: project, layer, and tileset
The first step within 16Tile is to save the project (Save, at the top), giving it any name. Then,
intheright-handpanel,theLayer sectionletsyounamethebackgroundlayeryou’reaboutto
build. Once the layer has been created, you need to assign it a tileset: in the Tileset section
of the same panel, the + button creates a new tileset, and the arrow icon lets you load the
image prepared in the previous step.
If the source tileset comes from graphics extracted with an emulator —a common source for
experimenting— it’s common for the colors to look wrong the first time they’re loaded into
16Tile: the emulator may export the RGB values on its own scale, which doesn’t necessarily
matchthesteps-of-32scale. Thefixistogobacktotheimageeditor,manuallyadjusttheRGB
valuesofeachcolorsotheyfallonthosesteps,savethecorrectedimage,deletetheprevious
tileset within 16Tile, and load the corrected version instead.
6. Painting the map: tile size, pasting, and flipping
With the tileset already loaded correctly, the right-hand panel lets you choose the tile size
to paste onto the main map: 8×8, 16×16, or 32×32 pixels, depending on the level of detail
neededforthatparticulartileset. Paintingthemapconsistsofleft-clickingatileinthetileset

downwhiledraggingthecursorletsyoupasteseveraltilesinarowinasinglemotion,without

10. The key change: replacing TILE_ATTR_FULL with the
tileset index
The most important change in this chapter happens in the call to MAP_create(). Up through
chapter11,thelastparameterofthatfunctionwasalwaysacalltoTILE_ATTR_FULL(palette,
priority, vertical_flip, horizontal_flip, index), manually specifying a single set of
attributes to be applied uniformly across the whole map:
MAP_create(&village_map, BG_B, TILE_ATTR_FULL(PAL0, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, ind));
A map exported from 16Tile, by contrast, already includes the palette, priority, and flip
information for each tile embedded directly within the map’s own PNG file, in a format
that rescomp recognizes automatically at compile time. This lets you replace the entire
TILE_ATTR_FULL(...) call with simply the tileset’s index variable (ind in this example), let-
ting the resource itself —rather than a single function call— determine each tile’s attributes
individually:
MAP_create(&village_map, BG_B, ind);
When you compile and run the result in an emulator, the map created in 16Tile appears on
screen as expected, with palette and priority already resolved tile by tile straight from the
resource itself.
11. Why use 16Tile instead of a generic image editor
For a simple map, building it directly with a generic image editor —as in previous chapters—
may even be faster. The reason to prefer 16Tile isn’t speed in a simple case, but three capa-
bilities that a generic image editor doesn’t offer, or offers only with much more difficulty:
1. Independent palette per tile. Instead of forcing a single palette for the whole back-
ground, each tile can use any of the active palettes. Since the Mega Drive can have up
to 4 palettes active simultaneously (with a combined total of 61 distinct colors visible
at once, discounting the transparent color of each palette beyond PAL0), this allows for
backgrounds far richer in color than what a single 16-color palette permits. Chapter 14
picks this technique back up in detail.
2. Independent VDP priority per tile. This allows for depth effects where the character
can pass in front of some parts of the landscape and behind others, a subject developed
in chapter 15.
65

=== PAGE 72 ===
3. Generating a collision array from the painted map itself, instead of having to define
it separately by hand, a technique revisited when covering level collision in chapter 40.

1. The problem: a background with more colors than fit in
a single palette

supports at most 16 colors (or 15 usable ones if it isn’t PAL0), a 29-color background cannot

2. Preparing two independent tilesets, each with its own
palette
The first step is to create two separate tilesets, each limited to the colors of a single palette:
one for the elements that will use PAL0 and another for the ones that will use PAL1. For this

3. Combining both tilesets into a single file, taking care
with copy order
16Tile imports a single tileset per layer, so the two tilesets prepared separately need to be

preserving their original colors.
68

=== PAGE 76 ===
The elements copied from the PAL1 tileset (the tree and the fence) take on incorrect colors

The solution is to reverse the order of the operation:
1. Paste the PAL0 palette into the PAL1 tileset itself, so that both momentarily share the
same active palette.
2. Only then copy the elements, now correctly converted, into the final tileset.
When combining tilesets intended for different palettes into a single file, it’s al-
ways best to first match the active palette of both and only then copy the graphics.
Copying the graphics before matching the palette is the most common cause of
an element changing color “for no apparent reason” when combined with another
tileset.
Doing it in this order, the color indices are preserved correctly and the elements keep their
original appearance when combined into the same file.

9. How to distribute the 4 palettes across a full game
Beyond this specific two-palette example, it’s worth thinking about how to distribute the
4 available palettes across a complete game. A common distribution — arising from prac-
tice rather than from any rule of the hardware or of SGDK — is to use PAL0 for the farthest
background, a combination of PAL0 and PAL1 for the playable foreground, PAL2 for the main

character (along with sub-weapons or other elements that can share that same palette, and
occasionally some enemy), and reserve PAL3 specifically for enemies.
Thisparticulardistributionisn’tafixedrule: it’sjustonepracticalconventionamongseveral
possible ones. How to distribute palettes in any given project is ultimately up to each devel-
oper’s judgment, depending on how many distinct elements need to be shown on screen at
once and how much it makes sense to share a single palette among them.

1. From plane priority to tile priority
InChapter7,prioritywasappliedtoanentireplane: changingpriotoTRUEinTILE_ATTR_FULL()
made all of BG_B draw in front of BG_A. That granularity is enough for certain effects, but
not for something as specific as “the character passes behind this trunk but in front of that
bush,” because the trunk and the bush live on the same plane.
Thesolutionistoassigntheprioritybittilebytile,usingexactlythesamemechanismChapter
14 used to assign palettes tile by tile: instead of setting a single TILE_ATTR_FULL() value
for the whole map inside MAP_create(), 16Tile stores, for each individual tile, whether that
particulartileshouldbedrawnwithhighpriorityornot,andexportsthatinformationtogether
with the map.

takes that as known and focuses directly on priority.

6. The priority parameter in SPR_addSprite()
The only code change needed for the character to respect tile priority happens in the call to
SPR_addSprite(),initsTILE_ATTR(palette, priority, vflip, hflip)argument. Thesecond
parameter,thesprite’sownpriority,determineswhetherthatspritebehavesintheusualway
(low priority, FALSE) or takes precedence even over background tiles marked as high priority
(high priority, TRUE).
SPR_addSprite(&mickeySprite, x, y,
TILE_ATTR(PAL2, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE));
81

=== PAGE 88 ===
Leaving the sprite’s priority at FALSE, the character passes behind any background tile that
does have high priority, which is the effect sought in this example: Mickey ends up hidden
behind the trunk marked in 16Tile.
7. What happens if the sprite also has high priority
To see the other side of this relationship, it’s enough to also change the sprite’s priority to
TRUE:
SPR_addSprite(&mickeySprite, x, y,
TILE_ATTR(PAL2, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE));
With both — the trunk tile and the character sprite — set to high priority, Mickey once again
appears in front of the entire background, including the tiles that previously covered him.
The general rule, then, is as follows:
A sprite only ends up hidden behind a background tile when the sprite has low
priority and, in addition, that particular background tile has high priority. If the
sprite has high priority, it is shown in front of any background tile regardless of
that tile’s priority.
Settingthesprite’sprioritybacktoFALSErestorestheintendedbehavior: Mickeyonceagain
passes behind the trunk marked as high priority.
8. Possible improvements: a second background layer
Thepriorityeffectisalreadyconvincingonitsown,butitcanbeintensifiedbyaddingasecond
background layer behind the foreground map already built: using BG_A for the map with
tile priority (the front layer) and BG_B for a more distant background with simple parallax
scrolling, using the technique already covered in Chapter 9. No tile scrolling is needed to
achieve this improvement — that technique is revisited in Chapter 17 — and combining both
resources (tile priority plus an additional parallax layer) is exactly what produces the multi-
layered sense of depth in the original World of Illusion scene.
If 16Tile or a similar tool is ever unavailable, the same per-tile priority can be assigned by
handinthecode,withoutrelyingonanexternalscript;thatalternativeiscoveredinChapter
16.

Chapter 16 — Manually Assigning
Tile Priority Without a Script
This chapter presents a manual method for assigning tile priority to a background, as an
alternative to the automated Lua script workflow that is picked up later, in Chapter 19. That
automated method works well, but it has a cost: on a large map, with many tiles marked as
priority, processing can take several minutes. The technique in this chapter aims at exactly
the same result —high- and low-priority tiles coexisting on the same background— but done
by hand, tile by tile, with more direct control over each step.
This is a brief addendum, not a new topic: it assumes familiarity with the row-based palette
structure already used to encode tile priority, so it’s worth having Chapters 14 and 15 fresh
in mind before continuing.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• ReadChapters14and15,onmultiplepaletteswithinasinglebackgroundandondepth
via tile priority, in order to understand what problem tile priority solves in terms of the
MegaDrivehardware, andwhattherow-basedpalettestructureis—normalrows, filler
rows, and priority rows— that this chapter completes by hand instead of with a script.
• Basic familiarity with Aseprite: layers, selection, copy and paste, and the difference
between RGB and Indexed color mode.
• SGDK installed; if you’re going to update it to version 2.11 following the last section of
thischapter,ithelpstohavetheproject’scodeeditoronhand,foritssearch-and-replace
features.
1. Analyzing the palette layout of a real-world example
A good exercise before applying the technique is to analyze how a commercial game dis-
tributes its colors across palettes. The first level of Alien 3 serves as a good example of tile
priority: there’s a single scrolling background and, on top of it, within the same foreground
layer, some columns let the character pass in front of them and others behind, which gives
the scene a sense of depth.
ThefirstlevelofAlien3: differentcolumnsintheforegroundusetileprioritysothecharacter
appears in front of or behind them.

there’s quite a bit of color duplication between palettes, with black and several shades of

A close-up of the level’s palette: black and several shades of gray repeat across more than

Goingdeeper: wheredoesthatmaximumof61comefrom,iffour16-colorpalettes
add up to 64? The color at index 0 of each palette is always the transparent color
for tiles using that palette, and of the four times that index 0 appears (one per
palette), only one actually ends up shown on screen, as the general background
color. The other three are, in practice, palette space that can no longer be used to
draw anything visible. Four 16-color palettes minus those three redundant entries
give exactly 61 colors available for simultaneous use. Going beyond that barrier of
61 simultaneous colors is possible with more advanced palette-management tech-
niques, which remain an interesting topic to explore further on your own.

Chapter 17 — Tile Scrolling
The Mega Drive has only two scrollable background planes, BG_A and BG_B. In principle, that
limits a game to just two independent parallax “layers” on screen at once. Tile scrolling
(tile scrolling) is the technique that lets you stretch that limit quite a bit further: instead of
shifting an entire plane as a single block — as was done in chapter 9 with HSCROLL_PLANE —
each 8-pixel-tall row of that same plane is shifted independently, with its own speed and its
own direction. Used well, the effect gives the impression that the console is handling four or
five parallax layers at once, even though the hardware still only has two.
Chapter 2 already introduced, at a conceptual level, that the VDP supports three levels of
granularity for horizontal scrolling — per plane, per tile, and per line — and two for vertical
scrolling — per plane and per column. Chapter 9 put code to the first of those variants, the
simplest one. This chapter picks up that foundation and extends it toward the intermediate
granularity: horizontal scrolling per tile. Along the way, it introduces two C tools that will
accompanythereaderfortherestofthemanual: arrays,mentionedinpassingbackinchapter
6 but not explained in detail until now, and for loops, which appear for the first time in this
manual with a dedicated explanation.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Completed chapter 9, “Scrolling and Parallax Scrolling,” since this chapter builds on
thesametypeofproject(abackgroundplanedrawnwithVDP_drawImageEx)anddirectly
reusesVDP_setScrollingMode,thethree-sectionorganizationof main(),andthepattern
of accumulating a displacement in fix16/fix32 and converting it to an integer before
passing it to the VDP.
• The three scrolling granularities introduced conceptually in chapter 2 (per plane, per
tile/column, and per line).
• The S16, U8, and FIX16 types from chapter 6.
• Basic notions of C: variable declaration, the structure of a while loop, and the use of
square brackets to index a position within a collection of values (explained in detail in
section 4 of this chapter).
1. What tile scrolling is and what it’s for
To see the effect clearly, it helps to have a test background where each 8-pixel-tall row is
numbered or easily distinguishable from the next, so you can immediately tell which row is
moving at any given moment.
The test background used in this chapter: each row of tiles is numbered, so you can tell at a
glance which one is scrolling at any moment and in which direction.
95

=== PAGE 102 ===
Figure 44: Test background with numbered tile rows
Thecoreideaissimpletostate,thoughithasmoremovingpartsthanplanescrolling: instead
of a single displacement variable for the whole plane, you need one displacement value per
visiblerowonthescreen. Withthestandardverticalresolutionof224pixels(seechapter10)
and8-pixel-talltiles,thatcomesoutto224÷8=28rows. Therestofthischapterdealswith
declaring those 28 values, updating them frame by frame, and doing so without repeating
code 28 times.
2. Turning on tile scrolling mode
ThefirststepistotellSGDKthat,fortheplaneyou’regoingtouse,horizontalscrollingshould
be handled row by row instead of moving as a single block. This is configured with the same
function already used in chapter 9, VDP_setScrollingMode(), but with a different value for
the horizontal mode:
VDP_setScrollingMode(HSCROLL_TILE, VSCROLL_PLANE);
Asarecapfromchapter2,thehorizontalscrollingoptionsareHSCROLL_PLANE(thewholeplane
as a single block, the variant from chapter 9), HSCROLL_TILE (each 8-pixel row independently,
theonecoveredhere),andHSCROLL_LINE(each1-pixellineindependently,thefinestgranular-
ity, revisited at the end of this chapter). For the vertical axis, the options are VSCROLL_PLANE
andVSCROLL_COLUMN—thelatterreplacingtheoldVSCROLL_2TILE,asalreadynotedinchapter
9. This chapter uses HSCROLL_TILE for the horizontal axis and VSCROLL_PLANE for the vertical
one, since only the horizontal displacement of each row is being worked with.
Combining horizontal tile scroll with vertical tile scroll: unconfirmed.
There’snopracticalverification,withinthescopeofthischapter,ofwhetherit’spos-
sibletocombineHSCROLL_TILEwithanindependentcolumnscroll(VSCROLL_COLUMN)
on the same plane at the same time. There’s reason to suspect it isn’t — the VDP
96

=== PAGE 103 ===
mightnotofferthatparticularcombination—butthat’sareasonablesuspicion,not
a confirmed fact checked against SGDK’s official documentation. Before designing
an effect that depends on that combination, it’s worth testing it first in a small
project and checking the result on screen.
3. Updating the scroll every frame: VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile
Turning on tile scrolling mode only tells SGDK what type of scrolling is going to be used;
you still need the function that actually moves each row, which has to be called inside the
main loop (while), since the displacement needs to be updated every frame. That function is
VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile(), and it takes five parameters:
void VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile(VDPPlane plane, s16 tileY, s16 *values, s16 num,
↪ u16 useDMA);
• plane: the background layer the tile scroll is applied to, BG_A or BG_B.
• tileY: the tile row, counted from the top, at which the effect starts being applied. With
0, the effect is applied starting from the first visible row, which is useful when there are
elements — clouds, for example — that need to move starting from the very top of the
screen.
• values: the array that holds the displacement value for each row, discussed in the next
section.
• num: the number of tile rows that need to be updated. With the standard vertical resolu-
tion of 224 pixels and tiles 8 pixels tall, that number is 28.
• useDMA (or the equivalent name for the transfer method): SGDK recommends using
DMA_QUEUE for this parameter, since several rows need to be updated every frame, and
queuing the transfer via DMA avoids blocking the CPU while the data is copied.
4. Arrays: declaring the position array
In chapter 9, a single variable was enough to store how much a plane had shifted along the
horizontal axis. That’s not enough here: since each of the 28 rows can move independently,
you need to store one displacement value per row, and for that you need an array instead of
a single variable.
An array is, essentially, a collection of variables of the same type, all grouped under a single
name and accessed via a numeric index. It’s declared similarly to an ordinary variable, but
with square brackets added containing the number of elements it will hold:
S16 tile_scroll_array[28];
This reserves space for 28 values of type S16 (a signed 16-bit integer, which is more than
enough for pixel displacements, whether positive or negative), all accessible through the
same name, tile_scroll_array. To access a specific element of the array, you use the name
followed by the index in square brackets, always starting from 0: tile_scroll_array[0] is
the first element, tile_scroll_array[27] is the last of the 28.
Indexes start at 0. Index 0 of an array corresponds to the first element, not the
second. Inthischapter,thatmeanstile_scroll_array[0]isthefirstvisiblerowon
screen, not the second; this is a common off-by-one mistake when you’re starting
out with arrays.
With all values at zero, which is the initial state before any movement code is written, no
row moves yet. To check that the array and VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile() are properly
97

=== PAGE 104 ===
connected, it’s enough to manually assign a value to a specific index: positive to move that
row to the right, negative to move it to the left. For example, tile_scroll_array[0] = 10;
shifts the first row 10 pixels to the right, while tile_scroll_array[1] = -5; shifts the next
row 5 pixels to the left. Once compiled, each row ends up shifted according to the sign and
magnitude of the value you assigned it.
5. Dynamic scrolling with += and -=
Assigning a fixed value, as in the previous section, produces a static, one-time displacement.
Toachievecontinuousmovement, eachrowneedstochangeitsdisplacementvalueframeby
frame, inside the while loop. The simplest way is to take the current value of an array index
and add or subtract a fixed amount on each pass, using the += and -= operators:
while(1)
{
tile_scroll_array[0] += 1; // row 0 advances 1 pixel per frame to the right
tile_scroll_array[20] -= 2; // row 20 advances 2 pixels per frame to the left
VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile(BG_B, 0, tile_scroll_array, 28, DMA_QUEUE);
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
Eachrowcanthushaveitsownoperatoranditsownspeed,movingcompletelyindependently
of the rest.
6. Fractional displacement with FIX16
One pixel per frame is a good pace for many elements, but for backgrounds that need
to move much more slowly — distant clouds, for example — it’s useful to be able
to add an amount smaller than a full pixel, such as 0.5 or 0.1. The problem is that
VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile()onlyacceptsintegervaluesthroughitsS16array,sothere’s
no direct way to add a fraction of a pixel to tile_scroll_array.
The solution is the same one already used in chapter 9 to solve the same problem for plane
scrolling, nowapplied rowbyrow: asecondarray, withthe samenumberof elements, butof
type FIX16 instead of S16. FIX16 is the 16-bit variant of the fixed-point types already covered
in chapter 6 (FIX32 was used in chapter 9 for the fractional displacement of an entire plane);
here the lighter version is enough, because background scrolling doesn’t need that much
precision. To distinguish it from the original array, it helps to add a suffix to the name:
FIX16 tile_scroll_array_as_f16[28];
// inside the while loop:
tile_scroll_array_as_f16[1] += FIX16(0.5); // accumulates half a pixel per frame
Addingavaluetothisarraydoesn’tmoveanythingbyitself,becauseVDP_setHorizontalScrollTile()
still works with the original integer array. What’s still needed is to convert the accumulated
FIX16 value into an integer and copy that result into the same position of the S16 array,
before it’s used in the scroll function. For that conversion, SGDK 2.11 uses F16_toInt() —
the FIX16 equivalent of the F32_toInt() function already used in chapter 9 for FIX32:
tile_scroll_array_as_f16[1] += FIX16(0.5);
tile_scroll_array[1] = F16_toInt(tile_scroll_array_as_f16[1]);
98

=== PAGE 105 ===
7. For loops to avoid repeating code
So far, every row you want to animate with fractional speed needs its own two lines of code:
one to add the speed to the FIX16 array, and another to convert that value to an integer and
copyitintotheS16array. Repeatingthatsamepairoflines28times—onceperrow—would
be a sure source of copy-paste errors and pretty messy code. This is the point to introduce,
with a dedicated explanation for the first time in this manual, the for loop.
Thesyntaxofaforloophasthreeparts,separatedbysemicolons,insidetheparenthesesthat
follow the word for:
for (U8 i = 0; i < 28; i++)
{
// loop body: runs once for each value of i
}
• The first part, U8 i = 0, declares a control variable and gives it an initial value. U8 is
used because that type goes up to 255 and the array only has 28 elements; the name i
is a very widespread convention in C, though it could be called anything else.
• Thesecondpart,i < 28,istheconditionevaluatedbeforeeachpass: aslongasit’strue,
the loop keeps repeating. With this condition, the loop runs through indexes 0 to 27,
which are exactly the 28 valid elements of the array.
• The third part, i++, is the instruction executed at the end of each pass: it adds one to i,
so that the condition will eventually stop being true and the loop will end.
The control variable only exists inside the loop. Avariabledeclaredinsidethe
parenthesesofafor,likeiintheexample,onlyexistswithinthebracesthatdelimit
that loop’s body. Outside of that, the compiler doesn’t recognize it. That’s why it’s
safe to reuse the same name, i, in several different for loops within the same file:
each one has its own copy, isolated from the others.
This chapter uses two for loops for different purposes.
The first is used inside main(), and therefore runs only once, when the program starts:
instead of writing 28 zeros by hand to initialize tile_scroll_array, and another 28 for
tile_scroll_array_as_f16, a single loop runs the index from 0 to 27 and assigns zero to
both arrays on each pass:
S16 tile_scroll_array[28];
FIX16 tile_scroll_array_as_f16[28];
int main()
{
// ... palette loading and background drawing, as in chapter 9 ...
for (U8 i = 0; i < 28; i++)
{
tile_scroll_array[i] = 0;
tile_scroll_array_as_f16[i] = FIX16(0);
}
VDP_setScrollingMode(HSCROLL_TILE, VSCROLL_PLANE);
while(1)
{
// ...
}
99

=== PAGE 106 ===
return (0);
}
It’s best to declare the arrays first, with empty braces (that is, without initializing their ele-
mentsyet),andwritetheforloopafterward: iftheloopappearedbeforethearraysexist,the
compiler flags an error.
The second for loop appears inside the while, and therefore runs every frame of the game.
This one isn’t for zeroing everything out — the previous loop already did that, just once —
but rather to replace the two lines that previously had to be repeated by hand for each row:
inside the loop’s body, the corresponding speed is added to the FIX16 array and the result is
converted to an integer with F16_toInt(), using the loop’s index i instead of a fixed number,
so that a single instance of those two lines is enough to update all 28 rows.
8. A third array for speeds, and named variables
Theloopfromtheprevioussectionneedsathirdarray: onethatstoresthescrollspeedofeach
row, in FIX16. This array can’t be initialized with a for loop like the previous two, because
itsvalues aren’t all thesame: some rows mightrepresent clouds, others mountains, others a
forest,andeachmovesatadifferentpace. Ithelpstocallitscroll_speed_array_as_f16,and
manually assign the speed value for each row:
FIX16 scroll_speed_array_as_f16[28] = {
FIX16(0.1), FIX16(0.1), FIX16(0.1), // rows 0-2: distant clouds
FIX16(0.5), FIX16(0.5), // rows 3-4: mountains
// ... the rest of the rows, each with its own speed
};
// inside the while loop, replacing the two repeated lines:
for (U8 i = 0; i < 28; i++)
{
tile_scroll_array_as_f16[i] += scroll_speed_array_as_f16[i];
tile_scroll_array[i] = F16_toInt(tile_scroll_array_as_f16[i]);
}
VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile(BG_B, 0, tile_scroll_array, 28, DMA_QUEUE);
Grouping repeated speeds under a named variable. When several consecu-
tive rows should always move at the same speed — for example, several rows that
together make up a layer of clouds — instead of writing the same numeric value
at each of those positions, it’s better to declare a named FIX16 variable, such as
cloud_speed, assign it the value once, and use it at every relevant position in the
array:
FIX16 cloud_speed = FIX16(0.1);
FIX16 scroll_speed_array_as_f16[28] = {
cloud_speed, cloud_speed, cloud_speed,
FIX16(0.5), FIX16(0.5),
// ...
};
That way, if the cloud speed needs adjusting later on, it’s enough to change a sin-
gle value in a single place, instead of hunting down and fixing that same figure
100

=== PAGE 107 ===
repeated across three, four, or five different positions in the array. If those same
rows needed to represent clouds moving in the opposite direction from the rest of
the background, it’s enough to give that variable a negative value, with no need to
create a new variable.
9. Beyond this chapter
With the three arrays and the two for loops in place, the final code ends up considerably
shorter than it would have been writing each row by hand, even though fractional displace-
ment and per-row speed management are, at bottom, repetitive tasks.
Combiningthistechniquewithtoolsalreadycoveredinearlierchapters—usingbothplanes,
BG_A and BG_B, each with its own tile scroll; adjusting tile priority between both planes, as
in chapter 16; and adding background sprites above or below certain rows — the number
of parallax layers you can simulate in practice grows well beyond the console’s two physical
layers.
Thehorizontaltilescrollingcoveredinthischapterhasanevenfinerequivalent,linescrolling
(HSCROLL_LINE,mentionedinsection2),which,insteadofmoving8-pixelrows,movesindivid-
ual 1-pixel lines. The code approach is equivalent to this chapter’s — an array of values, a
per-frameupdatefunction,thesameforloops—justwithmanymorepositionstoiterateover
(192linesinsteadof28rows,atthestandardresolution). Asanexercisetopracticethatfiner
variant, you can try recreating a Thunder Force IV-style parallax scene using HSCROLL_LINE
instead of HSCROLL_TILE.

Chapter 18 — Background Tile
Animation
Up to this point in the manual, VRAM has been treated as something that gets filled once,
when loading a level, and then stays fixed for the rest of the game’s execution. This chapter
breaks with that idea: it shows how to replace, at any moment and while the game keeps
running, one or several specific tiles within VRAM that has already been loaded. That capa-
bilityisthefoundationof backgroundtileanimation, the techniqueusedbygameslike Sonic
theHedgehogtogivecertainsceneryelements, suchastorches, water,orflowers, theirown
animation cycle independent of the rest of the background, without needing to touch sprites
or reload anything.
TheexampleusedthroughoutthechapteristheyellowflowersinthebackgroundofGreenHill
Zone, the first level of Sonic the Hedgehog, which spin continuously in place. The chapter
starts from a demo with that level’s background and foreground already loaded and with
parallaxscrollingbetweenthetwolayers,andbuildsthecompleteanimationofthoseflowers
step by step.
Prerequisites
• Having read chapter 7 (how to display backgrounds) and chapter 9 (scrolling and paral-

working.
• Having read chapter 2 (the VDP in depth), to have a clear picture of how VRAM is or-
ganized, and chapter 16 (multiple palettes and tile priority), to be familiar with the way
SGDK organizes a background’s tiles in VRAM when loading a level.
• Basic knowledge of C: arrays, conditional structures (if / else if), and increment oper-

• BasichandlingofAseprite,inparticularconvertingalayerintoatileset,alreadyusedin

2. Understanding the VRAM map with the ind variable
Before you can change specific tiles in VRAM, you need to understand how it’s organized.
When loading a level’s graphics, SGDK already uses a variable, usually called ind, to know
at which VRAM address it should write the background tiles, and then the foreground
tiles, without either one overlapping the other. That variable starts out with the value of
TILE_USER_INDEX, an SGDK constant marking the first VRAM position free for the program
to use (see chapter 2 for details on how VRAM is organized overall).
BlastEm’s VRAM debugger lets you see, tile by tile, what’s loaded at each position. In this
chapter’s demo, right before where the background tiles start, there are 16 tiles that at first
glance look a bit confusing: they’re actually the first 16 colors of the palette, represented as
solid-color blocks, rather than actual graphical tiles.
BlastEm’sVRAMdebugger: beforethebackgroundandforegroundtiles,16solid-colorblocks
103

=== PAGE 110 ===
Figure 46: BlastEm’s VRAM debugger, with 16 solid-color blocks before the background and
foreground tiles
appear, corresponding to the first 16 colors of the palette.
3. Experimenting with the base index
Those16tilesdon’thavetobekeptastheyare: inpractice,it’susuallysafetooverwritethem
with the background’s own tiles, gaining 16 tiles of VRAM that would otherwise go unused.
In general, it’s best not to touch SGDK’s default settings without a good reason,
since they’re usually set up that way for a reason. In this particular case, however,
overwriting those 16 tiles is safe.
To verify this, 16 is subtracted from the initial value of ind, so that the background starts
being written 16 positions earlier than usual, right where those color blocks used to be:
u16 ind = TILE_USER_INDEX - 16;
After compiling, those 16 solid-color tiles disappear from the VRAM debugger: the back-
ground now starts exactly where those blocks used to be, without leaving any gap.
It’salsoworthtryingtheoppositecase,asasanitycheck: insteadofsubtracting16,add100
to the initial value (u16 ind = TILE_USER_INDEX + 100;). The result is a gap of 100 unused
tiles between the color blocks and the start of the background tiles, immediately visible in
the VRAM debugger.
Finally, it’s worth understanding what happens if the adjustment is too aggressive: subtract-
ing 17 instead of 16. In that case, the background starts being written one position ear-
lier than it should, overwriting VRAM data that doesn’t belong to it, related to scrolling and
palettes, and the result on screen ends up visibly broken. In this particular case, then, 16 is
the exact margin available: that figure shouldn’t be exceeded.

With this single call, the flower immediately switches to its second position, with its tips

For the animation to alternate on its own, without manual intervention, a timer and a condi-

With the timer running inside the main loop, the if / else if pair checks its value: upon
reaching 60 frames (one second, at 60 frames per second), the flower switches to its second
position; upon reaching 120, it goes back to the first and the timer resets to zero. The timer
increment happens at the end of each pass through the loop, after these checks. The result
is the flowers alternating position once per second, continuously, exactly as in the original
level.
10. The risk of ALL compression with duplicate tiles
There’s an easy mistake to make when importing the animation images into resources.res:
usingtheALLcompressionoption, thesameonethatisindeedappropriateforordinaryback-
ground images, instead of NONE. With ALL, SGDK detects that the flower’s second image has
several tiles that are duplicates of each other (the four corners of the 4x4 tile square are left
completelyblank,andarethereforeidenticaltooneanother)andonlyloadsonecopyofeach
unique tile into VRAM, to save space.
The problem is that VDP_loadTileData expects to write exactly 16 distinct tiles, one for each
110

=== PAGE 117 ===
position in the 4x4 block; if SGDK only loaded, say, 12 unique tiles because it dropped the
4 blank duplicates, the function ends up reading tile data that doesn’t correspond to what it
should, and the result on screen ends up visibly broken: the flower appears deformed, with
parts incorrectly repeated.
Figure 52: The result of importing the animation image with ALL compression: the flower
ends up deformed
ThevisualresultofimportingtheanimationimagewithALLcompression: theflowerappears
deformed, with parts incorrectly repeated.
The solution is to use NONE as the compression option for any image that will be used with
VDP_loadTileData in this kind of animation, so that SGDK loads absolutely every tile of the
image into VRAM, including duplicates, and the number of tiles loaded always matches the
numberthefunctionexpects. Thisisalsothereasonwhy,earlierinthischapter,boththetest
tile and the two flower images were imported with NONE instead of ALL.
11. Other uses of this technique and its limits
Timer-drivenanimation,liketheoneinthischapter,isjustoneofthepossibleusesofchanging
VRAMinrealtime. Anothercommonusecaseisverylargelevels,withmoregraphicaldetail
variety than fits at once in the available VRAM: in that scenario, instead of triggering the
change with a timer, it’s best to trigger it based on the player’s position within the level,
discarding tiles that are no longer on screen and loading new tiles in their place, similar
to how chapter 17 shifted map tiles based on scrolling. This is possible with this chapter’s
method,butitrequirescarefulplanningofthetilesetitselfforittoworkwell;theseareVRAM
streaming techniques seen in some Mega Drive homebrew projects for handling levels with
more graphical variety than fits in VRAM at once.
There is one case, however, where this chapter’s technique falls short: individual destruc-
tible blocks. When those blocks are placed on the background layer (a common decision
111

=== PAGE 118 ===
when there are too many of them to handle as sprites, since the Mega Drive can’t display a
largenumberofspritesonscreenwithoutnoticeableflicker),changingaVRAMtilewiththis
chapter’s method affects every instance of that tile at once. That means destroying a single
blockwould,bymistake,destroyeveryidenticalblockinthelevel. Thiscaseneedsadifferent
solution, based on additional VRAM management techniques handled per block rather than
per shared tile; it’s a problem that has already been solved in various Mega Drive homebrew
projects, though it falls outside the scope of this chapter.

Chapter 19 — Complex Level
Maps with Aseprite
Chapters 13 through 16 showed how to build the map for a complete Mega Drive level with
16Tile: a free tool, designed specifically for this hardware, that lets you distribute a back-
ground’s tiles across several palettes and assign them priority relative to sprites. This chap-
terpicksupthosesametwoproblems—multiplepalettesandtilepriority—andaddsanew
one, generating a level collision array, but solves them with a different tool: Aseprite, the
graphics editor already used in Chapter 8 to create this manual’s first graphics.
Thechangeoftoolisnotawhim. 16Tilewasbornasaprojectmeanttocoveraspecificneed
and, although it was made available free of charge to the whole community, it retains the
typical limitations of a purpose-built program without much development time behind it: it
lacks copy and paste, and also undo, inside the map editor. Building a large level tile by tile,
without being able to repeat a piece already made or revert a mistake, turns what should be
mainly creative work into something tedious, and it also discourages experimenting with the
level design, because any change of mind means manually redoing everything already built.
Aseprite,beingacommercialpixelarteditorwithyearsofcontinuousdevelopment,hasnone
of those shortcomings: it offers copy, paste, and undo out of the box, and, since version
1.3 — released in early 2024 — also a native tileset tool, originally designed for indie PC
games. What Aseprite doesn’t include out of the box are Mega Drive-specific features: mul-
tiple palettes within a single tileset, tile priority, and level collision arrays. That gap can be
filled with scripts written in Lua, the scripting language built into Aseprite. Sections 6 and
7 of this chapter describe how a script of this kind would behave, in practice, for assigning
priority and another for generating the collision array, understood as a possible avenue of
automation within the editor and not as a piece of software with a single guaranteed source.
This chapter covers, in order, how to set up an Aseprite canvas as a tileset, how to paint it
while taking advantage of the Mega Drive’s four palettes within a single map, and how to
solve — with the help of Lua scripts — assigning priority to certain tiles and generating the
level’s collision array. By the end, readers will be able to judge, based on the complexity of
their own project, whether it’s worth sticking with 16Tile or switching to this Aseprite-based
workflow.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Aseprite 1.3 or a later version installed: the native tileset tool used in this chapter does
not exist in versions 1.2 or earlier.
• HavingreadChapters13through16,onbuildinglevelmapsandusingmultiplepalettes
and tile priority with 16Tile: this chapter assumes those same concepts are already
113

=== PAGE 120 ===
known, and only changes the tool used to apply them.
• Basic familiarity with Aseprite, covered in Chapter 8: layers, the color palette, and the
difference between indexed color mode and RGB mode.
• Some familiarity with SGDK’s resource compiler (rescomp), in order to interpret the
error message that appears in the section on palette mixing.
You don’t need to know how to program in Lua: the scripts mentioned in this chapter are
described as finished tools, without any need to write them or understand them line by line.
1. From 16Tile to Aseprite: what changes and what doesn’t
The underlying problem with 16Tile isn’t that the final result is worse: ultimately, both tools
producethesamekindoffile,anindexedimagethatSGDKconvertsintoatileset,sotheresult
is equivalent. The problem lies in the process of getting to that result. In a map built tile by
tile, with no way to copy or undo, repeating the same structure — for example, a building
that appears several times throughout a level — requires rebuilding it from scratch every
time, and a misplaced tile that isn’t caught in time can mean losing a good part of an entire
session’s work.
Figure 53: A level map in 16Tile, built tile by tile with no way to copy or undo
A level map assembled in 16Tile: each building was built tile by tile, with no way to copy or
move it as a block.
Two factors explain why it makes sense to solve this same problem with Aseprite. The first
is the release of version 1.3, which introduced a tileset tool designed to separate a map’s
logic (which tile goes in which cell) from a tileset’s logic (what each unique tile looks like),
something that until then only specialized tools like 16Tile or Tiled offered. The second is
the existence of Lua scripts capable of handling, within Aseprite, the two functions it lacks
for working with the Mega Drive: assigning priority to a tile and generating a level collision
array from a finished map.
114

=== PAGE 121 ===
2. Preparing the canvas and converting it into a tileset
The first step is to create a new file in Aseprite in RGB color mode, with a transparent back-
ground. Both the width and the height must be multiples of 16 pixels, not just of 8.
Attention: this requirement only makes sense once you reach section 7 of this
chapter: thecollisionarrayisgeneratedbycopyingthissamemapintoareference
tileset that works in 16×16 pixel blocks. If the canvas dimensions aren’t exact
multiples of 16, that copy ends up misaligned with the collision grid, and the final
result won’t match the actual map.
Withthecanvascreated, it’sagoodideatorenamethedefaultlayer—forexample, tofore-
ground — to distinguish it later from the other layers that will be added. The next step is
to convert that ordinary layer into a tileset layer: right-click on the layer, Convert to, and
Tileset.
That action opens a dialog box with several options. The grid’s width and height should both
be set to 8 pixels, since that’s the size of a Mega Drive tile. The base index decides whether
the first tile in the tileset is counted as number 0 or number 1; it isn’t entirely clear which of
thetwoconventionsAsepriteusesinternallyinthisdialog,soit’sbesttoleaveitatitsdefault
value,verifytheactualbehaviorinpracticebeforerelyingonit,andinanycasenotbaseany
step of the subsequent workflow on this number. Lastly, the two Allowed Flips checkboxes —
horizontal and vertical mirroring — tell Aseprite that, when counting unique tiles, it should
treat two tiles that only differ by being mirrored as the same tile.
Tip: this mirroring setting only affects Aseprite’s internal count of unique tiles
while drawing. When importing the final tileset into SGDK, rescomp does its own
independent mirroring analysis, without taking this checkbox into account.
3. Organizing the palette in index mode: four rows for the
four palettes
The Mega Drive has four hardware palettes — PAL0 through PAL3 — of 16 colors each.
Aseprite’s palette panel, on the other hand, can hold many more than 16 colors at once, so
it’sworthtakingadvantageofthatandorganizingall64possiblecolors(4rowsof16)within
a single panel: from then on, each row represents one of the four hardware palettes.
While defining this organization, it helps to assign each row a base color quite different from
the others — for example, red for the first row, green for the second, blue for the third, and
yellow for the fourth — without worrying yet about the actual colors that will be used in the
final artwork. This trick is just a temporary visual aid: it lets you spot at a glance where one
palette ends and the next begins, and it gets replaced later by the final colors.
The next step is to change the file’s color mode from RGB to Indexed (Sprite, Color Mode,
Indexed). The difference isn’t merely cosmetic: in RGB mode, each pixel stores a pure color
value, with no reference to which palette row it came from; in indexed mode, on the other
hand, each pixel stores the number of the palette slot it uses. That distinction is what makes
itpossible, lateron, toreliablydetectwhetheratilemixescolorsfromtwodifferentpalettes,
even when those two palettes share a visually identical color — black, for example — that
would look indistinguishable at a glance.
Finally, it’s worth creating a second file, separate from the tileset, in RGB mode, with a ref-
erence strip of the tones the Mega Drive reproduces accurately (an informal way to refer to
these tones is to call them “step-32” colors). Rather than typing the tileset’s RGB values by
hand and risking that they don’t match any real console tone, it’s better to copy the exact
colors from that reference file and paste them into the tileset’s indexed palette.
115

=== PAGE 122 ===
Tip: even if the exact colors aren’t copied from a reference file, SGDK automat-
ically adjusts any RGB value to the closest tone the console can reproduce when
importing the resource. The reference file isn’t mandatory: it’s a way to preview,
accurately, within Aseprite, what the colors will actually look like in the game, in-
stead of discovering it only after compiling.
4. Drawing the tileset: the two tile-creation modes
When painting onto a tileset layer, Aseprite offers, in a dropdown menu specific to this type
of layer, different tile-creation modes that change what happens each time you draw over a
tile that already exists on the map.
Inoneofthosemodes,everytimeatileismodified,anew,uniquetileisautomaticallycreated
within the tileset, without altering any other cell on the map that uses the original tile. This
is the recommended mode for adding new pieces to the map.
Theothermodeworkstheoppositeway: ifyoumodifyatilethat’salreadyusedinseveralcells
of the map, the change is applied to all those cells at once, because you’re actually editing
the tile’s shared definition rather than a new copy. This option is especially useful once the
map is practically finished and all that’s needed are small color tweaks to tiles that repeat
many times.

5. Using several palettes within a single tileset
Withthetilesetalreadyorganizedintofourpaletterows,thenextstepistoactuallydistribute
the map’s tiles across those four palettes, the same way it was already done with simple
backgrounds in earlier chapters, but now on a complete map built by hand in Aseprite. As
an example of how to allocate colors, consider an urban background that needs 6 colors —
including the screen’s overall background color — which leaves 10 free colors in that same
palette to reuse in the foreground.
Reusingacolorbetweenthebackgroundandtheforegroundisn’taprobleminitself—infact,
it’s what allows you to make better use of each palette’s 16 colors — as long as that reused
color doesn’t cause two different elements to visually blend together by ending up adjacent
and the same tone.
Attention: therulethattrulyadmitsnoexceptionsisadifferentone: withinasingle
8×8 pixel tile there can’t be colors coming from two different palette rows. A tile’s
palette attribute is a single value for the whole tile; if its pixels reference colors
from two different rows, the hardware will only honor one of those two palettes
when drawing it, and the tile will look wrong on the console even though it looks
correct in the editor.
This mistake is particularly easy to make, and hard to spot at a glance, when two palettes
share an identical color: for example, if both PAL0 and PAL1 include a pure black, you could
accidentallypaintapixelwithPAL1’sblackinsideatilethatshouldexclusivelyusePAL0,and
the result looks exactly the same on screen while you’re drawing it. A simple way to audit
this is to temporarily fill every color in one palette row with the same eye-catching color —
all green for PAL0, for example — and visually scan the whole map for pixels that haven’t
changed color: any pixel that keeps its original tone reveals that it actually belongs to a
different palette row.
Ifthismistakeisn’tcaughtintimeandyoutrytocompiletheprojectanyway,rescompdetects
it on its own while processing the tileset and halts compilation with a specific error message
that gives the exact pixel coordinates of the conflicting pixel within the image.
rescomp’s error message points to the exact pixel coordinates of the conflicting pixel within
the image.
Tip: that error message, cryptic as it may look at first glance, saves a lot of search
time: just open the tileset image and locate those exact coordinates to find the
misassigned pixel, instead of eyeballing the entire map.
Inatypicalsplitbetweenbackground,foreground,andsprites,palette0canbeusedforboth
the background and part of the foreground, palette 1 reserved exclusively for the rest of the
foreground, and palettes 2 and 3 assigned to different sprite groups — the player’s and the
enemies’, for example. This split highlights an idea already introduced in earlier chapters:
the Mega Drive’s four palettes are a resource shared between backgrounds and sprites, not
a resource exclusive to each one separately.
