6. Assigning tile priority with a Lua script
Chapters 15 and 16 showed what tile priority is — the bit that makes a background tile draw
infrontofspritesinsteadofbehindthem—andhowtoassignitwith16Tile. Asepritehasno
built-in equivalent concept to that priority. That function can be covered by a Lua script that
goes through the tiles marked as priority and applies a recognizable marker to them within
the image itself.
The mechanism such a script would use requires extending the palette: to the four rows of
16colorsthatalreadyrepresentthefourhardwarepalettes,youneedtoaddeightmorerows
of 16 colors each, always in that order and always present, even if the project ends up using
only one or two of the four real palettes. Of those eight new rows, the first four are filler —
their color doesn’t matter, because they won’t be used to paint anything — and the last four
arethepriorityrows,whichbyconvention(andonlyasAseprite’sdefaultcolorwhencreating
a new row) usually appear in pink.
In depth: it isn’t possible to confirm with certainty, from the code, exactly why
twelve palette rows are needed, but the observable behavior is consistent with a
reasonableexplanation: foreachtilemarkedaspriority,thescriptneedssomeway
toleavearecordofthatmarkwithinthefinalimageitself,withoutaddinganydata
outside the graphics file. If the four priority rows reserve a range of color indices
that’s never used for painting directly, the script can use that range as a recog-
nizable signal within the tileset itself. This reading is a reasonable inference from
observed behavior, not a confirmation of how the script actually works internally.
With that palette extension already in place, the workflow for marking tiles as priority, as-
sumingyouhaveaLuascriptinstalledinAseprite’sscriptsfolder(File,Scripts,OpenScripts
Folder,thenFile,Scripts,RescanScriptsFoldersoitshowsupinthelist),wouldbeasfollows:

1. Createanewlayerabovethetilesetlayer(New,NewLayer)andrenameit,forexample,
to priority.
2. Inthe tileset layer, withinthe color index panel(not the tilespanel), select the tiles that
should have high priority, copy them with Ctrl+C, and paste them with Ctrl+V onto the
new priority layer: this copies those same tiles, in the same map position, to the new
layer.
3. Saveabackupcopyofthefilein.asepriteformat—withanamelikeforeground_master,
for example — before continuing: the next step is irreversible, and without this backup
there would be no way to change which tiles are priority later on.
4. Convert the tileset layer back into an ordinary layer (right-click, Convert to Layer), be-
cause the script would work on ordinary pixels rather than on the internal structure of
a tileset layer.
5. With the priority layer selected, run the priority script from the File, Scripts menu.
Attention: onlargemaps,ascriptofthiskindcantakeseveralminutestoprocess

Once the process finishes, the final steps are: right-click on the priority layer and choose

7. Generating the collision array with a second script
Thesameway16Tileletsyouexportalevelcollisionarray,thatsameresultcanbeautomated
within Aseprite with a second Lua script, using a separate reference tileset made of 16×16
pixel tiles instead of 8×8, because this workflow’s collision array operates in 16×16 blocks.
That reference tileset is set up once and reused across all projects: in RGB color mode, it
contains one tile for each type of collision needed — for example, an S for a solid tile, a P for
a platform you can pass through from below but not from above, and additional variants for
slopes — and, in that same file’s palette, a distinct flat color for each of those tiles.
Attention: the order in which the tiles appear within the reference tileset and the
order in which the colors appear within the palette must match exactly: index 0
must be the transparent color and the transparent tile, index 1 the color and tile
for the S, index 2 the color and tile for the P, and so on. A script of this kind would
work by reading, for each 16×16 pixel block of the collision map, only the color of
its top-left pixel, and writing the index number of that color into the output array;
if the order of tiles and colors doesn’t match, the number that gets written won’t
correspond to the collision type that was actually drawn.
With the reference tileset already prepared, the procedure for generating the collision array
of a specific map would be as follows:
119

=== PAGE 126 ===
1. Open the finished map (the tileset layer with the background and foreground result),
select everything within the tiles panel, and copy it with Ctrl+A and Ctrl+C.
2. Open the collision reference tileset and adjust its canvas size (the C button, or Sprite
Size) so it matches exactly the pixel dimensions of the copied map.
3. Paste the copy (Ctrl+V) onto a new layer, as a visual guide, and paint onto a separate
collision layer the S, P, or slope tiles that correspond to each area of the level, using
that background copy as a guide to know where there’s ground, platforms, or elevation
changes.
4. Save a backup copy of the file before continuing, for the same reason as in the previous
section: the script step would be irreversible.
5. Delete the guide layer (the copy of the original map), leaving only the collision layer
visible, and change the file’s color mode to Indexed.
6. Run the collision script from the File, Scripts menu, and when prompted, provide an
output file name with the .txt extension.
The resulting text file would contain a declaration ready to paste directly into the code: a
const u8arraywithonenumberforeach16×16blockofthemap,and,attheend,aconstant
with the total length of that array, already calculated.
Tip: it’s worth checking whether there’s a trailing comma after the array’s last
number before pasting it into the code: the compiler generally tolerates it anyway,
but it’s a two-second check.
The result would be equivalent, in form and in index logic, to a collision array built by hand
with 16Tile: a linear array of unsigned 8-bit integers, with a fixed row width and one value
per collision tile. The logic for converting pixel coordinates into indices of that array, and
for interpreting each numeric value according to the collision type it represents, is the same
regardless of whether the array was built by hand or generated with a script.
8. When this workflow is worth it compared to 16Tile
Adopting this workflow has a real organizational cost: you have to set up the palette with a
specific row structure from the start, save a backup copy before every irreversible step, and
dependonLuascriptsthataren’tpartofeitherAsepriteorSGDK.Inexchange, yougetback
everything 16Tile doesn’t offer: copy and paste, undo, and generally, a more comfortable
editor for iterating on a level’s design.
Thisworkflowpaysoffmorethebiggerandmorechangeablethelevelis: aprojectwithmany
large levels, or with a design that’s still in a trial-and-error stage, benefits from being able
to copy repeated structures and undo mistakes without redoing work. For simpler projects,
there’s no need to feel obligated to add this complexity if 16Tile is enough for the size of
the level being built: it’s better to save the more elaborate techniques for when the project
actually needs them, rather than adopting them ahead of time just because they’re available.

Chapter 20 — Converting
Many-Color Images to the Mega
Drive Palette
Reducing a high-color-range illustration to the console’s four 16-color palettes through tile-
based quantization
All the previous chapters in this part of the manual started from a comfortable premise: the
sourcegraphicwasalreadydesignedwiththeMegaDriveinmind,drawnbyhandinaneditor
with an indexed color mode, with the 16-color-per-palette limit taken into account from the
very first stroke. This chapter closes out the part of the manual devoted to backgrounds,
tiles, palettes, and scrolling by tackling the reverse problem — one that’s considerably more
common than it might seem: what to do when the starting image wasn’t designed for the
console at all. A digital illustration, a render, or a screenshot from a modern game can have
thousandsofdistinctcolors, farbeyondthe61theMegaDrivecandisplayonscreenatonce.
Manuallyconvertingsuchanimage,colorbycolor,ispossiblebutextremelyslow;thischapter
presents an automated technique that reduces that work to a process of minutes, along with
its limits, which are worth knowing before relying on it for any kind of graphic.
TheexampleusedthroughoutthechapterisaSonicillustrationwithacolorrangefarbeyond
whattheconsolecanreproduce, treatedasifitweretheartworkforatitlescreenoracover.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, you should be clear on:
• Theconceptofanindexedpalette,thelimitoffour16-colorpalettes(PAL0throughPAL3),
and the idea that a tile doesn’t store color but rather an index into a palette, covered in
Chapter 2.
• Working with a graphics editor in indexed color mode — Aseprite or an equivalent —
including the use of a reference grid and an eyedropper-type tool to inspect the color
index of a specific pixel, covered in Chapter 8.
1. The problem: from an arbitrary color range to four
palettes per tile
Thealready-familiarrestrictionontheMegaDriveisthatanygraphiconscreenisbuiltfrom
8×8-pixel tiles, and each tile is assigned a single palette out of the four available. When a
graphicisdrawnfromscratchwiththeconsoleinmind,thatrestrictionisnaturallyrespected,
tile by tile, as the drawing progresses. The problem arises when the image already exists,
122

=== PAGE 129 ===
comes from another source, and has far more colors than any combination of four palettes
can represent.
Reducing that image by hand — choosing which 61 colors to keep and manually remapping
everypixel—isfeasibleforasmallillustration,butbecomesimpracticalasthesizeanddetail
of the graphic grow. The automated alternative is to use a color quantization algorithm that,
in addition to reducing the total number of colors, understands the Mega Drive’s particular
constraint: that the reduction isn’t done over the whole image as if it were a single palette,
but tile by tile, letting each 8×8 block use whichever of the four available palettes suits it
best. There are community tools, such as tile-based palette quantization generators, built
specificallyforthisproblem;theyusuallyrundirectlyinthebrowser,withnoinstallation,and
accept a plain PNG image as input. Since these are free projects maintained by hobbyists,
their exact name, address, or availability may change over time, so it’s worth searching for
whateveroptioniscurrentwhenyouneeditratherthanrelyingonafixedlink; whatmatters
here is understanding the parameters this kind of tool exposes and what each one means,
since they’re common to any implementation of the same problem.
2. Preparing the source image: canvas size, not image size
The first step, before touching any quantization tool, is to adjust the resolution of the source
image to the console’s screen size. In the graphics editor this is done through the canvas
sizeoption,nottheimagesizeorspritesizeoption: thelatterrescalesthecontent,distorting
or blurring the original drawing, whereas a canvas size change simply crops or adds space
around it without touching the existing pixels.
Thewidthissetto320pixels. Iftheaspectratioislocked,theresultingheightwouldbe240,
appropriate for a PAL project; for an NTSC project, that height should be manually adjusted
to 224. Since this is a canvas change rather than a scaling operation, the result crops a strip
off the original image (typically from the top and bottom) instead of distorting it, which is
usually preferable to losing proportions in a graphic that’s later going to be shown at actual
size.
Adjustingthecanvassizeto320pixelswide,withtheaspectratiostilllockedbeforemanually
correcting the height.
The color mode of the image at this point doesn’t matter much, because the quantization
tool used next accepts both RGB images and already-indexed ones. It’s enough to save the
cropped image as a regular PNG file.
3. Tile quantization parameters
Once the prepared image is loaded into the quantization tool, there’s a set of parameters
that define how the available color is going to be distributed. Although the exact name of
each field can vary depending on the specific implementation, the concepts behind them are
always the same and apply to any equivalent tool:
• Tile size: left at 8×8, which is the Mega Drive VDP’s native tile size. Any other value
wouldn’t make sense for this console.
• Number of palettes: 1 to 4 on the Mega Drive. When the image is going to be used
in isolation, such as a title screen with no other graphics sharing a palette with it, it’s
worthtakingadvantageofallfourfullpalettestomaximizetheamountofavailablecolor.
Iftheimageisgoingtocoexistwithothergraphics(enemysprites,itemcards,etc.) that
needtheirownpalettes,fewershouldbereserved—two,forexample—leavingtherest
for those other elements.
123

=== PAGE 130 ===
Figure 56: Adjusting the canvas size to 320 px wide
• Colors per palette: 16, the maximum the hardware supports.
• Bitsperchannel: 3,thecorrectvaluefortheMegaDrive,whichreproduces8intensity
levels per RGB channel (the same 9 total bits per color seen in Chapter 2). Other 8-bit
and16-bitsystemsusedifferentvaluesinthissametypeoftool—morebitsperchannel
onconsoleswithgreatercolordepth,feweronmorelimitedones—soit’sworthmaking
sure this is specifically configured for the Mega Drive and not for another system.
• Index-0 color behavior: determines what happens to the firstcolor of each of the four
palettes. If the graphic is a sprite or any element with transparency, it’s best to use the
transparentcoloroption(usuallyrepresentedasmagenta),makingsurethebackground

no need for transparency, it’s best to use the shared color option set to black: that way
index 0 matches across all four palettes, that black can be reused within the drawing
itself, and in practice you end up with 61 usable colors instead of 60.
• Sampled pixel fraction: controls how long the algorithm takes to produce the result.
Higher values are slower but, in theory, produce a more accurate quantization; in prac-
tice, the difference between a low value (0.1) and the maximum (1.0) is usually much
smaller than expected, so it’s best to start with a low value and raise it only if the result
isn’t convincing.
TheparametersalreadyadjustedforMegaDrive: 4palettes,16colorsperpalette,and3bits
per channel.
Besides these parameters, this kind of tool usually offers dithering options to smooth the
transition between colors when their count is reduced. It’s worth turning these on when
working with an isolated image, although the exact difference between the variants typically
offered — usually described as a “slow” mode and a “fast” mode — is best explored by trying
eachonedirectlyontheimageitself,ratherthanmemorizingafixedrule: theresultdepends

7. Manual touch-up: polishing the problem areas
Mostimagesquantizedthiswayaregoingtoneedsomedegreeofmanualtouch-up,especially
in high-contrast or fine-detail areas where the algorithm has less room to accommodate the
available color. How much time is worth investing in that polishing is up to whoever is doing
it: automatic quantization handles most of the work, but rarely one hundred percent of it.
A practical technique for deciding whether to merge or replace a color is, before making
the final call, to temporarily change it to a very bold tone quite different from the rest of
the image — an intense yellow, for example. That immediately reveals exactly where in the
image that color is used, information that’s otherwise hard to appreciate when the color in
question is very similar to another nearby one in the same palette. Once you’ve confirmed
the replacement doesn’t cause any noticeable loss, the final color is applied.

// All colors set to black before drawing, so the
// image doesn't suddenly appear with its real colors
PAL_setColors(0, palette_black, 64, CPU);
// Draw the already-quantized image, using all four palettes
VDP_drawImageEx(BG_A, &quantized_bg,
TILE_ATTR_FULL(PAL0, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TILE_USER_INDEX),
0, 0, FALSE, TRUE);
// Copy to RAM the four real palettes carried by the image
memcpy(palette, quantized_bg.palette->data, 64 * sizeof(u16));
// And apply them with a smooth fade-in
PAL_fadeIn(0, 63, palette, 100, TRUE);
while (TRUE)
{
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return 0;
}
Thepatternisalwaysthesame: setall64colorslotstoblackwithPAL_setColors(),drawthe
image with VDP_drawImageEx() (which internally already associates each tile with its corre-
sponding palette, as defined during quantization), copy the four real palettes carried by the
importedresourceintoanarrayinRAM,andapplythosepalettesgraduallywithPAL_fadeIn()
insteadofanabruptjump. Thissamefadingtechnique—settingeverythingtoblackandthen

=== PAGE 136 ===
bringing up the real palette progressively — can be reused in any other screen transition in
the game, not just in the image conversion covered in this chapter.
Oncecompiled,theROMfaithfullyreproducestheoriginalillustrationalreadyreducedtothe
MegaDrive’sfourpalettes,withasmoothfade-intransition. Theresultisremarkablerelative
to how little time it takes to get there, compared to a fully manual color reduction.

9. The limits of the technique
The example worked through in this chapter — an isolated illustration used as a title screen,
withallfourfullpalettesavailablejustforit—isthescenariowherethistechniqueperforms
best. The situation changes quite a bit when the graphic being converted is a playable-level
background that has to coexist with other elements: if only two of the four palettes can be
reserved for the background — leaving the other two for, say, enemy sprites and interface
elements—theresultoftheautomaticquantizationtendstolooknoticeablypoorerandmore
“washed out” than in the case of an image that has all four full palettes at its disposal. This
is especially noticeable in highly detailed art styles, with many color nuances and smooth
transitions — the kind of graphic you might see in an exploration-heavy platformer with a lot
ofenvironmentaldetail—wherehalftheavailablecolorcapacityisn’tenoughtopreservethe
visual richness of the original.
This automatic quantization works very well as a starting point and as a complete solution
for fixed, isolated graphics — covers, title screens, standalone illustrations — but it doesn’t
replacehand-donecolorreductionworkwhenthegraphicishighlydetailedandhastoshare
palettes with other elements in the game. In those cases, the most realistic approach is to
treat automatic quantization as a rough first draft and assume that a good part of the color
130

=== PAGE 137 ===
adjustment is going to end up being done by hand, tile by tile, with the same care you’d take
drawing a graphic designed for the console from the very start.
IntheMegaDrivehomebrewdevelopmentcommunity,thereareexperimentsfloatingaround
that take this same idea of tile-based quantization to full video sequences, frame by frame,
to achieve something resembling full-motion video (FMV) playable on the console, making
use of up to 61 colors per frame. It’s more a demonstration of the method’s possibilities
thana techniquein everydayuse: an actualvideo-playback projecton the MegaDrive would
probably also need additional hardware, such as the Mega CD add-on, to handle the data
volume and read speed that kind of content demands.
This chapter closes out the part of the manual devoted to backgrounds, tiles, palettes, and
scrolling. Thenextpartpicksbackupwithspritesandtheiranimation, buildingonthesame
vocabulary of tile, palette, and color index covered so far.

Chapter 21 — How to Display
Sprites
SGDK’s sprite engine, pixel coordinates, and automatic VRAM allocation
The previous chapters dealt entirely with background planes: how to display them, how to
scroll them, and how to draw them while respecting the hardware’s rules. Planes build the
game’s stage, but not what the player controls or what they play against. That role belongs
to sprites: the character that moves through the world, the enemies, the projectiles, any
graphical element that animates or moves independently of the background. This chapter
opens Part III by showing how to put a first sprite on screen, and along the way there turn
out to be as many similarities as differences compared to the background pipeline already
familiar to us.
Chapter 2 already introduced, at a conceptual level, the hardware behind sprites: their own
control table in VRAM (the Sprite Attribute Table, or SAT), independent of the planes’ name
tables; the 32×32-pixel size limit per hardware sprite, combining up to 4×4 tiles; and the
simultaneous limits depending on the resolution mode (80 sprites on screen and 20 per line
in H40; 64 and 16 in H32). That vocabulary is taken as known here; this chapter deals with
the code needed to put an actual sprite on screen.
Thespriteusedasanexampleinthischapteristakenasalreadyprepared,withoutrepeating
thecreationprocesscoveredinchapter8. Everythingsaidtherestillapplies: aspriteis,first
andforemost,agraphic,andassuchithastorespectthesize-multiple-of-8rule,the16-color-
per-palette limit, and the indexed PNG format. What this chapter adds is the other half of
thejob: howtodeclarethatfileasaresourceofadifferenttypethanabackground,andhow
to put it on screen through an SGDK mechanism completely separate from the one used for
planes, the sprite engine.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Completed chapter 7, “How to Display Backgrounds on the Mega Drive”: the resource
pipeline, the three sections of main(), PAL_setPalette(), and the concept of a palette
(PAL0 through PAL3) are taken as known.
• Completed, or at least reviewed, chapter 8, “Creating Graphics with Aseprite”: a sprite
is just another graphic, subject to the same size and palette rules.
• Anunderstandingofthespritehardwarepresentedinchapter2: theSAT,themaximum
size of 32×32 pixels per sprite, and the simultaneous quantity limits depending on the
resolution mode.
• AbaseSGDKproject,eitheremptyorbuiltfromoneoftheexamplesinpreviouschapters,
with a sprite PNG file already copied into the res folder.

1. The SPRITE Resource: What Sets It Apart from an IM-
AGE
LoadingaspriteintotheROMstarts,justaswithabackground,bycopyingthePNGfileinto
the res folder and declaring it in resources.res. But the directive is different: instead of
IMAGE, SPRITE is used, and its list of fields is longer.
SPRITE our_sprite "sonic.png" 6 6 FAST 0
Thefirsttwofields,thenametheCcodewilluse(our_sprite,inthisexample)andthepathto
thePNGfile,playthesameroleasinanIMAGE.Thethirdandfourthfields,ontheotherhand,
havenoequivalentthere: youhavetoexplicitlyspecifythewidthandheightofasinglesprite
frame, in tiles (6 and 6, in this case: a 48×48-pixel sprite). The reason for this difference
is picked up in detail in chapter 22, dedicated to creating animation sheets: a single sprite
file can contain several frames laid out side by side, and SGDK needs to know the size of an
individual frame in order to be able to separate them. With a static, single-frame sprite like
the one in this example, that size matches the size of the entire image.
The fifth field is, again, compression, with the same options as for an IMAGE — NONE, FAST,
and BEST — but with an additional consideration that is specific to sprites. NONE compresses
nothing;FASTprioritizesfastdecompressionatthecostoflessspacesavings;andBESToffers
thebiggestsavings, butdemandsmoreCPUworktodecompresseverytimethedataisused.
BEST corresponds, in the rescomp documentation, to the algorithm identified as APLIB; in re-
centversionsofSGDKthesamewordmayinsteadindicateanautomaticselectionofthemost
convenientalgorithmforeachresource. It’sworthconfirmingwhichofthetwobehaviorsap-
plies in the installed version before assuming that BEST always means the most aggressive,
and slowest, compression.
That distinction in decompression speed matters far more for a sprite than for a background.
Abackground,oncedrawn,normallystaysthesameinVRAMforagoodpartofthegame;the
cost of decompressing it is paid only once. An animated sprite, on the other hand, changes
frames several times per second, and each frame change can involve decompressing data
againanduploadingittoVRAM.Theeffectismeasurable: inaprojectwithseveralanimated
charactersonscreenatonce,changingtheirsprites’compressionfromFASTtoBESTcancause
a noticeable drop in frames per second, to the point of making the game perceptibly slower.
Fast compression for anything that animates often. The practical takeaway
is to prefer FAST for sprites that animate frequently, and to reserve BEST for data
that loads only once, like backgrounds. The alternative (loading every possible
animation frame into VRAM up front, so nothing needs to be decompressed during
gameplay) is also valid, but has the opposite cost: that VRAM space is no longer
availableforanythingelse,suchasmorebackgroundtiles. It’satrade-offbetween
space and speed, not a one-size-fits-all answer.
The last field on the line, left at 0 in this example, is the animation timing: how many frames
each animation frame lasts before moving on to the next one. At 0, automatic animation is
disabled,whichisexactlywhat’sexpectedforasingle-framespriteliketheoneinthischapter;
chapter 23, dedicated to animating sprites, returns to this field in detail.
2. The Three Sections of main() Again, and a Sprite That’s
a Pointer
With the resource already declared, it’s necessary, as with any resource, to include re-
sources.h in main.c so the code can refer to it by name. From there, the same three-section
133

=== PAGE 140 ===
organization used in chapter 9, on scroll and parallax scrolling, applies again: a global sec-
tion,beforeint main(),foranythingthatneedstoexistfortheentirelifetimeoftheprogram;
an initial setup section, between the opening of main() and the while(1), for anything that
runs exactly once; and the main loop, inside the while(1), for anything that repeats every
frame.
The first declaration in this chapter goes in the global section, and has a different form from
any variable used so far:
Sprite *player;
TheasteriskindicatesthatplayerisnotitselfaSprite,butapointer: avariablethat,instead
of storing a value, stores the memory address where another piece of data lives. The reason
forthisdesignbecomesclearerlookingahead: asshowninsection5,thefunctionthataddsa
spritetothescene(SPR_addSprite())doesn’tcreateanindependentcopyforthegamecode,
but instead returns a pointer to the Sprite that SGDK’s own sprite engine keeps managing
internallyframebyframe. Storingthatpointer,ratherthanavalueofitsown,iswhatletsthe
code, in later chapters, keep referring to this particular sprite in order to move it, animate
it, or query its state, without having to look it up again each time. For now, it’s enough to
follow the recipe: Sprite, asterisk, a name of your choosing (player, in this example, though
it could be called anything else), and a semicolon.
3. Initializing the Sprite Engine: SPR_init()
The sprite engine is the part of SGDK responsible for managing all active sprites at once:
which VRAM they’ve been allocated, what screen position they’re at, with what attributes,
and how to pack all that information into the format the VDP’s sprite hardware expects at
every vertical blank (VBlank). Before adding the first sprite, that engine has to be initialized,
and this is done exactly once, in the initial setup section, with SPR_init():
SPR_init();
Since SGDK 1.4 (May 2019), SPR_init() takes no parameters at all: internally it reserves
the maximum available number of sprites without needing to be told to. If older code or
documentation turns up calling it with three arguments (SPR_init(0, 0, 0), for example),
thatformstillexistsforbackwardcompatibilityunderadifferentname,SPR_initEx(),butit’s
nolongertherecommendedformfornewcode: SPR_init()withnoargumentsisthecurrent
form, and the one used throughout the rest of this manual.
There’s a more fundamental point beyond the difference in form: no other sprite function
— not PAL_setPalette() for the sprite’s palette, not SPR_addSprite(), not SPR_update() —
has any way of warning you that it’s failing because the engine isn’t ready. The symptom of
forgettingthiscallis,atbest,thatnothingappearsonscreen,withnoerrormessagepointing
to the real problem. Treat this line as non-negotiable in any project that uses sprites.
4. Assigning the Sprite’s Palette: The Same Function, a
Different Data Source
With the engine initialized, the next step is exactly the same function used for backgrounds
in chapter 7: PAL_setPalette(). The only thing that changes is where the color information
comes from.
PAL_setPalette(PAL2, our_sprite.palette->data, DMA);

andforenemies,respectively. TheVDPdoesn’tassignanyspecialmeaningtoanyofthefour

5. Adding the Sprite to the Scene: SPR_addSprite() and
Automatic VRAM Allocation
This is where a sprite’s workflow starts to diverge clearly from that of a background. To
display a background, chapter 7 needed a global variable (ind) to manually keep track of
which VRAM position belonged to each image, incremented by hand after every call to
VDP_drawImageEx(). For a sprite, that bookkeeping work isn’t necessary: the sprite engine
handles it on its own.
player = SPR_addSprite(&our_sprite, 0, 0, TILE_ATTR(PAL2, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE));
The first argument, &our_sprite, is the address of the sprite definition structure generated
from the SPRITE resource (hence the & symbol, “address of”). The next two, x and y, are the
sprite’s initial position on screen, with an important difference from VDP_drawImageEx() that
is picked up again in section 7. The fourth argument is the sprite’s attribute, built with a
different macro than the one used for backgrounds:
u16 TILE_ATTR(u16 pal, u16 prio, u16 flipV, u16 flipH);
TILE_ATTR()takesthesamefirstfourparametersasTILE_ATTR_FULL(),seeninchapter7for
drawingbackgrounds—thatis,palette,priority,verticalflip,andhorizontalflip—but,unlike
thatone,itdoesn’ttakeaVRAMindexatall. Thatabsenceisn’tanoversight: it’stheflipside
oftheautomaticresourceallocationthatSPR_addSprite()offersbydefault. Thespriteengine
decides on its own which VRAM position each sprite goes into, and it does so dynamically as
sprites are added, removed, or change animation frame; the programmer doesn’t have to
reserve or keep track of anything, unlike the manual discipline with TILE_USERINDEX that
backgroundsrequired. SGDKdoesofferafunction,SPR_setVRAMTileIndex(),tosetasprite’s
VRAMpositionbyhandincaseswherethatfine-grainedcontrolisneeded,buttheautomatic
behavior is the one used by default and is more than enough for practically any introductory
case like this one.
With this line, the sprite is added to the scene, and its pointer, returned by SPR_addSprite(),
isstoredinplayer,thevariabledeclaredinsection2. Onelaststepisstillneeded,insidethe
main loop, for the sprite to actually appear correctly on screen.

SPR_update() walks the internal list of active sprites, computes their updated state (position,

7. Compiling and Experimenting: Pixels, Not Tiles, and the
Flip Flags
With all six pieces now in place (resources.res with the SPRITE resource, the resources.h
include,theplayerpointer,SPR_init(),PAL_setPalette(),andSPR_addSprite()intheinitial
setup, and SPR_update() in the loop), saving both files and recompiling the project already
shows the sprite on screen, at position (0, 0), the top-left corner.
Agoodfirstexperimentistochangethesprite’sinitialpositionandobservetheresult. Chang-
ing x and y from (0, 0) to (10, 10) only shifts the sprite a little to the right and down. This
small a shift isn’t a coincidence: unlike the x and y coordinates of VDP_drawImageEx(), which
inchapter7weremeasuredintiles(avalueof5shiftedtheimage40pixels),thecoordinates
of SPR_addSprite() are measured directly in pixels. A value of 10 moves the sprite 10 pixels,
not 10 tiles (80 pixels); to get a shift visually comparable to that of a background plane, a
considerably larger number is needed, such as 100.
Tiles for planes, pixels for sprites. This difference in units between the two
functions isn’t a whim or an inconsistency in SGDK: it has to do with the fact that
sprites, unlike planes, move freely pixel by pixel across the whole screen (which is
why the Mega Drive’s own sprite hardware positions them in pixel units), whereas
a background plane, even though it can scroll in pixels (as seen in chapter 9), is
initially drawn tile by tile. Keep firmly in mind which of the two units applies to
each function: mixing them up produces sprites that barely move or backgrounds
that jump abruptly.
Thelasttwoparametersof TILE_ATTR(),flipVandflipH,letyouflipthespritewithoutneed-
ing another image file or any additional function. Changing flipV to TRUE flips the sprite
vertically, upsidedown; changing flipH to TRUE flipsit horizontally, facing theopposite direc-
tionfromtheoriginal. Placedsidebyside,theeffectiseasytopicture: thestandingsilhouette
exactly as it is in the PNG, that same silhouette flipped top to bottom with flipV, and that
same silhouette facing the opposite way with flipH, without any of the three variants requir-
ing a second sprite to be loaded or anything new to be drawn. It’s the usual way of handling,
for example, a character changing direction while walking.
The first parameter of TILE_ATTR(), priority, works the same way as seen in chapter 7 for
planes: by default, the Mega Drive’s drawing order goes from the background plane (BG_B)
at the back, the foreground plane (BG_A) in the middle, and sprites in front of everything.
Marking a sprite with high priority doesn’t change that overall order relative to the planes
(sprites are already drawn in front), but if the foreground plane is also marked with high
priority,asexplainedinchapter15whendiscussingdepththroughtilepriority,thatplanecan
end up being drawn in front of the sprite in the relevant areas. It’s the same tool that allows,
for example, a character to appear behind a lamppost or a tree trunk in certain columns of
the screen and in front of it in others.

1. A sprite’s canvas: the size of one frame, not the whole
sheet
Creating a sprite starts the same way as creating a background: a new canvas, in RGB mode
(for the same reason already seen in Chapter 8: avoiding color-banding issues when switch-
ing to indexed mode with a palette that’s still too large), but this time with a Transparent
background instead of white or black, since a sprite needs real transparency so it doesn’t
cover whatever is behind it in the game.

With the first frame drawn, adding a new one is as simple as pressing the corresponding

it). Whenenabled,theeditorshowstheprecedingandfollowingframesoverlaidanddimmed

Digital tracing paper (onion skinning) enabled: the current frame is drawn while seeing the

This makes it possible to keep trajectory and proportions consistent between frames without

3. Several animations on a single sheet: the problem and

sheet corresponds to one animation, and each column within that row, to a successive frame.

Here lies the most common source of confusion: the animation’s actual speed in the game
depends exclusively on the animation-timing field of the SPRITE line in resources.res (intro-
duced in Chapter 21 and detailed in Chapter 23), measured in screen frames (sixtieths of a
second), not in milliseconds.
Since both values use different units, going from one to the other requires a manual conver-
sion. IfananimationwastimedinAsepriteat60millisecondsperframe,thatvaluehastobe
convertedtoSGDK’sunitbydividingbytheapproximatedurationofonesixtiethofasecond
(16.67 ms): 60 ÷ 16.67 ≈ 3.6. The result is almost never a whole number, so it has to be
rounded up or down, with the resulting small difference between the pace previewed in the
editorandtheonethatultimatelyrunsinthegame. There’snowaytoavoidthismanualstep
withthetoolscoveredsofar;it’sbesttosimplykeepitinmindaspartoftheworkflow,rather
than assuming that the value seen in Aseprite is the one that will end up in the game.

6. Real hardware limits for sprites
With the file now ready to import, this section steps away from Aseprite to talk about some-
thing that has so far been left implicit: how big sprites can be, how many fit on screen at
once, andwhathappenswhenaprojectgoespastthoselimits. Toillustrateit, pictureafight
against a flying final boss — in the style of a Castlevania boss — that fires many fireballs at
once, while the playable character and the HUD are also on screen at the same time.
Figure 72: Scene with a final boss and many sprites on screen
A boss fight scene: the playable character, the flying enemy, several fireballs, and the HUD
on screen at the same time, all of them sprites.
Chapter 2 already mentioned that the VDP’s sprite hardware has a maximum size per indi-
vidual sprite of 32×32 pixels (4×4 tiles). A character visually bigger than that — like an
Alucard-style protagonist from Castlevania, or a final boss — isn’t, strictly speaking, a single
hardware sprite, but several sprites of up to 32×32 (or another allowed size, from 8×8 to
32×32 in any combination) combined to form the complete figure. That assembly doesn’t
have to be programmed by hand: SGDK’s sprite engine, already used in Chapter 21 through
SPR_addSprite(), takes care of automatically splitting a SpriteDefinition that’s too large
into however many hardware sprites are needed, and of moving and animating them as if
they were a single one from the code’s point of view.
Thatautomaticassembly,however,doesn’tremovethequantitylimitsalreadyseeninChapter
2: in 320-pixel-wide mode (H40), the VDP can display a maximum of 80 hardware sprites in
total per frame, and no more than 20 sprites (or 40 tiles wide, whichever comes first) on any
single horizontal line of the screen. Exceeding that limit on a particular line doesn’t produce
146

=== PAGE 153 ===
an error or halt the game: the VDP simply stops drawing the sprites that exceed that line’s
quota for that particular frame, and since the set of dropped sprites can vary from frame to
frame, the visible result is flickering (sprite flicker) in the affected elements. A scene with
several fireballs, a large boss, and a HUD all competing for sprites on the same horizontal
lines starts showing exactly that flicker as soon as enough projectiles pile up on screen, both
in an emulator and on real hardware.
Sprite flicker was a much more frequent and noticeable problem on 8-bit consoles like the
NES or the Master System, with considerably tighter per-line sprite limits; the Mega Drive,
with its 20 sprites per line in H40, suffers from it less often, but isn’t completely immune
either, as any scene deliberately loaded with sprites demonstrates.
6.1 Transparent space costs nothing
Comparingtwodifferentwaysoforganizingthesameanimationsheetoffersaspecificlesson.
Suppose a first version of a sheet where the character is drawn pushed up against one side
of each cell, so the cell is as small as possible, under the reasonable-looking assumption that
a smaller cell saves VRAM and reduces the risk of flicker.
Figure 73: Character shifted to one side of the cell
First version of the sheet: the character drawn shifted toward the left side of each cell, to
minimize the required cell size.
Thatadjustment,however,bringsacostofadifferentkind: sincethecharacterisn’tcentered
withinitscell,flippingithorizontally(withflipH,alreadyusedinChapter21)tomakeitface
the opposite direction also shifts its apparent position on screen, which forces the collision
codetoconstantlyaccountforwhetherthecharacterisfacingleftorrightinordertocorrect
for that shift. A second version of the same sheet, with the character properly centered in
eachcell—atthecostofalotmoretransparentspacearoundit—solvestheproblem: when
flipped, the apparent position no longer shifts.
147

=== PAGE 154 ===
Figure 74: Character centered in the cell
Second version of the sheet: the character centered in each cell, with considerable transpar-
ent space on the sides; when flipped horizontally, the apparent position no longer shifts.
The counterintuitive part is that this extra transparent space has no real cost at all: rescomp
detects the completely empty areas of each frame and excludes them both from the VRAM
tilecountandfromthenumberofhardwarespritesneededtorepresentthecharacter,inthe
samewayChapter8alreadyexplainedthatSGDKdetectsandreusesflippedtiles. Centering
the character on the sheet, then, doesn’t cost any extra memory or make flicker worse: it’s
a code-organization improvement (fewer special cases for left and right) that comes free in
terms of hardware resources. The same optimization applies to animation frames that are
nearly identical to each other — for example, if a character’s head doesn’t change position
between two consecutive frames: rescomp can recognize duplicate frames and avoid storing
them again in VRAM, with no extra manual work required, although more demanding cases
of space optimization may call for hand-tuning the sheet.
6.2 When it’s not worth using a sprite
For truly enormous characters — a final boss that takes up a large part of the screen, for
example—neitherautomaticVRAMallocationnortransparent-spaceoptimizationisenough
tofullyavoidthecostofsomanycombinedhardwaresprites. Inthosecases,atrickinherited
from the 8-bit era is still valid on the Mega Drive: instead of building the enormous charac-
ter entirely out of sprites, it’s worth using one of the two background planes (BG_A or BG_B,
seen in Chapter 2) to draw it, reserving sprites for the parts that genuinely need to move
independently and with the pixel-level positioning freedom that sprites provide.

3. Playing an animation: SPR_setAnim()
With the sprite properly positioned, what’s still missing is the core of the chapter: making it
playoneofitsanimationsinsteadofstayingonasinglefixedframe. Thefunctionthatchooses
which animation to play is:
void SPR_setAnim(Sprite *sprite, s16 anim);
The first parameter is the pointer to the sprite already returned by SPR_addSprite() (player,
in this example); the second, anim, is the index of the animation to play. To understand what
that index means, we need to look at the full sheet again: each row is a distinct animation.
On this particular sheet, from top to bottom: row 0 is a single static frame, with no real
animation; row1istheidleanimation; row2isthewalkcycle; androw3istheGrandUpper
punch, Axel’s signature move in Streets of Rage 2.
As is customary in programming, numbering starts at 0. Calling the function with index 0,
then, produces no visible motion, because that particular row contains only a single frame:
SPR_setAnim(player, 0);
Changingthesecondargumentto1should,inprinciple,playtheidleanimation. Butdoingso
and recompiling, the sprite still doesn’t move: there’s no error in this line, just a value that’s
still left unconfigured, as shown in the next section.
4. Animation speed: the last field in resources.res
Thereasonanimation1doesn’tmoveliesinthelastfieldoftheSPRITElineinresources.res,
theonethat’sbeenleftat0sofar. Thatfieldisthedurationofeachframe,expressedinscreen
frames (1/60 of a second on the NTSC variant of the console). At 0, automatic animation is
disabled entirely, which is why no animation index has produced any movement so far, so it
needs to be set to a value greater than zero for the sprite engine to advance frames on its
own.
Avalueof60turnsout,inpractice,tobetooslow: with60screenframesperanimation-frame
change, and running at 60 frames per second, the animation changes only once per second
— a noticeably slower pace than expected. Lowering the value makes the animation advance
more often; a value of around 15 for the idle animation gives a visually reasonable result:
SPRITE our_sprite "animated_sprite_15_16.png" 15 16 FAST 15
Changingtheanimationindexto2(thewalkcycle)andadjustingthespeedindependently,in
this case to 8 — noticeably faster than the idle animation’s — completes the example:
SPRITE our_sprite "animated_sprite_15_16.png" 15 16 FAST 8
SPR_setAnim(player, 2);
This mechanism, as used so far, has a limitation: the speed field in resources.res is a single
value per resource, not one per animation, so changing it affects all four rows of the sheet
equally. rescomp offers, for anyone who needs a different speed per frame or per animation
within the same sheet, a more advanced syntax with nested brackets that goes beyond the
scopeofthisintroductorychapterandispickeduplaterinthismanual. It’sworthknowingit
exists,becausesoonerorlaterthedifferencebetweenanimationsbecomesarealissue—for
example,aslowidleanimationcoexistingwithafastattackanimationonthesamecharacter.

5. From loose numbers to meaningful names: why #define
Up to now, the animation index was written as a loose number directly in the call to
SPR_setAnim(): 0, 1, 2, or 3. In programming this is known as a magic number (or, more
informally, hardcoding a value), and it’s a practice worth avoiding as code grows: a loose
number says nothing about its purpose, and finding and fixing every occurrence of that
number if its meaning ever changes becomes a tedious, error-prone task.
The natural first step is to replace the number with a variable:
int anim = 3;
SPR_setAnim(player, anim);
Thisalreadyimprovesreadability,butanordinaryvariable(int)canchangevalueatanypoint
intheprogram,andtheindexoftheGrandUpper animationonthisparticularsheetisnever
going to change: it will always be 3, no matter what else the rest of the code does. For that
case — a fixed value that should never change — C offers the const qualifier:
const int ANIM_UPPER = 3;
Besides fixing the value, changing the name from anim to ANIM_UPPER solves the other real
problem with a magic number: you no longer need to remember by heart that “the special
move animation is number 3” — reading the name is enough. The convention of writing
constants entirely in uppercase, with underscores between words, is a widespread practice
in C (though not required by the language) that helps you tell, just by looking at the code,
which identifiers are constants and which aren’t.
For this kind of value, though, it’s worth going one step further and replacing const with
#define. As explained in Chapter 6, the Mega Drive has very little RAM available — barely
64 KB in total (Chapter 1) — and that’s a resource worth actively conserving throughout the
game’scode. #defineisatextsubstitutionthatthepreprocessorresolvesbeforethecompiler
ever sees the code, so it doesn’t reserve any memory for the constant at run time; const, on
the other hand, depending on the compiler and optimization level used, can end up taking
up real space (the exact comparison between the two forms is well beyond what this chapter
needs, and depends on specific details of the toolchain; it’s enough to know that #define
is, in principle, the safer choice in such a memory-constrained environment). The syntax of
#defineisalsodeliberatelydifferentfromthatofavariabledeclaration: ithasnoequalssign
and no semicolon.
#define ANIM_STILL 0
#define ANIM_IDLE 1
#define ANIM_WALK 2
#define ANIM_UPPER 3
With the four constants now defined, the final code is considerably more readable than the
loose-number version from the start of the chapter:
SPR_setAnim(player, ANIM_UPPER);
ThebehaviorisidenticaltowritingSPR_setAnim(player, 3)directly,butthecodenowreads
on its own: anyone opening this file knows, without having to go check the animation sheet,
that this line plays the character’s special move. From here on, this manual uses #define
consistently for this kind of fixed value, including sound management later in the book.

new_camera_x = current_camera_x;
That same block of three cases (edge crossed on one side, on the other side, or no change)

conditionthattriggersdownwardmovementusesa“greaterthan,”whichatfirstglancemight
seem counterintuitive if you think in terms of “up” and “down” rather than in terms of the
numeric coordinate:

=== PAGE 165 ===

new_camera_y = player_y_map_integer - HOW_FAR_TO_DOWN_BEFORE_CAMERA_MOVES;
else if (player_y_position_on_screen < HOW_FAR_TO_UP_BEFORE_CAMERA_MOVES)

7. Applying the scroll: MAP_scrollTo() only when needed
Now that the camera’s new position has been calculated, we still need to decide whether
it actually changed from the previous position: if the character hasn’t moved far enough to
cross any of the limits, the camera doesn’t need to move, and calling MAP_scrollTo() every
frameunnecessarilywouldbeawasteofCPUwork. Thecomparisonusesthelogicalequality
operator (two equal signs, as opposed to assignment with a single one) and the logical “or”
operator (two vertical bars), since a change on either axis is enough to justify a new scroll:
if ((current_camera_x != new_camera_x) || (current_camera_y != new_camera_y)) {
current_camera_x = new_camera_x;
current_camera_y = new_camera_y;
MAP_scrollTo(level_map, current_camera_x, current_camera_y);
}
If the condition is true, the code updates the global variables with the new values (so that
next frame’s comparison has the correct reference) and only then calls MAP_scrollTo(), the
same function already used in chapter 11, this time with the freshly calculated coordinates.
8. First results, and the adjustment to center the character
With the camera function already written, we still need to add the call inside the main loop,
right after handle_input():

With that adjustment the camera now moves following the character, but there’s still a prob-
lem left: the sprite is still being drawn at its position within the full map, instead of at its
position relative to the current screen. The solution is the same subtraction already used to
calculate player_x_position_on_screen: SPR_setPosition() needs the character’s position
minus the camera’s position, not the absolute position on the map. This line is moved from
the main loop to the end of the camera() function itself, since that’s where it makes sense to
update it:
SPR_setPosition(link_sprite, F32_toInt(link_x) - new_camera_x, F32_toInt(link_y) -
↪ new_camera_y);
Using new_camera_x/new_camera_y instead of current_camera_x/current_camera_y works in
eithercase: whenthecameraactuallymoved,bothvariablesarealreadysynchronizedbythe

assignment in the previous step; when it didn’t move, new_camera_x/new_camera_y already

two already-calculated integers fits that type directly.
9. Keeping the camera from leaving the map
With the character now correctly centered, there’s still a visible problem when approaching
any edge of the map: the camera keeps scrolling beyond the map itself, showing repeated
tiles or visual artifacts in the areas that fall outside the actual bounds.
Figure 78: The camera scrolling past the actual edge of the map
Without bounding the camera, the graphics repeat incorrectly in the area that no longer cor-
responds to any valid map tile.
Thesolutionistoclampnew_camera_xandnew_camera_ytoavalidrange,whichrequiresfour
newconstants: thehorizontalandverticalscreenresolution,andthewidthandheightofthe
full map (1024 by 1024 pixels in this particular map, although the exact value depends on
each project):
#define HORIZONTAL_RESOLUTION 320
#define VERTICAL_RESOLUTION 224
#define MAP_WIDTH 1024
#define MAP_HEIGHT 1024
With those constants defined, the left and top limits are simple: if new_camera_x or
new_camera_y fall below 0, they’re set to 0. The right and bottom limits require a small
calculation: the camera can’t exceed the total width (or height) of the map minus the screen
resolution, since otherwise it would show content beyond the map itself:
160

=== PAGE 167 ===
if (new_camera_x < 0)
new_camera_x = 0;
else if (new_camera_x > MAP_WIDTH - HORIZONTAL_RESOLUTION)
new_camera_x = MAP_WIDTH - HORIZONTAL_RESOLUTION;
if (new_camera_y < 0)
new_camera_y = 0;
else if (new_camera_y > MAP_HEIGHT - VERTICAL_RESOLUTION)
new_camera_y = MAP_HEIGHT - VERTICAL_RESOLUTION;
This block goes after calculating new_camera_x/new_camera_y in step 6, and before the com-
parison against current_camera_x/current_camera_y in step 7. With this, the camera now
respects the map’s four edges: upon reaching any corner, it stops scrolling instead of show-
ing content outside the bounds.
10. Keeping the character itself from leaving the screen
Withthecameranowbounded,onelastdetailremains: eventhoughthemapnolongerscrolls

stoppedfollowingit. Thesolutionisanalogoustothecamera’sown,butappliedtolink_xand
link_y, and using the character sprite’s width and height (two additional constants) instead
of the screen resolution:

if (link_y < 0)

Sincelink_xandlink_yarefix32,thelimitsareexpressedwithFIX32()sothatcomparisons

tion. With this adjustment, both the camera and the character itself respect the map’s limits
in all four directions.

11. Adjusting the feel of the camera
Nowthatthefunctionisworkingwithouterrors,changingthefourHOW_FAR_TO_*_BEFORE_CAMERA_MOVES
constantsisthesimplestwaytoadjusthowstrictlythecamerakeepsthecharactercentered:
smaller values keep it almost always at the exact center of the screen, while larger values
giveitmore freedomof movementbeforethe camerareacts, atthe costof acharacter that’s
less centered at any given moment. How tight the camera should be is a design decision for
each particular game, not a fixed technical rule: more elaborate cameras, for example, push
the view ahead in the direction the character is facing to show more of the path forward,
although that behavior can feel uncomfortable if the camera shifts too abruptly every time
the character changes direction.
Thecompletesetofconstantsgoverningthecamera’sbehaviorarethefourscreen
margins, the horizontal and vertical resolution, and the dimensions of the map and
the sprite. Adjusting just the four margins is enough to completely change the feel
of the camera without touching the rest of the logic.
12. Adapting the camera to H32 resolution mode

so they still represent, roughly, half of the new horizontal resolution, so that the character
stays centered in this mode too. The rest of the camera() function needs no changes at all:
allthelimitandscrolllogicisalreadyindependentofthespecificresolution,becauseitrelies
on constants rather than on raw numbers written directly into the code.

Chapter 25 — Parallax Scrolling
Over a Camera
Combining a parallax background with the camera of a large map: inverted parallax, multi-
plication versus subtraction, and the real limit of a repeating image
Chapter 9 introduced basic parallax scrolling: two backgrounds moving automatically at dif-
ferent speeds, with no relation to any character. Chapter 24, for its part, showed how to
scroll a large map based on a character’s position, but without any additional background
behindit. Thischaptercombinesbothideas: aparallaxbackgroundthatscrollsaccordingto
the very same camera that already follows the character over the main map, with two new
complications that did not appear in either chapter on its own.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it’s a good idea to have on hand:
• Chapter 24 (“2D Camera”) already worked through: the camera() function, the cur-
rent_camera_x/current_camera_y variables, and the map and character limits.
• Chapter 9 (“Scrolling and Parallax Scrolling”): VDP_setScrollingMode() and the use of
two background planes (BG_A and BG_B).
• Chapter 7 (“How to Display Backgrounds on the Mega Drive”): the IMAGE resource and
VDP_drawImageEx().
1. Starting point: two different graphics resources
The example in this chapter combines a foreground map (the same kind of TILESET + MAP
resource already seen in Chapter 11) with a distant background image. The foreground map
measures 6176 pixels wide by 352 pixels tall — considerably taller than the screen’s 224
pixels, so as to also demonstrate vertical scrolling — while the background image respects
the already familiar limit of an IMAGE resource: 512×256 pixels at most.
Thestartingpointis,quitesimply,thefinishedcodefromthecamerachapter,withthegraph-
icsresourcesswappedoutandthemapandspritewidth/heightconstantsupdatedtothenew
values. On top of that code, it’s worth applying two minor adjustments as well:
Use s16 instead of int for the coordinates. As explained in Chapter 6, it’s always best to
use the smallest type that will do the job. This example’s map, at 6176 pixels wide, remains
well below the roughly 32,000-pixel limit of an s16, so declaring the camera coordinates as
s16 instead of int requires less CPU work and less ROM, without losing any useful range.
Simplifysingle-statementifs. InC,whenthebodyofaniforanelse ifcontainsasingle
statement,thebracesdelimitingthatbodyareoptional,andremovingthemtoleavethestate-
164

=== PAGE 171 ===
ment on the same line changes nothing about the program’s behavior. Blocks that execute
morethanonestatement(forexample,withininputhandling,whereit’softennecessaryboth
to move the character and, eventually, to change its animation) still need braces, since there
they are indeed mandatory.
2. Adding the background image: palettes and planes
WiththeforegroundmapalreadyonBG_AusingPAL1foritscolors—andnotPAL0,preciselyto
highlightausefuleffectworthrecognizing: thefirstcolorofanypaletteotherthan0isalways

VDP’s background color instead of its actual colors — adding the distant background image

PAL_setPalette(PAL0, bg_far.palette->data, DMA);
PAL_setPalette(PAL1, map_tileset.palette->data, DMA);

4. An unexpected problem: inverted parallax
Thesimplestwaytogiveb_hscrollandb_vscrollsomevalueistoassignthemdirectlyfrom
new_camera_x and new_camera_y, the same coordinates already used to scroll the foreground
165

=== PAGE 172 ===
map. Compiling with that change, vertical scrolling behaves as expected (background and
foregroundmovingexactlythesame,withnodeptheffectyet),buthorizontalscrollingreveals
aproblem: thebackgroundmovesintheoppositedirectionfromwhat’sexpected,aninverted
and visually unpleasant parallax effect.
The cause is conceptual: MAP_scrollTo() expects the camera’s position in order to scroll the
map in the correct direction, but VDP_setHorizontalScroll() interprets its parameter differ-
ently for a background image, so assigning it the same camera coordinate directly produces
the opposite of the intended effect.
5. Fixing the direction: multiplication versus subtraction
Themostintuitivesolutionistoflipthesignof new_camera_xbeforeassigningittob_hscroll,
by multiplying it by -1:
b_hscroll = new_camera_x * -1;
Thissolutionworks,butit’sworthkeepinganunderlyingissueinmind: theMegaDrive’sCPU
(aMotorola68000,which,asexplainedinChapter1,doesn’thaveamultiplicationordivision
unit as fast as its basic arithmetic and logic operations) isn’t especially quick at performing
multiplications or divisions, so it’s best to avoid them whenever a simpler alternative exists.
In this case, subtracting the value from 0 achieves exactly the same result as multiplying by
-1, without needing any multiplication at all:
b_hscroll = 0 - new_camera_x;
6. Depth with powers of two: bit shifting instead of divid-
ing
With the direction now fixed, the next step is to make the background scroll more slowly
than the foreground, to create a sense of depth: the farther away a background element is
supposed to be, the more slowly it should move relative to the character. The most intuitive
approach is to divide new_camera_x by some number — 2 for half speed, 3 for a third, and
so on — but division, like multiplication, is a relatively costly operation for this CPU. The
recommended alternative is bit shifting: shifting all the bits of a number one position to the
right is exactly equivalent to dividing it by 2; shifting two positions is equivalent to dividing
by 4; three positions, by 8; and so on, always in powers of 2. Since the CPU works in binary,
shifting bits is a much simpler and faster operation than a generic division:
b_hscroll = (0 - new_camera_x) >> 1; // half speed
Trying out different shift amounts is a quick way to fine-tune the sense of depth until finding
the one that best matches how distant that landscape element is supposed to be. For a back-
ground of distant mountains and forest, shifting three positions (dividing by 8) on both axes
tends to be a good starting point:
b_hscroll = (0 - new_camera_x) >> 3;
b_vscroll = (0 - new_camera_y) >> 3;
This value for b_vscroll, however, isn’t final yet: the next section adjusts it again to solve a
different problem with vertical scrolling.
166

=== PAGE 173 ===
7. A problem when scrolling vertically: the background
repeating
With horizontal parallax now working correctly, scrolling vertically reveals a different prob-
lem: at some point, the background image starts repeating vertically, showing its top part
againbeforefinishingshowingthebottom. Thisisavisuallyincorrecteffectforaplatformer,
though it might be acceptable in a vertical shooter where a repeating background makes
sense. The cause is the difference between the image’s height (256 pixels, the maximum al-
lowed for an IMAGE resource) and the screen’s height (224 pixels): a margin of only 32 pixels
before the vertical scroll exceeds the image’s actual height and starts showing it again from
the beginning.
Thesolutionistoclampb_vscrolltothat32-pixelrange,usingthesamelogicalreadyusedin
Chapter 24 to keep the camera from going outside the map: a lower limit of 0, and an upper
limit of 32 (the difference between the image’s height and the screen’s height):
if (b_vscroll < 0)
b_vscroll = 0;
else if (b_vscroll > 32)
b_vscroll = 32;
With this limit in place, the background stops repeating vertically no matter how far the
camera scrolls up or down, although — as was already the case with horizontal scrolling of
a repeating map — the background keeps repeating continuously along the horizontal axis,
which is perfectly correct for a background image meant to repeat along that axis.
Thislower-limitcheckmightturnouttobeunnecessaryifthecamera’sYcoordinate,
which new_camera_y depends on, is already clamped to a minimum of 0 inside the
camera() function from Chapter 24. Even so, keeping it costs nothing and leaves
the code safe against future changes to that function.
8. Why not use two maps instead of a map and an image?
A reasonable question is why not use two MAP resources (one for each plane) instead of com-
bining a MAP for the foreground with an IMAGE for the background, since in principle both
could be scrolled with MAP_scrollTo(). The reason is twofold. On one hand, an IMAGE re-
sourcesupportstheper-tileorper-linescrollingmodesseeninPartIIofthismanual,capable
of achieving visual effects that a MAP cannot reproduce, although this particular chapter only
used full-plane mode. On the other hand, and more importantly: a large map with no repe-
titions exists, above all, to define the level’s playable design (what obstacles there are and
where),whileabackgroundispurelydecorativeanddoesn’tneedthatsamelevelofdetail. A
512×256-pixelimagethatrepeatsindefinitelyisusuallymorethanenoughforabackground,
without spending extra memory on a full map that was never going to provide any relevant
gameplay information.

Chapter 26 — Transparency with
Shadow and Highlight
TheMegaDrivehasnogenuinewayofblendingcolorstoachievetransparency,thewaymore
modern consoles can with alpha layers. What the VDP does have is a special mode called
Shadow and Highlight, which darkens or lightens certain colors on screen in a controlled
way. Manycommercialgamestookadvantageofthismodetosimulatetransparency,lighting,
shadows, and ghosts, even though it isn’t real transparency in any technical sense.
It’s a feature with a reputation for being esoteric and hard to understand, but the program-
ming side of it is actually quite simple: enabling the mode takes a single line of code. The
real difficulty lies in understanding the particular rules that govern its behavior — which
palette is affected, which colors within that palette, and how it interacts with tile priority —
so you can make the most of it without surprises. This chapter covers those rules through a
smallpracticeproject: aghostthatcanturntranslucentagainstthebackgroundofahaunted
kitchen.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to be clear on two concepts already covered in this manual:
• The concept of the Mega Drive’s color palettes (PAL0 through PAL3, with the first color
of each palette reserved as transparent), covered in Chapter 2.
• The tile priority parameter (TILE_ATTR_FULL / TILE_ATTR), covered in Chapter 15.
1. Starting point: a background and two sprites
The project for this chapter starts out already with a haunted kitchen background and two
sprites loaded in resources.res: a ghost (spectre_sprite) and a sprite meant purely as a
visual palette reference (sh_palette_sprite), which is nothing more than a strip of colors
drawn specifically to clearly show the effect on each individual color. Handling both sprites
on screen and the D-pad controls to move them are already taken care of beforehand, so the
focus of this chapter is entirely on palette design and the effect itself.
The project’s resources.res file, with the kitchen background and the two starting sprites:
the ghost and the reference palette strip.
169

=== PAGE 176 ===
Figure 79: resources.res with the kitchen background and the starting sprites
2. The key palette: how to design a sprite for Shadow and
Highlight
The most important aspect of this chapter isn’t the code itself, but how each sprite’s color
palette is designed. The first color of the palette, as always on the Mega Drive, is ignored
and acts as the sprite’s transparent background color (it’s a good idea to draw it in a bright,
eye-catching color like blue, just so it’s clear where the actual artwork ends during editing).
The next thirteen colors are normal colors, which behave exactly the same as in any palette
without Shadow and Highlight enabled.
It’s the last two colors of the palette, color 15 and color 16, that have special behavior:
• Color 15 is used as the highlight.
• Color 16 is used as the shadow.
What matters about these two colors isn’t the hue assigned to them in the palette, but only
their position (15 and 16); they can, in principle, be any color at all, although it’s worth
picking hues that make the effect easier to visualize while testing.
The reference palette strip: the first color (blue) is transparent, the next thirteen are normal
colors, and the last two are the positions reserved for highlight and shadow.
3. Placeholder fill colors in the ghost sprite
In the ghost sprite, palette positions 15 and 16 can initially be filled with any flat color as a
placeholder,simplytooccupythosetwoindiceswhiletherestofthespriteisbeingdrawn. In
this project, the ghost’s white ends up taking the highlight slot, and the black of its outlines
and its own shadows takes the shadow slot. The only thing that matters at this point is the
positionofthosecolorswithinthepalette,nottheirapparenthueduringthedrawingprocess.

special effect yet, even though the palette is already set up for the mode.
Totesttheseeffectsproperly,it’sbesttodoso,asmuchaspossible,onrealhardwareoronan

6. Tile priority: how to keep an element’s original color
EnablingShadowandHighlightgloballydarkens,bydefault,everythingdrawnwithlowprior-

7. A key restriction: the effect only works on the fourth
palette (PAL3)
At this point, the ghost sprite shows no highlight or shadow effect at all, even though it also
hascolorsdefinedinpositions15and16ofitspalette. Thereasonisafundamentalhardware
restrictionofShadowandHighlightmode: theeffectonlytakesplaceontheMegaDrive’s
fourth palette, PAL3. Looking back at the project’s code, the reference palette strip (the
one that does show the effect) is assigned to PAL3, while the background uses PAL0, PAL1
isn’t used, and the ghost uses PAL2 — which is why it shows no effect.
This restriction is neither negotiable nor configurable: it’s a limitation of the VDP itself, and
it’s worth keeping in mind from the design stage of a project, since it effectively reserves an
entire palette (PAL3) for any element that needs this effect.

9. An additional limitation: which sprite covers which
There’sanimportantlimitationleftintheper-spritetransparencyeffect: iftwospritesoverlap

confirm this by reversing that order to see how it changes which sprite ends up in front.

Chapter 27 — Color Transparency
Without Shadow and Highlight
Flicker, mesh, and horizontal flip: three ways to simulate
transparency in any color
Chapter 26 showed how to use the VDP’s Shadow and Highlight mode (covered in detail in
Chapter2)tosimulatetransparency,butthatmodehastwoimportantlimitations. Thefirstis
about color: Shadow and Highlight can only darken (toward black) or lighten (toward white)

simply won’t do the job. The second is about overlap: as already shown, if a sprite with the
effect is drawn on top of another one, it completely covers it instead of casting a shadow or
highlight over it.
Thischaptercoversthreealternativetechniquesthatdon’trelyonShadowandHighlightand

The background with PAL0 and PAL1 active and the two sprites from the previous chapter,

176

=== PAGE 183 ===
2. First technique: flicker
The idea behind flicker is simple: if a sprite is made visible and invisible very quickly, alter-
nating frame by frame, the human eye perceives a blend between the sprite and whatever is
behind it, giving the impression of transparency. This effect looks better on an actual CRT
television than in a video recording or a screenshot, since a CRT’s image persistence and
refresh rate tend to smooth out the frame-by-frame alternation in a way that a camera or a
modern high-frequency display doesn’t always reproduce the same way.
Controlling that alternation requires a simple timer: a u8 variable (an unsigned 8-bit integer,
morethanenoughsinceitonlyneedstoalternatebetween0and1),initializedto0. It’sworth
organizing the flicker logic into a separate function, transparencyFunction(), declared with
its prototype before main() and defined at the end of the file, so it doesn’t get mixed in with
the rest of the main loop.
Inside that function, the key piece is SPR_setVisibility(), an SGDK function that takes the
sprite to affect and the desired state, using values of the SpriteVisibility type: VISIBLE to
show it and HIDDEN to hide it. The full logic alternates between two branches of an if: if the
timer is 0, the sprite is set visible and the timer is incremented by one; otherwise (that is, if
it’s 1), the sprite is set invisible and the timer is reset to 0. When writing this condition, be
careful not to confuse = (assignment) with == (comparison), an easy mistake to make even
though it’s a basic concept, and one that can leave the timer in an unexpected state without
the compiler warning you.
u8 timer = 0;
void transparencyFunction(void);
// ...
void transparencyFunction(void)
{
if (timer == 0)
{
SPR_setVisibility(spectre, VISIBLE);
timer++;
}
else
{
SPR_setVisibility(spectre, HIDDEN);
timer = 0;
}
}
Withthefunctionwritten, onelaststepremainsthat’seasytoforget: callingitoneverypass
of the game’s main loop, inside the while(TRUE), alongside the other per-frame update calls
(for example, reading input and SPR_update()).
The resulting behavior, frame by frame, is as follows: on the first frame the timer is 0, so
the sprite is set visible (no apparent change, since it already was) and the timer moves to 1;
on the second frame, since the timer is no longer 0, the sprite is set invisible; on the third
framethetimergoesbackto0andthecyclerepeats,alternatingvisibleandinvisibleoneach
successive frame.
The ghost alternating between visible and invisible frame by frame, letting the background
and the palette strip behind it show through.
177

=== PAGE 184 ===
Figure 85: The ghost flickering between visible and invisible
It’s worth keeping in mind that, when capturing or recording this effect to show it outside
of a CRT television, the result may not look as convincing as on real hardware, where the
frame-by-frame flicker tends to be perceived more smoothly and continuously. Even so, even
in a recording, the transparency effect is clearly noticeable.

4. Second technique: the mesh pattern
Theoriginalgamethatinspiredthisexample,StreetsofRage,doesn’tuseflickerforitssemi-
transparentlamp,butratherameshpattern: insteadofasolidcolor,thesprite’sowngraphic
is drawn with a pattern of alternating pixels (a checkerboard-style dithering), so that the
background color visually shows through the gaps in that pattern with no software trickery
needed at all.
It’s often mentioned that the Sega Saturn, generations later, has a dedicated hardware com-
mand for automatically converting a solid sprite into this kind of mesh pattern; this claim
could not be confirmed against technical documentation for that console, so it should be
taken with caution. In any case, the Mega Drive has nothing equivalent: the sprite’s own
graphic must already be drawn with the mesh built in from the start, in the graphics editor,
before converting it into an SGDK resource.
Figure 88: The lamp sprite redrawn with a mesh pattern
The lamp redrawn with a pattern of alternating pixels instead of a solid color, the technique
used by the original Streets of Rage.
The visual result of a mesh pattern depends heavily on the hardware or video filter used to
display it. With certain smoothing filters enabled in an emulator, the effect looks reasonably
convincing;turningthemoff,togetclosertowhatyou’dseewithacrispconnectionlikeRGB
on a real CRT, the pattern shows up as hard lines and the sense of transparency is lost. An
older or lower-quality connection, like RF, slightly blurs the whole image and, in the process,
also softens the mesh (historical examples of this phenomenon include the waterfall in Sonic
the Hedgehog, or, fittingly, the lamps in Streets of Rage). It’s a trade-off: a sharp image with
a very visible mesh, or a somewhat blurry image with a more disguised mesh. Since this
perception changes depending on the television or emulator, it’s worth testing the effect in
more than one environment before settling on it.
Combining this mesh pattern with the flicker technique from the previous section is also
possible, andgives an acceptable result, though not necessarily better thaneither technique
180

=== PAGE 187 ===
on its own.
5. Third technique: horizontal flip over the mesh pattern
There’s a variant that tends to give a more even result than the mesh pattern combined with
flicker: instead of alternating the sprite between visible and invisible, it’s kept visible at all
times, but flipped horizontally on every other frame using SPR_setHFlip(), another SGDK
function already used in earlier chapters of Part III. Since the mesh pattern isn’t perfectly
symmetrical, flipping it back and forth frame by frame makes the light areas and the pat-
terned areas seem to constantly swap positions, producing a smoother transparency effect
than simply flickering the whole sprite.
The change from the flicker technique is minimal: SPR_setVisibility() is replaced with
SPR_setHFlip() inside the same two branches of the if.
void transparencyFunction(void)
{
if (timer == 0)
{
SPR_setHFlip(lamp, FALSE);
timer++;
}
else
{
SPR_setHFlip(lamp, TRUE);
timer = 0;
}
}
Compilingwiththischange,theresultisusuallyconsideredthemostconvincingofthethree
techniques presented in this chapter for this kind of effect: the lamp looks evenly semi-
transparent, without the abrupt flicker of the first technique or the fixed visual harshness
of the static mesh pattern from the second. As with any comparison of this sort, the final
impression can vary depending on the television or emulator used to view it, so it’s worth
tryingallthreevariantsonthetargethardwareoremulatorbeforedecidingwhichonetouse
in a given project.
The lamp with a mesh pattern alternating its horizontal flip frame by frame: the most even
result of the three techniques.
Nothing stops you, moreover, from combining these techniques with Shadow and Highlight
withinthesameproject: forexample,usingShadowandHighlightforthepartsofaspritethat
need to look truly black or white in a transparent way, and one of this chapter’s techniques
for any other color. Which combination works best in each case depends on the visual needs
of the game in question.

Chapter 28 — Ranger X-Style
Dynamic Lighting
Chapters26and27coveredtwowaystosimulatetransparencyoversprites: firstwithShadow
andHighlight, thenwithalternativesoftwaretechniquesbasedonflickerandmeshpatterns.
This chapter returns to Shadow and Highlight, but this time applies it to the background
layers instead of individual sprites, in order to reproduce one of the most memorable effects
in the Mega Drive library: the light beams from Ranger X, which illuminate both the stage
and the player’s own robot as it passes beneath them. Another famous example of this same
technique is the stained-glass section in Castlevania: Bloodlines.
Unlike the version seen in Chapter 26, where priority was assigned sprite by sprite, here the
switch is the priority of the background tiles themselves: any tile marked with high priority
is shown with increased brightness, and any sprite that passes over that area is lit up along
with it. This difference brings one advantage (a single change lights up the background and
everything passing over it) and one new complication, because tile priority doesn’t only con-
trol Shadow and Highlight: it also decides the draw order between layers and sprites, and
the two functions can conflict with each other.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it’s worth having these points settled:
• The basic rules of Shadow and Highlight — PAL3 reserved for sprites with high-
light/shadow,colors15and16reservedforthosestates,andthecalltoVDP_setHilightShadow()
— were already covered in Chapter 26 and are assumed to be known here.
• Handling two background layers (BG_A and BG_B) and the concept of tile priority, pre-
sented in Chapter 15.
• Creating and importing maps with per-tile priority using 16Tile, covered in Chapter 13.
1. Starting point: a robot over a background with several
light sources
This chapter’s practice project uses, as its character, a sprite inspired by the robot from
Ranger X, over a simplified stage that revisits the setting of Revenge of Shinobi, chosen be-
causeitincludesseverallightsourceswellsuitedtothiseffect. Whenworkingwiththistype
of lighting, it’s also best not to exceed a map that’s 512 pixels wide by 256 pixels tall: larger
maps can cause performance problems, which are revisited later in this manual.
Thelayerstructurecomesalreadysetup: aregularbackgroundassignedtoPAL0anddrawn
