4. A color the effect doesn’t reach: palette position 15
Looking closely at the robot’s sprite as it passes under the lit area, there’s one detail that
doesn’t change brightness along with the rest: a small dot of color in its design. The cause
is an additional rule of the Shadow and Highlight mode applied to the background: for any
sprite, regardless of whether it uses PAL2 or PAL3, the color located at position 15 of its
palette is never affected by the effect. In this example, that dot was deliberately placed at
position 15 — a position not used in the original design — and position 16 was filled with
another color just to complete the 16-color palette.
Thereareatleastthreereasonablewaystodealwiththisrulewhendesigningaspritethat’s
going to receive the effect:
185

=== PAGE 192 ===
• Avoid using position 15 altogether, even if that means sacrificing an available palette
color.
• Accept that this particular color won’t be affected, when it takes up little space on the
sprite and is unlikely to be noticed during gameplay.
• Turn the limitation into a design asset: for example, a robot’s or an enemy’s glowing
eyescouldoccupyexactlyposition15,sothattheykeepstandingoutevenundershadow.
This is one option among the previous ones, not necessarily a better one, and it’s worth
choosing for whoever values that constant glow as part of the character’s design.
5. A difference from the original Ranger X: should the
player’s sprite be lit up?
Comparingtheresultobtainedsofarwiththeoriginalgamerevealsadifference: inRangerX,
the player’s own robot sprite isn’t affected by the lighting effect, and always keeps the same
brightness,whetherornotitpassesthroughalitarea. Thatbehaviorcanbereproducedwith
a single change: setting the robot sprite’s priority to high (TRUE) instead of low.
// High priority: the sprite is exempt from Shadow and Highlight
SPR_setAttribute(ranger, TILE_ATTR(PAL2, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE));
There’s no official confirmation of why the original game behaves this way, but there’s a
reasonable explanation: a player sprite that gets too dark under certain lights could make
it harder to see clearly during gameplay, so keeping it at a constant brightness would be a
design decision rather than a technical limitation. That said, the opposite stance is just as
valid: lettingtheplayer’ssprite(andtheenemies’sprites)beaffectedbytheeffecttoo,since
many consider it visually more appealing and it reinforces the feeling that the character is
part of the same lit space as the stage. Both are legitimate design decisions; for the rest of
this chapter, the robot’s priority is set back to low (FALSE), since lighting up the player’s own
sprite is the central goal of this technique.
6. Adding the remaining light sources
With the pattern already established, the rest of the stage’s lamps are added the same way:
painting,within16Tile,thetilesthatcorrespondtoeachadditionallightsourceathighprior-

which tiles are already at high priority and which are still at low.
With the new lights already painted in, however, a different problem shows up next to the
second light source: part of a wall and a trash can from the foreground, which should be
drawn in front of the robot sprite, end up appearing behind it when passing through that
area.
The robot should pass in front of the wall and the trash can, but ends up covered by them.
7. The underlying conflict: priority serves two purposes at
once
The cause of this problem is the same limitation already explained in Chapter 15: the pri-
ority parameter of a tile or a sprite serves two purposes at the same time. On one hand, it
determines whether that element is affected by Shadow and Highlight; on the other, it also
determines the draw order between background layers and sprites, since any high-priority
186

=== PAGE 193 ===
Figure 92: The robot ending up hidden behind the wall and the trash can near the second
light source
tileisdrawninfrontofanylow-prioritysprite,withoutexception. Markingthewallandtrash
can tiles at high priority to light them up had a side effect: those same tiles started being
drawn in front of the robot sprite, which is still at low priority. It’s the same mechanism that,
appliedtheotherwayaround, letsacharactercorrectlystaybehindoneforegroundelement
and in front of another within the same scene with several overlapping layers.
8. The solution: replacing the conflicting foreground with
low-priority sprites
The chosen solution avoids sacrificing either the lighting effect or the correct draw order:
within 16Tile, the foreground tiles causing the conflict — the wall and the right side of the
trash can — are removed and replaced with the transparent tile, so that the background
becomes directly visible in that area.
Atthispointthelightingeffectalreadyworkscorrectlyinthatarea,buttheactualdrawingof
the wall and the trash can, just removed from the foreground, is now missing. That’s where
the core of the solution comes in: instead of background tiles, those elements are recreated
asnewlow-prioritysprites,usingthesamegraphictheyhadaspartoftheforeground,placed
exactly where the removed tiles used to be.
// New sprites, using the same palette the foreground had (PAL1)
Sprite* ranger = SPR_addSprite(&sprite_ranger, x, y, TILE_ATTR(PAL2, FALSE, FALSE,
↪ FALSE));
Sprite* wall = SPR_addSprite(&sprite_wall, wallX, wallY, TILE_ATTR(PAL1,
↪ FALSE, FALSE, FALSE));
Sprite* bin = SPR_addSprite(&sprite_bin, binX, binY, TILE_ATTR(PAL1, FALSE,
↪ FALSE, FALSE));
187

=== PAGE 194 ===
Since these new sprites remain at low priority, just like the player’s robot, they are indeed
subjecttoShadowandHighlightandlightupalongwiththerestofthesceneunderthatlamp.
Being sprites just like the robot itself, moreover, the draw order between them is controlled
normally, without the previous conflict between background tile and sprite.
It’s best to add the robot sprite first and only afterward the new wall and trash can sprites,
so that the robot ends up correctly in front of them when it should: the order in which
SPR_addSprite() is called determines which sprite is drawn in front of which. It’s also nec-
essary to update the position of these sprites within the camera function, just like with any
other element that needs to scroll along with the map.
Replacing foreground tiles with sprites solves the conflict between lighting and
draw order, but it comes at a cost: each element turned into a sprite starts com-
peting for the same hardware resources as the rest of the sprites on screen. As
explained in Chapter 2, the Mega Drive can display around 80 simultaneous hard-
ware sprites before flicker starts showing up due to a lack of available slots on a
given scanline, so this resource should be used sparingly, and not every conflicting
foreground element should be turned into a sprite.
Withthesechanges,theproblemisresolved: thewallandtherightsideofthetrashcanonce
again appear in front of or behind the robot as appropriate, and all three light up correctly
when passing under the lamp.
9. Why the order of SPR_addSprite() matters
Tounderscoretheimportanceofthisorder,it’sworthdeliberatelytryingtoreverseit: adding
the robot sprite after the wall and trash can sprites, instead of before. With that change, the
player’srobotendsupdrawnbehindthetrashcaninsteadofinfrontofit,asitshouldbe,since
theorderof SPR_addSprite()directlydeterminestheorderofthehardwarespritetable,and
therefore what gets drawn over what. Reversing the order back — leaving the robot sprite
as the first one added — restores the correct result.

Chapter 29 — Palette Cycling
Animations
Palettecyclingwasaverycommontechniqueinthe16-biteraforbringingbackgroundstolife:
itwasusedtosimulatemovingwaterorfire,day-to-nightlightingtransitions,orsci-fiflickers.
Itsappealisn’tjustvisual. Sinceitdoesn’trequireextratilesinVRAMorupdatingthemframe
byframe,it’sanextremelycheaptechniqueintermsofsystemresources,andcombinedwith
other hardware tricks it can even contribute to pseudo-3D effects. This chapter covers how
to prepare graphics for this technique, how to program it in SGDK using PAL_setPalette(),
and how to get a quick preview of the effect in Aseprite before writing a single line of code.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, make sure you’re clear on:
• The use of PAL_setPalette() and loading a background image with VDP_drawImageEx(),
aswellashowCRAMisorganizedinto16-colorbanks(chap.2,“TheVDPinDepth”)and
how a background is displayed for the first time (chap. 7, “Displaying Backgrounds on
the Mega Drive”).
• Working with integer-based timers inside the main loop and the signed types s8/s16
(chap. 6, “C Applied to Retro Development”).
• How to work with indexed color mode in Aseprite (chap. 8, “Creating Graphics with
Aseprite”).
• How to extract a function from the main loop by declaring its prototype before main(),
a pattern already used in previous chapters on animation.
1. A conceptual starting point: “8-bit art”
Before diving into the code, it’s worth keeping in mind an idea that runs through much of
classic pixel art for animated backgrounds: the so-called “8-bit art,” understood not as a
reference to a system or console, but to the number of colors shown on screen: 256 in total.
Displaying that many simultaneous colors on the Mega Drive would require an add-on like
the 32X, but even with the 61 colors effectively available on the base console (four palettes
of 16 colors, with index 0 of each reserved for transparency), very convincing effects can be
achieved using palette cycling. The key is building the original artwork with color shifting
in mind from the start, so that the palette change reads as a smooth animation rather than
a simple pixel flicker. Achieving this is, above all, a palette design problem rather than a
programming one.
The“CanvasCycle”demo,with256colorsonscreenusingonlypalettecyclingoveracoastal
landscape.
189

=== PAGE 196 ===
Figure 93: Canvas Cycle, Mark Ferrari’s demo
2. Preparing the graphics: a background with an indexed
palette
The example in this chapter uses as its base a waterfall background, edited in Aseprite with
the color mode set to indexed (not RGB, as explained in the chapter on creating graphics
withAseprite),anessentialrequirementforbeingabletomanipulatepalettepositionsdirectly
insteadofthecolorofeachpixel. Thefirstcolorinthepalettecorrespondstothebackground
black,andthecolorsrelevanttotheeffectarethewhites,greens,andbluesthatmakeupthe
waterfall.
The waterfall background in indexed color mode, with the corresponding palette visible in
the left panel.
The advantage of palette cycling is that, instead of keeping many unique tiles in VRAM that
have to be swapped out to create an animation, it’s enough to shift the colors within the
palette positions to achieve the same visual effect. This can be verified right in Aseprite:
if you move the white color to the first position of the palette (for example, undoing and
redoing the change with Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y to compare before and after), the waterfall gives the
impression of movement, since all the colors in the gradient shift one position. Repeating
that shift several times completes the entire animation cycle.
Aftershiftingthecolorsbyoneposition,thewaterfall’swateralreadyshowsslightmovement
compared to the original state.
3. Saving each step of the cycle as a separate image
To keep the programming process as simple as possible, it’s better not to try to save the
palette animation as such, but instead to create a series of tiny images (8x8 pixels, i.e., a
190

=== PAGE 197 ===
Figure 94: The waterfall background in Aseprite
Figure 95: The waterfall palette after shifting a color
191

=== PAGE 198 ===
single tile), each with a slightly different (shifted) version of the waterfall’s palette. These
images aren’t used for their graphical content: they serve solely as containers from which
SGDK can read the palette data corresponding to each step of the cycle.
Thefirstfileissavedwiththepaletteinitsoriginalposition(inindexedcolormode,exported
asPNG);then,foreachsubsequentstep,thepaletteisshiftedonepositionfurtherandsaved
under a different filename, until seven files in total are completed, one for each step of this
waterfall’s full cycle. The number of steps depends directly on how many colors make up
thegradientyouwanttoanimate: awaterfallwithsevenrelevanttonesneedssevenstepsto
complete a full cycle.
4. The starting point in SGDK
The example project already includes the seven 8x8 images just described and the waterfall
background, all declared in resources.res. The background is called BG1, and each of the
small palette images is named PC0 through PC6 (from “palette cycle”):
IMAGE BG1 "gfx/shinobi_waterfall.png" NONE
IMAGE PC0 "gfx/pc0.png" NONE
IMAGE PC1 "gfx/pc1.png" NONE
IMAGE PC2 "gfx/pc2.png" NONE
IMAGE PC3 "gfx/pc3.png" NONE

Thestartingcodeinmain.cisdeliberatelysimple: itloadsthepaletteanddrawsthewaterfall
background on the BG_B layer, with no animation yet, just as was done when displaying a
background for the first time in chapter 7:
#include <genesis.h>
#include "resources.h"

↪ TILE_USER_INDEX), 0, 0, FALSE, TRUE);

Compiling at this point results in a completely static waterfall.
5. Creating the palette cycle timer
The first step in animating the effect is to create a timer: an integer variable called
palette_timer, initialized to 0 and declared before int main() so it can also be used inside
a separate function later on. As is typical with this kind of timer (chap. 6), it’s incremented
192

=== PAGE 199 ===
once per pass through the main loop using palette_timer++ (equivalent to palette_timer
+= 1), so its value advances from 0 to 1, 2, 3, and so on, once per frame.
static s16 palette_timer = 0;
int main(bool hardReset) {
// ...
while (TRUE) {
palette_timer++;
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return 0;
}
6. Changing the palette based on the timer
To make something happen when the timer reaches a given value, if statements are used
to compare palette_timer against a specific number. In the first step (when palette_timer
equals 0), the same PAL_setPalette() function already familiar from previous chapters on
backgrounds is used, but instead of taking the palette data from the background itself, it’s
takenfromoneofthesmallPC0toPC6imagescreatedearlier(inthiscase,PC0,thepalettein
its original position).
Fromthere,therestofthesequenceisbuiltwiththesamechainedelse ifpattern,deciding
howmanyframesshouldpassbeforethecycleadvances(tenframesinthisexample,i.e.,one-
sixth of a second at 60 frames per second) and changing, at each step, both the comparison
number and the palette file used: PC0 at frame 0, PC1 at frame 10, PC2 at frame 20, and so on
up to PC6 at frame 60:
if (palette_timer == 0)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC0.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 10)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC1.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 20)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC2.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 30)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC3.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 40)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC4.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 50)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC5.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 60)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC6.palette->data, DMA);
7. Restarting the cycle and choosing the right data type
With the seven conditions now in place, one problem remains: palette_timer will keep in-
crementing indefinitely past 60, with no condition set up to handle those future values. If it
had been declared as int (a 32-bit integer), the timer would take an extremely long time to
overflowandwrapbackto0onitsown,soinpracticethecyclewouldneverrestartnaturally.
193

=== PAGE 200 ===
The solution is to add an eighth condition that, upon reaching a reference value, manually
resets the timer.
There’s an important detail about how to reset it: since palette_timer++ runs at the end
of every pass through the loop, after all the if comparisons, assigning palette_timer = 0
directly in that condition would mean that, after the subsequent increment, the timer would
endupat1onthenextframe, completelyskippingthe palette_timer == 0 conditionandits
PC0palette. Thesolutionistoassignpalette_timer = -1instead,sothat,aftertheincrement,
the value effectively ends up at 0 for the following frame, closing the cycle correctly:
else if (palette_timer == 70)
palette_timer = -1;
There’s no fixed answer regarding the exact reference value for the reset (70 in
the example above): shifting that point to 69 could, in theory, produce a slightly
more even transition between the last step of the cycle and the first, but there’s
no definitive reason to prefer one value over the other. It’s worth trying both (69
and70)experimentallyonyourownprojectandkeepingwhicheverlookssmoother,
rather than assuming one is “the correct” one.
This need for a transient negative value also affects the data type used for palette_timer:
since int is a 32-bit integer, that’s more space than is needed for this purpose. An s8 (an
8-bit signed integer, roughly -128 to 127) would be more than enough for a 70-frame cycle,
but it’s better to use s16 (a 16-bit signed integer, with a range of several thousand in both
directions) as a more flexible option in case higher timer values are needed in the future (for
longerorslowercycles, forexample), withoutgoingaslargeasa32-bitint. Inanycase, the
essential point is that the chosen type must be signed, since without that, the -1 assignment
wouldn’t have the intended effect.
8. Compiling the result and extracting a function
Once saved and compiled, the resulting effect strongly resembles a waterfall animated by
movingwater. Whenreconstructingthepaletteofanexistingcommercialgamefrommemory
orfromascreenshot,it’snormalnottoachieveaperfectmatchwiththeoriginal: it’senough
for the result to be visually convincing for your own project. The effect looks even better
once foreground elements and sprites are added in front of the waterfall. By changing the
numbersusedintheconditions(boththeintervalbetweenframechangesandtheresetpoint),
the perceived speed of the cycle can be adjusted, faster or slower as the design requires.
Finally, since keeping all this palette-changing code directly inside the main loop is untidy,
it’s worth extracting it into a separate function, following the same pattern already used in
previous chapters: a prototype declared before main(), the function body defined afterward,
and a single call to that function inside the main loop:
#include <genesis.h>
#include "resources.h"
static s16 palette_timer = 0;
static void paletteCycler();
int main(bool hardReset) {
VDP_drawImageEx(BG_B, &BG1, TILE_ATTR_FULL(PAL0, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE,
↪ TILE_USER_INDEX), 0, 0, FALSE, TRUE);
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, BG1.palette->data, DMA);
194

=== PAGE 201 ===
while (TRUE) {
paletteCycler();
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return 0;
}
static void paletteCycler() {
if (palette_timer == 0)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC0.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 10)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC1.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 20)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC2.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 30)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC3.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 40)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC4.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 50)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC5.palette->data, DMA);
else if (palette_timer == 60)
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, PC6.palette->data, DMA);

Chapter 30 — Palette Fades
Thepreviouschaptercoveredpalettecycling: atechniqueforanimatingascenebyrepeatedly
alternating between several pre-prepared palettes. This chapter closes out Part III with a
related but distinct technique: instead of assigning palettes directly and immediately with
PAL_setPalette(), the color data is taken, stored in an array in RAM, and that array is used
togetherwithSGDK’sPAL_fadeIn()functiontomakethepaletteappeargraduallyfromblack,
rather than all at once.
Thepracticalgoalistoeliminatethe“flicker”orabrupt-loadeffectthatoftenoccurswhenthe
differentgraphicalelementsofascreen(background,foreground,sprites)loadtheirpalettes
in a staggered way that’s visible to the player. Many commercial games solve exactly this
detail so that a level’s opening screen looks polished instead of improvised.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to be clear on:
• The use of PAL_setPalette() to assign palettes to different planes and sprites from
graphicresourcesdefinedinresources.res(Chapter7,“Displayingbackgroundsonthe
Mega Drive”).
• TheconceptofCRAMastheVDP’scolormemory,withitsfourpalettesof16colorseach
(Chapter 2, “The VDP in depth”).
• TheconceptofanarrayinCasastructurecapableofstoringmultiplevaluesofthesame
type under a single name.
• SGDK’s build cycle via resources.res and resource generation.
• Basic handling of a graphics editor in indexed color mode (for example, Aseprite).
1. The problem: a staggered, visible palette load
A simple beat ’em up–style example serves as a starting point, with four palettes assigned
independently via PAL_setPalette(): one for the background (PAL0), another for the fore-
ground (PAL1), another for the player sprite (PAL2), and another for the enemy sprite (PAL3),
each pulling its color data from its own graphic resource.
PAL_setPalette(PAL0, background_image.palette->data, DMA);
PAL_setPalette(PAL1, foreground_image.palette->data, DMA);
PAL_setPalette(PAL2, player_sprite.palette->data, DMA);
PAL_setPalette(PAL3, enemy_sprite.palette->data, DMA);
ReloadingtheROMrepeatedlyintheemulatorshowsthattheentrytransitionlooksnoticeably
staggered: the background appears first, and then, with a slight offset, the foreground and
the sprites follow. The result feels unpolished. If instead the whole graphic set appeared
197

=== PAGE 204 ===
through a slow fade from black, the transition would look far more deliberate, and that’s the
effect built in this chapter.
2. Consolidating the four palettes into a single image
The first step is to comment out (disable) the four PAL_setPalette() calls used so far, since
they’ll be replaced by a different mechanism based on an array.
Instead of maintaining four independent palettes, the technique consists of storing all 64
availablecolors(16colorsforeachoftheMegaDrive’s4palettes)withinthepaletteofasingle
image — in this case, the background image. That image’s palette is expanded to 64 slots —
16perrow—sothatthefirstrowcorrespondstowhatwouldbePAL0,thesecondrowtoPAL1,
the third to PAL2, and the fourth to PAL3. The procedure essentially consists of copying and
pasting, in the graphics editor, the colors from the palettes of the other images (foreground,
player sprite, enemy sprite) into the corresponding rows of the background image’s palette.
Figure 97: Consolidated palette of the background image, with 64 colors in four rows of 16
The full consolidated palette, showing the range from 0 to 63 with the four rows of 16 colors
corresponding to the four original palettes.
Eachpalettemustoccupyexactlyitsrowof16colors, eveniftheoriginalgraphicusesfewer
colorsthanareavailable: theleftoverslotsarefilledwithblackoranotherfillercolor,andare
neverleftoutoforder,becauseotherwisethecolorsfromthedifferentpaletteswouldendup
mixed and misaligned relative to the indices the code will later use.
If the background image was already loaded previously in resources.res, SGDK
only regenerates resources when it detects a change in that file, or when a full
rebuild (clean) is requested. So, after modifying only the palette of an already-
existing image, it’s a good idea to force resource regeneration by adding and then
removing any character in resources.res (saving both times), or by doing a full
198

=== PAGE 205 ===
project clean before rebuilding. Otherwise, the ROM will keep using the previous
palette data.
3. Creating the array and copying the color data with mem-
cpy()
The next step takes place in main.c: an array is created that can hold the 64 color values.
Since each color is represented as an unsigned 16-bit integer, the array is declared as u16,
withadescriptivenameandasizeof64slots,declaredbeforemain()justlikeanyotherglobal
variable.
u16 our_level_palette[64];
To move the color data from the background image into that array in RAM, memcpy() is used
— a standard C function (not specific to SGDK) that copies blocks of memory and takes three
parameters: the copy destination, the copy source, and the number of bytes to copy.
memcpy(&our_level_palette[0], background_image.palette->data, 64 * 2);
The first parameter is the destination: the name of the array just created, preceded by the &
symbol (memory address) and with [0] as the starting position, since the write should begin
at the start of the array. The second parameter is the source of the data: taken from the
backgroundimage’spalette,usingthesameexpressionusedearliertoassignpalettesdirectly,
i.e., background_image.palette->data.
The third and final parameter indicates the size of the data to transfer, expressed in bytes.
Since each color takes up two bytes, it’s worth writing 64 * 2 explicitly rather than 128,
precisely to make the math itself document the fact that each of the 64 colors occupies two
bytesofdata. Theresultisequivalenttowriting128directly,butthe64 * 2formreadsbetter
as implicit documentation of the calculation.
At this point, the our_level_palette array already holds the color data in RAM, but that
copy by itself has no visible effect on screen: memcpy() only moves bytes in memory, without
interacting at all with the VDP or with the console’s active palette.
4. Applying the fade with PAL_fadeIn()
For the color data stored in the array to actually affect what’s shown on screen, and to do
so through a gradual transition, SGDK’s PAL_fadeIn() function is used, documented as an
effect that makes a palette appear gradually from black to the specified color (fade in, black
to specified color effect):
void PAL_fadeIn(u16 fromCol, u16 toCol, const u16 *pal, u16 numFrame, bool async);
The function takes five parameters:
• fromCol: the starting color index of the fade, within the range 0-63. Since the consol-
idated palette holds 64 colors in total, and each original palette (PAL0 through PAL3)
occupies 16 consecutive slots within that range (PAL0 from 0 to 15, PAL1 from 16 to 31,
andsoon),it’spossibletotreatthefadeasasinglecontinuousblockfrom0to63instead
of four separate blocks.
• toCol: the ending index of the fade, also within 0-63, and this last index is included in
the effect. To make all four palettes fade in at once from black, the values 0 and 63 are
used, covering all 64 colors (index 63 corresponds to the last of the palette’s 64 colors).
199

=== PAGE 206 ===
• pal: thesourceofthecolordata,i.e.,thenameofthearraycreatedearlier,withoutneed-
ing to prefix it with the & symbol or specify any position in brackets, since the function
expects a pointer to the whole array directly.
• numFrame: the duration of the fade expressed in frames. Since the Mega Drive runs at
60 frames per second (in the region used as the reference throughout this manual), a
value of 60 corresponds to one second of duration, 120 to two seconds, and 30 to half a
second.
• async: abooleanthatdetermineswhethertherestofthegame’sprocessescancontinue
while the fade is in progress (true), or whether, on the contrary, all other game logic
must wait for the fade to finish before continuing (false). For now it’s fine to leave it as
true; section 7 revisits this parameter in detail.
PAL_fadeIn(0, 63, our_level_palette, 60, true);
5. First test: the fade works, but with an initial flash
Withthe newPAL_fadeIn() callin place, the project is saved, built, and run. The fadecan be
seen,thoughit’shardtoobserveclearlyatadurationof60frames,soithelpstotemporarily
increase the frame count — say, to 300 — to make it much slower and more obvious during
testing:
PAL_fadeIn(0, 63, our_level_palette, 300, true);
For most screen transitions, a value between 20 and 30 frames tends to work better in prac-
tice, reserving much longer durations for deliberately dramatic effects, such as the gradual
appearance of an imposing enemy.
Although the fade itself works correctly, a brief flash of some graphic elements can still be
seen right at the start, before the fade becomes noticeable. The cause is the following: the
calltoPAL_fadeIn()happensasthelaststepbeforeloadingallthegraphicresources(tileset,
map, sprites), and memcpy() only moves the color data into RAM without touching the VDP’s
activepalette. Asaresult,whilethosegraphicresourcesareloading,theconsoleisstillusing
an SGDK default palette, and it’s precisely that default palette, briefly applied to the newly
loaded graphics, that shows up as an unwanted flash on screen before the fade begins.
The flash of the SGDK default palette, with colors clearly unrelated to the palette defined for
the level, briefly visible before the fade begins.
6. Removing the flash with PAL_setColors()
The solution is to explicitly set every color in the palette to black before loading any graphic
resources, so that even though the VDP uses its default palette during loading, that default
palette is already black and produces no visible flash. This is done with the PAL_setColors()
function, placed right before loading the tileset:
void PAL_setColors(u16 index, const u16 *pal, u16 count, TransferMethod tm);
PAL_setColors(0, palette_black, 64, DMA);
Thefirstparameter(index)isthecolorindextostartwritingat;sincethewholepaletteshould
be affected, 0 is used. The second parameter (pal) is the set of RGB intensities to apply; in-
steadofmanuallyspecifyingthevaluesforblack,SGDKalreadyprovidesapredefinedpalette
called palette_black, ready to use directly.
200

=== PAGE 207 ===
Figure 98: Flash of the SGDK default palette before the fade
The third parameter (count) behaves differently from how the first two parameters of
PAL_fadeIn()did: whereasPAL_fadeIn()tookastartingindexandaninclusiveendingindex,
in PAL_setColors() this parameter doesn’t represent an index at all, but a count of colors
to affect starting from the initial index. This is a difference in convention between the two
functions worth keeping in mind so as not to make a mistake by analogy: to cover all 64
colors of the palette (indices 0 through 63 inclusive), you don’t write 63, but 64, since you’re
counting 64 colors starting from index 0.
The fourth and final parameter (tm, transfer method) indicates the method used to transfer
to video memory; for this purpose, DMA is enough, with no need to dig into the available
alternatives yet (CPU, DMA_QUEUE, DMA_QUEUE_COPY).
With this change, the full sequence looks like this:
memcpy(&our_level_palette[0], background_image.palette->data, 64 * 2);
PAL_setColors(0, palette_black, 64, DMA);
VDP_loadTileSet(...);
// ... rest of graphic resource loading (map, sprites) ...
PAL_fadeIn(0, 63, our_level_palette, 60, true);
First the color data is copied into the our_level_palette array (no visible effect yet); then
every color of the active palette is set to black with PAL_setColors(); next the graphic re-
sources are loaded, which now produce no flash at all because the palette is already black;
and finally PAL_fadeIn() is applied to gradually bring in the real colors from that black.
Saving, building, and running the ROM again with this order produces a clean fade from
black, with no flash of graphic resources using the default palette.
Theorderoftheinstructionsisdecisive: ifPAL_setColors()isplacedafterloadingthegraphic
201

=== PAGE 208 ===
resources instead of before, the same default-palette flash observed originally reappears.
PAL_setColors() must always run before loading the graphic resources, never after.
7. The fifth parameter of PAL_fadeIn(): true versus false
Returning to the fifth parameter of PAL_fadeIn(), deferred from section 4: when it’s set to
true, the rest of the game’s processes (sprite updates, input handling, etc.) keep running
normally while the fade is in progress. When it’s changed to false, on the other hand, all
other game logic stays paused until the fade finishes completely.
PAL_fadeIn(0, 63, our_level_palette, 300, false);
Testing the ROM with this parameter set to false shows that, while the image fades in very
slowly from black, the sprites remain completely still: the main loop code responsible for
updating sprites and handling player input doesn’t run until the fade finishes.
Setting the parameter back to true, the sprites can move normally again while the fade’s
colors keep appearing gradually. In most cases true is the more suitable choice, reserving
false for specific scenarios where you deliberately want to fully pause the game’s logic for
thedurationofthetransition(forexample,anarrativetransitionscreenwherenointeraction
should be possible).
8. Partial fades: fading only part of the palette
The first two parameters of PAL_fadeIn() determine which range of color indices is affected
by the fade, and that range doesn’t have to cover the whole palette. If the range is set to
0 and 15, only the first 16 colors of the palette are faded (the ones that were PAL0, i.e., the
background), while the rest of the palette stays black:
PAL_fadeIn(0, 15, our_level_palette, 60, true);
With the range limited to 0-15, the background appears with its real colors while the fore-
ground and sprites remain black, as silhouettes.
Extending the range to 0 and 31 includes the first 32 colors of the palette — that is, both the
background and the foreground — while the player and enemy sprites (PAL2 and PAL3) still
remain black.
This is the foundation on which more elaborate staggered fade effects are built, where dif-
ferent parts of the scene appear at different moments instead of all at once. Achieving that
effect requires preparing additional arrays with different palettes and experimenting with
PAL_fadeIn() calls staggered over time (for example, triggering each call with a slight delay
relative to the previous one), though working out that example with full code is beyond the
scope of this chapter: the partial ranges 0-15 and 0-31 are already enough to demonstrate
the underlying principle.

Chapter 31 — D-Pad Controls
From sprites that are visible to sprites that move: position variables, a function of your own,
the if statement, and dynamic animation assignment based on player input
Part III left the graphical side of a playable character fully resolved: how to display it on
screen, how to animate it, and how to build its own animation sheet. What’s missing is the
piece that turns all of that into a game: letting the player control the character. This chapter
tackles that piece through the simplest possible example — the D-pad of a single joypad —
and along the way introduces two programming tools that will accompany the rest of this
manual: functions of your own and the if statement.
Thestartingpointisacharacteralreadyonscreen,standingstillatthecenter,playingafixed
animation. Everything that follows aims, first, to make that character move and, afterward,
to make that movement respond to what the player presses on the D-pad instead of being an
automatic motion.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it’s best to have covered:
• Chapter 21, “How to Display Sprites”: the Sprite* pointer, SPR_addSprite(),
SPR_setPosition(), and SPR_update(), which are reused directly here.
• Chapter 22, “Creating Sprites and Animation Sheets”: in particular, the idea that an
animationsheetisusuallydrawnfacingnaturallytowardoneside,andthattheopposite
side is handled with a horizontal flip instead of drawing a second sheet.
• Chapter 23, “Sprite Animation”: SPR_setAnim() and the practice of identifying each ani-
mation with a named constant (for example, via #define) instead of a bare number.
• Chapter 6, on data types: in particular, why it’s best to declare a screen coordinate as
s16 rather than int.
1. From fixed coordinates to position variables

3. Order matters: declare before use
Beforemovingon,let’sseewhathappensiftheorderisreversed,becausetheresultingerror

Unlikeother,moremodernlanguagesthatanalyzeanentirefilebeforerunninganything,the

reaches the line player_x += 1; inside handle_input(), if it hasn’t yet seen any declaration

further down: it simply doesn’t recognize it, reports the error, and halts compilation right
there.
Thepracticalruleissimple,anditappliesgenerally,notjusttothisparticularcase:
any variable (or function) has to be declared earlier, further up in the file, than the
first place where it’s used.
Moving handle_input() back to its original position, after the declarations of player_x and
player_y, makes the error disappear.

Chapter 32 — Button Controls
and Event-Based Reading
Chapter 31 solved character movement through continuous polling: on every frame, han-
dle_input() asks JOY_readJoypad() alloveragainwhat’sbeingpressedatthatinstant. That
approach works well for the D-pad, but it isn’t the only way SGDK offers to handle player
input, and in fact it isn’t the best fit for everything. This chapter introduces the second ap-
proach: an event-based mechanism, where the code doesn’t actively ask on every frame, but
instead SGDK automatically notifies it whenever something changed on the joypad.
The title speaks of “button controls” following the more common convention, but it’s worth
clarifying from the start that the real distinction isn’t D-pad versus buttons, but continuous
versus one-shot: in a menu navigated with the D-pad, the event mechanism is the right fit,
andinanattackthat’shelddown,continuouspollingistherightfit,eventhoughinbothcases
the physical control is the same kind of button. The second half of the chapter picks up this
distinctionwithaconcreteexample: anattackanimationthatneedstoplayoutinfullevenif
the player releases the button before it finishes, which requires introducing a timer.
Prerequisites
• Having completed Chapter 31 (“D-pad Controls”): the handle_input() function,
JOY_readJoypad(), the BUTTON_* constants, the & operator for reading a single bit, and
the use of if / else if / && / ! already explained there won’t be repeated in detail here.
• Having completed Chapter 6 (“C Applied to Retro Development: Data Types, Limited
Memory, and Pointers”): the u8, u16, and s16 types, and the criterion of choosing the
smallest type that fits the expected range of values, are revisited in this chapter for the
attack timer variables.
• Ideally,havingcompletedChapter23(“SpriteAnimation”): thetimingfieldofananima-
tion in resources.res is measured in sixtieths of a second per frame, a unit this chapter

1. Two ways of reacting to player input
Before writing code, it’s worth looking at how controls behave in existing games, because
thedifferenceiseasiertonoticebyplayingthanbyreading. Inatypicalplatformeroraction
game, moving with the D-pad is a continuous process: while the player holds the right side
down, the character keeps moving right, frame after frame, without needing to release and
press again. Attacking or jumping, on the other hand, is usually a one-shot event: pressing
thebuttononcetriggerstheactionexactlyonce,andeveniftheplayerkeepsthebuttonheld
down, the action doesn’t repeat until it’s released and pressed again.

Holdingdowntheattackbuttondoesn’tproducerepeatedhits: youhavetoreleaseandpress

There are, however, situations where the D-pad, normally associated with continuous move-

In an options menu, each D-pad press moves the cursor exactly one position, no matter how
long the button is held down.
In short, the choice between continuous polling and a one-shot event doesn’t depend on

2. The event mechanism: JOY_setEventHandler() and a func-
tion with a fixed signature
SGDKoffersasecondwaytoreadthejoypad, differentfromcalling JOY_readJoypad() inside
themainloop: registeringyourownfunctionthatSGDKwillcallautomaticallyeverytimethe
state of some joypad changes. That function has to have an exact signature, predefined by
SGDK through the JoyEventCallback type:
213

=== PAGE 220 ===
Figure 101: Options menu navigated with one-shot D-pad control
typedef void JoyEventCallback(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state);
Its three parameters indicate, in order, which joypad changed (joy), which buttons changed
state since the last reading (changed), and what the full current state is (state). Unlike han-
dle_input(), written with total freedom of name, parameters, and how it’s called, this func-
tion has to respect that exact three-parameter u16 signature so SGDK can invoke it correctly.
The function’s name is indeed free — in this manual it’s called joyEvent, but you can choose
any other name — as long as the order and type of the parameters are preserved.
Insideit,changedindicates,bitbybit,whichbuttonschangedstatesincethelastreading,and
stateindicates, alsobitbybit, whichonesarepressedrightnow. Combiningbothwiththe&
operator— forexample, changed & state & BUTTON_RIGHT —is equivalentto asking“did the
right button change state, and is that new state pressed?”, which is exactly the definition of
“the right button was just pressed”: if the button was already pressed on the previous frame,
changed would be zero for that bit and the whole expression would come out to zero, even
though state still marks the button as pressed.
It’s worth pausing on this expression for a moment, because there’s an alterna-
tive form, documented in the official SGDK wiki, that separates the two operators:
(changed & BUTTON_X) && (state & BUTTON_X). For a single button, both forms
are mathematically equivalent. Since BUTTON_X has a single bit set to 1, the result
of changed & state & BUTTON_X is nonzero exactly when that bit is set to 1 in
both changed and state; and that’s precisely the same thing evaluated separately
bychanged & BUTTON_X(nonzeroifthebitchanged)andstate & BUTTON_X(nonzero
if the bit is pressed), combined with &&. This equivalence holds only for testing a
single button at a time: it can’t simply be generalized to a mask that combines
several different buttons with | (for example, BUTTON_A | BUTTON_B). In that case,
changed & state & mask requires that there be a bit within the mask that’s set si-
multaneously in changed and in state, while (changed & mask) && (state & mask)
214

=== PAGE 221 ===
issatisfiedifsomebitofthemaskchangedandsomebitofthemask(notnecessar-
ily the same one) is pressed — two different conditions that can produce different
results. For a single button this distinction disappears, but it’s worth keeping in
mind before copying the pattern into a condition with multiple buttons.
The other point where this function departs from what’s been seen so far is how it gets trig-
gered. Thecustomfunctionsbuiltsofar,likehandle_input(), needanexplicitcallinsidethe
mainlooptorunoneveryframe. Thisfunction,bycontrast,isnevercalleddirectlyanywhere:
it’s registered once, in main(), with JOY_setEventHandler():
void JOY_setEventHandler(JoyEventCallback *CB);
passingitthefunction’sname(withoutparentheses,sincehereitisn’tbeingcalledbutrather
pointed out to SGDK):

From that registration onward, SGDK takes care of invoking joyEvent() automatically every
time it detects a change on the joypad, without the main loop having to actively ask about it.

The BUTTON_A, BUTTON_B, and BUTTON_C constants, just like BUTTON_RIGHT and the rest of the
direction constants already used in Chapter 31, remain unchanged in SGDK 2.11.
3. Commenting out code versus deleting it
A habit worth adopting early, and one that becomes especially relevant when switching back
and forth between testing movement in joyEvent() and returning it to handle_input(), is
tellingapartwhencommentingoutcodewith//makessenseandwhenitdoesn’t. Comment-
ing out code makes sense when there’s a real intention to bring it back later — for example,
to compare two alternative behaviors while deciding which one to use — but any line that’s
known to be useless going forward should simply be deleted rather than left commented out.
Commented-out code that piles up without a clear purpose is, over time, a source of bugs:
it becomes hard to tell at a glance which commented block is intentional and which is just
something that was never cleaned up, and a stray line that gets accidentally uncommented
along with the rest of a block can introduce unwanted behavior, such as a position variable
that keeps incrementing with no condition attached, hard to trace if the file has too many
commented-out fragments scattered without any criteria.
4. A first attempt at an attack, and why it falls short
With the event mechanism already tested, the rest of the chapter focuses on a more realistic
example: an attack animation triggered with the B button, using the character’s animation
sheetalreadyseeninpreviouschapters. Theleastelaboratereactionwouldbetoadd,directly
inside handle_input(), one more condition for the B button alongside the ones that already
exist for the four directions:
if (value & BUTTON_B) SPR_setAnim(player, ANIM_UPPER);
215

=== PAGE 222 ===
Theproblemwiththisapproachshowsupimmediatelywhentestingit: sincehandle_input()
re-evaluatesthisconditiononeveryoneofthe60framespersecondforaslongascontinuous
polling runs, holding down the B button plays the attack animation uninterrupted, instead of
a single hit. This is exactly the continuous behavior section 1 identified as unsuitable for an
attack action: the player would expect to press the button once, see the full hit play out, and
only then be able to attack again.
Simply pulling this code out of handle_input() and putting it into joyEvent(), using changed
& state instead of continuous polling, fixes the repetition problem but introduces a new one:
theeventonlytriggersSPR_setAnim()duringthesingleframeinwhichthechangeisdetected,
so the full animation never gets to play — you barely see one loose frame of the hit before
theidlecode(stillpollingcontinuouslyinhandle_input())interruptsitandinstantlysnapsit
back to the idle or walking animation.
What’s missing, then, isn’t simply choosing one of the two mechanisms, but combining them:
use the event to trigger the attack exactly once, and some sort of elapsed-time count to keep
thatanimationonscreenforaslongasitlasts,and,inthemeantime,tokeeptheD-padfrom
interrupting the attack or being interrupted by it.
5. A timer to sustain the animation: attack_timer and at-
tack_duration
The solution consists of adding two new variables, declared alongside the rest of the pro-
gram’s global variables: attack_timer, which starts at zero and keeps count of how many
frames the current attack animation has been running, and attack_duration, a constant in-
dicating how many frames that animation should last before returning to idle. Since both
quantities are always non-negative and small in range — there’s no need to represent large
or negative numbers — it makes sense to declare them as u16 rather than int, following the
same criterion from Chapter 6 about choosing the type best suited to the expected range of
values(it’salsothesametypealreadyusedbychangedandstateinthejoyEvent()signature):
u16 attack_timer = 0;
u16 attack_duration; // computed further below
The value of attack_duration isn’t picked by eye: it’s computed from the same data already
used in Chapter 23 to define an animation’s speed in resources.res. If the attack animation
has, say, seven frames, and each frame is configured to last eight sixtieths of a second (the
sametimingfieldoftheSPRITEresourceexplainedinthatchapter),thetotalduration,inthat
same unit of sixtieths of a second, is the product of both numbers:
#define ATTACK_DURATION (7 * 8) // 7 frames x 8 sixtieths of a second = 56
This calculation is exactly reproducible for any other animation: it’s enough to multiply the
number of frames by the configured duration of each frame in resources.res, as long as —
as is usually the case — all the frames of that animation share the same duration.
6. Starting the attack and suspending the D-pad while it
lasts
With both variables already declared, the code inside joyEvent() that triggers the attack
looks like this:
216

=== PAGE 223 ===
void joyEvent(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state)
{
if ((changed & state & BUTTON_B) && attack_timer == 0)
{
SPR_setAnim(player, ANIM_UPPER);
attack_timer += 1;
}
}
Besides changing the animation, the condition increments attack_timer by one as soon as
theBbuttonpressisdetected,andrequiresattack_timertobezerobeforestarting: without
thislastaddition,holdingBdowncouldrestarttheattackanimationoneveryframeinwhich
SGDK detected the button as just pressed. In practice this would no longer happen anyway,
because, as we’ll see next, handle_input() stays suspended during the attack; even so, it’s a
cheap check in terms of CPU that avoids restarting the count unnecessarily.
The other change is in the main loop: the call to handle_input(), which in Chapter 31 was
made unconditionally, is now guarded:
if (attack_timer == 0) handle_input();
Since this condition has just one line of code to run if it’s true, there’s no need to wrap it
in braces — both forms are equivalent in C, and using the brace-less version for a single
statement is simply a matter of style, though it’s worth going back to braces as soon as the
blockgrowspastoneline,toavoidmistakeswhenaddingcodelaterwithoutnoticingitended
up outside the if. As long as attack_timer is zero, handle_input() runs as usual and the D-
pad works just like in Chapter 31; as soon as the player presses B, attack_timer stops being
zero and handle_input() simply stops being called, which freezes the character’s movement
during the attack, exactly as intended.
There’s a syntax detail here that’s a classic source of bugs in C: the condition attack_timer
== 0 uses two equal signs, because it’s a logical comparison (“is it equal to zero?”), while
assigningavaluetoavariable—asinattack_timer = 0,whichappearsfurtherdown—uses
asingleequalsign. Confusingthetwooperatorsisaneasymistaketomake,onethecompiler
doesn’talwayscatch,sinceattack_timer = 0insideanifconditionisalsoavalidexpression
in C (it assigns zero and then evaluates that zero as false), only with a completely different
effect than intended.
7. Keeping the count going while the attack plays out
Incrementing attack_timer just once, when B is pressed, isn’t enough: it needs to keep
adding one for every frame that passes while the attack is in progress, so that it eventu-
ally reaches attack_duration and the D-pad is freed again. That continuous increment can’t
liveinjoyEvent(), whichonlyrunsattheone-offinstantthebutton’sstatechanges; ithasto
run frame by frame, like the rest of the main loop. The solution is to add, alongside the if
(attack_timer == 0) handle_input(); already written, an else if condition covering the
rest of the frames while the attack is underway:
if (attack_timer == 0)
handle_input();
else if (attack_timer > 0 && attack_timer < attack_duration)
attack_timer += 1;
This condition introduces two comparison operators — greater than (>) and less than (<) —
217

=== PAGE 224 ===
that haven’t appeared in this manual until now, though their meaning is the same as in ordi-
nary arithmetic. The full condition, attack_timer > 0 && attack_timer < attack_duration,
reads as “while the attack has already started but hasn’t finished yet,” and when it holds, it
simply adds one more to the counter, frame after frame.
Before tackling the missing step, it’s worth verifying that the attack_duration calculation
actually matters: deliberately changing it to a value that’s too high — 60 instead of 56, say,
for the example of seven frames at eight sixtieths of a second each — causes the animation
to complete its run and start over from the first frame before the counter gets around to
releasing the D-pad, producing a small, visible repeat of the hit.
Figure 102: A miscalculated attack_duration produces a repeat of the hit
With attack_duration set to 60 instead of 56, the seven-frame animation has already finished
its run but the timer still hasn’t released the D-pad, so the hit repeats from the start before
the character can move again.
8. Closing the loop: resetting the timer, and simplifying
with else
One step is still missing: at some point, attack_timer has to go back to zero so the cycle can
repeat. Without that last step, once the count up to attack_duration finishes, the counter
wouldsimplystopincrementing(becauseneitherofthetwoconditionsalreadywrittenwould
still be true), but it would never go back to zero, leaving the D-pad frozen forever.
The missing step is adding a third condition that detects when attack_timer has reached
exactly attack_duration, and in that case resets it to zero, freeing the D-pad again. That
conditioncouldbewrittenexplicitly,comparingattack_timer == attack_duration,butsince
it’sexactlytheoneandonlycasenotalreadycoveredbythetwopreviousconditions(neither
zero, nor a value between zero and attack_duration), a plain else, with no condition of its
own, is enough to catch everything left over:
218

=== PAGE 225 ===

handle_input();
else if (attack_timer > 0 && attack_timer < attack_duration)
attack_timer += 1;
else

This kind of simplification is convenient, but it demands close attention: an else with no
conditionrunsitscodeeverytimenoneofthepreviousbranchesheld,soyouhavetobesure

one. Inthisparticularcase,withonlythreepossiblestatesforattack_timer(zero,inprogress,
orfinished),thesimplificationissafeandsavesanexplicitcomparison,butitisn’tatechnique
to apply without thinking in more complex chains of conditions.
With the logic now complete and tested, one last purely organizational adjustment is worth
making, in the same spirit that already motivated creating handle_input() in Chapter 31:
rather than leaving these three loose lines inside the main loop, wrap them in their own
function and call it from there, so the main loop stays readable at a glance:
void attack_function(void)
{
if (attack_timer == 0)
handle_input();
else if (attack_timer > 0 && attack_timer < attack_duration)

else

}
And in main():

There’soneremainingdifferenceworthhighlightingbetweenthetwocustomfunctionscoex-

registered once with JOY_setEventHandler() and never called directly from your own code.
With this reorganization, the result behaves exactly the same as before — the D-pad moves
the character normally, the B button triggers a single hit that plays all the way through, and
only then does the D-pad respond again — but with a considerably tidier main loop.
9. So, handle_input() or joyEvent()?
With the full example already built, it’s worth revisiting the question from section 1 with
moretogoon. Thegeneralrule—continuousmovementinhandle_input(),one-shotactions
in joyEvent() — remains a good starting point, but this very chapter showed two concrete
exceptions worth keeping in mind when designing the controls of your own game. On one
219

=== PAGE 226 ===
hand, an options menu navigated with the D-pad is one of the few common situations where
it makes sense to move the direction code into joyEvent(), precisely because that’s where a
one-shot movement is wanted, one per press, rather than continuous. On the other hand, an
actionthatneedstomeasurehowlongabuttonishelddown(achargedattack, forexample)
has to rely on continuous polling inside handle_input() (or an equivalent function), since
joyEvent() only reports the instant something changes, not how long a state is held.
The choice, then, isn’t a mechanical rule but a design decision that depends on what each
particularactionneeds: iftheplayerexpectsholdingthebuttondowntoproduceacontinuous
effect, use polling; if they expect each press to count as an isolated event, use the event
mechanism. This chapter’s attack example, with its timer, also shows that both mechanisms
can be combined within a single action when needed: an event to trigger something once,
and continuous polling to sustain it over time.

matches the search tool reports: if the number doesn’t match what you expected, that’s a

same frame, so handle_input() runs twice in a row within the same frame. Since each run
moves both characters one more pixel in the pressed direction, the visible result is double
the displacement per frame for both of them, not just for one.

single handle_input()— conditioning how many times that entire function gets called from
outsidecanhavesideeffectsoneverythinginsideit,notjustonthepartyoumeanttocontrol.
When a condition depends on a specific element (for example, whether player2 is attacking),
that condition has to be applied precisely to that element’s code, not to the whole function
that also contains the others.
228

=== PAGE 235 ===
An acknowledged limitation: this doesn’t scale beyond two
players
The pattern used throughout this chapter —adding a numeric suffix to each variable (value2,
player2_x, attack_timer2, attack_duration2) and duplicating each code block— works rea-
sonably well for two players, but it’s worth being honest about its limits: it doesn’t scale
comfortably to three or more. Each additional player would require manually repeating the
same set of loose variables and the same block of code inside handle_input(), joyEvent(),
and attack_function(), with the same risk of copy-paste errors already seen in section 2,
multiplied by each new character.
The natural path to generalizing this pattern beyond two players is to group all of a charac-
ter’sinformation—theirsprite,theirposition,theirattacktimer—intoasingledatastructure,
and replace the loose variables with an array of those structures (for example, Player play-
ers[MAX_PLAYERS]), so that adding another player is a matter of increasing the array’s size,
not writing a new block of code. This manual doesn’t develop that tool yet: C structs are
introduced later, when the enemy data for the capstone project is organized (chap. 53). That
same approach solves, in a much cleaner way, the scaling problem this chapter solved by
hand.

Chapter 34 — The Sound Chips -
YM2612 and PSG
HowtheMegaDrive’ssoundisorganizedunderthehood,beforewritingthefirstlineofcode
to play it
This part of the manual is devoted entirely to sound: how to play music and sound effects
with SGDK, and how to create those assets from scratch. Before getting there, it’s worth
spending an entire chapter understanding the hardware behind it, the same way chapter 2
paused on the VDP before showing the first line of graphics code. Chapter 1 already gave a
briefpreview: theMegaDrive’ssoundishandledbyaZilogZ80coprocessorthatcontrolstwo
separate chips — a Yamaha YM2612 FM synthesizer and a programmable sound generator
(PSG). This chapter picks that idea back up with the depth needed to understand, in the
following chapters, why SGDK’s sound functions are organized the way they are.
This is a purely conceptual chapter: there’s no code yet. The goal is to build a mental map
of “what each chip does and why two are needed,” so that when chapter 35 starts showing
how to play music with the XGM and XGM2 drivers, those design decisions already have a
foundation.
1. A separate sound subsystem, not a simple speaker
On a modern computer, playing a sound usually comes down to handing a series of numbers
to an audio card. On the Mega Drive, sound depends on a whole subsystem with its own
processor: the Z80. That architecture shapes, from the outset, how any sound function has
to be written in SGDK.
The 68000, which runs the game’s main program, doesn’t have direct, permanent access to
the sound chips’ registers. To write to them, it first needs to hand control of the data bus
overtotheZ80(abusarbitrationmechanism: whilethe68000hascontrol,theZ80ishalted,
and vice versa). The Z80, for its part, has its own 8 KB of memory (already mentioned in the
memory table in chapter 1) where it can run its own program completely independently of
the 68000.
Thisenablestwowaysofworkingwithsound,andunderstandingthedifferencehelpsexplain
why sound drivers exist at all:
• Direct control: the 68000 requests the bus from the Z80, halts it for an instant, writes
directlytotheYM2612orPSGregisters,andhandscontrolbacktotheZ80. It’ssimpleto
understand,buteverynoteoreverysoundchangerequireshaltingtheZ80andspending
68000 cycles in the process.
• AresidentprogramontheZ80: the68000loads,justonce(typicallyatgamestartup),
a small program into the Z80’s own memory. That program then runs autonomously,
reading commands from a shared memory area and translating them into the low-level
230

=== PAGE 237 ===
writesthattheYM2612andPSGneed. The68000nolongerhastohalttheZ80forevery
sound event: it’s enough to drop commands into that shared memory whenever needed.
The second approach is, in essence, that of a sound driver, and it’s the one SGDK uses.
Section 4 of this chapter comes back to this idea; for now it’s enough to keep this in mind:
whilethe68000keepsrunningthegame, theZ80hasitsownprogramdedicatedexclusively
to coordinating the two sound chips described below.
2. The YM2612: frequency modulation synthesis
TheYamaha YM2612isthechipresponsiblefortheMegaDrive’smostrecognizablesound:
those metallic timbres, bells, thick basses, and orchestral textures that set much of its music
apart from other consoles of the era. It has 6 channels, each capable of playing in stereo
(that is, with its own balance between the left and right audio channels).
The technique the YM2612 uses is called frequency modulation (FM) synthesis. In very
general terms — and this is already a deliberate simplification, without going into formulas
or the exact details of the circuitry — FM synthesis doesn’t record or play back a preexisting
sound wave: it generates one mathematically by combining several simple waves (usually
called“operators”)insuchawaythatsomemodulatethefrequencyofothers. Dependingon
how those operators are connected to each other and with what parameters (a combination
known as an “algorithm”), the result can sound like a bell, a bass, an organ, or a completely
artificial timbre with no equivalent in any real instrument. That’s where much of the Mega
Drive’s sonic identity comes from: the music doesn’t try to imitate real instruments with
recorded samples, but generates its own timbres from scratch, chip by chip. The details
of how a specific FM instrument is designed — how many operators are involved, what pa-
rameters exist, and how they’re adjusted — are covered in chapter 36, dedicated to music
creation; for now it’s enough to know that each of the YM2612’s six channels can have its
own instrument configured independently.
There’s a second function of the YM2612 worth knowing about from the start: it can play
backdigitized audio samples (PCM),thatis,recordedsoundinsteadofsynthesizedsound.
But that capability has a direct cost: playing PCM on the Mega Drive always occupies the
chip’s sixth channel, which then becomes unavailable for FM synthesis for as long as the
sample lasts. In practice, this means a game that uses digitized voices, recorded gunshots,
or sampled percussion is giving up, during those moments, one of the six available melodic
channels. This is a sound-design decision that has to be factored in from the moment the
composition is conceived, not a secondary technical detail.
3. The PSG: four channels inherited from the previous gen-
eration
The second sound chip is the PSG (Programmable Sound Generator), a much simpler
sound generator than the YM2612, inherited directly from the Master System, Sega’s previ-
ous 8-bit console. The PSG has 4 channels:
• 3 tone channels,capableofgeneratingsimplesquarewavesatagivenfrequency. This
is the same kind of “chiptune” sound characteristic of many 8-bit consoles and comput-
ers.
• 1 noise channel, designed to simulate explosions, percussion, wind, or any effect that
needs a more chaotic texture than a tuned note. In several PSG chips of this family,
the noise channel can also be synchronized with the frequency of the third tone chan-
nel, which makes it possible to generate noises with a recognizable pitch instead of flat
231

=== PAGE 238 ===
noise; this is a relatively fine-grained usage detail that will be revisited, if relevant, in
the chapter devoted to creating sound effects.
ThePSGdoesn’thavethetonalrichnessoftheYM2612(there’snoFMsynthesisortheability
to shape a complex timbre), but it’s much simpler to work with and uses far fewer resources
to produce a sound. Its most common use in Mega Drive games is twofold: reinforcing the
YM2612’s music with additional melodic lines or arpeggios (adding up to three more voices
to the six FM channels), and above all, handling short sound effects — jumps, shots, coins,
hits — without having to sacrifice any of the FM synthesizer’s more valuable six channels.
Thetwochipshavedifferentorigins: theYM2612isexclusivetotheMegaDriveand
didn’t exist in earlier Sega hardware, while the PSG is the same type of chip that
was already used in the Master System. That continuity is one of the mechanisms
that lets the Mega Drive run Master System games in its compatibility mode: that
legacy mode only needs the Z80 and the PSG, without relying on the YM2612.
4. Why a sound driver is needed
With two chips of such different characteristics — six FM channels with PCM capability on
oneside,foursimpletone-and-noisechannelsontheother—coordinatingbothfromscratch,
writing directly to their registers every time a change is needed, would be impractical for a
real game. A game needs to simultaneously play a background music track (which may be
using several YM2612 and PSG channels at once) and trigger specific sound effects (a jump,
ashot, an explosion)withoutthoseeffectscutting offorsteppingon themusicthat’splaying.
This is why SGDK doesn’t expose sound as a simple function that “writes to the chip,” but
rather through a sound driver: a program that runs on the Z80 (following the second ap-
proach described in section 1) and is responsible for deciding, at every moment, which chan-
nelofwhichchipisdoingwhat. Thegamecode,runningonthe68000,doesn’tneedtoknow
exactly which YM2612 register to write to in order to play a given note: it asks the driver
to “play this music” or “play this effect,” and it’s the driver that internally figures out how to
distribute those requests among the available channels, including what to do when a sound
effect needs a channel that’s currently occupied by the music.
SGDK includes more than one sound driver, with different capabilities and different data for-
mats — the most important ones are XGM and its successor, XGM2 — and choosing between
them is one of the first practical decisions that will come up in chapter 35. For now, the im-
portant thing is to hold on to the concept: the driver is the layer that translates the game’s
intentions(“playthissong,”“playthiseffect”)intothelow-level,channel-by-channelhandling
of two chips with very different rules from each other.
5. Thinking in channels, not just instruments
A practical consequence of everything above, and perhaps the most important idea to take
away from this chapter, is that composing or programming the sound of a Mega Drive game
forces you to think in terms of concrete channels, not just abstract instruments. On a
modern computer with practically unlimited audio synthesis, a composer can think “I need
a bass, a drum kit, two melodic voices, and a background layer” without worrying about
whether there’s physical room for all of that at once. On the Mega Drive, that question has a
strict numerical answer: there are six FM channels and four PSG channels, period.
This has very concrete effects on how a game’s music and sound are designed:
• If a song uses all six of the YM2612’s channels to sound with its full tonal richness,
there’s no FM channel left free for a sound effect that needs to play over the music
232

=== PAGE 239 ===
without interrupting it; that effect will have to be handled by the PSG, or the driver will
have to decide to temporarily sacrifice one of the music channels.
• If the game needs to play a digitized voice or a PCM effect, you have to plan ahead for
that to consume the YM2612’s sixth channel for as long as it lasts, and compose the
music with the awareness that this channel may not always be available.
• Reinforcing a song with an extra PSG channel only makes sense if that channel isn’t
simultaneously needed for the game’s sound effects at that same moment.
Inotherwords,theprogrammerandthecomposerofaMegaDrivegameendupjointlymak-
ing channel-allocation decisions very similar to the ones a graphics programmer makes with
VRAM or the number of sprites on screen: a fixed, scarce resource that has to be allocated
deliberately, rather than assuming that “everything that should sound, will sound.” This way
ofthinkingaboutsound—intermsofavailablechannelsandhowthey’resplitbetweenmusic
and effects — underlies the tools and functions presented starting in the next chapter.

Chapter 35 — Music Playback -
XGM and XGM2 Drivers
Chapter 34 explained why the Mega Drive needs an intermediate sound driver: the YM2612
and the PSG are powerful but low-level chips, and programming them directly to play back
a full track—with all its channels, instruments, and PCM samples synchronized—would be
impractical for a game. SGDK solves that problem with two music drivers already built in:
XGM, the original one, and XGM2, added in an SGDK 2.00 update. This chapter compares
the two and walks through the functions needed to play music with each. The code itself is
short; what really deserves attention is the decision of which driver to use.
Prerequisites
• A working SGDK project, with resources.res and main.c, like the one used since the
early chapters of the manual.
• Anunderstandingofthegeneralstructureofaresources.resfilefordeclaringresources
(already covered in the chapters on graphics and maps).
• It helps to have read chapter 34, since this chapter assumes you already know what the
YM2612 and the PSG are and why a software driver is needed to handle them.
• No musical knowledge is required: this chapter is limited to playing back already-
composed tracks. Composing original music for the Mega Drive is covered in chapter
36.
1. Two drivers, one design decision
XGM is SGDK’s original music driver. It offers four PCM channels in total: one is normally
reserved for music, and the remaining three are available for sound effects.
XGM2wasaddedlater,inanSGDK2.00update,withaspecificgoal: reducingthefinalROM
size. In practice, music tends to be what takes up the most space on a cartridge, so any
savings there are significant. XGM2 achieves this in two ways: it uses smaller PCM samples
for sound effects, and it allows a single PCM sample to be shared across multiple tracks.
UnderXGM,ifthesamedrumsoundappearedinfourdifferenttracks,thatsamplehadtobe
includedfourtimesintheROM,oncepertrack;withXGM2it’sincludedonlyonce,andevery
track that needs it reuses it.
That advantage comes with a trade-off: XGM2 offers only three PCM channels in total (one
formusicandtwoforsoundeffects),onefewerthanXGM.Thismaymatterdependingonhow
manysimultaneoussoundsagameneeds,andit’sworthtakingintoaccountbeforechoosing
a driver for a project, since switching drivers later means redeclaring the audio resources.
234

=== PAGE 241 ===
These PCM channels are separate from the six FM channels of the YM2612 described in
chapter 34: the driver manages them independently, and this manual doesn’t go further into
the internal details of that management.
WhenXGM2wasintroduced,itgeneratedsomeexcitementinthecommunityovertwospecific
features: fade in/out and the ability to adjust the music tempo without having to manually
count frames. Of those two features, only fade in/out is actually exclusive to XGM2: tempo
adjustment already existed in the original driver, as shown later in this chapter.
2. Declaring the music resource in resources.res
Declaring a music track follows the same pattern as any other SGDK resource: first the type,
then a name to identify the track within the code, and finally, in quotes, the source file. For
the XGM driver:
XGM my_track "musica.vgm";
Both drivers require files in uncompressed VGM format; they do not accept compressed
formats such as MP3. If a downloaded file is in VGZ format (a compressed version of VGM),
it’s enough to decompress it with any common tool and then rename the resulting extension
from .vgz to .vgm.
If you’re going to use music from existing games in your own project, keep in mind
that a commercial project cannot include third-party music without authorization.
Non-commercialfanprojectstendtohavemoreleeway,butit’sworthcheckingthe
license of each track before distributing anything.
3. Playing music with the XGM driver
With the resource declared, starting playback takes a single line:
XGM_startPlay(my_track);
This call must be made only once, typically alongside the other initializations, after
SYS_init() and before the main game loop starts. A common mistake is placing it inside the
while(1): if that happens, the system would try to restart the track on every frame, instead
of letting it play normally.
int main(bool hardReset) {
SYS_init();
// ... other initializations ...
XGM_startPlay(my_track);
while (TRUE) {
// game logic, without calling XGM_startPlay() again here
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return 0;
}
235

=== PAGE 242 ===
4. Controlling the number of repeats: XGM_setLoopNumber()
Bydefault,XGM_startPlay()playsthetrackwith255repeats,whichinpracticeamountstoan
indefinite loop for most purposes. When different behavior is needed—for example, having a
titlescreenthemeplayjustonceandthenstop—youcanuseXGM_setLoopNumber(),specifying
the number of additional repeats desired:
XGM_setLoopNumber(0); // plays only once, without repeating
• -1 corresponds to the default behavior (255 repeats).
• 0 makes the track play exactly once.
• 1 plays it twice in total, and so on.
5. Adjusting the tempo: XGM_setMusicTempo()
XGM_setMusicTempo() allows changing the playback speed in real time. The default value is
60(60framespersecondonNTSC;50onPAL);halfthatspeedcorrespondsto30,anddouble
corresponds to 120:
XGM_startPlay(my_track);
XGM_setMusicTempo(120); // double speed
This function must be called after XGM_startPlay(), never before, otherwise it has no effect.
It’s rarely essential, but it can be useful in genres like shoot ’em ups, where it might make
sense to speed up the music as the ship’s speed increases or as more enemies appear on
screen.
6. Pausing and resuming: XGM_pausePlay() and XGM_resumePlay()
XGM_pausePlay()stopsplaybackwithoutresettingit,whichisusefulforexampleforcutscenes
or pause menus. XGM_resumePlay() picks the track back up right where it left off:
if (paused) XGM_pausePlay();
else XGM_resumePlay();
Unlike the previous functions, meant to be called only once before the main loop, these are
normally invoked inside the game loop, conditioned on some event such as a button press.
DuetothenatureoftheFMchip,resumingisn’talwaysperfect: somenotesmaybelostuntil
the next key event in the track itself.
7. Switching to the XGM2 driver
Moving from XGM to XGM2 doesn’t require restructuring anything: in resources.res it’s
enough to replace the keyword XGM with XGM2, leaving the rest of the line unchanged:
XGM2 my_track "musica.vgm";
In main.c, the function equivalent to XGM_startPlay() is XGM2_play():
XGM2_play(my_track);
The rest of the functions covered so far have direct equivalents with the XGM2_ prefix:
XGM2_setLoopNumber(), XGM2_pause(), and XGM2_resume() cover, respectively, the number of
repeats, pausing, and resuming, with the same behavior described for the original driver.
236

=== PAGE 243 ===
8. What’s truly exclusive to XGM2: fade in and fade out
Fade in and fade out is indeed an XGM2-exclusive feature, with no equivalent in the original
driver. The syntax is straightforward: XGM2_fadeIn() takes as a parameter the number of
frames the transition should last. At 60 frames per second, 120 equals 2 seconds:
XGM2_play(my_track);
XGM2_fadeIn(120); // 2-second fade in
XGM2_fadeOut() works analogously, with the same type of parameter, to fade the track out
insteadofcuttingitabruptly. Iftheeffectseemsbarelynoticeablewithlowvalues,increasing
the duration (for example to 240 frames, about 4 seconds) usually makes it more evident
during testing.
