Chapter 37 — Programming
Sound Effects
Along with music, graphics, and animation, sound effects are one of the elements that bring
the most life to a game, even when they serve no gameplay function whatsoever. Think of a
platformerwherethecharactermakesasmallsoundwhilewalking,orwherecertainelements
ofthesceneryreactwithasoundeffectwhensteppedonortouched: noneofthataffectsthe
mechanics, but it reinforces the feeling that the represented world is real.
ThischaptercovershowtouploadsoundfilestotheROM,assignthemanidentifyingnumber
within the range reserved for effects, play them in response to controls, and — the most
importantpointofthechapter—howtomanagesoundchannelsandprioritieswhenseveral
effects might play at the same time.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• ReadChapter35,“MusicPlayback: theXGMandXGM2Drivers”: thischapterassumes
familiarity with the XGM driver and the resources.res file, since sound effects are also
declared there and played with functions from the same family.
• ReadChapter32,“ButtonControlsandEvent-BasedReading”: theexampleinthischap-
ter reuses that same joystick event-handling structure to trigger the effects.
• An understanding of using #define to associate readable names with constant numbers,
already covered in the chapter on sprite animation (Chapter 23).
1. Starting Point: Handling Several Buttons with Indepen-
dent if Statements
The example in this chapter starts from a joyEvent() function like the one in Chapter 32,
whichcheckswhetherbuttonsA,B,orCwerepressed. There’sanimportantdesigndetailin
that structure: the three buttons are checked with three independent if statements, never
with else if.
void joyEvent(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state)
{
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_A)
{
// play effect A
}
245

=== PAGE 252 ===
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_B)
{
// play effect B
}
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_C)
{
// play effect C
}
}
The reason for using independent if statements instead of else if is that, with else if,
only one sound effect could ever play at a time, even if the player presses two or three but-
tons simultaneously. With independent if statements, each button can trigger its own effect
regardless of the state of the others.
To illustrate the rest of the chapter, three example sound files are used, with generic names
you can replace with your own: sfx_shout.wav, sfx_rise.wav, and sfx_yell.wav. They don’t
needtobeoriginalorespeciallyelaboratesoundstofollowalongwiththechapter: anythree
short WAV files will do for experimenting with channels and priorities.
2. Uploading Sound Effects: the WAV Keyword in re-
sources.res
The first step in programming a sound effect is uploading it to the ROM by declaring it in
resources.res. Unlike music (which uses the XGM or XGM2 keyword, as seen in Chapter 35),
individual sound effects are declared with the WAV keyword, in uppercase, since the source
file must be in uncompressed .wav format.
After the keyword comes a freely chosen name to identify the resource within the code, fol-
lowed by, in quotes, the file name with its .wav extension. The last piece of data the declara-
tion requires is the sound driver associated with the effect:
WAV sfx_shout "sfx_shout.wav" XGM
WAV sfx_rise "sfx_rise.wav" XGM
WAV sfx_yell "sfx_yell.wav" XGM
This chapter uses the XGM driver instead of XGM2. Besides the fact that, as explained in
Chapter 35, XGM2 has one fewer PCM channel than XGM, XGM2 is a more recent addition
to SGDK and its documentation on effect playback is still even sparser. The procedure for
making sound effects under XGM2 would be similar to what’s shown in this chapter: declare
the resource with XGM2 instead of XGM and use the equivalent functions from that API. It isn’t
covered in detail here; it’s left as an exercise for anyone who prefers that driver.
Regardingtheexactformatthesource.wavfilemusthave(samplerate,bitdepth),thischap-
ter can’t provide concrete, verified figures. In practice, rescomp (the SGDK tool that pro-
cesses resources.res) usually accepts the WAV file as exported from a common audio editor
and automatically adjusts it to the format the sound driver needs; if you notice distortion or
unexpected noise when testing an effect of your own, it’s worth checking the quality of the
source file first before suspecting the console’s sound driver.
246

=== PAGE 253 ===
3. The Sound Effect Number Range: Why Start at 64
Within SGDK, each sound effect in a game receives a unique identifying number, within a
range from 0 to 255. However, the numbers from 0 to 63 are reserved exclusively for music,
so sound effects must use numbers between 64 and 255: a total of 192 available numbers,
more than enough for practically any game.
This distinction becomes clearer when using the playback functions: the declaration in re-
sources.res (seen in the previous section) identifies the sound file itself, while the number
defined in this section identifies the effect within the game’s playback system. They are two
related but distinct concepts.
4. Naming Effect Numbers with #define
Rather than using the numbers 64, 65, and 66 directly in the code — a practice that quickly
becomes confusing when you have to remember which number corresponds to which effect
—it’sbettertodefineareadablenameforeachonewith#define,followingthesamepattern
alreadyusedinChapter23forspriteanimation. It’salsoagoodideatochoosenamesdifferent
from those used in resources.res, so as not to confuse the file resource’s name with the
effect’s identifying number within the game:
#define SFX_SHOUT 64
#define SFX_RISE 65
#define SFX_YELL 66
5. Associating Each Effect Number with Its File: XGM_setPCM()
With the files already declared in resources.res and the effect numbers already defined, the
next step is to tell SGDK which file corresponds to which effect number. This is done with
the XGM_setPCM() function, which takes three pieces of data: the sound effect identifier (for
which the name defined with #define can be used directly instead of the number), the name
of the sound resource as declared in resources.res, and the size of the file in bytes.
For this last piece of data, rather than calculating the size manually, it’s best to use the C
language’sownsizeof()function,passingitthenameofthesoundresourceasanargument;
SGDK resolves that calculation automatically at compile time:
int main()
{
XGM_setPCM(SFX_SHOUT, sfx_shout, sizeof(sfx_shout));
XGM_setPCM(SFX_RISE, sfx_rise, sizeof(sfx_rise));
XGM_setPCM(SFX_YELL, sfx_yell, sizeof(sfx_yell));
// ... rest of initialization
}
These three calls go before the main loop, along with the rest of the game’s initialization.
247

=== PAGE 254 ===
6. Playing the Effect: XGM_startPlayPCM(), Priority, and
Channel
The last step is to tell the system when to play each effect, inside the joyEvent() function
presented at the start of the chapter. The function used is XGM_startPlayPCM(), which also
takes three pieces of data: the sound effect identifier (again, using the defined name instead
of the number), the effect’s priority, and the sound channel it should play on.
Priority is a value from 0 to 15, where 15 is the highest priority. This value determines what
happensiftwosoundeffectstrytoplayatthesametimeonthesamechannel. Asforthechan-
nel,theXGMdriverhasfoursoundchannelsintotal(SOUND_PCM_CH1throughSOUND_PCM_CH4),
but the first of these is usually reserved for music, so under normal circumstances it’s best
to avoid it and use channels 2, 3, or 4 for effects.
Assigning each effect to a different channel, with the same priority for all three:
void joyEvent(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state)
{
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_A)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_SHOUT, 15, SOUND_PCM_CH2);
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_B)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_RISE, 15, SOUND_PCM_CH3);
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_C)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_YELL, 15, SOUND_PCM_CH4);
}
Whencompiledandtestedintheemulator,allthreesoundeffectsworkcorrectlyontheirown
andcanalsoallplayatthesametimeifallthreebuttonsarepressedatonce, sinceeachone
occupies a different channel. If the same button is pressed repeatedly, each new playback
cuts off the previous one and restarts it from the beginning, since both share a channel.
7. What Happens When Several Effects Share the Same
Channel
In a real game, it’s common to need more than three simultaneous sound effects — for ex-
ample, severaldifferentenemiesonscreenatonce—whicheventuallyforcesmorethanone
effect to share the same sound channel. To see what happens in that case, it’s enough to
modifythepreviousexamplesothatallthreeeffectsusethesamechannel, leavingthesame
priority for all three for now:
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_A)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_SHOUT, 15, SOUND_PCM_CH2);
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_B)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_RISE, 15, SOUND_PCM_CH2);
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_C)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_YELL, 15, SOUND_PCM_CH2);
When compiled and tested, the result is that any new effect cuts off whatever was playing at
that moment on the same channel, regardless of which one it was: since all three have the
same priority, the most recent one always replaces the previous one.
248

=== PAGE 255 ===
8. Controlling Which Effect Wins: Adjusting Priority
Depending on the game’s design, it may not be desirable for any new effect to interrupt the
previous one on the same channel; priority allows this to be controlled more precisely. For
example, youcouldleavethefirsteffectwiththelowestpriorityofthethree(13), thesecond
at an intermediate level (14), and the third with the highest priority (15):
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_A)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_SHOUT, 13, SOUND_PCM_CH2);
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_B)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_RISE, 14, SOUND_PCM_CH2);
if ((changed & state) & BUTTON_C)
XGM_startPlayPCM(SFX_YELL, 15, SOUND_PCM_CH2);
Thepracticaleffectisthat,whilethepriority-15soundisplaying,nootherlower-priorityeffect
caninterruptitonthatchannel;thepriority-13one,ontheotherhand,canbeinterruptedby
both the priority-15 and priority-14 ones; and the priority-14 one can only be interrupted by
the priority-15 one.
Ahigher-priorityeffectcanalwaysinterruptalower-priorityoneonthesamechan-
nel; two effects of equal priority interrupt each other, with the most recent one
always winning.
The concrete way to apply channels and priorities in a real game depends entirely on each
project’sdesign. Asanexample,inanactiongamewithamaincharacter,itmightmakesense
toassignthecharacter’sowneffectsandtheir“takedamage”soundtoachannelwherethat
damage sound has high priority over their own attacks (so it isn’t lost while the character
is attacking), reserve another channel for enemies, and a third for scenery elements like
interactive objects or collectibles, so that these different types of sound don’t interrupt each
other.
There’s a common mistake in this kind of design: if an enemy’s attack and its final speech or
screamuponbeingdefeatedendupassignedtothesamechannelwiththeattackatahigher
priority, it can happen that, if the attack is still playing at the moment the enemy is defeated,
thesecondeffectgetscompletelycutoffandneverplaysatall. It’saneasyoversighttomake
and a hard one to notice during testing unless specific attention is paid to the assignment of
channels and priorities among effects that might coincide in time.

Chapter 38 — Creating Sound
Effects
The previous chapter showed how to program sound effects that were already prepared for
a SGDK project: how to declare a .wav file with the WAV keyword in resources.res and how
to trigger it from code with the corresponding sound driver. This chapter deals with the step
before that: creating those sound files from scratch, using the free program Audacity.
Thefocushereisdeliberatelykeptnarrow,limitedtothespecificrequirementsandlimitations
of the Mega Drive’s sound hardware. For more general sound design techniques, how to
convincingly create the sound of a punch, a sword, or a synthetic voice, it’s worth turning
to more general sound design resources once the console’s own technical requirements are
understood, which is precisely the subject of the following sections.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to be clear on:
• How to declare a WAV resource in resources.res and play it from code with the corre-
sponding sound driver (chapter 37, “Programming Sound Effects”).
• Having Audacity installed (free) or an equivalent audio editor that lets you change a
track’s sample rate, convert it to mono, and export it as unsigned 8-bit PCM.
• Amicrophoneorsomeaudiosourcetorecordwith. It’salsoperfectlyvalidtostartfrom
an existing sound file instead of recording your own.
1. Where to draw inspiration from
Many sound effects from the classic Mega Drive library have a less handcrafted origin than
they might seem at first listen. The first Golden Axe, for example, is known for lifting sound
effectsdirectlyfrom1980sHollywoodmovies,whileitssequel,GoldenAxeII,withnoticeably
weaker enemy death effects, illustrates the other end of the spectrum.
The practical takeaway from these examples is simple: while taking sounds from movies
or someone else’s music might have gone unnoticed in the eighties, today it’s preferable
to create your own original sound effects, whether by recording your own voice, everyday
objects, or by turning to properly licensed sound banks. The rest of this chapter proceeds
from that premise: a sound effect is recorded from scratch with Audacity and adapted step
by step to the Mega Drive’s requirements.

8. Does the file always need to be converted manually?
It’s possible to add a .wav file to resources.res that doesn’t meet the recommended format
(in stereo and at a sample rate other than 16000 Hz, for example) and have the project still
compile. SGDK appears to perform some automatic conversion of .wav files at compile time,
even when they aren’t mono or at the recommended sample rate, as long as the file is rea-
sonably small; it isn’t precisely documented exactly how far this goes or under what exact
conditions that automatic conversion kicks in, so it’s best to treat it as a fallback behavior
rather than a reliable way of working.

That’s why, even though the final result might sound equivalent (the same voice effect, com-

can turn out to be practically indistinguishable once played back from the ROM in an emula-
tor), it’s generally best not to rely on that automatic conversion and to always carry out the
manual process described in this chapter, because there’s no guarantee that behavior will
work equally well in every case.
It’s also worth keeping source files as short and as low in quality as is acceptable, since this
reducesthefinalsizetakenupinsidetheROM,eventhoughSGDKalreadycompressesthese
sound files reasonably well. On that note, the XGM2 driver (covered in chapter 35, “Playing

sound effects than the original XGM driver used throughout this chapter, although the exact
comparison between the two formats hasn’t been verified here in detail and should be taken
as a general reference rather than a precise figure.
9. Adjusting the sound effect’s volume
One important recommendation to close out the chapter: SGDK doesn’t offer any way to
adjust a sound effect’s volume directly from code, so any volume adjustment has to be made
beforehand in the audio file itself, within Audacity. This is a common problem with sound
effects taken from external sources, which often turn out too quiet or too loud relative to the
rest of the game’s music and effects.

Chapter 39 — The Resource
Compiler in Depth
A unified view of rescomp: resource types, compression modes, and the organization of re-
sources.res
From Chapter 7 through Chapter 38, practically every chapter of this manual used rescomp,
SGDK’s resource compiler, to solve a specific problem: displaying a background, assembling
alargelevel,animatingasprite,playingmusic,ortriggeringasoundeffect. Ineachofthose
cases, rescomp appeared as a tool in service of a concrete goal, and each chapter explained
onlywhatwasneededforthatgoal. ThischapterclosesPartVIbytakingastepback: instead
of adding a new resource, it brings together in one place the complete map of what rescomp
can do, what each resource type is for relative to the others, and what general criteria are
worthapplyingwhenchoosingcompressionandorganizingaresources.resfilethat,inareal
project, ends up growing well beyond two or three lines.
There is no new code to learn in this chapter: every keyword, function, and structure that
appears here was already used in some earlier chapter. The goal here is different — this is
a reference chapter, a chapter of judgment, meant to be revisited whenever a real project
forces a decision, such as whether to compile a giant map with BEST or FAST, or how to keep
a three-hundred-line resources.res from becoming impossible to maintain.
1. What rescomp is and its place in the pipeline
Chapter 7 first introduced the central idea: a graphic, audio, or level resource does not auto-
matically become available inside a Mega Drive program. Before it can be used from main.c,
it has to be declared in a text file — by convention, resources.res, inside the project’s res
folder — and left for rescomp to process during compilation.
The full circuit always has the same shape, regardless of the type of resource involved:
1. A source file (PNG, WAV, VGM, TMX, depending on the type) is placed in the project’s
res folder.
2. A line in resources.res declares the resource: its type, a name chosen by the program-
mer,thepathtothesourcefile,and,dependingonthetype,additionalparameters(com-
pression, frame size, sound driver, etc.).
3. When the project is compiled, rescomp reads resources.res, processes each source file,
andgeneratestwonewfiles,resources.handresources.c,withintheprojectstructure.
4. main.c includes resources.h and, from that point on, can refer to each resource by the
name given to it in the .res file, as if it were a global variable already initialized with
the data from the original file.
5. Theprocessedcontent—alreadyinthebinaryformatexpectedbytheMegaDrivehard-
ware, and compressed as indicated — ends up embedded in the final ROM (rom.bin)
258

=== PAGE 265 ===
when the project is linked.
AsChapter7alreadypointedout,the.resfileisthesourcethatgetseditedbyhand,whilere-
sources.h/resources.c are products generated automatically on every build: they are never
editeddirectly,andanychangehastobemadeinthesource.resfile. Also,anewlydeclared
resource name is not available to the editor or to the compiler for main.c until the project is
saved and built at least once.

decision for any new graphic or sound, even before thinking about compression.
3. Compression modes, in a unified view
Several of the resource types from the table above — IMAGE, TILESET, MAP, SPRITE — accept
a compression field, and Chapters 7 and 21 already introduced, separately, the same three
alternatives:
• NONE: the resource is included uncompressed. It takes up more space in ROM, but re-
quires no decompression work at runtime: the data is already in the final format the
hardware expects.
• FAST: a lighter compression algorithm, which produces a smaller file than NONE but not
as compact as BEST, in exchange for decompression that is quick and cheap in terms of
CPU at runtime.
• BEST: the mode that produces the smallest file. In rescomp’s documentation this corre-
sponds to the APLIB algorithm, though in recent versions of SGDK the same keyword
mayalsoimplyanautomaticselectionofwhicheveralgorithmbestsuitseachparticular
260

=== PAGE 267 ===
resource — a behavior Chapter 21 already pointed out, and one worth checking against
the actually installed SGDK version before assuming BEST is always synonymous with
“the most aggressive compression and the slowest to decompress.”
The criterion for choosing among the three doesn’t change depending on the resource type:
what changes is how many times per second that resource will be decompressed during the
game, and how much CPU time is available at that moment.
• Aresourcethatgetsdecompressedonlyonce,typicallywhenloadingascreenoralevel
— a static background, the tileset and map of a full level, a menu’s palette — can afford
the cost of BEST with no perceptible impact: the decompression happens once, during
a loading screen or a transition, and after that the data already lives decompressed in
VRAMorinworkingRAM.ThisisexactlythecaseoftheIMAGEresourcefromChapter7
and the TILESET/MAP from Chapter 11: there’s no practical reason not to use BEST there.
• A resource that gets decompressed many times per second — the central case being
an animated sprite, which changes frames several times per second and may need to
decompress data on every change — pays the cost of BEST over and over, frame after
frame. Chapter21alreadyshowedthatthiscostismeasurable: inaprojectwithseveral
animated characters on screen at once, switching their sprites from FAST to BEST can
causeanoticeabledropinframerate. Forthistypeofresource,FASTisusuallythemore
sensible choice, reserving BEST for cases where ROM size is a more pressing constraint
than speed.
• NONE makes sense in two specific situations: when the resource is already so small that
compressing it wouldn’t yield a meaningful saving, or when the fastest possible access
isneededandthere’snoroomevenforthelightcostof FAST—forexample,datathatis
read extremely frequently and where every additional CPU cycle is critical.
The question worth asking about each resource, then, is not “how big is this file?” but “how
many times per second does it need to be decompressed, and how tight is the CPU budget
at that moment in the game?” A huge level background, even though it’s a heavy file, gets
decompressed only once when entering the level and can safely go in BEST; a small sprite, if
it’s animated constantly, may justify FAST even though it weighs much less in raw terms.
This same trade-off between space and speed reappears, in another form, in the alternative
already mentioned in Chapter 21 for sprite compression: loading every possible animation
frameintoVRAMupfront,therebyavoidinganydecompressionduringgameplay,atthecost
of permanently occupying the VRAM space those frames need — space that then becomes
unavailableforanythingelse. Thisisn’tabetterorworsealternativetoadjustingcompression:
it’s the same space-versus-speed trade-off, resolved at the opposite end of the problem.
4. Organizing a growing resources.res
Every example in this manual, chapter after chapter, worked with a resources.res of just a
few lines, designed to introduce one resource at a time. A real project ends up accumulating
dozens or hundreds of lines: tilesets and maps for several levels, sprite sheets for every
characterandenemy,amusictrackperscene, andalonglistofsoundeffects. Withoutsome
extra care, that file quickly becomes hard to navigate and maintain, especially on a team of
more than one person.
The safest way to keep that file organized, within what this manual can confirm based on
the information already used in earlier chapters, is a discipline of organization within a sin-
gle resources.res file, rather than relying on splitting resource declarations across several
separate files. Specifically:
• Group lines by area of the game,withacommentmarkingeachblock—forexample,
one block for the playable character’s resources, another for each level, another for the

=== PAGE 268 ===
interface, and another for audio — in the same order in which it makes sense to review
them.
• Adopt a consistent prefix in resource names that identifies which area or which
leveleachonecomesfrom—forexample,lvl1_tileset,lvl1_map,lvl1_paletteforthe
firstlevel, and player_walk, player_idle forthe character’s animation sheets— so that
the resource name is already readable in main.c’s code without having to go back to
resources.res to remember what it corresponds to.
• Keep related resource lines together, as already shown in Chapter 11 with TILESET,
PALETTE,andMAPforthesamemap,orinChapter12withTILESET,PALETTE,andTILEMAP
for a level designed in Tiled: declaring those lines one right after another makes the
relationship between them far clearer than scattering them across the file.
• Review compression at the end of each block, since it’s easy to copy and paste a
line from an already-declared resource as a starting point for a new one and forget to
adjustthecompressiontomatchtheactualusecaseforthatnewresource(forexample,
copying the line for a background compressed with BEST as the basis for a sprite that
would actually need FAST).
Asforthepossibilityofsplittingresourcedeclarationsacrossmorethanone.resfileperarea
of the game — a reasonable idea in the abstract, especially in large projects — this manual

Chapter 40 — Level Collision for
a Top-Down 2D Game
With backgrounds, large maps, sprites, the camera, controls, and sound already covered,
there’s one problem left that shows up in practically any game with free movement: keeping
the character from walking through walls, furniture, or any other obstacle in the scene. This
chapter opens Part VII of the manual, dedicated to physics and collisions, and builds a level
collision system from scratch for a game viewed from above, in the style of the early Zelda
titles.
Theexampleinthischapterreusesthesingle-screenroomscene(320×224pixels)withbeds,
furniture, and walls as obstacles. That scene, with its narrow gaps between objects, works
as a good stress test for the code we’re about to build: if the collision correctly resolves the
tightcornersbetweentwonearbypiecesoffurniture,itwillhavenotroublewiththesimpler
cases.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have already covered:
• Chapter6, ondatatypes(u8, u16, s16, const)andtheMegaDrive’smemoryconstraints.
• Chapter 13, on creating maps with 16Tile, since this chapter reuses that workflow to
generate an additional layer.

1. Where to place the collision box within the sprite
The first conceptual step, before writing a single line of code, is deciding where the colli-
sion box will sit within the character’s sprite: the rectangle whose four corners are checked
against the map to decide whether a movement is valid. That box doesn’t have to match the
full sprite; in fact, it’s almost always better for it to be smaller.
Foratop-downcharacter,itusuallyworksbesttoplaceitaroundthefeetratherthanoverthe
entiresprite. Thatway,thecharactercanvisuallyoverlapwiththetopofapieceoffurniture
or the headboard of a bed without that counting as an actual collision — something already
possiblethankstotilepriority,coveredinChapter15: atilewithprioritycanbedrawnontop
of the sprite even though, in the pixels further down, the character is still physically blocked.

The reference box marks where the collision box will be placed: around the character’s feet,
smaller than the full sprite.
2. A second map layer, dedicated solely to collision
The core technique in this chapter is to create, within the same 16Tile project used for the
background (Chapter 13), a second layer dedicated exclusively to collision. That layer uses
itsowntileset,completelydifferentfromthegraphicalone: afileof16blocksof16×16pixels,
each a distinct flat color. Each color will represent a type of collision.
For the purposes of this chapter, two colors are enough: one (black, for example) for a free
tile,throughwhichthecharactercanmovewithoutrestriction,andanother(red,forexample)
for a fully solid tile. The remaining 14 colors in the tileset stay available for more elaborate
collision types that aren’t needed yet: a water tile passable only with certain equipment, or
a one-way tile that lets you drop down a ledge without being able to climb back up, like the
ones found in several classic games from that era.
With the layer created and named (collision, for example), the painting itself works exactly
like any other 16Tile layer you’ve already used: select the red block and paint it over every
map tile that should behave as solid, leaving the rest in the color that represents “free.” The
layer’s visibility icon (shaped like an eye) lets you toggle between viewing it opaque, semi-
transparentoverthebackground,orhidden,whichmakesiteasiertopaintthecollisionwhile
still seeing the actual background as a reference.

3. Exporting the layer as a collision array
Before exporting, the collision layer needs a special setting within 16Tile’s layers panel: an
option that tells the tool this particular layer should be exported as a data array rather than
as a graphical background. When you export the full project, the result is two quite distinct
files: oneforthebackgroundlayer(animage, justliketheonesseeninearlierchapters)and
another for the collision layer, which is a plain text file with C array syntax, ready to paste
into the project: a series of 1s (solid tile) and 0s (free tile), one per map tile, in row order.
Automating this step is one of the reasons 16Tile becomes especially valuable as levels grow
larger: writing the collision array by hand, tile by tile, is slow and error-prone, especially on
maps bigger than a single screen, like the ones worked with using MAP_create() in Chapter
11.
4. The collision array in main.c: const u8, not u16
Thetextfileexportedby16Tiledeclaresthearrayasu16bydefault. Sinceinthisexampleits
onlypossiblevaluesare0and1,it’sworthshrinkingittou8,whichtakesuphalfthespacein
ROM without losing any information: for a 320×224 map (20×14 tiles, 280 elements), that’s
already 280 bytes saved, and it scales proportionally with the size of the level.
The second adjustment, even more important, is declaring the array as const, as explained
in Chapter 6 on data types and memory. A value marked const records in the code that
it won’t change during gameplay, and in practice it makes the compiler place that array in
ROM instead of copying it to RAM, a far scarcer resource on this console (only 64 kilobytes
total). Since the collision map never changes during the game, it’s a perfect candidate to
live permanently in ROM. There’s no published measurement confirming how many cycles it
coststoreadfromROMinsteadofRAMforanaccesslikethis,soit’sworthnotassumingthe

=== PAGE 272 ===
differenceisnegligible;eitherway,declaringthearrayasconstcarriesnopracticaldownside
and does save real RAM, so it’s the recommended way to declare it.

6. The collision box offsets

four values are measured once, on the reference sprite, and declared as constants alongside
PLAYER_WIDTH and PLAYER_HEIGHT:
#define PLAYER_WIDTH 32
#define PLAYER_HEIGHT 32
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_LEFT 10
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_RIGHT 23
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_TOP 18
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_BOTTOM 31

8. From pixels to tiles: dividing by 16 with a bit shift

s16 xtilecoord_right = player_right_collision_coord >> 4;
s16 ytilecoord_top = player_top_collision_coord >> 4;
s16 ytilecoord_bottom = player_bottom_collision_coord >> 4;
9. From tile coordinates to array index

continuously from 0 to 279, row by row. The formula is:
index = (row × level_col_width) + column
A couple of concrete examples help confirm the formula is correct: a tile in column 0, row 1
gives(1 × 20) + 0 = 20; atileincolumn2,row6gives(6 × 20) + 2 = 122. Bothmatchthe

11. Resolving leftward movement
Inside collision(), an if (player_move_left) block brings together three steps in order:
movethecharactertotheleft,calculatewhetherthatmovementcausesthetop-leftorbottom-
left corner of the collision box to land on a solid tile, and if so, correct the position so it ends
up flush against the edge of that tile. Since all of this happens within the same animation
frame, the player never actually sees the character visually penetrating the obstacle before
being pushed back.
It’s worth moving the pixel, tile, and index calculations for the left side into this block, since
there’s no point calculating them if the character isn’t moving in that direction:
if (player_move_left)
{
player_x = F32_sub(player_x, FIX32(PLAYER_SPEED));
s16 left_coord = F32_toInt(player_x) + PLAYER_COLBOX_LEFT;
s16 top_coord = F32_toInt(player_y) + PLAYER_COLBOX_TOP;
s16 bottom_coord = F32_toInt(player_y) + PLAYER_COLBOX_BOTTOM;
s16 xtile_left = left_coord >> 4;
s16 ytile_top = top_coord >> 4;
s16 ytile_bottom = bottom_coord >> 4;
u16 idx_topleft = (ytile_top * level_col_width) + xtile_left;
u16 idx_bottomleft = (ytile_bottom * level_col_width) + xtile_left;
if (level_col[idx_topleft] == SOLID_TILE || level_col[idx_bottomleft] ==
↪ SOLID_TILE)
{
// Align the left edge of the collision box (not the sprite)
// with the right edge of the solid tile it collided with.
s16 blocked_coord = (xtile_left << 4) + 16 - PLAYER_COLBOX_LEFT;
player_x = FIX32(blocked_coord);
}
}
The calculation for the bounce-back position takes the tile column where the obstacle lies,
multiplies it by 16 using a left bit shift (multiplying by a power of 2 allows the same shortcut
as dividing), adds another 16 — the width of a tile, to land on its right edge instead of its left
edge — and finally subtracts the collision box offset, since player_x describes the position
of the full sprite, not the box. Skipping that final subtraction leaves the character pushed
noticeably farther from the obstacle than expected, so it’s worth paying attention to it: the
correct result stops the character exactly where the green reference collision box touches
the edge of the furniture, with no visible extra bounce.
12. Right, up, and down
Rightward movement follows the same logic as leftward movement, with two differences: it
uses the coordinates of the box’s right corners instead of the left ones, and its bounce-back
formula doesn’t need to add the full width of a tile, since aligning the box’s right edge with
the solid tile’s left edge doesn’t require that extra adjustment (though it does still subtract
the corresponding offset, in this case PLAYER_COLBOX_RIGHT):

=== PAGE 276 ===
s16 blocked_coord = (xtile_right << 4) - PLAYER_COLBOX_RIGHT;
player_x = FIX32(blocked_coord);
Verticalmovement(upanddown)repeatsthesamestructure,usingthetoporbottomcorner
coordinates as appropriate.
Horizontalmovementisdeliberatelyresolvedbeforeverticalmovement: sinceboth
axessharesomeofthesametilecoordinates,resolvingthehorizontalcollisionfirst
simplifies the code needed later for more advanced collision types, such as slopes.
Thisisareasonabledesigndecisionforthiscase,notamandatoryenginerule: with
other collision schemes, the reverse order might be preferable, or even resolving
both axes together.
13. The “wall jump” problem and its fix
With all four movement directions now working individually, a problem shows up when com-
biningtwodirectionsatonce: holdingdown,forexample,rightandupatthesametimenear
awallmakesthecharactermomentarilygetstuckagainstit,insteadofslidingsmoothly. This
happensbecause,whenthehorizontalaxisisresolvedfirst,thecorrectedpositionleavesthe
character flush against the edge of the solid tile (zero distance), and that exact same coinci-
dence can cause the vertical axis calculation, right afterward, to interpret that position as a
collision all over again.
The fix is to subtract a fraction of a pixel (0.1) from the character’s coordinate immediately
after resolving the horizontal collision — just enough to nudge it slightly away from the wall
without the human eye noticing the difference, but enough that the vertical axis no longer
gets stuck against it:
if (level_col[idx_topleft] == SOLID_TILE || level_col[idx_bottomleft] ==
↪ SOLID_TILE)
{
s16 blocked_coord = (xtile_left << 4) + 16 - PLAYER_COLBOX_LEFT;
player_x = F32_sub(FIX32(blocked_coord), FIX32(0.1));
}
The same adjustment, subtracting 0.1 from player_y after vertical collision, fixes the equiva-
lent problem when combining downward movement with horizontal movement.
14. The final result
Withallfourmovementdirectionsandboth“walljump”fixesinplace,thecharactercanmove
around the entire scene, consistently colliding with beds, furniture, and walls, including the
narrow gaps between objects mentioned at the start of the chapter.
Aftersubtractingthecollisionboxoffsetintheformula, thecharacterstopsrightattheedge
of the obstacle, with no visible bounce or penetration.

function capable of converting pixels into indices of that array to stop movement in all four

thatdefinedalargepartofthe16-bitcatalog: theside-scrollingplatformer. Mostoftheheavy
lifting — converting pixel coordinates to tile coordinates, the array index formula, checking
each corner of the collision box — is already solved; what changes is how that information
getsused. Inatop-downgametheplayerisfreetodecidetomoveupordown;inaplatformer,
gravity constantly pulls the character downward, and the player can only fight it by jumping.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to already have covered:
• Level collision for a top-down 2D game (chapter 40): this chapter directly reuses and
modifies that code, in particular the collision() function and the collision array.
• Buttoncontrolsandevent-basedreadingwithJoyEvent()(chapter32): thejumpbutton
is added following that same pattern.

1. From top-down to side-scrolling: what changes and what
stays the same
Thetilesetusedasanexampleinthischapter—possiblyrelatedtotheonefromChakan: The

— includes common ground tiles, some fully solid platforms (meant for practicing jumping:
they can’t be passed through from the sides, from above, or from below), and a semi-solid
platformtype,commoninthegenre,thatletsthecharacterpassfreelythroughthesidesand
from below but stops them when they fall onto it from above. This chapter focuses on the

left for chapter 43, and adapting this same system to a larger sprite is left for chapter 42.
The tileset used in the chapter, with its ground tiles, solid platforms, and semi-solid platform

zeros. Since this map is considerably larger than the single-screen room from the previous

row length of the collision array needs to be recalculated (the new map width divided by 16),
and both the array’s contents and the total element count declared in brackets need to be
replaced. A collision bug that shows up erratically on a new map is almost always caused by
getting one of those two numbers wrong.
2. Removing free vertical movement
The first real change toward a side-scrolling platformer is eliminating the vertical move-
ment that made sense in a top-down game but not in this genre: the boolean variables
player_move_up and player_move_down, along with the lines in handle_input() that acti-
vated them using the D-pad directions, are removed entirely. Horizontal movement stays
unchanged.
The collision calculation against the ground and the ceiling, however, isn’t discarded: much
of that work gets reused later on. The upward collision block is temporarily commented out
(it’spickedbackupinsection6ofthischapter, forceilingcollisionwhenjumping), whilethe
downward collision block gets restructured from the ground up. In the top-down game, that
code only ran if the player pressed the down direction; in a platformer, gravity acts on the
character every single frame, whether or not any button is pressed, so the if that used to
guard it goes away and the ground collision calculation stays permanently active.
3. Gravity as a constant vertical velocity
The heart of this chapter is a new variable, gravity, of type fix32, with an initial test value:
273

=== PAGE 280 ===
fix32 gravity = FIX32(0.8);
Also, since the character now has its own vertical velocity — independent of whether the
player is pressing a key — another fix32 variable is needed:
fix32 player_y_vel = FIX32(0);
This exposes a naming problem: the variable player_vel, inherited from chapter 40, repre-
sented the fixed horizontal speed at which the character moved. To avoid confusing it with
the new vertical velocity, it should be renamed to player_x_vel everywhere it appears.
The gravity logic itself is surprisingly simple: each frame, the value of gravity gets added
to player_y_vel (the falling speed progressively accelerates, frame by frame), and then
player_y_vel gets added to the player_y coordinate itself. Since the vertical axis on the
Mega Drive grows downward (0 at the top, larger values toward the bottom), adding a
positive velocity pulls the character downward:
// Gravity: accumulates onto the vertical velocity every frame
player_y_vel += gravity;
player_y += player_y_vel;
It’sagoodideatoresetplayer_y_veltoFIX32(0)atprogramstart,alongwiththerestofthe
character’s variables, and to adjust the character’s starting position to fit the actual size of
the new map before compiling for the first time. With this change, the character falls from
its starting position until it hits the ground and can move freely side to side, but once on the
ground there’s no way to go back up: just like in real life, jumping is needed to counteract
gravity.
The values 0.8 for gravity and, later on, 12 for jump velocity don’t come from any exact
physicsformulaoranystandardSGDKconvention: they’reareasonable,hand-pickedstarting
point,meanttobetunedexperimentallytomatchthefeelyou’reafter. Ahighergravityvalue
producesasharperfallandashorterjump;aloweroneproducesafloatierjump. Treatthem
as fine-tuning knobs, not constants to memorize.
4. The jump button
Adding the jump requires, first, a new fix32 variable:
fix32 jumping_vel = FIX32(12);
theupwardvelocitygiventothecharacterthemomentthejumpbuttonispressed. Next,but-
tonhandlingneedstobesetupthroughJoyEvent(),followingthesamepatternalreadyseen
in chapter 32: a function prototype, JOY_setEventHandler() inside main(), and the function
itself at the end of the file. Any action button works for this (C, B, or one of the extra buttons
on the 6-button pad); what matters is the logic inside the handler. Pressing the jump button
subtracts jumping_vel from player_y_vel (subtracts, rather than adds, because any upward
movement in this coordinate system requires a negative value):
void handle_joy_event(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state)
{
if (changed & state & BUTTON_C)
{
player_y_vel -= jumping_vel;
}
}

=== PAGE 281 ===
Withthischangethecharactercannowjumpandclimbbackupoverthemap’sstepsandplat-
forms. A problem shows up right away, though: pressing the button repeatedly and quickly
enough lets the character rise indefinitely, since each press subtracts 12 from the vertical
velocity while gravity only adds 0.8 per frame, and that difference isn’t enough to offset very
rapid presses.
This isn’t necessarily a bug that needs fixing in every case: some games deliberately offer
double or triple jumps, and others use the jump button to control the character’s buoyancy
underwater, pressing it repeatedly to avoid sinking. For this chapter’s example, though, the
goal is to limit the character to a single jump until it touches the ground again.
5. Limiting the jump to a single use
The solution is a new boolean variable, initialized to false:
bool jumping = false;
When the jump button is pressed, in addition to subtracting jumping_vel, this variable gets
settotrue. Thebutton’sconditionisextendedwithan&&torequire,besidesthebuttonbeing
pressed, that the character not already be in the air (!jumping is a common, shorter way of
writing jumping == false):
void handle_joy_event(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state)
{
if ((changed & state & BUTTON_C) && !jumping)
{
player_y_vel -= jumping_vel;
jumping = true;
}
}
The only remaining step is setting jumping back to false at the right moment: when the
characteractuallytouchestheground,insidetheexistinglowercollisionblock,alongsidethe
rest of the position and velocity corrections applied there. With this change the character
can only jump once per ground touch, without chaining jumps in mid-air.
6. Re-enabling ceiling collision
With the jump now limited to one use, a problem becomes obvious: since the upper collision
block was left commented out in section 2, the character can jump straight through any plat-
form above instead of bumping its head against it. To re-enable it, it helps to first reorder
the lower collision block, and then reuse the same six lines of calculation (pixel coordinates,
tilecoordinates,arrayindices)alreadyusedfortheground,adaptingthemtothetopcorners
of the collision box. The commented-out block gets uncommented and added right after the
lower collision block, this time as an else if rather than a standalone if, since in any given
framethecharactercanonlybetouchingeitherthegroundortheceiling,neverbothatonce:
if (player_bottomleft_col == SOLID_TILE || player_bottomright_col == SOLID_TILE)
{
// Ground collision: snap the position to the top edge of
// the solid tile, just like in chapter 40, and stop the fall
player_y = FIX32((ytilecoord_bottom << 4) - PLAYER_COLBOX_BOTTOM);
player_y_vel = FIX32(0);
jumping = false;

}
else if (player_topleft_col == SOLID_TILE || player_topright_col == SOLID_TILE)

// Ceiling collision: snap the position to the bottom edge of
// the solid tile and stop the ascent

The tile coordinates (ytilecoord_bottom, ytilecoord_top) and the collision box offsets
(PLAYER_COLBOX_BOTTOM,PLAYER_COLBOX_TOP)arethesameonesalreadycalculatedinchapter

7. A design dilemma: what happens when the character
hits its head
With upper collision working, a curious side effect appears: when the character bumps its
head against a platform mid-jump, instead of falling immediately it seems to stay “stuck” for
amomentagainsttheceilingbeforestartingtofall. Theexplanationissimple: whenjumping,
player_y_vel starts at -12, and gravity only adds 0.8 per frame (-12, -11.2, -10.4, and so on);
as long as that velocity stays negative, the character keeps “trying” to rise every frame, and
theceilingcollisionsimplyblocksitinplaceuntilthevelocityreaches0,atwhichpointgravity
finally starts pulling it back down.
There’s no single correct answer here, and both behaviors show up in real games on the
console. At one extreme, hitting your head doesn’t immediately cut the upward momentum,
whichisallowedtorunitscoursenormally;leveldesignthataccountsforthisbehaviormight,
for example, avoid placing hazards directly beneath a low platform. At the other extreme,
the character falls immediately the moment it hits its head, with no “stuck” moment against
the ceiling at all. Achieving this second behavior is as simple as resetting player_y_vel to
FIX32(0) at the same point where jumping already gets reset to false inside the upper colli-
sion block, exactly as is already done in the lower collision block upon touching the ground,
as shown in the snippet from the previous section. Choosing between one behavior and the
other is a design decision, not a matter of technical correctness.
8. A real danger: when velocity exceeds 16 pixels per frame
Since the collision system works with 16×16 pixel tiles and checks positions only once per
frame (not continuously throughout the movement), any velocity — horizontal or vertical —
that exceeds 16 pixels per frame runs the risk of completely skipping over a single-tile-thick
layerwithoutthecollisioncodeevendetectingit. Raisinggravitytoahighvaluecanletfalling
speed exceed 16 within a few frames and pass straight through a platform without stopping
on it; likewise, a jumping_vel that’s too high can let the character pass through a platform
from below if its upward velocity on the exact frame of impact still exceeds that limit.
With terminal velocity set to a low value, the fall becomes noticeably slow and “floaty” com-
pared to a fall without that limit.
The solution has two parts. The first is simply keeping jumping_vel below 16, which guar-
antees the character never jumps faster than the collision system can detect. The second is
introducing a terminal velocity: an upper limit on player_y_vel, checked every frame right
after gravity is added to it, so that falling speed can never exceed that value no matter how
long the character has been falling:
276

=== PAGE 283 ===
Figure 124: The character falling with terminal velocity set to a low value
fix32 terminal_vel = FIX32(8);
// ... inside the physics loop, every frame:
player_y_vel += gravity;
if (player_y_vel > terminal_vel)
{
player_y_vel = terminal_vel;
}
player_y += player_y_vel;
A very low terminal velocity value (say, 4) produces a visibly slow, almost floaty fall, which
mightsuitaglidingpower-up;mostconventionalgameswouldprobablypreferahighervalue,
such as 8, 10, or 12. Since this example’s horizontal movement stays fixed and below 16
pixels per frame, it’s in no danger of passing through tiles on that axis; but any game with
acceleration-basedhorizontalphysicswouldneedtoapplythesamespeed-limitingprecaution
on that axis too.
There’s still an edge case that the system built in this chapter doesn’t fully resolve: because
of the exact order in which jumping and the character’s position get updated (between the
moment it leaves the ground and the first collision frame already in the air), it would still be
possible to jump again without having touched the ground. If the game requires it, the most
direct way to close that gap is an additional flag (for example, already_jumped) that gets set
to true at the very instant of the jump and is only explicitly cleared upon confirming ground
contact on the following frame, rather than relying solely on jumping.

3. Redrawing the collision box: new offsets and a higher
jump
The next step, just as in chapter 40, is to go back into the graphics editor and manually
draw, on top of the sprite, the rectangle considered to be the character’s actual collision
box. It’s usually somewhat narrower than the full sprite, since the hat, the sword, or other
decorative details shouldn’t block the character against the scenery. Exactly where to draw
thatrectangleisadesigndecision,notamathematicalcalculation: itdependsonthespecific
look of each sprite, and there’s no general formula for deriving it.
From that rectangle, the four constants PLAYER_COLBOX_LEFT, PLAYER_COLBOX_RIGHT,
PLAYER_COLBOX_TOP, and PLAYER_COLBOX_BOTTOM are measured, always as pixel offsets
measured from the top-left corner of the full sprite (the reference point the Mega Drive uses
to position any sprite on screen). For this sprite, for example:
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_LEFT 16
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_RIGHT 32
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_TOP 6
#define PLAYER_COLBOX_BOTTOM 60

character enough momentum to clear the new sprite’s extra height. Like the collision box
offsets, this value is an empirical adjustment based on the look of this particular sprite, not
the result of a general formula.
fix32 jumping_vel = FIX32(14);
4. First results: jumping works, but the character passes
through platforms from the sides
Compiling at this point, the result is partially encouraging: the character can jump and fall
normally, and collision against the ground and against the ceiling, that is, the top and bot-
tom corners of the box, works correctly. The problem shows up when moving sideways: the
characterpassesstraightthroughsolidplatformsfromtheside,bothleftandright,asifthey
weren’t there.
The cause is easy to spot by looking at the code inherited from chapter 40: for each side of
the collision box, the system only checks two points, the top corner and the bottom corner of
that side. With the compact sprite from chapter 41, those two points were enough, because
the entire height of the collision box fit within a single 16-pixel collision tile. With this much
taller sprite, the collision box spans several tiles in height, and there’s a considerable gap
betweenthetopcornerandthebottomcornerthatneitherpointmanagestocheck: ifasolid
platform happens to sit at exactly that intermediate height, the character can pass through
it without the game detecting it.
Jumping and vertical collision already work, but the character still passes through platforms
when moving sideways.
5. A first intermediate point: one alone isn’t enough
The conceptual solution is to add extra checkpoints between the top and bottom corners of
each side. Conveniently, the tile coordinate of the top corner has already been calculated, so

10. What if 8×8 collision tiles were used instead of 16×16?
Acommonquestionatthispointiswhynotjustuseafinercollisiongrid,8×8pixelsinsteadof
16×16, since that would eliminate the problem of gaps between checkpoints at the root. It’s
perfectlypossible(you’djustneedtoadaptthepixel-to-tileconversionformulasandallrelated
calculations), but it brings some downsides that explain why 16×16 is the more common
convention.
On one hand, since there would be twice as many tiles both horizontally and vertically, the

Chapter 43 — Semi-Solid
Platforms
Almost every platformer from the 16-bit era includes a very particular kind of tile: the semi-
solidplatform. Unlikeafullysolidfloororwalltile,thistypeofplatformcanbefreelypassed

This chapter adds that behavior to the collision system built in the previous chapters of this

Thereasonissimple: thecopiedcodeblockdoesn’tdistinguishwhichdirectionthecharacter

5. The conceptual solution: comparing the current posi-
tion with the previous frame’s
One possible solution would be to simply check whether the character’s vertical velocity is
positive or negative, similar to how the mid-air jump bug was solved in chapter 41. However,
checking only the sign of the vertical velocity, instead of comparing against the previous
frame’s position, can end up causing bugs in certain particular circumstances with this type
of platform. That’s why a different approach is preferable: storing, on every frame, the char-
acter’sYpositionfromthepreviousframe,beforegravityandtherestofthatframe’svertical
movement are applied.
By comparing that previous position with the current one, it’s possible to know for certain
whether the character is moving downward (falling) or upward (jumping): since the Mega
Drive’s Y axis grows downward, if the current position is numerically greater than the previ-
ous one, the character is moving downward.
fix32 previous_player_y;
This variable is declared at the beginning of collision() and is updated to the value of
player_y before gravity and the rest of that frame’s vertical movement are applied. With it
declared,thePLATFORM_TILEblock’sconditionisexpanded: besidesrequiringthatthebottom-
leftorbottom-righttilebeofplatformtype,itnowalsorequiresthatplayer_ybegreaterthan
previous_player_y,meaningthecharactermustactuallybefallingonthatframeandnotris-

if ((tile_left == PLATFORM_TILE || tile_right == PLATFORM_TILE)
&& player_y > previous_player_y)
{
// collision against the semi-solid platform
}
Withthischange,theresultisnowasexpected: thecharactercanjumpandpassthroughthe
semi-solid platform freely upward, and only gets caught on top of it when falling.
6. A design nuance: how far should the character sink
before getting caught?
With the basic mechanic working, a detail comes up that isn’t exactly a bug, but rather a
design decision: as the code stands at this point, as soon as the character’s feet touch any
part of the platform — even its lowest edge — the character is immediately pushed up to the
platform’s surface. For a fairly thick collision tile, like the one in this example, that behavior
canfeelunnatural: it’sprobablybetterforthecharactertoonlygetcaughtiftheirfeetreach
a reasonably close distance to the platform’s top edge, and if they fall much further below
that, they should simply keep falling through it normally.
This is also a good time to reorganize the code: since in a given frame the character can
only be colliding with the floor, with the ceiling, or with a platform (never two at once), the
standalone if block for PLATFORM_TILE becomes another else if in the same chain already
used for SOLID_TILE, saving unnecessary CPU checks.

7. Implementing the pixel margin before getting caught
Tobeabletocomparethecharacter’spositionagainsttheplatform’stopedgeinwhole-pixel

With a tolerance margin of a few pixels like this one, the character only gets caught if their
feet land within that distance from the platform’s top edge; if they fall further below that,
theysimplykeepfallingthroughit. Thisvalue—likeothersinthischapter,suchasthetimer

in the actual game and tuned according to the desired feel of the jump, rather than derived
from a fixed formula. A margin that’s too wide (say, 8 pixels) can make the character get
caught sooner than expected; one that’s too narrow may require increasing jumping_vel so
the character can more easily reach that narrow band when jumping from below.
8. A serious bug: passing through platforms at high speed
Playing around with the result a bit more reveals a much more serious bug, directly related

margin in a single frame, without the collision code ever detecting it. The result is that the
character passes straight through the platform as if it weren’t there.
One possible solution would be to simply lower the terminal velocity below that margin, but
thatoptionisn’trecommended: withsuchalowterminalvelocity,thecharacter’sfallbecomes
noticeably slow and floaty, an undesirable effect for this type of game. Instead, it’s better to
add an exception to the existing condition.
This problem is, in essence, the same kind of “high-speed tunneling” that already came up
whensolvingaxis-by-axislevelcollisioninchapter40: whenaframe’sdisplacementisgreater
than the detection margin, the object can skip clean over the contact zone.

expanded to also check whether dpad_down is active at that moment, and if so, instead of

The solution is a timer: two new variables, declared alongside the rest of the character’s
physics variables (gravity, jumping_vel, terminal_vel):
bool dpad_down = FALSE;
bool fall_through_platform = FALSE;
u8 fall_through_platform_timer = 0;

fall_through_platform_timerisacounterthatstartsat0,andmax_fall_through_platform_time

few frames, so a long timer isn’t necessary; a value of 4 frames turns out to be enough in
practice, although — like the other values in this chapter — it’s worth tuning experimentally
based on the game’s actual falling speed.
Inside collision(), while fall_through_platform is true, the counter is incremented
every frame, and as soon as it reaches its maximum value, both the counter and
fall_through_platform itself are reset (the latter to false), reactivating normal collision
against the next platform the character encounters:
if (fall_through_platform)
{
fall_through_platform_timer++;
if (fall_through_platform_timer >= max_fall_through_platform_time)
{
fall_through_platform_timer = 0;
fall_through_platform = FALSE;
}
}
With the timer in place, the final result works as expected: holding down and jumping, the

any further than necessary.

Chapter 44 — DMA - Direct
Memory Transfers
The VDP’s DMA controller, SGDK’s dma.c/dma.h unit, and the transfer queue as an optimiza-
tion technique
The dma parameter has already shown up several times in earlier chapters without much
attention being paid to it: in PAL_setPalette(PAL0, bg1.palette->data, DMA) and in
VDP_drawImageEx(BG_B, &bg1, ..., TRUE),whereitwasexplainedinpassingthatDMAstands
for Direct Memory Access and that it’s a copy mechanism that, unlike copying with the CPU,
is cheaper in terms of processor time. That explanation was enough to keep moving forward
with backgrounds and sprites, but it leaves out questions that become unavoidable as soon
as a game grows: why is DMA faster than a CPU copy if, at some point, the same bytes still
have to be moved? Can DMA be controlled more finely than with a simple TRUE/FALSE? What
happens if, in a single frame, more VRAM needs to be updated than DMA can move?
ThischapteropensPartVIIIofthemanual,dedicatedtoVRAMoptimizationandperformance,
andanswersthosequestionsindetail. Thereisn’taflashynewfunctiontolearnfromscratch
here — the underlying mechanism has already been used, unknowingly, since chapter 7 —
but rather a deeper understanding of something that was already being used only halfway,
plus access to an SGDK unit, dma.h, that until now has stayed completely hidden behind the
dma/DMA parameter of other functions.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• An understanding of the VDP, VRAM, CRAM, and VSRAM as presented in chapter 2.
• Some prior experience, even without going deep, using the dma/DMA parameter of func-
tions like PAL_setPalette() or VDP_drawImageEx(), covered in chapter 7.
• A general sense of how SGDK organizes its resources in ROM (chapter 39), since the
examples in this chapter load tilesets generated from an IMAGE resource.
1. What DMA does at the hardware level
The Mega Drive’s CPU, a Motorola 68000, can write data to the VDP’s VRAM, but it can only
do so one word (16 bits) at a time, and each of those writes is one more instruction within
the program: it involves decoding the instruction, calculating the destination address, and
executing the write, all of which consumes 68000 clock cycles. Copying an entire tileset of
several thousand bytes this way, word by word, in a software loop, is a slow operation that
keeps the processor busy the whole time.
294

=== PAGE 301 ===
The VDP solves this with its own DMA controller: a dedicated circuit, separate from the
68000’slogic,capableoftakingcontrolofthesystembusandmovinganentireblockofdata
from memory (the cartridge ROM or the 68000’s working RAM) directly into VRAM, CRAM,
or VSRAM, without the 68000 having to execute one instruction per word transferred. The
programmer simply tells the VDP where to copy from, where to copy to, and how much, and
the VDP itself takes care of the rest.
It’s worth being precise about what this does and doesn’t mean. It’s tempting to imagine
DMAassomethingthathappens“inparallel,”leavingtheCPUfreetokeepcalculatinggame
logic while the data travels to VRAM on its own. That’s not exactly how it works: during a
DMAtransfer,theDMAcontrollertakesthesystembusforitself,andthe68000iseffectively
halted — unable to access memory or keep executing — until the transfer finishes. The gain
from DMA isn’t that the CPU“does something else in the meantime,” but rather two distinct,
more concrete gains:
• ThedatamovementitselfismuchfasterthantheequivalentloopwritteninCorassembly,
because it’s done by a circuit dedicated to that single task, without the cost of decoding
instructions.
• That pause time can be deliberately placed at a moment when the CPU had nothing
better to do: the vertical blank period (vblank), the instant between when the VDP fin-
ishes drawing one frame and starts the next, during which there’s nothing on screen to
update, and much of the time games are already waiting for that moment anyway with
SYS_doVBlankProcess().
It’spreciselythatsecondpointthatexplainswhy,inchapter7,itwassaidthatDMA“doesn’t
take up CPU time”: in practice, when the transfer is triggered during vblank, it isn’t taking
useful time away from any game calculation, because that time was already earmarked for
waiting. The nuance this chapter adds is that this claim depends on when the transfer hap-
pens, and it isn’t free if DMA is triggered in the middle of game logic, during active screen
drawing.
2. Beyond the boolean: TransferMethod
Thefunctionsseensofar,likeVDP_drawImageEx(),exposeDMAinthesimplestpossibleway: a
bool dmaparameterthat’seitherTRUE(useDMA)orFALSE(copywiththeCPU).Buttheactual
mechanism behind it, which other SGDK functions expose directly, is a richer enumerated
type:
typedef enum
{
CPU = 0,
DMA = 1,
DMA_QUEUE = 2,
DMA_QUEUE_COPY = 3
} TransferMethod;
PAL_setPalette(),infact,wasalreadyreceivingthistypebackinchapter7(PAL_setPalette(PAL0,
bg1.palette->data, DMA)), although at that point only two of its four possible values were
used:
• CPU — copies the data with the CPU itself, word by word. It’s the slowest option, but
it doesn’t require the source data to remain intact after the call: the copy is already
finished by the time the function returns.
• DMA — triggers a DMA transfer immediately, in a blocking way: the function doesn’t
return until the VDP has finished moving the data. This is the option used so far in this
295

=== PAGE 302 ===
manual.
• DMA_QUEUE — instead of transferring right away, queues the operation to run automati-
cally during the next vblank.
• DMA_QUEUE_COPY—avariantofthepreviousonemeantfordatathatisn’tstableinmemory
(for example, a temporary buffer or a local variable): before queuing, it copies the data
into an internal area reserved by SGDK, so that the original content can be modified or
discardedimmediatelyafterthecallwithoutaffectingtheactualtransfer,whichwillonly
happen at the next vblank.
These last two values are the gateway to the real subject of this chapter: the DMA queue.
3. The dma.h unit and its low-level functions
Everythingabove—thebool dmaofVDP_drawImageEx(),theTransferMethodofPAL_setPalette()
— is, underneath, a convenience layer over an SGDK unit dedicated specifically to DMA:
dma.h. This unit exposes functions to trigger transfers explicitly, without going through
a higher-level drawing function, which is useful when you need to move data that isn’t
necessarily a whole image (for example, updating just part of a tileset, or writing data
generated at runtime).
The most direct function is DMA_doDma(), which triggers an immediate, blocking transfer —
the explicit equivalent of using DMA as the TransferMethod:
void DMA_doDma(u8 location, void *from, u16 to, u16 len, s16 step);
• location — the destination of the transfer within the VDP: DMA_VRAM, DMA_CRAM, or
DMA_VSRAM.
• from — a pointer to the source data (in ROM or in the 68000’s RAM).
• to — the destination address within VRAM, CRAM, or VSRAM, depending on location.
• len — the amount of data to transfer, measured in 16-bit words (not bytes).
• step—howmuchthedestinationaddressadvancesaftereachwordwritten;foranormal,
contiguous copy the usual value is 2.
There’s also DMA_transfer(), which adds a TransferMethod parameter at the front and del-
egates to CPU, DMA, DMA_QUEUE, or DMA_QUEUE_COPY as appropriate, acting as the single entry
point used internally by functions like PAL_setPalette():
bool DMA_transfer(TransferMethod tm, u8 location, void *from, u16 to, u16 len, u16
↪ step);
To upload, for example, the tileset from an IMAGE resource to VRAM without going through
VDP_drawImageEx(), the explicit call would be:
u16 ind = TILE_USERINDEX;
// Immediate, blocking transfer of level1's tiles
// into VRAM, starting at tile index 'ind'.
DMA_doDma(DMA_VRAM, level1.tileset->tiles, ind * 32,
level1.tileset->numTile * 16, 2);
The calculation ind * 32 converts a tile index into a byte address in VRAM (each tile takes
up 32 bytes), and numTile * 16 converts the tile count into the number of 16-bit words that
need to be transferred (32 bytes per tile equal 16 words). These are the same calculations
VDP_drawImageEx() performs internally when called with dma = TRUE; the difference is that
here they’re visible and under the programmer’s direct control.
296

=== PAGE 303 ===
4. The DMA queue: queuing instead of forcing
Triggeringanimmediatetransferliketheoneintheprevioussectionhasapracticallimitation:
if a single frame needs to upload several tilesets, several palettes, and maybe also update
VSRAM for a scroll effect, each DMA_doDma() call blocks execution until it finishes, one after
another, with no centralized control over how much total time is being used or over exactly
when each transfer happens within the frame.
SGDKsolvesthiswithaqueuingsystem. Insteadoftriggeringthetransferatthemomentit’s
requested, it gets recorded in an internal list:
bool DMA_queueDma(u8 location, void *from, u16 to, u16 len, u16 step);
The parameters are the same as those of DMA_doDma(), with one fundamental difference:
DMA_queueDma() doesn’t move any data at the moment it’s called. It just stores the operation
(destination,source,length,step)inaninternalqueue. Thatqueueisprocessedautomatically,
as a batch, during the next vblank — the same period during which SYS_doVBlankProcess()
runs — at which point SGDK’s engine triggers, one after another, all the transfers that have
been queued since the previous vblank.
This has an important consequence for the source data: since the actual transfer happens
later, the from pointer passed to DMA_queueDma() needs to keep pointing to valid, unmodified
data until the vblank actually processes it. For a tileset living in ROM this isn’t a problem,
since its content never changes. But if the source is a temporary buffer, a local variable,
or any data the program is going to modify or discard before the next vblank, you need the
variant that copies the data immediately into an internal area reserved by SGDK:
bool DMA_copyAndQueueDma(u8 location, void *from, u16 to, u16 len, u16 step);
DMA_copyAndQueueDma() copies the data pointed to by from into an SGDK-owned buffer at
the moment it’s called (a CPU copy, fast since it’s usually a small block) and queues the
actualtransferfromthatinternalbuffer,notfromtheoriginalfrom. It’sthesameideabehind
DMA_QUEUE_COPY as a TransferMethod, and it’s the option to pick whenever the source data
isn’t a constant resource in ROM.
That internal copy buffer has a limited size, configurable with:
void DMA_setBufferSize(u16 value);
u16 DMA_getBufferSize(void);
void DMA_setBufferSizeToDefault(void);
Andthequeueitself—thenumberofdistinctoperationsitcanhold,notthenumberofbytes
— also has a configurable size:
void DMA_setMaxQueueSize(u16 value);
u16 DMA_getMaxQueueSize(void);
void DMA_setMaxQueueSizeToDefault(void);
Sizing both values is, essentially, a trade-off decision between available RAM and the
amount/sizeoftransfersagameneedstogroupintoasingleframe: agamethatonlyupdates
palettes and the occasional stray tile per frame can get along perfectly well with the default
values; a game that loads entire tilesets at once when changing levels may need a bigger
queue, or may need to resort directly to a copy buffer with more room if much of that data is
assembled at runtime rather than already coming packaged in ROM.
297

=== PAGE 304 ===
5. The real limits of the VDP’s DMA
DMAisn’tmagic: it’sstillsubjecttothelimitationsofrealVDPhardware,andunderstanding
them avoids surprises when deciding how much VRAM to update at once.
The source data can’t be just any memory address. The VDP’s DMA controller can only
read from the cartridge ROM or from the 68000’s working RAM; it can’t, for instance, read
directlyfromtheZ80’sRAM(thesoundprocessor)orfromanyothermemoryregionoutside
that map. On top of that, real Mega Drive hardware has a well-known quirk: a DMA transfer
can’t cross a 128 KB boundary within that source memory without the address “wrapping
around” incorrectly within that same 128 KB block. It’s a real limitation of the chip, not
of SGDK, and SGDK handles it transparently: when a queued or immediate transfer would
cross one of those boundaries, DMA_queueDma() and DMA_doDma() automatically split it into
twoconsecutiveoperations, oneon eachsideof theboundary, withoutthecode callingthese
functions having to worry about detecting it.
The vblank time available for DMA is finite. The VDP can only move a limited amount of
data during a single vblank period — on the order of a few thousand bytes per frame, with a
somewhat higher figure on PAL systems than on NTSC due to a longer vblank — and SGDK
exposes that figure as a configurable limit:
u16 DMA_getMaxTransferSize(void);
void DMA_setMaxTransferSize(u16 value);
void DMA_setMaxTransferSizeToDefault(void);
Whenthesumofallthetransfersqueuedforagivenframeexceedsthatlimit,notallofthem
get processed in the immediate vblank: depending on how the behavior for that overflow
is configured (DMA_getIgnoreOverCapacity() / DMA_setIgnoreOverCapacity()), the excess is
either ignored or left pending. Either way, SGDK’s queue doesn’t automatically spread
the leftover work across the following frames: it’s the game code’s own responsibility
not to queue, all at once, more than a single vblank can process, and to deliberately split a
largeloadacrossseveralframeswhenneeded—forexample,uploadingoneportionofanew
level’s tileset per frame over a handful of frames, instead of all at once.
During active drawing, DMA is even slower still. Outside of vblank, while the VDP is
busy reading VRAM to draw the screen, it can only spare DMA the memory access slots left
over between one video read and the next, which are very few. The practical result is that a
transfer triggered in the middle of active drawing crawls along at a fraction of the speed it
wouldhaveduringvblank,ontopofriskingpausingthe68000atamomentwhenit’sprobably
in the middle of some time-sensitive calculation, such as a frame’s physics. That’s why the
general recommendation — and the reason the DMA queue exists — is to concentrate large
transfersintovblankasmuchaspossible,ratherthanfiringthemoffindividuallyduringgame
logic.
Thought of as a timeline, a video frame is split into an active-drawing period, fairly long,
followed by a vblank period, much shorter but with all of its capacity available for DMA.
Whentheamountofdatatomoveexceedswhatfitsintothatvblank,theleftoverportionisn’t
transferredinthatframe: it’sleftpendingforthenextone,unlessthegamecodeitselftakes
care of splitting it up beforehand.
6. Why queuing is an optimization technique
With the pieces above in place, it’s now possible to answer the question that motivated this
chapter: why queue DMA transfers instead of forcing them all immediately?
The short answer is that queuing moves control over when each transfer happens from the
298

=== PAGE 305 ===
point in the code where what to transfer is decided to a single place, vblank processing,
where SGDK can take the frame’s real capacity limit into account. If a game needs, at the
same instant of game logic, to update a new enemy’s palette, upload an animated tile, and
refresh a row of a scrolling map, forcing three immediate transfers with DMA_doDma() one
after another blocks execution three times in a row, with no guarantee that the whole set
will comfortably fit into the next vblank. Queuing all three with DMA_queueDma() (or with
DMA_QUEUE/DMA_QUEUE_COPY in the higher-level functions that support it) lets the game code
keep running without pauses until vblank, at which point all three are processed together,
respecting the frame’s capacity limit.
This same mechanism becomes even more relevant when the amount of data to move isn’t
small, as happens when loading the entire graphics set for a new level at once: several tile-
sets, several palettes, and potentially several tile maps, all ready for the first frame in which
the level becomes visible. It’s easy for that amount of data to exceed what a single vblank
can process. The DMA queue doesn’t solve that problem automatically — as noted in the
previous section, it doesn’t spread the excess across future frames on its own — but it does
provide the tools (DMA_canQueue() to find out whether an operation fits within the frame’s
remainingbudget,DMA_getQueueSize()/DMA_getQueueTransferSize()toinspecthowmuchis
already queued) on which an explicit strategy of loading in stages across several frames can
be built. That concrete strategy — how to spread out the loading of a new level across sev-
eral frames without it showing up as a noticeable pause — is picked up in detail later in this
manual, in the chapter dedicated to loading graphics for a new level.

Chapter 45 — Managing VRAM
Limits
How VRAM is divided between background and sprites, how to spot an allocation conflict,
and how to adjust that split with SPR_initEx()
Chapter 44 showed how DMA moves data into VRAM without stopping the CPU. But before
askinghowapieceofdatagetsintoVRAM,it’sworthaskingsomethingmorebasic: whether
there’s room for it. Chapter 2 already established that VRAM has 64 KB in total, and that, in
theory,thisisenoughfor20488×8-pixeltilesifallofthatmemorywerededicatedexclusively
to storing them. In practice, that theoretical figure is never fully available: part of VRAM is
reserved for the plane name tables, the sprite attribute table (SAT), and other internal data,
and SGDK, on top of that, automatically splits whatever remains between background tiles
and sprite tiles. That automatic split usually goes unnoticed while the graphics are modest,
but as soon as a project starts using backgrounds with many unique tiles (a full illustration
converted to tiles, for example, rather than a level tileset with repeating patterns), it can
becomearealproblem: spritetilesendupbeingwrittenontopofbackgroundtiles,producing
visual corruption.
This chapter explains that automatic split, how to detect when it runs out, how to measure
ahead of time how many unique tiles a graphic needs, and how to take manual control of the
allocation with SPR_initEx().
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• The VRAM, tile, and palette vocabulary introduced in Chapter 2.
• The manual VRAM accounting and use of TILE_USERINDEX covered in Chapter 7, since
thischapterrevisitsthatsameideaof“occupiedspace”butappliedtothesplitbetween
background and sprites.
• Basic use of the sprite engine (SPR_addSprite(), SPR_update(), SPR_init()) introduced
in Chapter 21.
• Basichandlingofapixel-arteditorwithindexedpalettesupport(Chapter8),and,inpar-
ticular, of Aseprite’s tileset tool already introduced in Chapter 19, which in this chapter
is reused only for counting tiles, without revisiting how it works internally.
• An emulator with VDP/VRAM debugging tools, such as the Gens emulator introduced in
Chapter 4.
