1. A typical scenario: a nearly full background and an over-
lapping sprite
Picture a project that already has a finished background (a full illustration converted to the
Mega Drive palette, not a level tileset with lots of repeating patterns) and that adds a new
element as a sprite: a title-screen logo, a UI icon, a large character. The sprite itself is
declared, loaded, and drawn without any compile errors, and when the ROM runs it appears
correctly on screen. The problem shows up somewhere else: in the part of the background
that was located “furthest along” in the memory occupied by its tiles, fragments of graphics
appearthatdon’tbelongthere,asifsomethinghadbeenwrittenontop. Ifthenewspritehas
an animation, even one as simple as alternating between two frames, the problem becomes
even more visible: the corrupted area of the background changes appearance in step with
the sprite’s animation, because it’s literally the sprite’s tiles that are showing up there.
Thisisn’tacoincidenceorahardwarebug: it’sanexactsymptomofthebackgroundtilesand
the sprite tiles competing for the same VRAM positions.
2. Why it happens: two automatic allocations sharing the
same space
SGDK doesn’t reserve one fixed block of VRAM for the background and another fixed, inde-
pendent block for sprites: it automatically splits the available space between both uses, and
that split has a limit. Background tiles, loaded through IMAGE, TILESET, or MAP resources,
areplacedstartingat TILE_USERINDEX(seeninChapter7)andmovingforward, occupyingas
many positions as the image has unique tiles. The sprite engine, for its part, automatically
reservesitsownblockofVRAMtouploadthetilesofactivespritesinto, andthatblockhasa
default size.
As long as the background uses few tiles, both blocks coexist without any problem: there’s
plenty of room for both. But if the background gets close to the tile limit that the automatic
split assigns to it, the block reserved for sprites starts to overlap with the tail end of the
backgroundtiles, andthespriteengineendsupwritingitsowndatathere, overwritingback-
ground tiles that were already in use. The result is exactly the corruption described in the
previoussection: it’snotthatthebackgroundisphysicallydamaged, butratherthatanother
set of data now occupies that same VRAM address.
3. How much VRAM is available: rough figures, not uni-
versal constants
To be able to reason about this problem without memorizing memory addresses, it helps to
have a reference figure in mind: in a typical configuration, the VRAM available for user tiles
can be thought of as a space of roughly 1,400 tiles in total, of which SGDK automatically
assigns around the first 1,000 to the background and leaves the remaining 400 for sprites,
throughadefaultreservationof 420tilesthatSPR_init()applieswheninitializingthesprite
engine.
It’sworthstressingthatthesenumbersarearoughsimplification,notaguaranteedconstant
ofthehardwareorofSGDK:thetheoreticalmaximumfigureforVRAM,perChapter2,is2048
tiles if all of memory were dedicated exclusively to tiles, but in practice that figure shrinks
becauseofthespacetakenupbytheplanenametables,theSAT,andotherinternaldata,and
the exact split between background and sprites can vary depending on the resolution mode,
how many planes are in use, and other details specific to each project. Take these figures
301

=== PAGE 308 ===
as a practical guide for reasoning about the problem, and for getting a rough sense of how
muchheadroomthereisbeforetheautomaticsplitstartstofail,notasanexactlimitthatwill
always match, tile for tile, in every configuration.
The practical rule worth remembering. A background built from a fully con-
verted image (as opposed to a level tileset with repeating patterns, where many
tiles get reused) tends to use a number of unique tiles very close to the total num-
ber of tiles the image occupies, because almost no 8×8 cell repeats. That type of
graphicis,byfar,theonemostlikelytoapproachtheavailablelimitandtriggerthe
conflict described in the previous section.
4. Counting unique tiles with Aseprite’s tileset tool
Beforetouchingasinglelineofcode,it’sworthmeasuringhowmanyuniquetileseachimage
in the project actually uses. Chapter 19 already introduced, within Aseprite, the editor’s
native tileset tool (available since version 1.3) as a way to paint a level map while taking
advantage of several palettes at once; that same panel, without needing to revisit how it
works internally, serves here for something much simpler: counting how many distinct tiles
are in an image.
When converting an image to a tileset within Aseprite and enabling the 8×8 grid over the
canvas,thetilesetpanelnumberseachuniquetileitdetectsandletsyouvisuallymatcheach
celloftheimagetoitscorrespondingnumber. Inafullyconvertedimage,likethebackground
in the scenario laid out in section 1, the vast majority of tiles turn out to be unique, except
for the occasional coincidence in areas of very flat color (a plain white surface, for example),
whereseveralcellsshareexactlythesametile. Abackgroundofthiskindcanenduparound,
say, 1,000 unique tiles: a figure that, compared with the automatic background reservation
mentionedintheprevioussection,immediatelyexplainswhythere’salmostnoheadroomleft
before the sprite block starts to overlap.
Repeatingthesameprocedureonthesprite’sgraphic(thelogooraddedelement)mightturn
up, for example, a considerably lower figure, somewhere in the low hundreds of unique tiles.
Addedtothebackgroundtiles,thatfiguremightstillfallwithintherough1,400-tiletotallimit,
andyettheconflictstilloccurs,becauseSGDK’sautomaticsplitdoesn’tknowinadvancehow
many tiles the background is actually going to need: it simply applies a fixed reservation of
420tilesforsprites,regardlessofwhetherthebackgroundendsupusing600or1,000. When
the sum of both actual uses exceeds the total available, the excess is what gets written over
the tail of the background.
5. Adjusting the split with SPR_initEx()
The solution isn’t to shrink the background or sacrifice the sprite, but to tell SGDK exactly
howmuchVRAMtoreserveforthespriteengine,insteadofacceptingtheautomaticvalueof
420 tiles. Instead of the usual function:
SPR_init();
you use:
SPR_initEx(300);
SPR_initEx() takes a single parameter, vramSize, indicating how many VRAM tiles to re-
serve for sprites; passing 0 is equivalent to using the default value of 420 tiles, the same one
SPR_init() applies internally. By lowering that number — from 420 to 300, for example —
302

=== PAGE 309 ===
additional space is freed up for background tiles before the area reserved for sprites begins,
and the sprite tiles start being written further along in VRAM, leaving the tail end of the
background tiles untouched.
Only one of the two sprite-engine initialization functions should be used, never both: if the
project already calls SPR_init(), that call is replaced with SPR_initEx() rather than being
added alongside it.
After recompiling with this change, the background from the scenario laid out at the start of
the chapter should now display without visible corruption, with the sprite — animated or not
— occupying an area of VRAM that no longer interferes with the background tiles. Opening
the emulator’s VDP/VRAM viewer again (Chapter 4) lets you confirm this visually: between
the end of the background tiles and the start of the sprite tiles there should now be a gap
of free space, instead of an overlap. Lowering the vramSize value even further — to 200, for
example — pushes the start of the sprite tiles even further along in memory, widening that
gap.
Figure 130: VDP/VRAM viewer after adjusting to SPR_initEx(300)
The emulator’s VDP/VRAM viewer after the change to SPR_initEx(300): between the end of
the background tiles and the start of the sprite tiles there is now a gap of free space, instead

6. How much VRAM to reserve in a real project
SPR_initEx() doesn’t have a single correct value: how much VRAM to reserve for sprites
depends entirely on the project’s needs. A game with very detailed backgrounds, close to
using a full screen as a single illustration with few repeated tiles, will need to reduce the
sprite reservation to leave more room for the background. A game with large sprites, highly
detailed ones, or many distinct animation frames on screen at once — several enemies with
303

=== PAGE 310 ===
elaboratesprites,forexample—willneedtheoppositeapproach: keepingorevenexpanding
the sprite reservation, at the cost of a simpler background or one with more repeated tiles.
Thattension—moreVRAMforthebackgroundmeanslessforthesprites,andviceversa—is,
toalargeextent,unavoidable: there’snocombinationthatmaximizesbothresourcesatonce,
because they share the same physical space. What’s generally worth avoiding is needlessly
exhausting either side: reserving far more VRAM than a sprite actually needs leaves less
roomforthebackgroundwithnorealbenefit,andthesameholdsinreverse. Justaswiththe
number of colors in a palette, the practical recommendation is to measure first — using the
tilesettooldescribedinsection4—howmuchVRAMeachpartoftheprojectactuallyneeds,
and set SPR_initEx() to that real number, leaving just a small margin, rather than reserving
extra “just in case” or thoughtlessly accepting the automatic value of 420.

1. VRAM anatomy: what’s there, and in what order
Beforetouchinganyconfiguration,it’sworthwalkingthroughtheentiretyofVRAMusingan

see exactly what information lives in each area. In a typical SGDK project, that walkthrough
reveals a fairly consistent order:
1. Sixteen solid-color tiles at the very start, reserved for SGDK’s internal use.
2. The background and foreground tiles of the current level or screen.
3. The tiles that change constantly: the sprites, both the player’s and those of enemies or
other animated elements.
4. SGDK’sbasictextfont, usedtodisplaynumbersandlettersonscreen(thesamedefault
font that already appeared when drawing the first graphics back in Chapter 2).

Don’t mistake the “corrupted”-looking blocks for an actual error. The scroll ta-

2. config.h: a file for reconfiguring SGDK
InsidetheincfolderoftheSGDKinstallation—thesamefolderthatheaderfilesusedearlier
in this manual, like genesis.h, come from — you’ll find config.h, designed specifically to let
you enable or disable certain SGDK features before compiling it.
Among the options config.h offers that this chapter doesn’t touch are, for example, one that

The option that matters here is LEGACY_FONT_LOCATION, which is enabled by default (with a

after SGDK’s 16 internal-use tiles, and frees up the space it used to occupy.
// config.h, inside the inc/ folder of the SGDK installation
#define LEGACY_FONT_LOCATION 0

4. Why it matters: space reserved even when unused
The font changing position within VRAM might seem like a detail with no real practical con-
sequence, but it isn’t. Consider, for example, a level that doesn’t need to display any text
on screen, and where you decide, manually, not to load the font tiles at all. With SGDK’s
oldconfiguration(LEGACY_FONT_LOCATIONsetto1),thatleaveswhatlooks,atfirstglance,like
empty space in VRAM, located right before the background foreground plane’s scroll table.
The intent in not loading the font is usually to make that free space available for additional
sprites. Andforawhile,itdoesseemtowork: asmorespritesaregenerated,theemptyspace
shrinks normally. But at some point, it stops shrinking no matter how many new sprites are
generated; instead, SGDKstartslookingforfreespaceinotherareasofVRAM,reusinggaps
left behind by earlier sprites that are no longer in use.
The reason is that the old configuration reserves that space for the text font unconditionally,
regardless of whether the program ever actually loads a single font tile. That reservation,
invisible to the programmer but very real from SGDK’s point of view, means that neither
the sprite engine nor the background tile loader can ever use that range, no matter how
completely free it appears to be.
5. Recalculating the starting point of available VRAM
With LEGACY_FONT_LOCATION set to 0, that space is finally no longer held captive. To take
advantage of it in your own project’s code, it’s worth revisiting how the starting index of
available VRAM is calculated at the beginning of the routine that loads a level’s graphics.
Until now, that index was usually initialized with the value of TILE_USERINDEX, the SGDK
constantmarkingthefirsttilefreefortheprogrammerafterthetilesreservedbythesystem
(introduced in Chapter 7). Looking at its definition in SGDK’s code, that value is calculated
asthesumofthreeparts: TILE_SYSTEM_INDEX(thepositionwheresystemtilesstart,typically
0), plus TILE_SYSTEM_LENGTH (the length of those system tiles), and FONT_LENGTH (the length
of the font).
In the SGDK 2.11 installation used for this manual, TILE_SYSTEM_LENGTH was 16 and
FONT_LENGTH was 96, but these two numbers should be treated as illustrative, not fixed:
they’re internal SGDK constants and could change in future versions of the framework.
Before relying on a specific numeric value, it’s worth checking it directly in your own
installation, either by letting your editor show the value of TILE_USERINDEX when hovering
over the constant, or by checking its definition in SGDK’s source code.
With those reference values, the example from the previous section wasted 96 whole tiles,
reservedforafontthatthisparticularleveldidn’tevenload. WithLEGACY_FONT_LOCATIONset
to 0, there’s no longer any need to reserve that space before starting to load the level’s own
tiles. SubtractingthatnumberoftilesfromTILE_USERINDEXworksasafirsttest,butitleaves
the code unexpressive and fragile against future SGDK changes. A cleaner alternative is to
use the TILE_FONT_INDEX constant directly as the starting value, since it represents exactly
thepositionwherethefontusedtostartandwhichisnowavailablefortherestoftheproject:
// In the routine that loads the current level's graphics,
// before reserving space for the background and sprites
u16 vram_index = TILE_FONT_INDEX;
The SGDK maintainer recommends not going any further than this and not overwriting the
16 system tiles at the start of VRAM, since doing so can cause problems in certain map-
handling functions. This is an explicit recommendation from the SGDK project itself, so it’s
worth taking seriously in any production-bound code; anyone who still wants to experiment
308

=== PAGE 315 ===
withthatmargincanuseTILE_SYSTEM_INDEXinsteadof TILE_FONT_INDEXasthestartingpoint,
knowingly taking on that risk:
// Riskier: ignores the 16 system tiles.
// When in doubt, prefer TILE_FONT_INDEX.
u16 vram_index = TILE_SYSTEM_INDEX;

Chapter 47 — Reducing Tiles and
Saving VRAM
Uptothispoint,thismanualhasalmostalwaysassumedthatalevel’sgraphicsfitcomfortably
intotheavailableVRAM.Thatassumptionisreasonablewhiledesigningagamefromscratch
for the Mega Drive, because the art creation process itself tends to stay within reasonable
budgets: the artist knows from the start what the platform’s limitations are and draws ac-
cordingly. But sooner or later, anyone tackling a more ambitious project — a port, a demake
of a game designed for more powerful hardware, or simply a game with very detailed back-
grounds — runs into the opposite problem: the graphics already exist, they already look the
waythey’resupposedto,andthenumberofuniquetilestheyneedsimplydoesn’tfitinVRAM.
This chapter deals with what to do in that scenario: how to detect redundant or nearly iden-
ticaltileswithinanalready-finishedtileset, andhowtomergethemtoreclaimspacewithout
sacrificing the visual quality of the final result. Unlike most chapters in this manual, the con-
tent here doesn’t revolve around C code or SGDK functions, but around a technique applied
directly to the artwork itself, supported by tile-editing tools.
Prerequisites
• Understanding what VRAM is and what a unique tile means, covered in chapter 2.
• Familiarity with Aseprite as a tile-based graphics editor, already used in chapters 8 and
19 to create graphics and level maps.
• It’s worth having read chapters 45 and 46, on managing VRAM limits and configuring
VRAM in SGDK 2.x, since this chapter assumes that context and focuses on a comple-
mentary technique: reducing the number of unique tiles at the source, before they ever
take up space on the console.
There’s no need to have any open-source project set up or compiling: the content of this
chapter is independent of whatever C program is being developed and applies to any Mega
Drive project in general.
1. Why it matters: the real limit on unique tiles in VRAM
In theory, the Mega Drive’s 64 kilobytes of VRAM are enough to store up to 2048 unique
tiles, as explained in chapter 2. In practice, however, that theoretical number is never fully
availableforlevelgraphics,becausepartofVRAMisreservedforotherstructuresthesystem
needs,suchasscrolltables(seechapter45fordetailsonhowVRAMisdividedbetweenthose
structures and graphics tiles).
A useful rule of thumb, born out of experience porting games from more powerful hardware
to the Mega Drive, is this: if the combined unique tiles between a level’s background and
311

=== PAGE 318 ===
foreground exceed a thousand, it’s time to start worrying about not having enough room
left for the player’s sprites, enemies, power-ups, and everything else that also consumes
VRAM. The concrete recommendation that follows from that experience is to keep the sum
of background and foreground unique tiles below a thousand, and preferably below eight
hundred, leaving a comfortable margin for everything else a level needs to display on screen
at the same time.
This figure isn’t an exact hardware rule, but a design guideline learned through practical
experience, and it should be treated as such: a useful reference point, not an absolute limit
etched into the console’s silicon.
ThedistinctionbetweenmakinganoriginalgamefortheMegaDriveandportingor
remaking a game originally designed for more powerful hardware is central to this
chapter. Whendesigningfromscratch,thetilebudgettendstoberespectedalmost
as a matter of habit. When remaking a 32-bit game, on the other hand, the goal is
toresembletheoriginalascloselyaspossible,andthatgoalcompetesdirectlywith
theneedtokeepthenumberofuniquetileslow: youdon’talwayshavethefreedom
to simplify the art as much as you’d like. That’s why tile-reduction techniques are
far more relevant in this second scenario.
2. How many tiles professional backgrounds use: some
reference points
Beforedivingintothetechniqueitself,it’sworthgettinganintuitivesenseofhowmanyunique
tilesareneededdependingonthetypeofscene. Afairlyconsistentobservationacrossdiffer-
ent games of the era is that nature is more expensive in tiles than human-made structures:
a natural landscape, with its organic variation of shapes and shadows, resists tile repetition
much more than a brick wall or a regular architectural structure does.
Figure 134: Cave background with rock formations
312

=== PAGE 319 ===
Acavebackgroundwithorganicrockformations: about390uniquetiles,reflectinghowcostly
it is in VRAM to convincingly represent a natural environment.
As an illustrative example (the specific numbers vary a lot from project to project and
shouldn’t be taken as an exact table, just as a sense of scale), a cave background with rock
formations might come in at around 390 unique tiles, a relatively high number that reflects
how expensive it is to convincingly represent a natural environment. A more artificial or
architectural scene — a castle, a corridor, a building façade — on the other hand, tends to
achieve visually rich results with far fewer tiles: a foreground of just 147 tiles alongside a
background of 105, adding up to around 250 in total, or even a foreground of 86 tiles and a
background of 129, both well below the recommended limit of a thousand combined tiles.
The most extreme case of tile economy usually shows up in well-designed repeating pat-
terns: a castle corridor with a wall-and-tower pattern can be achieved with as few as twenty-
one unique tiles in total, despite including trees, different wall heights, and shading on the
stonework. It’s a good reminder of just how much a well-thought-out pattern — with pieces
thatfittogetherandrepeatwithsubtlevariations—candelivervisually,farbeyondwhatthe
actual tile count in VRAM would suggest.

When, despite every design precaution, a background or foreground ends up exceeding the

content. There are community scripts and tools for Aseprite that can automatically detect

5. Similarity search: merging nearly identical tiles
The second function automates exactly this kind of correction. Unlike the frequency search,
herethethresholddoesn’trepresentanumberofoccurrencesbutadegreeofvisualsimilarity
between tiles: the lower the number, the more alike two tiles must be to each other to be
flagged as merge candidates.
Before using this function, it’s always worth turning on the option to create a new layer
with the changes (create diff layer or equivalent), so the original layer stays intact in case a
change needs to be reverted. Always working on a copy is a cheap precaution against the
cost of losing or damaging a level’s original graphic.

Running the similarity search highlights pairs of nearly identical tiles, indicating for each

Thescriptdetectsapairofnearlyidenticaltiles,differingbyjustacoupleofpixels,candidates

As an illustrative example of the typical magnitude of savings achievable with this kind of

This technique is especially useful for those porting or remaking an existing game, because

Chapter 48 — Saving VRAM
Through Manual Sprite Loading
Chapter21showedthemostdirectwaytoputaspriteonscreen: defineit,addittothescene
with SPR_addSprite(), and let the SGDK engine handle everything else, including uploading
the graphic’s tiles to the VDP’s VRAM. That convenience has a cost that isn’t always obvious
until many sprites are needed on screen at the same time, especially when several instances
share exactly the same graphic. This chapter makes that cost concrete and teaches how to
take manual control of VRAM so that repeated instances of the same sprite share a single
copy of their tiles.
The case study is a background decoration element (trees that scroll with parallax between
the background and foreground) within a sample project. The same reasoning applies to any
sprite that repeats many times on screen with the same graphic: clouds, stars, collectible
items, projectiles, and so on. Understanding this technique is also the gateway to a broader
topic: themanual,strategicmanagementofVRAMasaresourcesharedbetweenbackground,
foreground, and sprites, which was already raised in chapters 45 through 47 and continues
to be developed here from another angle.
Prerequisites
• Knowledge of C and prior experience with SGDK: creating a project, compiling, and
running it in an emulator.
• FamiliaritywiththebasiclifecycleofSGDK’sspriteengine: SPR_init(),SPR_addSprite(),
SPR_update(), and the concept of SpriteDefinition as a container for a sprite’s anima-
tion frames (chapters 21 and 23).
• AgeneralunderstandingoftheVDP’sVRAMandwhatatileis(the8x8-pixelgraphiccell,
the minimum unit of VRAM storage), covered in chapter 2, along with manual VRAM
accounting and TILE_USERINDEX from chapter 7. This chapter does not explain those
conceptsfromscratch, butgoesdeeperintohowtheyaremanagedwhentheautomatic
engine is no longer enough.
• An emulator with a VRAM debugger (BlastEm, for example), which lets you view in real
time which tiles are loaded and in what position.
1. The hidden cost of the automatic sprite engine
By default, SGDK’s sprite engine assumes it’s best to stream each sprite’s animations from
ROM to VRAM as they’re needed, frame by frame. This is one of the great advantages of
cartridge-based systems over CD-based ones: ROM is read with the almost instantaneous
latency and bandwidth of the system bus, while a CD-ROM drive of the era was too slow to
feed VRAM on the fly with that same agility.
320

=== PAGE 327 ===
Deep dive: why the CD complicated animation
Consoles like the Mega CD, PlayStation, and Saturn couldn’t rely on nimble tile
streaming because accessing a CD-ROM is much slower and less predictable than
accessingcartridgeROM.Theusualsolutionwastoloadacharacter’sentireanima-
tion sheet into VRAM during the level-loading stage, instead of bringing in frames
on the fly. The best-known side effect of this limitation is the “stutter” suffered by
some fighting games of the era — Mortal Kombat is a frequently cited case — dur-
ingfinalbattles,whenthegameneedstoloadthefullanimationofanewcharacter
entering the scene into VRAM.
On the Mega Drive, however, the fact that animation can be streamed from ROM doesn’t
meanit’salwaysadvisabletodoso. WatchingtheVRAMdebuggerwhilevariouscommercial
games run reveals a pattern:
• In Mortal Kombat (Mega Drive version) there is constant VRAM activity: each char-
acter’s animation tiles are continuously streamed from ROM, being replaced frame by
frame.
• InE-SWAT,theplayer’sanimationisstreamedthesameway,buttheenemies’animations
arefullypreloaded: evenifanenemymovesorattacks,there’snonewactivityinVRAM,
because those tiles were already there from the start.
• In The Revenge of Shinobi something similar happens and is easy to observe: if the
player moves, new tiles enter VRAM and the scroll table shifts; but if the player stands
still and only the enemies move, there is no change whatsoever in VRAM, because the
enemy ninjas’ animations were already preloaded beforehand.
Figure 142: The Revenge of Shinobi alongside the VRAM debugger
TheRevengeofShinobirunninginBlastEmalongsidetheVRAMdebugger: theplayer’stiles
are streamed live as they move, while the enemies’ tiles are already preloaded and don’t
change even as they move or attack.
The most telling case is that of the rings in Sonic the Hedgehog. When many instances of
321

=== PAGE 328 ===
a ring appear on screen at the same time, they don’t each stream their own copy of the
animation: it is preloaded a single time, and every visible instance reuses it. In the VRAM
debugger those tiles appear colored red instead of the yellow they show on screen, because
thedebuggerdoesn’tapplythecolorpaletteinrealtime—itonlyshowstherawpixelpattern
as it’s stored.
Two reasons to prefer preloading over streaming
1. Performance: streaming tiles to VRAM every frame consumes DMA time and
CPUcycles;overusingthistechniquewithmanyspritesatoncecancauseslow-
downs.
2. VRAM savings: when the same graphic is needed for several simultaneous
instances (rings, clouds, background trees), uploading it once and having all
instancespointtothatsamecopyisstrictlymoreefficientthanlettingthesprite
engine upload an independent copy for each instance.
2. The problem in concrete terms: four trees, four copies
Thesampleprojectaddsathirdparallaxlayerbetweenthebackgroundandforegroundusing

with some irregularity so the scrolling looks natural. The problem appears when you look at
VRAM.
Figure 143: Four decorative trees and the VRAM debugger

Allfourtreesuseexactlythesamegraphic. However, sinceeachonewasaddedtothescene

3. Modeling reusable background sprites
Before solving the VRAM problem, it’s worth looking at how the code that manages
these background sprites is organized, since the solution builds directly on that struc-
ture. The design closely follows the one typically used for a game’s enemies: a
header file (background_sprites.h) with the data types, and an implementation file
(background_sprites.c) with the concrete data and functions.
3.1 The data types
Two structures are defined. The first describes each unique background sprite graphic that
exists in the game (a tree, for example, and later on clouds and stars):
struct BGSpriteType {
const SpriteDefinition* image;
Palette palette;
bool highPriority;
};
The image field points to the graphic’s SpriteDefinition. The palette field indicates which
of the VDP’s four color palettes that sprite uses, under the assumption that all instances of a
giventypeshareapalette. ThehighPriorityfielddetermineswhetherthespriteisdrawnin
front of or behind the foreground plane: the trees, clouds, and stars in this chapter use low
priority because they must stay behind the foreground, but the field exists because that isn’t
always the case.
When a background sprite needs high priority
ThehighPriorityfieldisnotsuperfluous: therearelegitimatecaseswhereadeco-
rative element must be drawn in front of everything. The arcade version of Mortal
Kombat, for example, has hanging chains that appear in front of the player in a
particularstagetoreinforcethesenseofdepth. Thesamebackground-spritemech-
anismdescribedinthischaptercanbeusedforthatkindofeffectjustbychanging
this field.
The second structure describes each concrete instance of a background sprite within a level:
struct BGSprite {
u8 status;
u8 type;
fix32 x;
fix32 y;
Sprite* sprite;
};
status indicates whether the instance is active or inactive (unlike enemies, which also have
attack, chase, or recovery states, background sprites for now only need these two possibili-
ties). type identifies, via an enum, which of the unique types in BGSpriteType it corresponds
to. x and y are the position in fixed-point (fix32), and sprite holds the pointer to the actual
instance managed by the SGDK engine once it’s created.
323

=== PAGE 330 ===

Also notice that this level’s entries use the type CLOUD_BG_SPRITE, even though the graphic it

NUM_BG_SPRITES_PER_LEVEL is not the actual number of active sprites
Thisconstantsetsthemaximumsizeoftheper-levelarray(10,intheexample),not

without having to resize arrays, at the cost of a bit of unused ROM memory.
3.3 From ROM to working RAM
The data above lives in ROM and is read-only. To manipulate the state of background sprites
during gameplay (activating them, moving them, assigning them their Sprite instance), a
working copy in RAM is needed:
struct BGSprite current_bg_sprites[NUM_BG_SPRITES_PER_LEVEL];
which is filled, when each level loads, by the function copyBGSpriteArray():
324

=== PAGE 331 ===
void copyBGSpriteArray() {
for (u8 i = 0; i < NUM_BG_SPRITES_PER_LEVEL; i++) {
current_bg_sprites[i] =
bg_sprites[all_levels[current_game_section].background_sprites][i];
}
}
This function walks through the ROM template corresponding to the current game section
(current_game_section) and copies it into the working array in RAM.
4. Integration with the level loader
Enemies appear, to a greater or lesser extent, in practically any section of the game. Back-
ground sprites are the exception: in a game with hundreds of sections (title screens, menus,
levels), perhaps only a handful have background sprites. Reserving a background-sprite ar-
ray entry for every section, as is done with enemies, would waste ROM in the vast majority
of cases where it isn’t needed.
For that reason, the Level structure (used to describe each game section in the all_levels
array) includes an additional field:
struct Level {
// ...
const u8 background_sprites;
};
This field takes a value from an enum listing the different background-sprite zones in the
game (for example, the zone corresponding to the city or the one for the harbor), with a
special value NO_BG_SPRITES for sections that have none. The function that loads each level,
levelLoader(), checks this field before creating the background sprites:
void levelLoader() {
// ...
createPlayer();
createEnemies();
if (all_levels[current_game_section].background_sprites != NO_BG_SPRITES)
createBGSprites();
current_game_state = RUNNING_LEVEL;
// ...
}
Why this field is optional and the enemies one isn’t
This design asymmetry is not accidental. In a full game with several hundred sec-
tions, only a minority tend to include background sprites, while almost all include
some enemy. A mandatory field for background sprites, analogous to the one for
enemies,wouldmeanreservinganemptybackground_spritesentryinROMforev-
ery section without background sprites — a systematic waste. The sentinel value
NO_BG_SPRITES solvesthe problem at a minimal memory cost (a single byte per sec-
tion) in exchange for an extra check at load time.
The other key element for what follows is the variable u16 vram_ind, declared as extern in
levels.h. It keeps track of the position (the tile index) up to which VRAM is occupied as the
325

=== PAGE 332 ===
various graphic elements of a level are loaded, in order:
• It’sinitializedtoTILE_USERINDEX,thefirstfreeindexafterthetilesreservedbythesystem
(see chapter 7).
• It’s used to load the background image (VDP_drawImageEx) and is then incremented by
the number of tiles that image occupied.
• It’s used to load the foreground tileset (VDP_loadTileSet) and is incremented again.
• From that point on, it’s available so that createBGSprites() (or any other system that
uploads tiles manually) knows from which index it can write without overwriting data
already loaded.
vram_ind is a manual counter: getting it wrong throws everything off
Sincevram_indismanagedbyhand,addingthenumberoftilesusedaftereachload,
an accounting error (forgetting to increment it, or incrementing it by too much or
too little) causes two different elements to end up writing over the same VRAM re-
gion. The symptom is predictable: tiles from one element replacing or mixing with
those of another, producing corrupted graphics. Section 7 of this chapter deliber-
ately shows that error so it’s recognizable if it happens by accident.
5. The naive version: one copy per instance
With the data model already built, the first version of createBGSprites() (the function re-
sponsible for putting a level’s active background sprites on screen) is as straightforward as
possible: copy the level’s template and, for each active entry, ask the sprite engine to add it.
void createBGSprites() {
copyBGSpriteArray();
for (u8 i = 0; i < NUM_BG_SPRITES_PER_LEVEL; i++) {
if (current_bg_sprites[i].status != INACTIVE_BG_SPRITE) {
current_bg_sprites[i].sprite = SPR_addSprite(
bg_sprites_list[current_bg_sprites[i].type].image,
F32_toInt(current_bg_sprites[i].x),
F32_toInt(current_bg_sprites[i].y),
TILE_ATTR(bg_sprites_list[current_bg_sprites[i].type].palette,
bg_sprites_list[current_bg_sprites[i].type].highPriority,
FALSE, FALSE));
}
}
}
This code compiles and works: the four trees appear on screen exactly in the expected po-
sitions. The problem, as already shown in section 2, is that each call to SPR_addSprite()
independently uploads the tiles of bg_sprites_list[...].image to VRAM, with no instance
aware that another has already uploaded exactly the same graphic. Four instances of the
same tree produce four identical copies in VRAM.
6. The solution: load once and share the VRAM index
SGDK offers a mechanism designed exactly for this scenario: manually upload a SpriteDef-
inition’s tiles a single time, then tell each Sprite instance to use that same copy instead
of managing its own. Three pieces work together here: the function SPR_loadAllFrames(),
whichperformsthemanualload,andthemethodsSPR_setAutoTileUpload()andSPR_setVRAMTileIndex(),
326

=== PAGE 333 ===
which reconfigure a Sprite instance so that it no longer manages its own tiles and instead
points to the ones already loaded.
6.1 SPR_loadAllFrames(): uploading the tiles a single time
The function’s signature, according to the SGDK documentation, is:
u16 SPR_loadAllFrames(const SpriteDefinition *sprDef, u16 index, u16
↪ *totalNumTile);
sprDefistheSpriteDefinitionwhosetilesaretobeuploadedtoVRAM;indexistheposition
(thetileindex)wherethey’llbewritten;totalNumTile,ifnotNULL,letsyouretrievehowmany
tiles in total were occupied by all the loaded animation frames. The function also returns a
dynamically allocated index table that reveals the VRAM position of each frame of each ani-
mation;sincethischapterdoesn’tneedtomanipulateanimationsframebyframe,thatreturn
valueandthetotalNumTileparameteraresetasidefornow(passingNULL)andrevisitedlater
in this manual.
This function can take several frames: call it only during loading
The SGDK documentation itself warns about this: SPR_loadAllFrames() can take
quite a while (several game frames) because it uploads via DMA the entirety of the
tiles from every animation in the given SpriteDefinition. For that reason it must
be called during initialization or level loading, never inside the game’s main loop.
In the project’s code, this call is added a single time, before the loop that iterates over the
backgroundsprites: unlikeSPR_addSprite(),thisloadmustnotberepeatedforeachinstance.
void createBGSprites() {
copyBGSpriteArray();
SPR_loadAllFrames(bg_sprites_list[current_bg_sprites[0].type].image,
vram_ind = vram_ind + 10, NULL);
for (u8 i = 0; i < NUM_BG_SPRITES_PER_LEVEL; i++) {
if (current_bg_sprites[i].status != INACTIVE_BG_SPRITE) {
current_bg_sprites[i].sprite = SPR_addSprite(/* ... as before ... */);
SPR_setAutoTileUpload(current_bg_sprites[i].sprite, FALSE);
SPR_setVRAMTileIndex(current_bg_sprites[i].sprite, vram_ind);
}
}
}
Two details of this call deserve explanation. The first is where the graphic to load
comes from: rather than writing the tree graphic’s name literally, the code takes
bg_sprites_list[current_bg_sprites[0].type].image, i.e., the graphic used by the ar-
ray’s first active entry. This keeps the code a bit more flexible than a hardcoded value,
though it only works correctly as long as all the background sprites in a given level share a
single graphic, which is the case in this example.
This technique assumes a single graphic shared per level
Taking the graphic from current_bg_sprites[0] is only correct if, within a given
level, all background sprites use the same SpriteDefinition. If a level needed to
mix, say, trees and clouds with different graphics at the same time, this scheme

=== PAGE 334 ===
would need to be extended by calling SPR_loadAllFrames() once for each distinct
graphic present in the level, rather than once for the whole array.
6.2 The spacing margin in vram_ind
Theseconddetailistheadditionof10positionstotheaccumulatedvalueof vram_indbefore

Care should be taken with expressions like vram_ind = vram_ind + 10 used directly as a

6.3 SPR_setAutoTileUpload() and SPR_setVRAMTileIndex(): reconfiguring
each instance
With the tiles already uploaded a single time, each Sprite instance created with
SPR_addSprite() still needs to be told not to manage its own copy of tiles but instead
to use the one already in VRAM. This is achieved with two additional calls, placed inside the
loop, one per active background sprite:
void SPR_setAutoTileUpload(Sprite *sprite, bool value);
Thevalueparametersetto TRUE(thedefaultbehavior)tellsthespriteenginetokeepupload-
ing this sprite’s tiles automatically; set to FALSE, it tells the engine that responsibility now
rests with the programmer. That is exactly what’s needed here: it’s called with FALSE so the
engine stops trying to upload its own tiles for this instance.
The second call, SPR_setVRAMTileIndex(sprite, index), tells the engine which VRAM posi-
tion to look at for that instance’s tiles when drawing it, instead of the position the engine
would have chosen on its own. The value passed to it must be exactly the same index used
earlier in SPR_loadAllFrames():
SPR_setAutoTileUpload(current_bg_sprites[i].sprite, FALSE);
SPR_setVRAMTileIndex(current_bg_sprites[i].sprite, vram_ind);
The two indices must match exactly
If the index used in SPR_setVRAMTileIndex() doesn’t match the one used in
SPR_loadAllFrames(), the instance will end up displaying on screen whatever
tiles happen to be at that other VRAM position, which could belong to any other
elementofthegame,insteadofthecorrectgraphic. It’sasilenterror: theprogram
compiles and runs without failing, but the visual result is wrong.
Why keep using SPR_addSprite() if VRAM is managed by hand?
Itmightseemthat,ifautomatictileuploadingisgoingtobedisabledanyway,there’s
no need to go through SPR_addSprite(). However, that call is still necessary: it’s
what reserves the Sprite instance within the engine, assigns it a hardware slot,
incorporates it into the priority/depth ordering, and makes it available for the rest

oftheengine’sfunctions(position,animation,flipping). Theonlythingbeingtaken
over is VRAM management, not the rest of the sprite’s lifecycle (see chapter 21).

The difference is in VRAM, where there is now a single copy of the tree tiles instead of four.

Same sample program after the change: where there used to be four identical strips of tree

Chapter 49 — Profiling and CPU
Load
How to know, while the game is running, whether a frame’s work fits into the time available
The previous three chapters of this part each dealt, from a different angle, with the same re-
source: videomemory. Chapter44showedhowDMAmovesdataintoVRAMwithoutstalling
theCPU;chapters45and46explainedhowmuchVRAMisactuallyavailableandhowtosplit
it between background and sprites; chapter 47 showed how to reduce the number of unique
tilesagraphicneedsinordertofitintothatspace. Thischapter,thelastinPartVIII,shiftsthe
axis: instead of asking how much memory something takes up, it asks how much CPU time
it consumes. These are two different questions — a game can have plenty of VRAM to spare
andstill run slowly, or it canhave plenty of free CPUtime tospare and still not fitin memory
— but both answer the same underlying need: making the game work within the hardware’s
real limits, not just within the limits that happen to be convenient to program against.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to keep in mind:
• The main loop and the role of SYS_doVBlankProcess() in synchronizing with the VDP,
introduced in chapter 5.
• Emulatorswithdevelopmenttools—GensKMod,BlastEm—andtheirVDPviewersand
68000 debuggers, introduced in chapter 4.
• DMA as a mechanism for moving data to VRAM without blocking the CPU (chapter 44),
and managing VRAM limits (chapters 45 through 47), as a reference for the other half
of optimizing a Mega Drive game.
• Bit shifting as an alternative to multiplication and division, seen when calculating paral-
lax depth for a background in chapter 25.
• Collision arrays traversed frame by frame, introduced in Part VII (chapters 40 through
43).
1. A frame’s budget: what “frame budget” means
A console doesn’t draw a continuous image: it draws a succession of complete frames, one
afteranother,atafixedrateimposedbythevideohardwareitself. OnaMegaDriveconfigured
for NTSC output, that rate is 60 frames per second; on one configured for PAL, it’s 50. That
figure isn’t a performance target to aim for: it’s literally the rate at which the VDP sweeps
the screen, the same regardless of how simple or complex the scene is.
A direct calculation follows from that figure. At 60 frames per second, each frame has 1/60
of a second — about 16.7 milliseconds — to complete. At 50 frames per second, that margin
332

=== PAGE 339 ===
risesto20milliseconds. Thatinterval—theframebudget—isallthetimetheprogramhas
to do absolutely everything a frame needs: read the controls, update the game logic, resolve
physicsandcollisions,decidewhatneedstoberedrawn,andgetallofthatworkreadybefore
the VDP starts drawing the next frame.
Chapter5alreadyintroducedthepieceofcodethatembodiesthatlimit: SYS_doVBlankProcess(),
called once per loop iteration, which synchronizes pending work with the VDP’s vertical
blanking interval — the brief span between one drawn frame and the next during which
it’s safe to modify certain graphics data. That call isn’t a mere formality: it’s, in practice,
the point where each frame’s budget gets settled. If all the work in one iteration of the
main loop — reading input, moving characters, resolving collisions, updating animations —
finishes before the next vblank arrives, SYS_doVBlankProcess() simply waits out whatever
time is left and the game keeps running at 60 (or 50) frames per second without anything
being noticeable. But if that work stretches past the vblank it was supposed to meet,
SYS_doVBlankProcess() ends up waiting for the next vblank, a full frame later: the game
drops an entire frame, the sense of smoothness suffers, and if this happens persistently, the
actual game speed perceived by the player falls below the nominal 60 (or 50) frames per
second.
Dropping a frame is not the same as running “a bit slower.” A game that
occasionallygoesoveritsbudgetdropsisolatedframes,whichgenerallyreadsasa
small, one-off jolt. A game that systematically goes over its budget — for example,
because a poorly written collision routine inherently takes more than 16.7 millisec-
onds in a level with many enemies — ends up running at a constant fraction of its
nominalspeed(30framespersecondinsteadof60,forinstance),andanyanimation
or movement that isn’t designed to be independent of frame rate starts to look and
feel different depending on how many elements are on screen at a given moment.
Within that frame budget there is, moreover, an even narrower margin: the vblank interval
itself,justafractionofthewholeframe,istheonlywindowinwhichit’ssafetowritetoVRAM
withoutriskingcorruptingwhatevertheVDPisdrawingatthatinstant. Thisisexactlywhere
the DMA covered in chapter 44 comes into play: the faster VRAM transfers complete, the
more room is left within that narrow window to queue up graphics updates without having
them cut off halfway through. The frame budget and the vblank window are, in that sense,
two sides of the same timing problem: one bounds how long the game’s complete logic can
take, the other bounds specifically how long writes to VRAM can take.
2. Measuring CPU load: SYS_getCPULoad() and VDP_showCPULoad()
Knowing that a frame budget exists is useful as a concept, but it says nothing about whether
a specific project is respecting it. For that, SGDK offers a way to estimate, frame by frame
and while the game is running, what percentage of that budget is actually being used.
SYS_getCPULoad() returns a value that estimates the CPU load for the most recent frame,
expressed as a percentage: SGDK measures how much time is left idle while waiting for
vblank and compares it against the total time available in that frame, so that a value close to
100% indicates that nearly the entire frame budget is being used, while a value well above
100% indicates that the frame is going over its budget and, consequently, frames are being
dropped.
Checking that number manually, frame by frame, isn’t very practical during normal devel-
opment, so SGDK also offers a way to display it directly on screen: VDP_showCPULoad(),
which draws that percentage as overlaid text, using the same default font already used to
display any other text on screen (chapter 5). As with any on-screen debugging information,
it’s best to call it once per iteration of the main loop, typically right alongside the call to
333

=== PAGE 340 ===
SYS_doVBlankProcess():
while (1)
{
// input reading, game logic,
// sprite and animation updates...
VDP_showCPULoad(1, 1); // <!-- VERIFY: exact parameter names -->
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
With that overlay active, it’s enough to play the project’s most demanding level — the one
withthemostenemiesonscreen,themostelaborateparallaxbackground,theexplosionwith
the most particles — and watch how the number reacts: if it stays stable and comfortably
below 100%, there’s margin to spare; if it starts approaching or exceeding 100% in the most
demandingsituations,it’stimetoinvestigatewhichpartoftheframeisconsumingthatexcess,
before the problem becomes noticeable to the player.
3. Measuring real frames per second: VDP_showFPS()
The CPU load percentage is an internal estimate, calculated from how much idle time is left
beforevblank. Adirectandmoreintuitivecomplementtothatestimateistodirectlymeasure

60 (NTSC) or 50 (PAL) and the counter shows a consistently lower number, that’s the most
concrete confirmation possible that frames are being dropped, with no need to interpret any
percentage.
SGDKoffersVDP_showFPS()forthispurpose,withthesameusagepatternasVDP_showCPULoad():
it’scalledonceperiterationofthemainloopanddrawstheframes-per-secondcountdirectly

}
In some projects it may be useful to get that number without drawing it directly on screen

Usedtogether,theCPUloadpercentageandtheframes-per-secondcounteranswerdifferent,

4. Emulators as a complement: visual profiling with
BlastEm and Gens KMod
The CPU load percentage and the frames-per-second counter tell you whether a frame is
goingoverbudget,buttheydon’tautomaticallytellyouwhichpartofthecodeisresponsible.
For that second step, the development tools of the emulators introduced in chapter 4 are a
direct complement.
Both BlastEm and Gens KMod include a 68000 debugger capable of pausing execution, step-
ping instruction by instruction or frame by frame, and placing breakpoints at specific code
addresses. CombiningthatcapabilitywiththeVDP_showCPULoad()overlayitselfmakesitpos-

The VDP viewer in both emulators, already used in chapters 45 and 46 to visually inspect
VRAM, plays a different but related role here: it doesn’t measure CPU time, but it does let
you confirm with certainty how many VRAM transfers are happening in a given frame and
howlargetheyare—ausefulpieceofdatafordecidingwhethertherealbottleneckisonthe
computation side (the CPU resolving logic) or on the data-transfer-to-VRAM side (a problem
revisitedinthenextsection). Noemulatorreproducesrealhardwaretimingswithperfectac-

5. What typically eats into a frame’s budget in practice
With the measurement tools already introduced, it’s worth reviewing the usual suspects in
a real Mega Drive game when the CPU load percentage starts approaching the limit. This
manual has already presented, in earlier chapters, the concrete solution for each of these
three cases; what this chapter adds is the judgment needed to recognize them as the real
cause of a performance problem, rather than treating them as an isolated technical curiosity.
Avoidable multiplications and divisions. The Mega Drive’s Motorola 68000 resolves a
multiplication or a division in considerably more cycles than an addition, a subtraction, or a
bit shift. Chapter 25 already showed the concrete case of dividing a parallax background’s
position to achieve a sense of depth: replacing that division with a bit shift (>>) when the
divisor is a power of two — 2, 4, 8, and so on — achieves exactly the same numeric result
at a fraction of the cost. Any calculation that repeats once per frame, and even more so if
it repeats once per sprite or per active entity on screen, is a natural candidate to review for
multiplications or divisions that could be replaced with a lighter operation.
VRAM transfers without using DMA. Chapter 44 showed that copying data to VRAM by
driving the CPU directly — instead of delegating that copy to the DMA — keeps the CPU
fully occupied for the entire transfer, unable to do any other work in the meantime. A large
transfer done this way, especially if it happens within the narrow vblank window described
in section 1, can by itself consume a considerable portion of that frame’s budget. DMA frees
up the CPU during the transfer and, by completing it faster thanks to hardware dedicated to
that task, leaves more margin available for the rest of that frame’s work.
335

=== PAGE 342 ===
Traversing large collision arrays every frame. Part VII of this manual (chapters 40
through 43) built level collision from an array that represents, tile by tile, which areas of
the map are walkable. Checking that array for the few positions relevant to a character —
the corners of its collision box, nothing more — is a cheap operation; traversing the entire
array, or checking it for far more positions than strictly necessary, once per active entity and
once per frame, is a pattern that scales poorly: the cost grows with the number of enemies
or objects on screen, exactly the kind of growth that can go unnoticed with a handful of test
enemies and only become a real problem once a finished level packs in many at once — the
scenario revisited in Part IX of this manual.
None of these three cases is, by itself, a reason to rewrite code preemptively: optimizing be-
foremeasuringriskscomplicatingcodethatwasn’tactuallyresponsiblefortheproblem. The
correct approach is the reverse of how these three sections are ordered: first measure with
VDP_showCPULoad() and VDP_showFPS(), then confirm with the emulator’s debugger which
specific routine fires exactly when the percentage rises, and only then apply the appropriate
technique — bit shifting, DMA, or narrowing an array traversal — at the actual point of the
problem.

1. A brief graphical analysis: how Streets of Rage achieves

Before diving into code, it’s worth pausing for a moment on the graphics of Streets of Rage,
one of the most memorable beat ’em ups on the console, because they explain a good part
of the art decisions worth making in a project of this genre. Zooming in on a brick in a wall

3. The cause: plane size and scroll that repeats
The explanation goes back to something already seen in the chapter on parallax scrolling:
when the scroll coordinate of a background plane advances far enough in one direction, that
planestartsrepeatingfromthebeginning. Theexactpointatwhichthescreenstartsrepeat-
ing depends on the plane’s size, configurable with VDP_setPlaneSize(). By default, that size
is64tileswideby32tilestall,whichequals512×256pixels—preciselythemaximumlimitof
an IMAGE resource mentioned in the previous chapter. And what happens to the background
also happens, in practice, to any sprite positioned in map coordinates: once that repetition
limit is reached, the scroll engine shows the same content again from the origin, and the en-
339

=== PAGE 346 ===
emy gives the impression of having been placed again, even though there’s still only a single
instance of it in the code.
VDP_setPlaneSize() takes the width and height of the plane in tiles (with possible values of
32,64,or128)andathirdbooleanparameterrelatedtotheinternalVRAMaddressingmode.
A plane 128 tiles wide, for example, spans 1024 pixels: quite a bit more than the 320-pixel
screenwidthinhigh-resolutionmode,buttherepetitionpointstillexists,justpushedfarther
away.
4. Does changing the plane size solve the problem? No,
and it also has its own drawbacks
Wideningtheplane to128 tileswith VDP_setPlaneSize(128, 32, TRUE) looks, at first glance,
like a reasonable solution. In practice, the result visibly scrambles both the background
and the foreground —the map data already loaded doesn’t fit the same way into a plane of
a different size— and as for the enemy repetition, the change makes no difference at all:
plane size affects background layers, not sprite positions. Furthermore, even if it worked,
increasingtheplanesizerequiresmoreVRAMfortheplaneitself,soitwouldn’tbeagoodfit
for this particular problem either way.
Evenso,VDP_setPlaneSize()doeshavealegitimateandfairlyspecificuse: introorcutscene
sceneswheregraphicalelementsneedtobekeptoffscreenbeforeslidingthemin. Consider,
forexample,ascenewhereseveraldifferentcharactersslidedownfromthetopofthescreen,
one by one, before the level starts. With the default plane size (256 pixels tall), there isn’t
enough vertical space to keep all those characters hidden above the screen before the ani-
mation. The solution, in a case like that, is to increase the plane’s height from 32 to 64 tiles
while keeping the width at 64:
VDP_setPlaneSize(64, 64, TRUE); // 512x512 instead of 512x256, for cutscenes
This gives a 512×512 pixel space instead of the usual 512×256, enough vertical margin to
hide several elements before bringing them down one by one via vertical tile scrolling, a
techniquerevisitedinalaterchapter. Thepracticaltakeawayisthatchangingtheplanesize
isbestreservedforthiskindofone-offcutsceneorintro,whereextraspaceisneededtohide
elementsoffcamera;forthegameitself,it’sbesttoleaveitatitsdefaultsizeandsolveenemy
repetition another way.
5. Revisiting SPR_setPosition() and why a custom function
is needed
With the plane-size option ruled out, the problem needs to be tackled from another angle.
The function SGDK provides to position a sprite, SPR_setPosition(), takes three pieces of
data: the sprite to move and its X and Y coordinates as signed 16-bit integers (s16). The
problem is that the position of the player and the enemies in this project is handled as fix32,
in order to represent fractional positions —essential as soon as jump or smooth-movement
physics are added, as seen in previous chapters— so it needs to be converted to an integer
with F32_toInt() before it can be used with SPR_setPosition(). In addition, the actual on-
screenpositionofanyspritehastosubtractthecameraposition(new_camera_x/new_camera_y):
withoutthatadjustment,thespritestaysfixedatthesamepointonthescreennomatterwhere
the camera moves, instead of moving along with the rest of the stage.
Repeating that conversion and subtraction by hand every time an enemy needs to be po-
sitioned works, but it’s exactly the kind of repetitive code that’s worth wrapping in a cus-

tomfunction,especiallyconsideringthatthisprojectwilleventuallyhaveseveralenemieson
screen at once.
6. Writing a custom function: set_enemy_position()
The solution is to write a custom function, similar in spirit to handle_input() or camera(),
that takes the enemy’s fix32 coordinates directly —instead of requiring the conversion to
integer before calling it— and does that conversion internally. While at it, it’s worth having
thefunctionalsotakethewidthandheightofthespriteinquestion,sincethosetwovaluesare

looks like this:
static void set_enemy_position(Sprite* enemy_sprite, fix32 enemy_x, fix32 enemy_y,
s16 enemy_width, s16 enemy_height);
It’sworthrememberingapointaboutvariablescope: thenamesusedasfunctionparameters
—enemy_sprite, enemy_x, enemy_y, enemy_width, enemy_height— only exist inside that func-
tion. Trying to use them anywhere else in the code, such as inside the main loop, produces a
compilation error stating that the variable is undefined. Any variable that needs to be used
across several different functions, on the other hand, has to be declared globally, outside of
any function.
Inside the body of the function, the first step is to convert the received fix32 coordinates
to s16 integers, with descriptive names that make clear they’ve already gone through the
conversion:
static void set_enemy_position(Sprite* enemy_sprite, fix32 enemy_x, fix32 enemy_y,
s16 enemy_width, s16 enemy_height) {
s16 enemy_x_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_x) - new_camera_x;
s16 enemy_y_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_y) - new_camera_y;
SPR_setPosition(enemy_sprite, enemy_x_as_s16, enemy_y_as_s16);
}
7. A second scope problem: the camera variables
When trying to subtract new_camera_x and new_camera_y inside the new function, the same
kind of error shows up as with the parameters: those two variables had, until now, been
declared inside the camera() function itself, so they only exist there and can’t be used inside
set_enemy_position(). The solution is the same as in any other case of this kind: move the
declaration of new_camera_x and new_camera_y outside of camera(), to the global variables
area near the beginning of the file, alongside current_camera_x and current_camera_y, to
which they are related:
// Camera variables (now global, no longer local to camera())
static s16 current_camera_x;
static s16 current_camera_y;
static s16 new_camera_x;
static s16 new_camera_y;
The body of camera() doesn’t need any other changes: since those two variables already
existed under those names inside the function, pulling their declaration out and leaving it

=== PAGE 348 ===
outside doesn’t change the logic at all, it just widens their scope so that any function in the
program —including set_enemy_position()— can read them.
With this change, the function compiles without errors. Calling set_enemy_position() with
the boss’s coordinates instead of the manual call to SPR_setPosition() from section 2, the

8. The real solution: hiding the enemy when it falls outside
the camera
Thesolutiontotheunderlyingproblemistotakeadvantageof SPR_setVisibility(),already

soon as it re-enters those bounds. The logic boils down to four checks inside a single if,
joined with || (logical “or”): if the enemy’s on-screen X coordinate is less than 0, or greater
thanthescreenwidth, oriftheYcoordinateislessthan0, orgreaterthanthescreenheight,
the enemy is off camera and must be hidden; otherwise, it must be shown:
static void set_enemy_position(Sprite* enemy_sprite, fix32 enemy_x, fix32 enemy_y,
s16 enemy_width, s16 enemy_height) {
s16 enemy_x_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_x) - new_camera_x;
s16 enemy_y_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_y) - new_camera_y;
if (enemy_x_as_s16 < 0 || enemy_x_as_s16 > HORIZONTAL_RESOLUTION ||
enemy_y_as_s16 < 0 || enemy_y_as_s16 > VERTICAL_RESOLUTION) {
SPR_setVisibility(enemy_sprite, HIDDEN);
} else {
SPR_setVisibility(enemy_sprite, VISIBLE);
SPR_setPosition(enemy_sprite, enemy_x_as_s16, enemy_y_as_s16);
}
}
Note the use of HORIZONTAL_RESOLUTION and VERTICAL_RESOLUTION, the same constants al-
readydefinedinthecamerachapter(320and224inhigh-resolutionmode),insteadofwriting
thosenumbersdirectlyintothecondition: iftheprojectweretoswitchresolutionmodelater
on, it’s enough to update those two constants in a single place. It’s also worth paying atten-
tion to the comparison operator (==, with two equal signs, not one) and being careful, when
writingthefourchecks,nottomixupanXforaY—aneasymistaketomakewhencopyingand
pasting the same condition four times. And if the project used the low-resolution mode (256
pixels wide instead of 320), the horizontal limit adjusts on its own, because it now depends
on the constant rather than on a fixed number.
Compiling with this logic, the result is already fairly good: the enemy stops repeating across
the whole map and only appears once, exactly where the code places it.

9. A subtle bug: the enemy disappears before actually leav-
ing the screen
Moving the camera carefully, however, reveals a small flaw: on the left side of the screen,
the enemy sprite disappears an instant before actually leaving the visible area, leaving a
noticeable gap. This is a common behavior in games from earlier generations, but it looks
out of place in a 16-bit game.
A good trick to clearly reproduce this flaw is to move the enemy’s starting position
muchfartherawayonthemap,sothere’splentyofroomtoslowlyapproachitwith
the camera and observe the exact moment it appears or disappears.
10. The cause and the solution: using the sprite’s width
and height as the margin, not 0
The explanation for the flaw lies in how the Mega Drive positions any sprite: its coordinates
alwayscorrespondtothetop-leftcorneroftheanimationframe. Iftheenemymovesleftand
its on-screen X coordinate reaches 0, at that moment its left edge exactly coincides with the
edge of the screen, but a good part of its body —the sprite’s entire width— is still visible to
the right of that corner. Since the condition hides the sprite as soon as its X is less than 0,
the enemy disappears too soon, while it should still be visible on screen.
Thesolutionistoreplacethatlimitof0withanegativevalueequaltothesprite’sownwidth,
so that the enemy remains visible as long as any part of it —including its right edge— is still
withinthevisiblearea,andonlygetshiddenonceithascompletelyleftthescreen. Thesame
reasoning applies to the top limit: if the map included vertical scrolling, the enemy would
disappear too soon at the top as well, unless that limit is replaced with the sprite’s negative
height instead of 0. Although this particular project’s map only scrolls left to right for now,
it’sworthapplyingthesameadjustmenttotheverticallimittokeepthefunctionreadyforany
kindofmapinthefuture. Thisispreciselywhyset_enemy_position()takesenemy_widthand
enemy_height as parameters, instead of having those values hardcoded inside the function:
static void set_enemy_position(Sprite* enemy_sprite, fix32 enemy_x, fix32 enemy_y,
s16 enemy_width, s16 enemy_height) {
s16 enemy_x_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_x) - new_camera_x;
s16 enemy_y_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_y) - new_camera_y;
if (enemy_x_as_s16 < -enemy_width || enemy_x_as_s16 > HORIZONTAL_RESOLUTION ||
enemy_y_as_s16 < -enemy_height || enemy_y_as_s16 > VERTICAL_RESOLUTION) {
SPR_setVisibility(enemy_sprite, HIDDEN);
} else {
SPR_setVisibility(enemy_sprite, VISIBLE);
SPR_setPosition(enemy_sprite, enemy_x_as_s16, enemy_y_as_s16);
}
}
// Actual width and height of each sprite, used as the visibility margin

Chapter 51 — Organizing the
Project with Header Files
How to split the code of a growing game into several .c and .h files, instead of piling it all up
in main.c
The previous chapter left this beat ’em up project with the player, two enemies (boss_sprite
andfat_man_sprite),thecamera()function,theset_enemy_position()function,andahand-
ful of global variables, all living together inside a single main.c file. It works, but it’s already
startingtoshowthetypicalproblemofanygrowingproject: itgetsharderandhardertofind
a function among so much code, and every new enemy, weapon, or mechanic added is going
topilemorelinesontoafilethat’salreadydifficulttonavigate. Thischapterstepsawayfora
moment from the game’s specific content to address something more general, applicable to
any project written in C: how to split that code into several files, organized by topic, without
changing the program’s behavior in the slightest.
It’s worth clarifying from the start that none of what follows is a feature specific to SGDK
or the Mega Drive: header files are a mechanism of the C language itself, and everything
explained in this chapter would apply equally to any other project written in that language.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Chapter 50 (“VDP planes and enemies in a beat ’em up”) completed, since this chapter
picksupexactlyfromthecodeleftattheendofthatone: player_sprite/player_x/player_y,
boss_sprite, fat_man_sprite, set_enemy_position(), and camera().
• The basic C concepts covered in chapter 6: what a declaration is versus a definition,
what a function prototype is, and what the #include directive does.
• Chapter 39 (“The resource compiler in depth”), about how rescomp generates a header
file from a .res file.
1. Why split the code into several files
Thecentralideaofthischaptercanbesummedupinonesentence: insteadofwritingallofa
game’s code inside main.c, it’s better to group it by topic into separate sets of files. One set
of files for everything related to the player, another for the enemies, another for the camera,
and so on as the project requires. Each of these sets usually has, at minimum, a header file
(.h extension) and a corresponding code file, with the same name but a .c extension.
With a project as small as the ones from the early chapters of this manual, splitting the code
intofilesdoesn’tgainmuch: everythingfitscomfortablyonascreenortwo. Butabeat’emup
346

=== PAGE 353 ===
withaplayer, severalenemytypes, acamera, levels, andlatersecondaryweaponsoragame
state system is a different case, and it’s exactly the kind of project this mechanism exists for.
A common problem when setting up a new SGDK project in Visual Studio Code is
thatfunctionautocompletion(IntelliSense)stopsshowingSGDK’sowndescriptions
andsuggestions. Theproblemisalmostalwaysinthesettings.jsonfile,insidethe
project’s.vscodefolder: thesimplestwaytofixitistocopythatfilefromaprevious
project where autocompletion does work, and paste it into the new project.
2. Splitting resources into several .res files
Beforetouchingthecodeitself,it’sworthapplyingthesameideatoresources. Uptonow,this
manual has declared sprites, backgrounds, and music inside a single resources.res file. For
a project with resources for the player, each enemy type, backgrounds, and music, it’s also a
goodideatosplitresourcesintoseveral.resfiles,followingthesamecriteriaasforthecode:
oneresourcefilepertopic. Forexample,res_player.resfortheplayerandres_enemies.res
for the enemies:
// res_player.res

// res_enemies.res
SPRITE boss_sprite_def "enemies_assets/boss.png" 7 10 FAST

Also note the organization into subfolders within res: player_assets for the player’s images
and enemies_assets for the enemies’, instead of leaving all the image files loose directly in
res. This doesn’t change anything about the rescomp mechanism already covered in chapter
39; it just requires writing the full path starting from res in each SPRITE line, including the
subfolder name.
Thefirsttimeitcompileswiththesefiles,rescompautomaticallygeneratesthecorresponding
header files, res_player.h and res_enemies.h, with the same logic it already used to gen-
erate resources.h when there was a single resource file. There’s no need to touch those
generatedfilesbyhand,butit’sworthreviewingtheircontents,becausetheyuseexactlythe

automatically generated from the file’s name.
3. Quotes or angle brackets: two ways to include a file
Any file that uses SGDK functions needs to include genesis.h, the library’s general header,
with #include <genesis.h>. The project’s own header files, on the other hand, such as
res_player.h or the ones created in this very chapter, are included using quotes: #include
"res_player.h".
Thisdifferenceinsyntaxisn’tanaestheticwhim. Anglebracketstellthecompilertosearchfor
thefileamongthesystem’sorthelibrary’sstandardincludepaths(that’swhereSGDKlives),
while quotes tell it to search first in the project itself, next to the file doing the including. As
apracticalconvention: <genesis.h>andanyotherlibraryheadergobetweenanglebrackets;
anything that’s the project’s own code goes between quotes.
347

=== PAGE 354 ===
4. From static variables to variables shared across files
Before splitting the code into several files, there’s a problem the previous chapter left pend-
ing without naming it: a good part of this project’s variables and functions (player_sprite,
boss_sprite, camera(), set_enemy_position()) were declared with the static keyword.
Within a single file, static on a global variable or function limits its scope to that same file,
preventing it from accidentally clashing with an identical name defined elsewhere in the
project. It’s good practice when everything lives in main.c, because that file is, in effect, the
only place those variables are used.
Theproblemisthat,assoonasthatsamecodeissplitintoseveralfiles,thatrestrictionstops
making sense: if camera() needs to call set_enemy_position(), which is now going to live in
another file, or if set_enemy_position() needs to read new_camera_x, which is going to live
inathirdfile, noneofthosevariables orfunctionscanremain static anymore. Thekeyword
that replaces static for this purpose is extern, and the rest of this chapter is devoted to
showing exactly where and how to use it.
5. The include guard
Every new header file created in this project — player.h, enemy.h, camera.h — has to start
with a repetitive but indispensable block called an include guard:
#ifndef PLAYER_H
#define PLAYER_H
// (the file's content goes here)
#endif // PLAYER_H
This guard exists to prevent the same header file from being included more than once within
a single program. A file like player.h can end up included, indirectly, from many different
places in the project: for example, enemy.h might need to include player.h to make an en-
emy react to the player’s position, and camera.h might need to include it too for some other
reason. Without an include guard, each of those repeated inclusions would redeclare the
same variables and functions, producing compilation errors — typically redefinition errors —
that are sometimes hard to trace back to their real cause. The guard solves this by mark-
ing, with #define, that the file has already been included once; if the compiler encounters a
second inclusion, #ifndef detects that the marker already exists and jumps straight to the
corresponding #endif, without processing the content again.
The name of the marker (PLAYER_H in the example) is a convention, not a language require-
ment: it just needs to be unique within the project, and using the file’s name in uppercase,
with an underscore instead of the dot, is the simplest way to guarantee that.
It doesn’t matter much whether #include directives are written inside the include
guardorbeforeit(thefilesrescompgeneratesautomatically,forinstance,puttheir
#include <genesis.h> before the guard); both ways work the same. What does
always need to be respected is that the rest of the content (variable, sprite, and
function declarations) stays between the #define and the #endif.
6. Splitting out the player: player.h and player.c
With the guard now clear, the first set of files worth creating is the player’s. Inside the
project’s inc folder, player.h is created, with declarations for everything other files are go-
348

=== PAGE 355 ===
ing to need from the player: the pointer to the sprite, its position in map coordinates, and a
create_player() function that groups the code that used to be loose inside main().
The important difference from how these variables were written in the previous chapter is
that, inside a header file, both the variables and the functions that need to be usable from
other files are declared with the extern keyword in front:
// inc/player.h
#ifndef PLAYER_H
#define PLAYER_H
#include <genesis.h>
#include "res_player.h"
// Player sprite and its position in map coordinates
extern Sprite* player_sprite;
extern fix32 player_x;
extern fix32 player_y;
// Creates the player's sprite and adds it to the scene
void create_player(void);
#endif // PLAYER_H
extern tells the compiler that this variable or function exists and can be used from any file
that includes this header, but that its actual definition (the place where memory is actually
reserved for it, or where the function’s body is written) is somewhere else. That somewhere
else is, by convention, a .c file with the same name, in the src folder:
// src/player.c
#include "player.h"
Sprite* player_sprite;
fix32 player_x = FIX32(40);
fix32 player_y = FIX32(160);
void create_player(void) {
player_sprite = SPR_addSprite(&player_sprite_def, F32_toInt(player_x),
↪ F32_toInt(player_y),

Chapter 52 — Adding Enemies to
the Game
From loose per-enemy variables to arrays, and how to decide how many enemies the screen
can sustain at once
The previous chapter left the project already split into header files: player.h/player.c for
the player, enemy.h/enemy.c for the enemies, and camera.h/camera.c for the camera, with
boss_sprite and fat_man_sprite as the only two enemies on the map, each with its own
pointer to Sprite, its own fix32 position variables, and its own width and height constants.
That pattern — one loose variable for each piece of data for each enemy — works perfectly
well for two named characters, but a beat ’em up needs something more: waves of common
enemies that appear, move, and disappear without each one deserving its own hand-written
setofvariables. Thischapteraddsthatwaveofenemies,showswhytheloose-variablepattern
stops being sustainable as soon as the number of enemies grows, and replaces it with arrays
traversed with a for loop. It closes by returning to a more practical question: how many
enemies can be on screen at the same time before the hardware, or the frame budget itself,
starts to notice.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Chapter 51 (“Organizing the project with header files”) completed, since this chapter
picks up directly from player.h/player.c, enemy.h/enemy.c, and camera.h/camera.c
exactly as they were left there, including set_enemy_position() and the variables
boss_sprite, fat_man_sprite, boss_x, boss_y, fat_man_x, and fat_man_y.
• Arraysandforloops,coveredindepthinchapter17(“Tile-basedscrolling”);thischapter
assumes that syntax is already known and focuses on applying it to a new problem.
• Thelimitsonsimultaneousspritesdependingonresolutionmode,introducedinchapter
10 (“H40 and H32 resolution modes”), and VRAM management and CPU profiling cov-
ered in Part VIII (chapters 45 to 49), which are briefly revisited toward the end of this
chapter.
1. The limit of the “one variable per enemy” pattern
Adding a third enemy using the same approach as boss_sprite and fat_man_sprite is me-
chanical: a Sprite* variable, two fix32 variables for position, two constants for width and
height, a line inside create_enemies() to register it with SPR_addSprite(), and a call to
set_enemy_position()insidecamera(). Noneofthatishard,butit’sexactlythekindofwork
that doesn’t scale: adding a wave of four common enemies — a ninja, a sniper, a stealth
354

=== PAGE 361 ===
ninja, and a boomerang-throwing enemy, all four recruited from the same remake the previ-
ous chapters have been using — would multiply each of those steps by four, and adding ten
moreenemieswouldmultiplythemagain. Thecodeincreate_enemies()andcamera()would
endupasalongstringofnearlyidenticallines,oneperenemy,withtheaddedriskthatcopy-
ing and pasting those lines is also the most common way to introduce silent bugs: a palette
changedbymistake,aYcopiedwhereanXshouldhavegone,acalltoset_enemy_position()
left pointing at the wrong enemy.
The solution to this kind of repetition already appeared earlier in this manual, applied to a
different problem: instead of one variable per enemy, an array with one position per enemy,
traversed with a for loop.
2. Assets for a wave of common enemies
Followingthesameapproachalreadyusedforboss.pngandfat_man.png,thefournewgraph-

SPRITE line for each of them, alongside the two that already existed:

The four common enemies are deliberately small in their number of animation frames, in
keeping with an 8-bit game style: three of them measure 3×4 tiles (24×32 pixels), and the
boomerang-throwing one, a bit wider because of its throwing animation, measures 4×4 tiles
(32×32 pixels). When compiled, rescomp adds the four new definitions to res_enemies.h,
alongside the ones that already existed for boss_sprite_def and fat_man_sprite_def.
The enemies_assets subfolder, with the graphics for boss, fat_man, and the four common
enemies already copied inside.

5. manage_enemies(): a first artificial intelligence with ar-

Withthepositionsalreadyinarrays,updatingthemframebyframebecomesasinglefunction
with a single loop, instead of one addition per enemy:
void manage_enemies(void) {
// Each common enemy advances according to its own horizontal speed,
// read from enemy_velx[i]: positive values move to the
// right, negative ones to the left
for (u8 i = 0; i < NUM_ENEMIES; i++) {
enemy_x[i] += enemy_velx[i];
}
}
This is, deliberately, the simplest possible version of an artificial intelligence: each common
enemy walks in a straight line, at a constant speed, without reacting to anything. It’s only a
startingpoint—thefollowingchaptersaddreactiontotheplayer,patrollimits,andbehavior
states — but it’s enough to confirm that the speed array works: if enemy_velx were a single
value instead of one per slot, the four enemies would move at exactly the same speed and in
the same direction, losing the variety they had when each one was an independent variable.

writing a different addition for each one.
