7. How many enemies the screen can sustain at once
Before adding more enemies, how far can this be pushed? To answer that, it helps to revisit
two hardware limits already seen in Part VIII.
The first is the number of simultaneous hardware sprites the VDP can draw, introduced in
chapter 10: up to 80 in H40 mode (320 pixels wide) or 64 in H32 mode, with a maximum
of 20 per horizontal line in H40 (16 in H32). That limit isn’t counted per character, but per
hardwaresprite,andanSGDKSpritelargerthan32×32pixels(4×4tiles,themaximumsize
of a hardware sprite) is actually made up internally of several chained hardware sprites.
It’sworthdoingthemathwiththeproject’sactualsizes: player_sprite(5×5tiles)
takes up 2×2 = 4 hardware sprites; boss_sprite (7×10 tiles) takes up 2×3 = 6;
fat_man_sprite (6×8 tiles) takes up 2×2 = 4; each of the three 3×4-tile common
enemies takes up 1×1 = 1, and the boomerang-throwing one, at 4×4 tiles, takes
up another 1×1. In total, this chapter’s full scene uses 4 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 18
hardware sprites, comfortably under the 80 available in H40.
Themarginiscomfortabletoday,butitshrinksfastasprojectiles,items,andeffectsgetadded,
each with its own sprite. The per-line limit is, in practice, the easiest one to hit without
noticing: if several large enemies happened to overlap vertically within the same screen
band,thesumofhardwarespritestheyoccupyonthatlinecouldgetclosetothe20available,
and the VDP simply stops drawing the excess ones on that line, causing flicker. Spreading
enemies across different screen heights, and avoiding stacking several large enemies one
below another, helps keep that margin.
The second limit isn’t the VDP’s but the frame budget itself, covered in chapter 49: every
active enemy adds CPU work on each pass of the main loop — its own movement logic, its
animationupdate, andlateron, collisiondetectionagainsttheplayer—andthatworkhasto
fit,alongwitheverythingelse,withinthe16.7millisecondsofaframeat60framespersecond.
The correct way to know whether a given number of simultaneous enemies is sustainable
isn’ttoguessit,buttomeasureitwithSYS_getCPULoad()whilethegamerunswiththatmany
enemies active and moving, as explained in that chapter.
It’s also worth remembering the VRAM cost of each new enemy type, covered in chapters
45 to 48: every distinct graphic adds its own unique tiles to video memory, and a common
enemy that repeats many times on screen — unlike boss_sprite or fat_man_sprite, which
are unique — is exactly the use case for the manual sprite loading from chapter 48, where
severalinstancesofthesameenemyshareasinglecopyoftheirtilesinsteadofreservingone
per instance.
Inpractice,theconcretefigureof“howmanyenemiesatonce”isn’tafixednumberthatholds
foranyproject: itdependsonthesizeofthesprites,howmuchelseisonscreen(background,
effects, HUD), and how much logic runs per enemy. NUM_ENEMIES is 4 in this chapter because
that’s the size of the wave being added right now, but nothing prevents defining it larger as
360

=== PAGE 367 ===
the project needs it, as long as the hardware-sprite-per-line count and the SYS_getCPULoad()
measurement confirm there’s still margin.
8. The problem coming up: too many parallel arrays
The position array and the speed array already solve this chapter’s problem, but they raise a
new one as soon as you think about what else each common enemy is going to need later on:
hit points (something the common enemies in this remake don’t need, since they die in one
hit, but which bosses will need), whether it’s alive or already defeated, which direction it’s
facing, which animation state it’s in. Each of those attributes, following the same approach
used in this chapter, would require yet another four-slot array, indexed with the same enemy
number as the others but declared and maintained separately. Even enemy_sprite is already,
in effect, one more of these parallel arrays.
Technically, continuing down that path would work, but it would quickly become unmanage-
able: nothing in the language would prevent, for example, updating enemy_x[2] and acciden-
tallyreadingthehitpointsfromenemy_life[1],becausethecompilerhasnowayofknowing
that both slots should refer to the same enemy. The tidy way to solve this — grouping all of
an enemy’s attributes in one place, instead of keeping them spread across parallel arrays of
the same size — is to create a custom data type with a structure (struct), a topic revisited
later in this manual.

Chapter 53 — C Structs Applied
to Game Entities
Replacing an enemy’s parallel arrays with a single, purpose-built data type capable of gath-
ering all of its information in one place
Thepreviouschapterleftaproblemonthetablethatwasonlygoingtogetworseovertime: to
handle several enemies at once, instead of a lone boss_sprite and fat_man_sprite, an array
was needed for every attribute — one for the sprite pointers, another for the X coordinates,
another for the Y coordinates, another for the horizontal speed, another for each enemy’s
graphic resource. It works, but every new attribute needed down the line (hit points, a be-
haviortype, itsowntimer)isgoingtorequireaddingyetanotherarray, allthesamesizeand
always walked in parallel, with the constant risk that a position drifts out of sync between
one array and another. This chapter introduces the C language tool designed exactly for this
problem: thestructure,orstruct,whichwasalreadymentionedinpassingbackinchapter6
asoneofthedatatypesavailableinC,butwhichisonlynowusedindepthtomodelsomething
as concrete as an enemy in the game.
Astructureletsyoudefineyourowndatatypethatgroupsseveralrelatedvalues—potentially
of different types — under a single name, so that each enemy becomes a single variable with
several fields inside it, instead of a repeated position across half a dozen separate arrays.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Chapter 52 (“Adding enemies to the game”) completed, since this chapter picks up di-
rectly from the problem it leaves open: several parallel arrays — one per attribute — to
handle more than one enemy on screen.
• Chapter51 (“Organizing the project with header files”), covering extern syntaxand the
project’s organization into player.h/.c, enemy.h/.c, and camera.h/.c.
• Chapter 6 (“C applied to retro development”), covering the u8, s8, and fix32 types, and
Cstructuresingeneral—althoughthischapterrevisitsthedotoperator(.) fromscratch
for anyone who hasn’t used it yet.

By the end of the previous chapter, enemy.h and enemy.c had grown beyond the original two
enemiesfromchapter50(boss_spriteandfat_man_sprite),inordertohandleasmallwave
ofenemiesatonce. Themostdirectwaytoachievethat,withoutanynewtools,wastoreplace
each standalone variable with an array of the same type, all indexed the same way: position

// Project state at the end of the previous chapter: one array per attribute

The problem isn’t that this code is badly written: it compiles and works just as well as be-
fore. The problem shows up the moment one more attribute needs to be added. Hit points,
for instance, would require declaring a sixth array, s8 enemy_hitpoints[MAX_ENEMIES], and
remembering,ateveryplaceinthecodewhereanenemyiscreatedorupdated,totouchthat
array in addition to the other five. The more attributes pile up, the easier it is to forget one
whenwritinganewfunction,orworse,toaccidentallymisalignonearray’sindexagainstthe
others—forexample,byinsertinganenemyinthemiddleofthearrayandforgettingtoshift
one of the five arrays along with the other four.
2. Defining struct Enemy
Thesolutionistostopthinkingintermsof“fivearraysthatliveinsync”andstartthinkingin
terms of “an array of a single thing, which already carries its five attributes inside it.” That
“single thing” is exactly what defining a structure in C lets you do. The syntax is simple: the
struct keyword, whatever name you want to give the new type, a pair of braces with the
attributes inside, and a semicolon at the end.
Anyone already familiar with C might prefer typedef struct instead of the plain
struct TypeNameformusedinthischapter. Thedifferenceismostlystylistic—with
typedef you can write Enemy instead of struct Enemy in every declaration — and
thismanualstickswiththeformwithouttypedefbecauseit’sabitmoreexplicitfor
anyone encountering structures for the first time.
The new type is called Enemy, and it’s defined in enemy.h, alongside the sprite-size constants
that have already been there since chapter 51. The first attribute worth adding is a state
(status), as an unsigned 8-bit integer (u8): for now two values are enough, 0 for an inac-
tive enemy and 1 for an active one, although the data type leaves room to represent other
behaviors later on, such as attacking, taking damage, or chasing the player.
Next come the attributes that already existed as parallel arrays: the x and y coordinates
and the horizontal speed vel_x, all three as fix32, and a pointer to the enemy’s sprite, of
type Sprite*. An attribute meant for future use is also added, hit points (hitpoints), as a
signed 8-bit integer (s8) — most of the regular enemies in this project are going to die in a
single hit, but this attribute is going to matter more for tougher level bosses — along with
each enemy’s graphic resource, graphic, of the same type const SpriteDefinition* already
usedbyboss_sprite_defandfat_man_sprite_def. Finally,sothatset_enemy_position()can
keepcalculatingeachenemy’svisibilitymarginwithoutdependingonafixedmacropertype,
it makes sense for the sprite’s width and height to travel as part of the structure too:
// inc/enemy.h (excerpt)
struct Enemy {
u8 status; // 0 = inactive, 1 = active
fix32 x;

3. An array of structures, instead of an array per attribute
With the Enemy type already defined, you can declare an array of elements of that type using
exactly the same syntax already used for the fix32 arrays in section 1, except that now the
datatypeisstruct Enemyinsteadof fix32. Thearrayiscalledcurrent_enemies,anditkeeps
the same size, MAX_ENEMIES, that the parallel arrays it replaces already had:
// inc/enemy.h (excerpt)
extern struct Enemy current_enemies[MAX_ENEMIES];
Like any other variable that needs to be used from several files, it’s declared with extern
inside the .h file and defined, with its actual contents, in the corresponding .c file.
4. Filling in the enemy data
In enemy.c, the actual contents of the array are defined. Each element is written between
braces, with its nine values in the same order in which the structure’s attributes were de-
clared: status, X position, Y position, speed, sprite, width, height, hit points, and graphic.
The sprite attribute is left as NULL for all six enemies, because at this stage no sprite has
been set up on screen yet — that only happens inside create_enemies(), in the next section.

position of the boss and the fat man that already existed since chapter 50, and the following
two add a second pair of the same graphics, further along the map, with a nonzero vel_x so
they move on their own in addition to following the camera. The last two elements are left
inactive (status set to 0), reserved for adding more enemies in the future without having to
enlarge the array or recompile with a different size.
Storing a width and height of 0 for inactive enemies causes no problem: as long
as status is 0, neither create_enemies() nor manage_enemies() ever reads those
fields, thanks to the check added in the next two sections.
5. The dot operator: how to access an element’s attributes
Toaccessanattributeofanarrayelement,thedotoperator(.) isused: current_enemies[i].status
accesses the state of the enemy at position i, current_enemies[i].graphic accesses its
graphic, and so on for any other attribute of the structure. The reading is literal: first the
array is indexed as usual (current_enemies[i]), and then you navigate inside that element
to the field you need (.status, .x, .sprite, etc.).
This syntax replaces, in a single step, what the parallel arrays required: instead of en-
emy_sprite[i], enemy_x[i], enemy_y[i], and enemy_graphic[i] — four separate arrays, co-
ordinated only by convention — there is now a single array and a single index, and the dot
operator picks the attribute within that element.
6. Simplifying create_enemies() with the dot operator
With all six enemies already defined in the array, create_enemies() can walk through them
with a single for loop, instead of one call to SPR_addSprite() per enemy. Before creating
each sprite it makes sense to check that the corresponding enemy is active: if its status
is nonzero, it’s set up with SPR_addSprite(), taking the graphic resource and the starting
position directly from that array element’s attributes.
// src/enemy.c (continued)
void create_enemies(void) {
for (u8 i = 0; i < MAX_ENEMIES; i++) {
if (current_enemies[i].status != 0) {
current_enemies[i].sprite = SPR_addSprite(current_enemies[i].graphic,
F32_toInt(current_enemies[i].x), F32_toInt(current_enemies[i].y),
TILE_ATTR(PAL3, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE));
}
}
}
It’s worth paying attention to a detail that’s easy to overlook: the value returned by
SPR_addSprite() — the pointer to the newly created sprite — has to be stored in cur-
rent_enemies[i].sprite, not discarded. If that assignment were missing, the pointer would
be lost as soon as that loop iteration ended, and manage_enemies() would have no way to
move or hide that sprite later on: the sprite attribute would keep being NULL forever, and
any later call to SPR_setPosition() or SPR_setVisibility() with that pointer would end up
in a runtime error.

7. Simplifying position updates: manage_enemies()
The same approach applies to the function that updates the enemies’ position every
frame. Instead of a loop that added the speed to an array of positions and then called
set_enemy_position() for each individual sprite (as camera() did directly at the end of
chapter51,withonecallforboss_spriteandanotherforfat_man_sprite),asingleloopnow
walks through the six elements of current_enemies, adding current_enemies[i].vel_x to
current_enemies[i].x and delegating to set_enemy_position() — the same function from
chapter50,unchanged—thecameraadjustmentandthehidingofspritesoutsidethevisible
bounds.
This loop, as it stands, would also try to move the inactive enemies, whose sprite attribute
is still NULL because no sprite was ever created for them; doing so would produce the same
runtimeerrormentionedintheprevioussection. Thesolutionistoaddthesamecheckalready
used in create_enemies(): process only the enemies whose status is nonzero.
// src/enemy.c (continued)
void manage_enemies(void) {
for (u8 i = 0; i < MAX_ENEMIES; i++) {
if (current_enemies[i].status != 0) {
current_enemies[i].x += current_enemies[i].vel_x;
set_enemy_position(current_enemies[i].sprite, current_enemies[i].x,
↪ current_enemies[i].y,
current_enemies[i].width, current_enemies[i].height);
}
}
}
void set_enemy_position(Sprite* enemy_sprite, fix32 enemy_x, fix32 enemy_y,
s16 enemy_width, s16 enemy_height) {
s16 enemy_x_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_x) - new_camera_x;
s16 enemy_y_as_s16 = F32_toInt(enemy_y) - new_camera_y;
if (enemy_x_as_s16 < -enemy_width || enemy_x_as_s16 > HORIZONTAL_RESOLUTION ||
enemy_y_as_s16 < -enemy_height || enemy_y_as_s16 > VERTICAL_RESOLUTION) {
SPR_setVisibility(enemy_sprite, HIDDEN);
} else {
SPR_setVisibility(enemy_sprite, VISIBLE);
SPR_setPosition(enemy_sprite, enemy_x_as_s16, enemy_y_as_s16);
}
}

With the functions already rewritten, the parallel arrays from section 1 (enemy_sprite, en-
emy_x, enemy_y, enemy_vel_x, and enemy_graphic) are removed from enemy.h and enemy.c,
since all of that information now lives inside current_enemies. When compiled, the result
on screen is the same as at the end of the previous chapter — the same four active enemies,
moving and hiding correctly according to the camera — but organized in a way that’s much
simpler to extend: adding a seventh attribute to each enemy, from now on, means adding a
single field to struct Enemy, instead of a new array coordinated by hand with the rest.
8. A problem that remains unsolved: data repeated per
enemy type
Structures solve the parallel-array problem, but they leave a different one unresolved. If it
laterbecamenecessarytochangeoneofthearray’senemiestoadifferenttype—forexample,
turning the second fat_man into a third boss — changing the graphic attribute isn’t enough:
width,height,andhitpointsalsohavetobeupdatedbyhand,separately,sincethosevalues
depend on the enemy type and end up repeated, independently, in every array element that
uses that type. With only two enemy types and four active elements, the risk of forgetting
one of those fields already exists; with more types and more enemies on screen, that risk is
only going to grow.
Rememberingwhichstatusnumbercorrespondstowhichbehaviorisalreadyabit
confusing even with just two possible values (0 and 1); as soon as more states are
added — attacking, taking damage, dying — that problem is also going to need its
own solution.
The solution to both problems — the data repeated per type and the magic numbers used for
status — comes through a related tool that this manual revisits later on: a fixed list of the
possibleenemytypes,eachwithitsownconstantcharacteristics(graphic,hitpoints,size),so
thatchanginganenemy’stypewithincurrent_enemiesisreducedtochangingasinglevalue,
instead of several separate fields at once.

Chapter 54 — C Enumerations
(enums)
Replace the loose numbers in the status field with readable names, and use #define for the
quantities that repeat throughout the code
Thepreviouschapterlefteachenemy’sstatusfieldasaplaininteger: 0foraninactiveenemy,
1foranactiveone,withthepromiseofaddingmorevaluesinthefuturetorepresentdifferent
behaviors(attacking, hurt, dying, andsoon). Theproblemisthatmemorizingwhichnumber
represents which behavior becomes, as more values are added, increasingly hard to follow
justbylookingatthecode: anif (current_enemies[i].status != 0)saysnothingonitsown
about what that zero means. This chapter solves that problem with another tool from the C
language that hasn’t been used yet in this manual: the enumeration, or enum, which lets you
give a readable name to each of those numbers.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Chapter 53 (“C structs applied to game entities”) completed, since this chapter works
directly on the Enemy structure and the current_enemies array created there.
• Chapter 52 (“Adding enemies to the game”), where the createEnemies and manageEne-
mies functions were first written, and which this chapter will simplify even further.
• Basic knowledge of C: the #define directive, already used in earlier chapters to create
named constants.
1. Why #define isn’t enough for a list of related values
Before showing enums, it’s worth reviewing the alternative this manual already knew about:
using #define to give a name to each number, for example #define ENEMY_INACTIVE 0 and
#define ENEMY_IDLE 1, and then replacing the loose numbers in the code with those names.
That technique works, but it falls short when dealing with a more or less long list of values
relatedtooneanother,suchasthedifferentpossiblestatesofanenemy. Declaringeachvalue
separatelywithitsown#defineforcesyoutorepeatthekeywordoverandover,saysnothing
anywhere in the code about those names being part of the same closed set of options, and
leaves it up to the programmer not to accidentally repeat the same number in two different
#defines. Whenthevaluesarerelatedtoeachother,it’susuallycleanertogrouptheminside
an enumeration instead of declaring each one separately.

=== PAGE 376 ===
2. Defining the EnemyStates enum
The syntax of an enum is similar to that of a struct: the enum keyword, the name you want to
give the list, a pair of braces, and a semicolon at the end. This enum is called EnemyStates,
and it’s declared inside enemies.h, alongside the existing Enemy structure:
// enemies.h
#pragma once
#include <genesis.h>
#include "res_enemies.h"
// Possible values for an enemy's status field
enum EnemyStates {
ENEMY_INACTIVE,
ENEMY_IDLE,
ENEMY_ATTACK,
ENEMY_HURT,
ENEMY_DYING
};
Inside the braces you write the list of possible values, one per line and separated by com-
mas, following the usual C convention of writing them in uppercase. The order chosen, EN-
EMY_INACTIVE, ENEMY_IDLE, ENEMY_ATTACK, ENEMY_HURT, and ENEMY_DYING, leaves room to add
more states in the future, as the enemies’ artificial intelligence becomes more elaborate.
It’s possible to manually assign a number to each value of the enum, by writing an
equals sign followed by that number after each name. But if no number is spec-
ified, the compiler automatically assigns consecutive values starting from 0: the
first value in the list becomes 0, the second 1, and so on, following the same order
in which they were written. It’s best to let the compiler handle this automatic as-
signmentratherthanwritingthenumbersbyhand,unlessthere’saspecificreason
not to follow that consecutive order.
Withthisdeclaration,ENEMY_INACTIVEisworth0andENEMY_IDLEisworth1,exactlythesame
values that had already been used since the previous chapter, only now they have a name.
ENEMY_ATTACK,ENEMY_HURT,andENEMY_DYINGendupdefinedwiththevalues2,3,and4respec-
tively, ready to be used as soon as the project incorporates those behaviors.
3. Replacing the array’s numbers with the enum’s names
With the enum already defined, you can go back to the current_enemies array, in ene-
mies.c, and replace the 0 and the 1 that appeared as the first value of each element with
ENEMY_INACTIVE and ENEMY_IDLE respectively:

4. The behavior doesn’t change
The names in an enum are, ultimately, just a more readable way of writing the same num-
bers as always: the compiled program behaves exactly the same as before this change. It’s
worth confirming this by compiling first without touching anything else, and checking that
the on-screen result matches what you had at the end of the previous chapter. Afterward,
as a test, you can change the state of one of the already active enemies from ENEMY_IDLE
to ENEMY_INACTIVE and compile again: the expected result is that fewer enemies appear on
screen, since that enemy no longer gets registered in createEnemies. Once that behavior is
confirmed, it’s best to set those values back to ENEMY_IDLE before continuing.
5. Simplifying the checks in createEnemies and man-
ageEnemies
The same enum can be used to simplify the if checks that already existed in cre-
ateEnemies and manageEnemies since the previous chapter. Instead of writing if (cur-
rent_enemies[i].status != 0), you now write if (current_enemies[i].status !=
ENEMY_INACTIVE), with exactly the same meaning but much easier to read for anyone
reviewing the code later on:
void createEnemies(void) {
for (u8 i = 0; i < MAX_NUMBER_CURRENT_ENEMIES; i++) {
if (current_enemies[i].status != ENEMY_INACTIVE) {
current_enemies[i].sprite = SPR_addSprite(current_enemies[i].graphic,
F32_toInt(current_enemies[i].x), F32_toInt(current_enemies[i].y),
TILE_ATTR(PAL2, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE));
}
}
}

6. A named constant for the array’s size

reduced to modifying a single value, in a single place in the code. The createEnemies
and manageEnemies snippets from the previous section already show the final result, with
MAX_NUMBER_CURRENT_ENEMIES instead of the number 10 repeated in several places.
After modifying a header file this way, it’s a good idea to do a project clean before
compilingagain. Insomecases,changesmadetoa.hfilearen’tcorrectlyreflected
in the build unless that cleanup is forced first.
7. What’s coming next: structs and enums, once again
Boththestructsfromthepreviouschapterandtheenumsfromthischapterwillbeusedmany
more times later on in this project, and not just for enemies. As an early example, consider
theplayer’sanimations: inaspritewithseveralanimationframes,insteadofreferringtothe
idleframeasnumber0andthewalkingframeasnumber1,anenumwouldallowyoutowrite
something like PLAYER_IDLE and PLAYER_WALKING, with the same gain in readability seen in
this chapter for enemy states. That same pair of tools, a struct to group the fixed attributes
ofathingandanenumtoreplaceitsnumericvalueswithnames,comesupagainlaterinthis
manual to solve a different problem: that of the different enemy types (the basic ninja, the
sniper, the stealth ninja, the one that throws boomerangs), each with its own typical graphic,
hit points, and speed, instead of having those values repeated by hand in each element of
current_enemies.

Chapter 55 — Permanent Enemy
Types
The previous two chapters introduced two tools from the C language: structs, to group an
enemy’sattributesinasingleplace,andenums,togivereadablenamestothedifferentvalues
ofthestatusattribute. Thischaptercombinesbothtoolstosolveaproblemthatwasleftopen
at the end of the chapter on structs: the Enemy struct mixes together, in the same place, data
that changes constantly while a level is being played — position, velocity, current state —
with data that is actually permanent and specific to each enemy type, such as which graphic
it uses, how many hit points it has at the start, or which color palette it’s assigned.
Thesolutionistocreateasecondstruct,EnemyType,exclusivelyforthatpermanentdata,and
a catalog of enemy types built from it. That way, changing an enemy’s type within a level
comesdowntomodifyingasinglevalue,insteadofmanuallyupdatingseveralseparatefields
at once.
Prerequisites
• Chapters53(“CStructsAppliedtoGameEntities”)and54(“CEnumerations(enums)”),
since this chapter works directly with the Enemy struct, the current_enemies array, the
EnemyStates enum, and the createEnemies and manageEnemies functions defined there.
• The difference between ROM and RAM on the Mega Drive, covered in chapter 6, and in
particularwhythe64kilobytesofavailableRAMareamuchmorelimitedresourcethan
the cartridge ROM.
1. Separating what’s permanent from what changes during
the level
The starting point is to go over the Enemy struct field by field and ask which of those fields
belong to each individual enemy instance within a level, and which, instead, belong to the
enemy type and shouldn’t change from one instance to another.
Thestatusfield—whethertheenemyisinactive,active,attacking,etc. —changesconstantly
during the level, so it stays in Enemy. The same goes for the x and y coordinates, the vel_x
velocity, and the sprite pointer, which identifies a specific instance already added to the
screen. The graphic an enemy uses, on the other hand, is something permanent, specific to
the enemy type rather than to any particular instance: the boomerang-throwing enemy will
always use the same boomerang graphic, no matter how many instances of that type exist in
a level.
374

=== PAGE 381 ===
2. Defining the EnemyType struct
Thenewstruct,EnemyType,startswiththegraphicfield—thesameconst SpriteDefinition*
pointer that Enemy already had — because that data really is permanent for each enemy type.
Two more fields are added next: that type’s starting hit points, and the palette it uses.
// enemies.h
// Permanent data for an enemy type: it doesn't change between instances,
// only between different types (boomerang, ninja, sniper, etc.)
struct EnemyType
{
const SpriteDefinition* graphic;
s8 max_health;
u8 palette_used;
};
The hit points field needs to exist in both structs at once, though with a slightly different
nuance in each: in Enemy it represents an instance’s current hit points, which go down as
the player hits it; in EnemyType, instead, it represents how many hit points any instance of
that type should start with when created. To avoid confusing the two meanings, the field in
EnemyType is called max_health instead of hitpoints.
Regarding the palette: it would be possible to reserve, say, PAL3 exclusively for all enemies,
following a simple scheme where PAL0 is for the background, PAL1 for the foreground, and
PAL2 for the player. But there’s no need to follow that scheme rigidly. Each enemy type can
use any of the four palettes available on the Mega Drive, which is why it makes sense for the
palette to be just another field of the enemy type, instead of always assuming the same one
for everybody.
3. A catalog of enemy types, stored in ROM
With the EnemyType struct already defined, an array of that type is declared, enemyTypesList,
following the same syntax already used for current_enemies. It’s given ten slots, on the
assumptionthatagameofthissizeprobablywon’tneedmorethantendifferentenemytypes,
counting level bosses; that number can be expanded later if needed.
// enemies.h
extern const struct EnemyType enemyTypesList[10];
There’s an important difference from current_enemies: this array is declared with the const
keyword before struct. A variable marked as const stays in the cartridge ROM and is never
copied to the console’s RAM. This makes sense for enemyTypesList because its content —
which graphic, how many maximum hit points, and which palette each enemy type gets — is
fixed and never changes during play, unlike current_enemies, whose values change all the
time and therefore do need to live in RAM.
The Mega Drive has only 64 kilobytes of RAM, a much scarcer resource than the
cartridge ROM. That’s why it’s worth marking any data that won’t change during
play as const, so it stays in ROM and doesn’t take up RAM space unnecessarily.

Chapter 56 — Function Pointers
for Enemy AI
How to store an enemy’s behavior, not just its data, inside its type
Chapter 55 solved a real organizational problem: it separated the permanent data of each
enemy type (its graphic, its maximum health, its palette) into a struct of its own, EnemyType,
and gathered them into a catalog, enemyTypesList, indexed by the enemy_type field of each
instance inside current_enemies. Thanks to that, changing an enemy’s type within a level
wasreducedtochangingasinglevalueoftheEnemyNamesenum,insteadofmanuallyupdating
several separate fields.
However, that chapter left a pending problem, and a fairly obvious one at that: regardless
of an enemy’s type, manageEnemies() still applies exactly the same artificial intelligence (AI)
to all of them. That AI, inherited from earlier chapters of the project, simply adds vel_x to
the enemy’s x coordinate and updates its sprite’s position. That’s a reasonable behavior as
a starting point, but it makes no sense for a boomerang-throwing enemy, a regular ninja, a
stealth ninja, and a sniper to all move the exact same way.
This chapter solves that problem in two stages. First, in the most straightforward way possi-
ble: a distinct AI function for each enemy type, selected with a chain of if / else if. That
solutionworks,butitdoesn’tscalewellasnewenemytypesgetadded. That’swhythesecond
stage brings in a C language mechanism that hasn’t been used yet in this manual: function
pointers, which allow the AI of each enemy type to be stored as just another piece of data
inside struct EnemyType, alongside the graphic, health, and palette, and invoked directly
without first asking what type it is.
Pointers in general (what they are, how they’re declared, how they point to data in memory)
were already explained in depth in chapter 6 of this manual. This chapter assumes that
content is already known and focuses on what’s new: a pointer that, instead of pointing to a
piece of data, points to a function.
1. One AI function per enemy type
Thefirststepistocreate,foreachofthefourenemytypesdefinedinthecatalog(boomerang,
basic ninja, stealth ninja, and sniper), an independent function with its own movement
logic. Each of these functions needs a single piece of data: the enemy’s position within
current_enemies, that is, a number between 0 and MAX_ENEMIES - 1. That parameter is
called enemy_number and is declared as u8; the name is a stylistic choice, not a language
requirement.
The prototypes are added in enemies.h, alongside the already existing ones for createEne-
mies() and manageEnemies(), following the pattern enemyName + AI:
381

=== PAGE 388 ===
// enemies.h (excerpt)
void createEnemies(void);
void manageEnemies(void);
// AI functions, one per enemy type
void boomerangAI(u8 enemy_number);
void basicNinjaAI(u8 enemy_number);
void stealthAI(u8 enemy_number);
void sniperAI(u8 enemy_number);
It’s worth remembering that extern only makes sense in a function’s declaration inside a
header file; it should never appear in its definition inside the corresponding .c file, since
that’s where the function’s body is actually written. With that in mind, the bodies are filled
in in enemies.c. For now the goal isn’t a definitive, elaborate AI for each enemy (that will
be revisited later in this manual), but simply to verify that the selection mechanism works,
giving each function a visible difference from the others: some move along the x axis, and at
least one moves along the y axis.
// enemies.c (excerpt)
void boomerangAI(u8 enemy_number) {
current_enemies[enemy_number].x += FIX32(1.5);
SPR_setPosition(current_enemies[enemy_number].sprite,
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].x),
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].y));
}
void basicNinjaAI(u8 enemy_number) {
current_enemies[enemy_number].x += FIX32(2.5);
SPR_setPosition(current_enemies[enemy_number].sprite,
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].x),
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].y));
}
void stealthAI(u8 enemy_number) {
// Unlike the others, this one moves along the y axis
current_enemies[enemy_number].y += FIX32(0.5);
SPR_setPosition(current_enemies[enemy_number].sprite,
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].x),
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].y));
}
void sniperAI(u8 enemy_number) {
// Combines both axes
current_enemies[enemy_number].x += FIX32(1.0);
current_enemies[enemy_number].y -= FIX32(0.5);
SPR_setPosition(current_enemies[enemy_number].sprite,
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].x),
F32_toInt(current_enemies[enemy_number].y));
}

insteadofreadingthevel_xfieldof current_enemies[enemy_number]. Thisisintentional. The
vel_xfieldwasdefinedinearlierchaptersasaper-instanceeditablevalue,meantforastage
of the project where the concept of enemy type didn’t exist yet; if two instances of the same

=== PAGE 389 ===
type (two boomerang enemies, for example) had different vel_x values loaded by hand into
current_enemies, they would move at different speeds despite being the same type, which
is inconsistent with the central idea of chapter 55: that an enemy’s behavior depends on its
type, not on loose values loaded per instance. That’s why each AI function defines its own
speed as an internal constant. The vel_x field can still exist in struct Enemy for other future
uses(forexample,anAIthatdoesneedtomodifyitsspeedatruntime),butitisnolongerthe
source that the functions in this chapter draw their movement from.
2. Choosing the right AI in manageEnemies()
With the four functions already written, the next step is to modify manageEnemies() so it de-
cides which one to run based on the current enemy’s enemy_type field. The most direct way
is a chain of if / else if, comparing that field against each value of the EnemyNames enum:
void manageEnemies(void) {
for (u8 i = 0; i < MAX_ENEMIES; i++) {
if (current_enemies[i].status != ENEMY_INACTIVE) {
if (current_enemies[i].enemy_type == BOOMERANG_ENEMY)
boomerangAI(i);
else if (current_enemies[i].enemy_type == BASIC_NINJA_ENEMY)
basicNinjaAI(i);
else if (current_enemies[i].enemy_type == STEALTH_ENEMY)
stealthAI(i);
else if (current_enemies[i].enemy_type == SNIPER_ENEMY)
sniperAI(i);
}
}
}
In every branch, the argument passed is i, the loop variable of the for loop, which is ex-
actlythesamevaluethateachAIfunctioninternallycallsenemy_number: theenemy’sposition
within current_enemies.
Figure 1: The four enemy types on screen, each moving according to its own AI function.
With only four enemy types, this block is perfectly readable, and there’s nothing wrong with
leaving it as is. The problem appears when thinking about the scale of the full project: if the
enemyTypesListcatalogendeduphaving,say,fiftydifferentenemytypes—themaximumthe
array size would allow — manageEnemies() would end up with fifty conditions in a row just to
decide which function to call. It’s the same kind of scalability problem that’s already been
solved earlier in this project: with enums instead of a long list of #defines, and with structs
insteadofindependentparallelarrays. Themoreenemytypesthegamehas,themoreobvious
the need for a tidier solution becomes.
3. Storing behavior, not just data
The AI an enemy uses is, at bottom, a feature just as permanent to its type as its graphic,
its maximum health, or its palette: every boomerang enemy always uses boomerangAI, every
stealth ninja always uses stealthAI, and that association never changes during gameplay.
If the graphic, health, and palette already live inside struct EnemyType, it makes sense for
the AI function to live there too, instead of being decided every frame through a chain of
comparisons inside manageEnemies().
ThedifferencefromtheotherEnemyTypefieldsisthat,insteadofstoringanumberorapointer
383

=== PAGE 390 ===
Figure 150: The four enemy types on screen, each moving according to its own AI function
to a graphical resource, what gets stored now is the function itself that must be executed.
That’swhatfunctionpointersarefor: variablescapableofstoringtheaddressofafunction,
as long as that function has the exact signature the pointer expects (same return type, same
number and type of parameters).
3.1. The syntax of a function pointer
Declaring a field of this type inside struct EnemyType is written like this:
void (*enemyAI)(u8 enemy_number);
The syntax looks a little strange at first glance, because of the extra parentheses and the
asterisk, but it’s easier to understand by comparing it line by line with the normal prototype
of one of the AI functions:
void (*enemyAI)(u8 enemy_number); // the function pointer
void boomerangAI(u8 enemy_number); // a normal function, for comparison
The underlying structure is the same in both cases: first the return type (void, returns noth-
ing), then a name, and between parentheses the parameter list (a single u8 enemy_number).
The only real difference is that, in the function pointer, the chosen name (enemyAI) is en-
closed in parentheses together with an asterisk to its left: (*enemyAI). That asterisk is what
indicates that this isn’t declaring a normal function, but rather a variable capable of storing
the address of any function that matches that signature: one that returns void and takes a
single u8 parameter.
The general pattern for declaring a function pointer is returnType (*cho-
senName)(parameters);. The parentheses around *chosenName are mandatory:
without them, void *enemyAI(u8 enemy_number); would mean something com-
384

=== PAGE 391 ===
pletely different (a normal function, called enemyAI, that returns a pointer to
void).
With that, the field is added to struct EnemyType, right after palette_used:
// enemies.h (excerpt)
struct EnemyType {
const SpriteDefinition* graphic;
u8 max_health;
u8 palette_used;
// AI function that any instance of this enemy type runs
void (*enemyAI)(u8 enemy_number);
};
3.2. Assigning the AI for each type in enemyTypesList
With the field now declared, the next step is to fill it in for each existing entry of enemy-
TypesList, adding the corresponding function name at the end of each brace block, after
the graphic, health, and palette. In C, the name of a function used without parentheses or
arguments evaluates to a pointer to that function, so no special syntax is needed for this
assignment: writing the name is enough.
// enemies.c (excerpt)
const struct EnemyType enemyTypesList[MAX_ENEMY_TYPES] = {
{ &boomerang_sprite, 10, PAL3, boomerangAI },
{ &basic_ninja_sprite, 15, PAL3, basicNinjaAI },
{ &stealth_ninja_sprite, 12, PAL3, stealthAI },
{ &sniper_sprite, 8, PAL3, sniperAI },
// Filler slots, waiting for new enemy types
{ &boomerang_sprite, 10, PAL3, boomerangAI },
{ &boomerang_sprite, 10, PAL3, boomerangAI },
{ &boomerang_sprite, 10, PAL3, boomerangAI },
{ &boomerang_sprite, 10, PAL3, boomerangAI },
{ &boomerang_sprite, 10, PAL3, boomerangAI },
{ &boomerang_sprite, 10, PAL3, boomerangAI },
};
Since the prototypes of the four functions are already declared in enemies.h, and enemies.c
includesthatheaderatthetop,thecompileralreadyknowseachone’ssignaturebythetime

3.3. manageEnemies() reduced to one line

void manageEnemies(void) {

}

The expression enemyTypesList[current_enemies[i].enemy_type].enemyAI(i) reads from
the inside out: current_enemies[i].enemy_type gives the enemy type’s position within the
catalog; enemyTypesList[...] accesses that entry; .enemyAI retrieves the function pointer
stored there; and (i) invokes it, passing i as enemy_number. Since the body of the if is now
reducedtothissinglestatement, thebracesthatusedtosurrounditarenolongernecessary
and can be removed, leaving the whole statement on a single line.
The result on screen is identical to the one obtained with the if / else if chain: each enemy
still moves according to the function corresponding to its type. What changed is the way of
reaching that result. Now, adding a new enemy type to the game — enemy number fifty, if
it came to that — doesn’t require touching manageEnemies() at all: it’s enough to write its
AI function, declare its prototype in enemies.h, and add a new entry to enemyTypesList with
thatfunctionassignedtotheenemyAIfield. manageEnemies()isdoneforgood,nomatterhow
many enemy types the game ends up having.

Chapter 57 — Game States
A minimal state machine to separate loading a level from running it, put to double use by
turning the player into a struct along the way
Up to this point in the project, the main loop always does the same thing on every pass: it
processes the controls, moves the player, updates the enemies in the current_enemies array,
and refreshes the sprites on screen. That assumption—that the game is always playing a
level—was convenient while the project was limited to a single scrolling screen, but it stops
holdingupassoonasthegameneedstodosomethingotherthanplay: loadanewlevel,show
amenu,orpresentapausescreen. Iftheplayer-controlcoderunsunconditionally,itwillkeep
movingthecharacterevenwhilethegameshouldbebusyloadingdata,whichmakesnosense
and can produce strange behavior.
This chapter introduces the concept of a game state: a variable that indicates at all times
what the game is doing, and which both the main loop and the control functions check be-
fore acting. It’s a simple idea to state, but it’s the foundation on which the actual transition
betweenlevelswillbebuiltinthecomingchapters. Alongtheway,andbecauseit’sworthre-
solving before moving further, this chapter also refactors the player’s data—until now, loose
variables with hand-written coordinates—into a struct Player, following the same pattern
already used for the enemies.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have on hand:
• Theproject as organizedin Chapter 51(“Organizing the project withheader files”): the
player.h/player.c,enemy.h/enemy.c,andcamera.h/camera.cpairs,usingexterntoshare
variables and functions between files.
• Chapters 52 through 56 of this part, which already turned the enemies into a cur-
rent_enemies array of struct Enemy (Chapter 53, “C structs applied to game entities”),
with their own types and states declared as an enum (Chapter 54, “C enumerations
(enums)”) and their AI resolved with function pointers (Chapter 56).
• The two control functions already used in this manual, handle_input() and joyEvent(),
covered respectively in Chapters 31 (“D-pad controls”) and 32 (“Button controls and
event-based reading”), along with the controls.h/controls.c pair where this project’s
input code lives.
• The difference between fix32 (32-bit fixed point) and s16 (16-bit signed integer), ex-
plained in Chapter 6.

1. Why the main loop needs to know what state the game
is in
Attheproject’scurrentstage,theplayerandseveralenemiesalreadymoveonscreenthanks
towhatwasdevelopedinpreviouschapters. Allthecontrolcoderunsunconditionally: aslong
as the program is running, the D-pad moves the player and the enemy AI keeps advancing.
Thisworksbecause,sofar,thegameonlyknowshowtodoonething—playthelevelcurrently
loaded in memory—so there has never been a need to distinguish any other situation.
Theproblemappearsassoonasyouthinkaboutwhatcomesnext: loadinganewlevel,show-
ing a title screen, pausing the game. Each of these situations requires the game to stop
behaving as if it were playing a level. Without an explicit way to tell what situation the pro-
gram is in, there’s no way to tell the control code, “don’t move the player right now, we’re
still loading.”
Thesolutionistoaddavariablethatexplicitlyrecordswhatstatethegameisinatanygiven
moment, and to make both the main loop and the control functions check it before acting.
This idea—a program that is, at all times, in one of several possible states, and that reacts
differently depending on which state that is—is, in essence, a finite state machine, an ex-
tremely common design pattern in game development. It already showed up, without being
named as such, when each enemy was given its own state enum in Chapter 54; now the exact
same approach is applied, but at the scale of the whole game.
2. The GameStates enum and the current_game_state vari-
able
2.1. Declaring the possible states
Followingthesameapproachalreadyusedforenemystatesandenemytypes,thegamestates
are declared as an enum. This avoids representing states as bare numbers: a 0 or a 1 with no
namecommunicatesnothingonitsown,whileLOADINGandRUNNING_LEVELdo. Inlevels.h,a
new enum called GameStates is created with two values to start: LOADING, which represents
the moment when the game is loading the resources for a level or a new screen, and RUN-
NING_LEVEL, which represents the moment when a level that’s already loaded is in progress.
// inc/levels.h
#ifndef LEVELS_H
#define LEVELS_H
#include <genesis.h>
// Possible game states. Just two for now: loading data,
// or playing the level that's already in memory. More will
// be added later: a title screen, a menu, maybe a level
// select map.
typedef enum {
LOADING,
RUNNING_LEVEL
} GameStates;
// Current game state, checked from controls.c and from
// the rest of the project before moving the player or the enemies
extern u8 current_game_state;
391

=== PAGE 398 ===
#endif // LEVELS_H
It’sworthnotingthat,althoughthecartridgedoesn’thavethelongloadingtimesofanoptical
medium—loading a level’s data can take as little as one or two sixtieths of a second—a dedi-
catedloading state isstill necessary. Thereason isn’t the lengthof the wait, butthe need for
the loading process not to be interrupted by the rest of the game’s code: while data is being
copied to VRAM or structures are being initialized, it’s best that player control or enemy AI
don’t run at the same time.
For now only these two values are needed, but since the enum already exists, adding a new
state in the future—a title screen, a menu—comes down to writing one more name inside its
braces, without touching the rest of the code that already distinguishes between states by
name.
2.2. Storing the current state in a variable
Declaringthepossiblestatesisn’tenough: thegamealsoneedsavariablethatrecordswhich
of them is the current state at any given instant. For this, current_game_state is created as
an unsigned 8-bit integer (u8), the same type already used for each enemy’s state in Chapter
54: with a range of 0 to 255 there’s more than enough room for any reasonable number of
game states, and using a larger type would waste memory for no benefit.
Like any variable, current_game_state needs an initial value. In levels.c it’s assigned RUN-
NING_LEVEL, so the game starts out directly playing the level that’s already on screen:
// src/levels.c
#include "levels.h"
u8 current_game_state = RUNNING_LEVEL;
This choice is consistent with the project’s current state—there’s still no real level-loading
mechanism, a subject picked back up in Chapter 58 (“Loading different enemies per level”)
and in Chapters 60 and 61—but once real loading is implemented, it will make more sense
for the game to start directly in the LOADING state.
Going deeper. It’s worth naming the pattern explicitly, because it’s going to keep
coming back throughout this manual: what’s being built here is a finite state ma-
chine, a model in which a system can only be, at any given instant, in one of a
fixedsetofstates,andwherespecificevents,likepressingtheStartbutton,trigger
transitions from one state to another. In game engines, almost any element with
complex behavior (the flow of the game, an enemy with AI, an options menu) ends
upbeingmodeledthisway,becauseitkeepsthecodeorganized: insteadofatangle
of conditions stepping on each other, each state knows what to do and which other
states it can move to.
3. Changing state from joyEvent()
Withthestatealreadydeclared,amechanismisneededtochangeitinresponsetotheplayer’s
action. As already seen in Chapters 31 and 32, SGDK distinguishes between two input func-
tions with different purposes: joyEvent(), which fires once per button press and is suited to
one-off actions, and handle_input(), which runs on every pass of the main loop and is suited
to continuous actions, such as moving the player while the D-pad is held down. Advancing
392

=== PAGE 399 ===
to the next screen when Start is pressed is exactly the kind of one-off action joyEvent() is
meant for.
Inside joyEvent(), the transition logic is added: if the current state is RUNNING_LEVEL and
the button that changed in this event was Start, current_game_state is set to LOADING. The
check on the current state isn’t a minor detail: it’s what will allow pressing Start to mean
different things depending on what part of the game you’re in—jumping to the next screen
during gameplay, but perhaps confirming an option inside a menu. Each new state added in
future chapters will likely need its own branch inside these two control functions.
// src/controls.c
#include "controls.h"
#include "levels.h"
#include "player.h"
void handle_input(void) {
if (current_game_state != RUNNING_LEVEL) return;
u16 value = JOY_readJoypad(JOY_1);
if (value & BUTTON_RIGHT) {
player_character.x_f32 += FIX32(2);
} else if (value & BUTTON_LEFT) {
player_character.x_f32 -= FIX32(2);
}
}
void joyEvent(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state) {
if (current_game_state == RUNNING_LEVEL && (changed & state & BUTTON_START)) {
current_game_state = LOADING;
}
}
Watch out. A common mistake when introducing a new variable in a file other
than the one where it was declared is forgetting the #include for the correspond-
ing header. In this case, controls.c needs current_game_state, RUNNING_LEVEL,
andLOADING,andnoneofthethreeliveincontrols.h: theyliveinlevels.h. Ifthat
#include "levels.h" were missing, the compiler would flag each of those three
identifiers as unrecognized, an error that disappears as soon as the missing #in-
clude is added. It isn’t a conceptual problem with the state machine: it’s simply a
consequenceofhowCsharesknowledgeofsymbolsbetweenfiles,andit’sthesame
kindoferror—anidentifierthatexists,butwhoseheaderwasn’tincludedwhereit’s
needed—that already came up when the project was split apart in Chapter 51, and
one worth recognizing at a glance whenever it reappears.
controls.h, for its part, only needs to declare the two functions (their bodies, and therefore
their internal dependencies, stay in controls.c):
// inc/controls.h
#ifndef CONTROLS_H
#define CONTROLS_H

4. From loose variables to a struct Player
4.1. Defining struct Player
Before wrapping up player control, it’s worth resolving a design problem that had been
dragging on since the earliest chapters of this project: the player’s data—its sprite and its
coordinates—stillexistasloosevariables, withitsinitialcoordinateswrittendirectlyasfixed
numbers at the moment the sprite is created. Just as Chapter 53 grouped each enemy’s at-
tributes into a struct Enemy, here it makes sense to group the player’s into a struct Player.
Thenewstructincludestheplayer’sspriteandtwoversionsofitsXandYcoordinates: onein
fix32, the 32-bit fixed-point type, and another in s16, a 16-bit signed integer. The reason for
keepingbothversions,ratherthanjustone,wasalreadyexplainedinChapter6: theplayer’s
movement needs numbers with a fractional part (fix32) because an acceleration of 0.5 or
a jump with gravity rarely advances in whole pixel numbers; however, SPR_setPosition()—
and,lateron,thelevelcollisionroutinesandthecollisionboxcalculations—expecttoreceive
16-bitintegers. Keepingbothversionsavoidsconvertingbetweentypesoneveryuse,though
it requires remembering to keep them in sync.
// inc/player.h

Chapter 58 — Loading Different
Enemies per Level
Everything built so far around enemies —the Enemy struct, the permanent type catalog ene-
myTypesList, and the AI selected through function pointers— coexists with a limitation that
becomes obvious as soon as you think about a complete game: the current_enemies array
representsasingleenemyconfiguration,theonecurrentlyonscreen,anduntilnowthatcon-
figuration could only be changed by editing the code by hand and recompiling. A real game,
however, has dozens of screens or sections, each with its own combination of enemies, and
recompilingtheentireROMeverytimetheplayeradvancestoanewlevelisnotareasonable
option.
This chapter separates two things that until now lived mixed together in a single array: on
one hand, the complete catalog of which enemies correspond to each level or section of the
game —data that never changes during a playthrough and can therefore live permanently in
the cartridge’s ROM—, and on the other, the enemy configuration for the section currently
being played, which continues to live in current_enemies, in RAM, because that is the only
placewherethedatacanbemodifiedwhilethegameisrunning. Thebridgebetweenthetwo
is a new function, copyEnemyArray(), which copies the data for the corresponding section
from the catalog into current_enemies.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have already covered:
• The Enemy struct and the current_enemies array, as they stood at the end of chapter 53
(“C Structs Applied to Game Entities”), and the EnemyStates enum together with the
MAX_NUMBER_CURRENT_ENEMIES constant from chapter 54 (“C Enumerations (enums)”).
• The enemyTypesList catalog, the EnemyType struct, and the practice of using const to
keep permanent data in ROM, from chapter 55 (“Permanent Enemy Types”).
• The enemyAI field within EnemyType and the functions boomerangAI, basicNinjaAI,
stealthAI, and sniperAI from chapter 56 (“Function Pointers for Enemy AI”).
• FamiliaritywithmultidimensionalarraysinC(anarrayofarrays),althoughhavingused
them before is not strictly required: this chapter introduces them in practice.
• The GameStates enum and the notion of game state from chapter 57 (“Game States”),
since current_game_section relies on the same idea of a variable that the rest of the

1. The problem: a single array isn’t enough for multiple
levels
As things stand today, main.c calls createEnemies(), and that function takes the data from
current_enemiesandusesittodisplaytheenemiesonscreen. Thisworksperfectlyaslongas
thegamehasasinglescreen,becausecurrent_enemiesonlyneedstorepresentthatonecon-

represent a single combination at a time— isn’t enough to store all of them simultaneously.
Thesolutionisn’ttomakecurrent_enemiesbigger,buttoseparatetwodistinctquestionsthat
until now were answered by the same array. The first is which enemies exist in each section
of the game, a fixed answer known ahead of time. The second is which enemies are active
rightnow,inthesectioncurrentlybeingplayed,somethingthatchangesconstantlyastheAI
acts. The first question is solved with a new catalog; the second remains current_enemies.
2. A complete catalog: the all_enemies array
2.1. Declaring an array of arrays
Thecatalogisdeclaredinenemies.hbycopyingthesyntaxalreadyusedforcurrent_enemies,
with three changes. First, the name becomes all_enemies, to reflect that it contains the
enemiesforthewholegameandnotjustthecurrentscreen. Second,asecondpairofbrackets
is added: current_enemies is an array of ten Enemy structs (one for each possible enemy on
screen),whereasall_enemiesisanarrayofarrays,withonerowpersectionofthegameand,
within each row, the same ten slots that current_enemies already has.
The number of sections is, in itself, a number that is best not left loose in the code, following
the same approach already used for MAX_NUMBER_CURRENT_ENEMIES in chapter 54. That’s why
a new constant, NUMBER_OF_SECTIONS, is defined. This manual illustrates it with four sections
—as many as the reference project’s levels— but nothing prevents expanding it later if the
game grows: it’s enough to change a single value.
The third change is adding the word const before struct Enemy. Unlike current_enemies,
whosevalueschangeconstantlyastheAIactsoneachenemy,theall_enemiescatalogrepre-
sentstheinitialconfigurationofeachsection,datathatisnevermodifiedduringaplaythrough.
Marking it as const —the same approach already applied to enemyTypesList— ensures that
the entire array is stored in the cartridge’s ROM and doesn’t take up space in the mere 64
kilobytes of available RAM.

easy to lose count and write one block too many or too few. The compiler catches
the mismatch and warns with a message along the lines of “too many initializer

3. The copyEnemyArray() function: moving data from ROM
to RAM
Having the complete catalog in all_enemies is useless if createEnemies() and manageEn-
emies() keep reading exclusively from current_enemies, which is where the data actually
shown and modified on screen truly lives. What’s needed, then, is a function that, given
the current section number, copies the corresponding block from all_enemies into cur-
rent_enemies. That function is copyEnemyArray(), already declared as a prototype in the
enemies.h listing in the previous section, alongside createEnemies() and manageEnemies().
Thebodyof copyEnemyArray()walksthroughthetenslotsof current_enemieswithaforloop
and, on each pass, replaces the contents with those of the corresponding enemy within the
indicated section of all_enemies. The expression all_enemies[current_game_section][i]
usestwoindices: thefirstselectsthegamesection,andthesecond,thesameifromtheloop,
selects which of the ten enemies in that section is being copied.
void copyEnemyArray(void)
{
for (u8 i = 0; i < MAX_NUMBER_CURRENT_ENEMIES; i++)
{
// Copy entry i of the current section into current_enemies.
current_enemies[i] = all_enemies[current_game_section][i];
}
}
The C language offers a generic function for copying blocks of memory, mem-
cpy(), which in principle could replace this for loop with a single line, some-
thing like memcpy(current_enemies, all_enemies[current_game_section],
sizeof(current_enemies)). Both approaches are valid in C; this manual prefers
theexplicitloopbecauseitmakesvisible,elementbyelement,whatisbeingcopied
and to where, without depending on the source and destination sizes matching
exactly in bytes. If the reader tries memcpy() and finds it more convenient, there’s
no reason not to use it.
4. Linking with the current level: current_game_section
One piece is still missing: where does the section number that copyEnemyArray() uses as an
indexcomefrom? Forthat,anewvariablecalledcurrent_game_sectionisaddedinlevels.h,
in the same style as current_game_state from chapter 57: an unsigned 8-bit integer that
records which section of the game the player is currently in. With 8 bits there’s room for
256 different sections, more than enough even for a game with a great many levels; if some
project needed more, a u16 would offer up to 65 thousand sections at no significant cost.

This decision does, however, leave a small design detail unresolved: both copyEnemyArray()
and createEnemies() walk through the ten slots of current_enemies with an identical for
loop, which means that, in practice, the same range is traversed twice in a row. It would be
possibletomergebothloopsintoasingleoneandeliminatecopyEnemyArray()asastandalone
function, gaining a bit of efficiency. The criterion adopted here prioritizes clarity: keeping
copyEnemyArray() as a separate function, with a name that describes exactly what it does,
turnsouttobemorereadablethanasingleloopthatdoestwothingsatonce,andthecostof
traversingaten-elementarraytwiceperlevelis,inpractice,negligiblecomparedtothetime
available per frame.
This kind of decision —code clarity versus a marginal savings in CPU cycles— will
come up again throughout this manual. As a general rule, it’s best to prioritize
readability while the performance cost is negligible, and reserve aggressive opti-
mization for code that truly runs with a frequency or data volume that justifies it,
such as routines that run once per frame over many elements at once.

Chapter 59 — Preparing Level
Graphics
Where the art for each level of a game with several distinct stages comes from, and how to
organize tilesets, palettes, and maps by level within a single SGDK project
The previous chapters of this part left the project with the player and the enemies organized
into separate files (chapter 51), and with the logic for each enemy to position and hide itself
correctly relative to the camera (chapter 50). The next step in building this beat ’em up is
to let the player move on from one level to the next, each with its own background, its own
foreground,and,likely,itsowncastofenemies. Beforewritingthattransitionlogic,it’sworth
solving a more basic problem, one that none of the previous chapters had to face yet: where
the art for each of those levels comes from, and how it’s organized in the project so that
loading level 2 doesn’t depend on still having level 1’s tiles in memory.
This chapter deals with those two questions. The first part is more a matter of artistic judg-
mentandworkflowthanofcodeitself;thesecondpicksupdirectlyfromtheresourcehandling
alreadycoveredwiththerescompcompiler(partVI)andtheVRAMlimits(partVIII),applying
them to the specific case of a game with multiple backgrounds that are shown, never two at
once, over the course of the game.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it’s worth having fresh in mind:
• TheTILESET,PALETTE,andMAPresources,andtheVDP_loadTileSet(),PAL_setPalette(),
MAP_create(), and MAP_scrollTo() functions, introduced in chapter 11.
• The Tiled workflow and the TILEMAP resource from chapter 12, as a valid alternative to
the MAP resource when a level is designed by painting tiles rather than starting from a
single, already-composed image.
• The split of the project into several .res files by topic, seen in chapter 51, which this
chapter extends from “one resource file per character” to “one resource file per level.”
• The palette and VRAM constraints covered in the chapters on multiple background
palettes (14), managing VRAM limits (45), SGDK 2.x’s new VRAM configuration (46),
and tile reduction (47).
• Basic familiarity with a tile-based graphics editor, such as the Aseprite already used in
chapter 8.
1. Where a level’s art comes from
Noteverylevelofagameneedstobedrawnentirelyfromscratch. Reusingandadaptingart
from an existing game — one’s own, or, in hobby projects made for learning purposes, some
407

=== PAGE 414 ===
well-known classic — is a common production strategy in homebrew development: it lets
youfocuseffortonimprovingandexpandingartthat’salreadyproven,insteadofgenerating,
from a blank page, the sheer volume of tiles a full level needs. An illustrative case, common
in Mega Drive projects made by hobbyists, is starting from the graphics of an 8-bit game on
anearlierconsoleandadaptingthemtotheMegaDrive’scapabilitieswhilekeepingthesame
drawing style and the same tile and sprite size, rather than redesigning the art at a higher
level of detail.
Whatever the source of the art, it’s worth settling two criteria before you start preparing a
level’s tiles:
• The sprite size for the player and the enemies doesn’t change between levels. If
a level’s background art is drawn at a different level of detail than the rest, the player
and enemies will look disproportionate as soon as they’re moved over that background.
Anyreferenceartbeingadapted—whetherfromanearliergameofyourownoranother
source — has to be respected at the same scale the project’s sprites already use.
• Tiles are still 8×8 pixels,theminimumunittheVDPworkswith,asexplainedinchap-
ter 2. This doesn’t change from one level to the next: it’s a hardware constraint, not a
design decision.
Whenthereferenceartcomesfromanexistinggamethatisn’tavailableasaneditableimage
file, a practical technique for gathering reference material is to capture the game running
inside an emulator that supports frame advance, rather than letting it run at normal speed.
Freezing the image frame by frame avoids capturing a screen in the middle of a scroll move-
ment or with an animated element in an unrepresentative in-between position, and lets you
go through a level screen by screen to later combine those captures in a graphics editor and
reconstruct the full layout as a single continuous image. Practically any emulator with an
equivalent frame-advance feature works for this purpose: there’s no technical dependency
on any particular emulator, beyond the convenience of using one you already know.
Oncethatreferenceimagehasbeenassembled,theeditingworkgoesthroughaconventional
tile-based graphics editor (Aseprite, already used in chapter 8): cleaning up the result, snap-
ping it to an 8×8 grid, and starting to apply the color improvements described in the next
section.
2. Making the most of the extra color: contrast and plane
separation, now multiplied per level
The Mega Drive offers four hardware palettes of 15 colors each plus a shared background
color, for a total of 61 simultaneous on-screen colors compared to the 31 of a typical 8-bit
console. Thatdifferenceisn’tputtousebyhavinganindividualtileorspritedrawfrommore
thanonepalette—eachoneisstilllimitedto15colorsplusthebackgroundcolor,asexplained
in chapter 14 — but by spreading different palettes across different elements of the scene so
they contrast clearly.
In this project, the four hardware palettes already have a fixed assignment inherited from
previous chapters: PAL1 for the player and PAL3 for the enemies (chapters 50 and 51). That
leavesPAL0andPAL2availableforlevelbackgrounds,andit’sworthkeepingthatassignment
constant across the thirteen chapters of this part: PAL0 for the foreground (BG_A), where the
level’scollisionlives,andPAL2fortheparallaxbackground(BG_B),whichispurelydecorative.
Eachnewlevelreplacesthecontentsofthosetwopalettes,butneverchangeswhichhardware
palettecorrespondstowhichplane: thatsimplifiestheloadingcode,becausethere’snoneed
to decide again, level by level, which palette number to use.
Withinthosetwoper-levelpalettes,thesameseparationcriterionalreadypracticedinchapter
408

=== PAGE 415 ===
14nowalsoappliesbetweentilesthatcoexistonthesameplane: it’sworthreservingclearly
distinct color ranges for walkable terrain and for the vegetation or decorative elements sur-
rounding it, so that a player can tell at a glance where they can step and where they can’t,
instead of both kinds of tile sharing a similar color range and blending together. That con-
trast matters even more in a game with continuous horizontal scrolling like this one, where
the player doesn’t have time to stop and carefully examine the scenery.

Tilesetofaharborarea: structures,aboat,andwater,eachwithitsownpalettesotheystand

Splittingintobackgroundandforegroundplanesisalsoarequirementforapplying
parallax scrolling (chapter 9): if a level’s reference art comes from a game that
showed everything on a single layer, you have to explicitly decide, while preparing
the tiles, which elements move to the distant background and which stay in the
walkable foreground, before declaring any resource.
3. Organizing resources by level
With the artistic criteria already set, the next step is to bring each level into the project as

void load_level_graphics(u8 level_index) {

VDP_loadTileSet(level->background_tileset,
TILE_USER_INDEX + level->foreground_tileset->numTile, DMA);

TILE_ATTR_FULL(PAL0, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TILE_USER_INDEX));
background_map = MAP_create(level->background_map, BG_B,
TILE_ATTR_FULL(PAL2, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE,
TILE_USER_INDEX + level->foreground_tileset->numTile));

their palettes to change completely. The if (foreground_map != NULL) check prevents the
first time the function is called from trying to free a structure that doesn’t exist yet; on any
later call, however, that pointer already points to the previous level’s map and needs to be
freed before it’s replaced, so as not to leave allocated memory unused.
Note that the VRAM index where the background is loaded (TILE_USER_INDEX + level-
>foreground_tileset->numTile) is calculated from the actual tile count of that particular
level’s foreground, taken from the numTile field of the TileSet structure, rather than a fixed,
hand-written number. This matters because different levels are almost certainly not going
to have the same number of unique tiles in their foreground, so a fixed offset that works for
level 1 could cause level 2’s background to partially overlap its own foreground if the latter
turned out to have more tiles.
5. The VRAM budget is no longer for a single background,
it’s for the whole level
The chapters on managing VRAM limits (45), SGDK 2.x’s new configuration (46), and tile
reduction (47) already explained how to calculate how many unique tiles fit into the space
available starting from TILE_USER_INDEX. With a single background on screen, that calcula-
tion was done once. With a level split into a foreground and a parallax background, the
number that matters is the sum of the unique tiles in both: level->foreground_tileset-
>numTile + level->background_tileset->numTilecan’texceedtheVRAMspacefreeforuser
tiles,afteralsosubtractingthetilesalreadyusedbytheplayer’sandenemies’sprites, which
share the same tile memory even though they’re managed with SPR_addSprite() instead of
VDP_loadTileSet().
Thisdoesn’tchangeanyofthetechniquesalreadycovered—reducingduplicatetileswiththe
TILESET’s ALL mode, reusing mirrored variants instead of drawing new tiles, or falling back
onthemanualspriteloadingfromchapter48ifmorespaceneedstobefreedup—butitdoes
change the arithmetic: in a single-level game, that budget was calculated once and stayed
fixed; in a multi-level game, each level has its own combined foreground-plus-background
budget, and it’s worth checking it level by level as levels are added to the catalog, rather
than assuming that whatever fit in the first one will automatically fit in all the rest.

1. The main loop based on the game state
The first change happens in main.c, where up to now the main loop always called the same
functions on every pass, with no condition. From this chapter on, the body of the loop is
414

=== PAGE 421 ===
organized as a chain of if/else if statements that check the value of current_game_state
beforedecidingwhattodo. IfthestateisRUNNING_LEVEL,theloopprocessesthecontrols,up-
datestheplayerandtheenemies,andrefreshesthesprites,exactlyasithasbeendoinguntil
now. If the state is LOADING, on the other hand, the game needs to do something completely
different: load the data for the new level.
One function is deliberately left out of this branching: SYS_doVBlankProcess(), the call that
synchronizes screen updates with the console’s vertical blank interval. This function needs
to run on every pass of the loop regardless of the game’s state, so it’s left outside of any if,
running unconditionally.
// src/main.c
#include <genesis.h>
#include "levels.h"
#include "player.h"
#include "enemies.h"
int main(bool hard_reset) {
VDP_setScreenWidth320();
JOY_init();
JOY_setEventHandler(joyEvent);
SPR_init();
while (TRUE) {
if (current_game_state == RUNNING_LEVEL) {
handleInput();
managePlayer();
manageEnemies();
SPR_update();
} else if (current_game_state == LOADING) {
levelLoader();
}
// Runs always, regardless of the game's state
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return 0;
}
Before writing the branch for the LOADING state, it’s worth reviewing which existing func-
tions should run only once when the program starts (setting the screen resolution, initializ-
ingthecontroller,initializingSGDK’sspriteengine)andwhichonesshouldberepeatedevery
time a new level is loaded. The former stay where they are, before the main loop; only cre-
atePlayer() and createEnemies() need to run on every level load, and it’s precisely those
two that get reorganized in the next section.
2. levelLoader(): a function that groups level loading to-

in levels.h. This grouping isn’t just about tidiness: as loading a level grows more complex

the loading process, instead of having to remember to update the main loop every time.

indirect #includes. The include guard already used in every header of this project ensures

as soon as the program starts, what’s needed is to load a level, not run it; the latter is left at

2.2. The body of levelLoader()
The body of levelLoader(), in levels.c, for now simply calls createPlayer() and createEn-
emies() (the same two functions that used to be called directly from main.c) and, as a final
step, changes current_game_state back to RUNNING_LEVEL. This last step is essential: if lev-
elLoader() never updated the state, the game would keep loading the same level over and
over on every pass of the main loop, never moving on to run it.
// src/levels.c
#include "levels.h"
u8 current_game_state = LOADING;
u8 current_game_section = 0;

void levelLoader(void) {
createPlayer();
createEnemies();
// With the level now loaded, the next pass of the main loop
// will run the RUNNING_LEVEL branch
current_game_state = RUNNING_LEVEL;
}
3. Testing the initial load
With levelLoader() now being called from the LOADING branch of the main loop, it’s enough
to compile and test the ROM to verify the full flow: the program starts in the LOADING state,
runs levelLoader() once (which places the player and the section 0 enemies on screen and
changes the state to RUNNING_LEVEL), and from then on each subsequent pass of the loop
runs the RUNNING_LEVEL branch, allowing the player to move around and the enemies to be
observed behaving normally.
4. Changing sections by pressing Start
Withlevelloadingnowautomated, whatremainsisconnectingtheStartbuttontoadvancing

increments the section number by one every time the button is pressed.
// src/controls.c (fragment of joyEvent(), already existing since the
// chapter on game states)
void joyEvent(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state) {
if (current_game_state == RUNNING_LEVEL) {
if (changed & state & BUTTON_START) {
current_game_state = LOADING;
current_game_section++;
}
}
}
The next time the main loop enters the LOADING branch, levelLoader() will call createEne-

new value of current_game_section and copy, from all_enemies, the enemies corresponding
to the next section.
Compiling and testing this change, the initial result is encouraging: the first level loads nor-
mally, and pressing Start does advance to the next section, with its own enemies as defined
in all_enemies. However, a slightly closer look reveals a problem.
5. A common bug: sprites that don’t disappear between
levels
Pressing Start several times in a row, the enemies of the new section appear correctly, but
the player and the enemies from the previous section remain visible on screen instead of

=== PAGE 424 ===
disappearing, piling up each time a level is advanced. The cause is easy to explain: every
time levelLoader() calls createPlayer() and createEnemies(), these functions allocate new
spritesviaSPR_addSprite(), butatnopointisSGDK’sspriteenginetoldtoreleasetheprevi-
ous section’s sprites before creating the new ones.
Figure 154: Sprites piling up on screen after pressing Start several times
Thespritesfromprevioussectionsremainonscreentogetherwiththoseofthecurrentsection,
instead of being replaced.
Beyond the anecdotal sight of dozens of overlapping sprites on screen before the problem is
noticedorthesystemcrashes,thisbugillustratesageneralprinciplevalidinalmostanysprite
engine: allocatingaresource(inthiscase,ahardwaresprite)withoutreleasingtheprevious
one will sooner or later exhaust that resource, whether it’s memory, sprite identifiers, or any
other finite limit of the system.
6. The fix: SPR_reset()
SGDKoffersafunctiondesignedexactlyforthisscenario: SPR_reset(),whichreleasesevery
sprite allocated so far along with the resources associated with them. The fix consists of
callingSPR_reset()asthefirststepinsidelevelLoader(),beforeanythingelse,sothatevery
level load starts from a clean state, with no leftover sprites from the previous section:
// src/levels.c
#include "levels.h"

u8 current_game_section = 0;

// Releases every sprite allocated so far —the player and the

// enemies from the previous section— before creating the
// ones for the new section
SPR_reset();
createPlayer();
createEnemies();

}
After recompiling with this change, the problem disappears completely: the player and the
enemiesfromeachprevioussectionareremovedfromthescreentheinstantthenextsection
is loaded, and only the sprites belonging to the current section remain visible.
SPR_reset() releases absolutely every sprite allocated so far, without distinguishing what
category they belong to. As long as the only thing on screen is the player and the enemies,
thisisexactlywhat’sneeded;butifinafuturechapterthegameaddsalifecounterorascore
