of which sprites get released and which don’t would need to be rethought.
Lookfortheexistingfunctionfirst. Anyfunctioninanengineorframeworkthat
allocates a resource is usually accompanied by an equivalent function to release it.
Faced with a resource-accumulation bug like the one in this section, it’s worth ask-
ing first: does the framework being used already have a function designed exactly
forthisproblem? InSGDK,theanswerisalmostalwaysyes,andlookingitupinthe
documentation usually saves a lot of time compared to trying to solve the problem
by hand—for example, keeping a custom array of pointers to Sprite just to be able
to loop through it and call SPR_releaseSprite() sprite by sprite.
7. A deliberate crash: what happens when the level array
overflows
To close out the chapter, a question asked with a bit of mischief: what happens if Start is
pressed more times than there are sections defined in all_enemies? That catalog was de-
clared with capacity for ten sections (indices 0 through 9), so pressing Start eleven times
brings current_game_section to the value 10, an index that falls outside the array’s valid
bounds.
The result, the first time the array overflows by a single position, isn’t an immediate crash:
a single enemy appears on screen, with data that clearly doesn’t correspond to any section
designed on purpose. This happens because index 10 falls right into the memory contiguous
to all_enemies, which at that moment happens to contain some data that can be interpreted
as a valid enemy. Continuing to press Start and overflowing the array by one more position,
the program finally crashes with an address error message.
Thisiswhattheaddresserrorproducedbythe68000lookslikewhenreadingmemoryoutside
the bounds of all_enemies.
An address error of this kind is how the Mega Drive, more precisely its Motorola 68000 pro-
cessor, reacts when the program tries to access a memory address in a way the hardware
doesn’tallow, somethingthathappensfrequentlywhenanarrayoverflowsandendsupread-
ing memory that doesn’t belong to that array.
It’s tempting to think that an immediate, loud crash is the worst possible outcome for a bug
419

=== PAGE 426 ===
Figure 155: Emulator address error when overflowing the all_enemies array
like this, but it’s worth considering the opposite argument: the intermediate result (a single
enemywithcorrupteddata,withnoerrormessageatall)isactuallymoredangerous,because
itinviteslookingforthecauseoftheprobleminthewrongplace—theAIlogic,forinstance—
instead of correctly suspecting an array overflow. An immediate, explicit crash, even though
it’s alarming the first time it’s seen, unambiguously signals that something was written or
readoutsidethememoryboundsitwassupposedtostaywithin,narrowingdownconsiderably
where to look for the bug.
This chapter closes without fixing the ten-section limit: this is a problem that naturally gets
resolvedasthegame’sdevelopmentprogressesanddefinesitsactualnumberoflevels,andit
doesn’t warrant further concern for now. It is worth remembering this behavior, though, the
next time a strange, inconsistent bug shows up in a project of your own: before suspecting
more complex logic, it’s worth ruling out an array overflow first.

1. A level’s graphic resources: background, foreground,
and a separate palette
Each level in the game is made up of two independent images —a background and a
foreground— prepared following the artistic criteria already explained in the chapter on
preparing level graphics: separating both layers is precisely what enables parallax scrolling
between them later on. A third, much smaller image is added to those two, whose sole
purpose is to store color information: the screen’s overall background color and the four
systempalettes(PAL0throughPAL3)infull,sixty-fourcolorsintotal. Inthisproject,PAL0and
PAL1 are reserved for the level’s background and foreground, PAL2 for enemies, and PAL3 for
the player and the HUD.
Storing the palette as a separate resource, instead of letting each image carry its own, has
a concrete advantage: it allows combining the same background with different foregrounds
that use different palettes for PAL1, which will come in handy the day a single scene needs
lighting or section variants. The three resources for each level are declared using the same
.res file mechanism already used in previous chapters for sprites and backgrounds:
// res_levels.res
IMAGE level1_palette "levels/level1_palette.png" NONE
IMAGE level1_background "levels/level1_background.png" BEST ALL

MAP level1_fg_map "levels/level1_foreground.png" level1_fg_tileset BEST 0
IMAGE level2_palette "levels/level2_palette.png" NONE
IMAGE level2_background "levels/level2_background.png" BEST ALL
TILESET level2_fg_tileset "levels/level2_foreground.png" BEST ALL
MAP level2_fg_map "levels/level2_foreground.png" level2_fg_tileset BEST 0
IMAGE level3_palette "levels/level3_palette.png" NONE
IMAGE level3_background "levels/level3_background.png" BEST ALL
TILESET level3_fg_tileset "levels/level3_foreground.png" BEST ALL
MAP level3_fg_map "levels/level3_foreground.png" level3_fg_tileset BEST 0
Thelevel1_paletteresourceusestheNONEcompressionmodebecauseit’satinyimage: com-
pressingitprovidesnorealsavingsandonlyaddsanunnecessarydecompressionstep. When
compiled,rescompgeneratesres_levels.hfollowingthesamelogicalreadyseenforanyother

3. Loading the graphics in levelLoader()
With the catalog already complete, the loading process is added inside levelLoader(). The

createEnemies();

Throughout this sequence, vram_index plays the same role already seen in the chapter on

writing from, and that position depends on how much space the resources uploaded earlier
in that same load already took up. Keeping track in a single variable, instead of computing
separate offsets on each call, is what lets the same block of code work unchanged no matter
which level is being loaded at any given moment.

4. Why the colors come out wrong: manual palettes versus
per-level palettes
If you open the emulator’s palette debugging screen at this point, PAL2 and PAL3 —the en-
emy’s and the player’s palettes— show up with their correct colors, while PAL0 and PAL1
remain white and red. The reason is that createPlayer() and createEnemies() still call
PAL_setPalette() manually to set their own palettes, something that made sense before a
level system existed, but which now conflicts with the idea of loading all of a level’s palettes
in a centralized way.
The fix is to remove those manual calls to PAL_setPalette() from both createPlayer() and
createEnemies(). The goal is for the game’s four palettes to be loaded from a single, cen-
tralized place inside levelLoader(), instead of each function responsible for creating an on-
screen element managing its own palette separately.
The first step of that centralization is copying the information from the current level’s small
palette image —accessible as all_levels[current_game_section].palette->data— into the
already-declared palette_full array, using memcpy() to copy all 64 colors in one go:
memcpy(palette_full, level->palette->data, sizeof(palette_full));
With the colors already copied, the final step is to call PAL_fadeIn() at the end of level-
Loader(), passing it palette_full as the color source and a short duration, measured in
frames:
PAL_fadeIn(0, 63, palette_full, 15, FALSE);
The 0, 63 range covers all four palettes at once, since palette_full carries the 64 colors in
thesameordertheyliveininCRAM.Afterrecompiling,thelevelfinallyshowsupwithitsreal
colors from the very first visible instant on screen.

5. Clean transitions: fade-out and memory release
With the fade-in already working, one detail still remains unresolved: when switching levels,
theplayerbrieflygetstoseehalf-loadedtileswhilethenewdataisbeingcopiedtoVRAM.The
fixistoaddafade-out, PAL_fadeOut(), atthestartoftheloadingprocess, sothescreengoes
black before the new graphic data starts being written, and the new level is only revealed
once everything is ready.
There’s also a loose end of a different nature: every time MAP_create() is called to generate
fg_map_def, SGDK allocates dynamic memory for that structure. If that memory is never
freed before preparing the next level’s map, every level transition leaves behind allocated
memory that’s no longer used and never reclaimed —something that isn’t noticeable today
because the game is small, but that would eventually cause an out-of-memory crash as the
gamegrows. ThefixistocallMEM_free(fg_map_def)beforecallingMAP_create()againwhen
loading the next level.
These three cleanup tasks —fade-out, sprite reset, and memory release— are grouped into
a separate function, screenResetManager(), whose sole purpose is to leave the screen and
memory in a clean state before loading any new level:
// levels.c
void screenResetManager(void) {
PAL_fadeOut(0, 63, 10, FALSE);
SPR_reset();
if (fg_map_def != NULL) {
MEM_free(fg_map_def);
fg_map_def = NULL;
}
// Leaves all four palettes black between one fade and the next,
// to rule out any chance of a leftover color from the previous
// level bleeding through visually while the new data is loading
PAL_setColors(0, palette_black, 64, DMA);
}
screenResetManager()isn’tcalledfromlevelLoader(),butfromcontrols.c,insidethesame
condition that already increments current_game_section and changes current_game_state
to LOADING when Start is pressed:

6. From a blocking transfer to the DMA queue
Everything above already leaves the level-change cycle working end to end, but it’s
worth taking a closer look at what’s happening under the hood of VDP_drawImageEx() and
VDP_loadTileSet()whenuploadingthegraphics,becausethisisexactlythescenariochapter
44 left pending for this point in the manual.
Both VDP_drawImageEx(..., DMA) and VDP_loadTileSet(..., DMA) trigger, underneath, an
immediate, blocking transfer equivalent to DMA_doDma(): the 68000 is halted until the VDP
finishescopyingthetiles. InlevelLoader()thisisn’taproblem,becauseithappensonlyonce
per transition and with the screen already black thanks to screenResetManager(): there’s
nothing on screen depending on the CPU continuing to run at that exact instant. The real
cost isn’t visual, it’s about time: while the DMA is busy copying a level’s tiles, no other game
calculation moves forward, and since this load doesn’t necessarily happen during vblank —
it could start in the middle of a frame’s active drawing, depending on exactly when level-
Loader()runswithinthemainloop—thetransferalsorunsatthereducedspeedthatchapter
44 described for that period.
For a level with a modest background and foreground, a few thousand bytes in total, this
speed difference isn’t noticeable. The problem shows up with the LEVEL_DOUBLE_MAP level
type anticipated in the enum: an indoor scene with two independent tile maps can easily
accumulatemoreuniquetilesthanasinglevblankisabletomove,basedonthefigureexposed
by DMA_getMaxTransferSize(). Forcing that amount of data through DMA_doDma() all at once
doesn’t produce any error, but it does produce a proportionally longer CPU stall, potentially
spilling partly into the active drawing of the next frame, with the speed penalty that implies.
The alternative, as laid out in chapter 44, is to split the load across several frames using the
DMA queue instead of an immediate transfer, checking before each chunk how much budget
remains available in the current frame with DMA_canQueue():
// Uploads a full TileSet to VRAM in chunks that respect a single
// vblank's transfer limit, instead of one blocking call.
// Meant for large tilesets (for example, a LEVEL_DOUBLE_MAP), where
// a single DMA_doDma() call might not comfortably fit within one frame.
static void loadTileSetFractioned(const TileSet* tileset, u16 index) {
u16 words_left = tileset->numTile * 16; // 16 words (32 bytes) per tile
u16 words_sent = 0;
u16 dest = index * 32;
while (words_left > 0) {
u16 max_chunk = DMA_getMaxTransferSize();
u16 chunk = (words_left < max_chunk) ? words_left : max_chunk;
// If the chunk doesn't fit within the current frame's remaining
// budget, wait for the next vblank before trying again
while (!DMA_canQueue(chunk)) {
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
DMA_queueDma(DMA_VRAM, (u8*) tileset->tiles + words_sent * 2, dest, chunk,
↪ 2);
words_sent += chunk;
words_left -= chunk;
dest += chunk * 2;

// Lets this chunk be processed on the next vblank before
// queuing up the next one
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
}
Replacing the call to VDP_loadTileSet(level->foreground_tileset, vram_index, DMA) with
loadTileSetFractioned(level->foreground_tileset, vram_index) spreads the same total
amountofdataacrossseveralvblanksinsteadofjustone,withoutthescreen—alreadyblack
thanks to screenResetManager()— showing any hint that the load is happening in several
steps. For this chapter’s LEVEL_PARALLAX levels, whose data volume is modest, the blocking
versionremainsperfectlyreasonable; thefractionedversionisthetooltoreachforthedaya

1. The project as it stands

Put another way: the project in this part is not a finished game, but the backbone of one. It

Chapter 63 — HInterrupts and
Raster Effects
The VDP’s horizontal interrupt, SYS_setHIntCallback(), and differential scroll by screen
bands
ThischapteropensPartXofthemanual,devotedtoadvancedtopicsthatdidn’tfitcomfortably
into the previous parts: they aren’t a direct continuation of a topic already underway, but
rather specific tools worth knowing once the rest of the foundation — the VDP, DMA, the
general structure of an SGDK project — is already settled. The first of these tools is the
horizontal interrupt, or HInterrupt (also called HInt, or in English-language documentation,
horizontal interrupt).
Uptothispoint,anychangemadetotheVDP—movingaplane,changingapalette,updating
a tile — has always happened at one of two possible moments: during the main loop, while
the screen has already been drawn and what’s showing is still the previous frame, or during
the vertical blank (vblank), the interval between when one frame finishes drawing and the
next one begins, which is what SYS_doVBlankProcess() targets. The HInterrupt adds a third,
muchfiner-grainedpossibility: reactinginthemiddleofthedrawingofasingleframe,exactly
whentheVDP’sscanbeamfinishesonelineofvideoandisabouttostartthenext. Thatmakes
it possible to change the VDP’s state — the background color, a plane’s horizontal offset, in
theory almost any register — at a precise point on the screen, and it’s the basis for a classic
familyofeffectsgenericallyknownasrastereffects: waterthatrippleswithadifferentscroll
offset on each horizontal strip, a starry sky that scrolls at a different speed than the ground,
a split screen where a HUD area stays fixed while the rest keeps scrolling.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, you should be comfortable with:
• UnderstandingoftheVDP,itsBG_A/BG_Bplanes,andthethreegranularitiesofhorizontal
scroll(HSCROLL_PLANE,HSCROLL_TILE,HSCROLL_LINE),introducedinchapter2andputinto
code in chapters 9 and 17.
• Having worked with VDP_setScrollingMode() and VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile(),
from chapter 17, since this chapter extends the same idea to the finest granularity, per
line.
• The general structure of an SGDK program, with its main loop organized around
SYS_doVBlankProcess().
• Ideally, having read chapter 44 on DMA, because one of this chapter’s precautions is
precisely which transfer mechanisms cannot be used inside an HInterrupt.

1. What a horizontal interrupt is at the hardware level
The Mega Drive’s VDP draws the screen line by line, top to bottom, sweeping each line from
left to right before moving to the next. That process is exactly the same mechanism, in-
herited from analog television, that makes the very concept of vblank possible: when the
scan reaches the last visible line and has to return to the top for the next frame, there’s
an interval with nothing to draw, and that’s where the vertical interrupt (VInt) that triggers
SYS_doVBlankProcess() occurs.
Thehorizontalinterruptisthesameidea,butappliedtoeachindividuallineinsteadoftoeach
complete frame. The VDP has an internal line counter and a dedicated register — register
0x0A,intheVDP’sinternalregisternumbering—thatspecifieshowmanylinesshouldelapse
between interrupt triggers. SGDK exposes that counter with:
void VDP_setHIntCounter(u8 value);
The value loaded there isn’t “every how many lines,” but “how many lines to wait before the
first one”: with value = 0 the interrupt fires on every line, and in general, loading N makes
the HInterrupt occur every N + 1 scan lines. That counter reloads itself automatically after
each trigger, so once configured it keeps producing interrupts at regular intervals without
the program having to reprogram it line by line.
The interrupt itself has to be enabled separately, with:
void VDP_setHInterrupt(bool value);
VDP_setHInterrupt(TRUE) enables the trigger; VDP_setHInterrupt(FALSE) turns it off
completely, without touching the counter value (which stays saved for the next time it’s
re-enabled). An important detail for understanding where it makes sense to use this mech-
anism: the HInterrupt fires while the VDP is scanning through the screen’s active drawing
area, line by line; when it reaches the end of the frame, it’s the vertical interrupt that takes
over during the vblank, not the horizontal one. This is precisely what makes the HInterrupt
useful for this chapter: it provides a hook point exactly where the VInt doesn’t reach, in the
middle of the frame’s own drawing, rather than only before or after it.
A necessary clarification: it’s not magic, it’s real time. The CPU doesn’t
“pause” the VDP’s drawing to handle the interrupt at leisure. The screen’s scan
keeps going exactly at the pace set by the video clock, whether or not program
code runs in the meantime. If the interrupt handler takes too long to finish, the
VDP will already have started drawing the next line with the old state, or the mo-
menttoupdateitintimewillsimplybemissed. Section5ofthischapterreturnsto
this idea in more detail.

3. Per-line scroll: the other half of the effect
Chapter 17 showed HSCROLL_TILE, which allows an independent horizontal offset for each 8-
pixelrowofaplane. TheVDPsupportsanevenfinergranularity,HSCROLL_LINE,whichallows
a different horizontal offset value for each individual line of the screen, without grouping
them in sets of 8. It’s enabled with the same function already covered:
VDP_setScrollingMode(HSCROLL_LINE, VSCROLL_PLANE);
and updated with the equivalent of VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile() for this granularity:
void VDP_setHorizontalScrollLine(VDPPlane plane, u16 line, s16 *values, u16 len,
↪ TransferMethod tm);
The parameters are analogous to those of VDP_setHorizontalScrollTile(): plane is BG_A or
BG_B; line is the first screen line, counted from the top, from which the values are applied;
values is an array holding one offset per line; len is the number of lines to update; and tm is
the transfer method (CPU, DMA, DMA_QUEUE, or DMA_QUEUE_COPY, as covered in chapter 44).
Here’s a key point worth emphasizing, because it tends to cause confusion: this table of per-
lineoffsetsisreadbytheVDPonitsown,automatically,everytimeitdrawseachscreenline.
Thatmeansaripplingeffect—liketheclassicwaterreflection,witheachhorizontalstripoff-

it’s enough to compute the entire table of values once per frame, during the vblank, and up-
load it all at once with a single call to VDP_setHorizontalScrollLine(). The VDP then takes
care, in real time throughout the whole active drawing pass, of reading a different value for
each line without the program having to intervene line by line. This is, in fact, the simplest
and most common way to achieve a rippling water effect in SGDK, and it needs none of what
was explained in sections 1 and 2.
So what is the HInterrupt needed for? For everything that table can’t resolve on its own:
• Changing something that has no per-line table. The VDP’s background color

The rest of this chapter builds an example combining both pieces: a fixed “sky” strip at the

4. Full example: differential scroll by bands
The example divides the screen into bands 8 lines tall (to simplify the calculations, although
HSCROLL_LINEwouldalsoallowsingle-linebands). Aboveacutoffline, WATER_START,theback-
ground is shown with no additional offset. Below that line, each 8-line band receives a differ-
ent horizontal offset, taken from a precomputed wave table, which also rotates by one step
each frame to give a sense of motion: the classic water effect.
#include <genesis.h>
#define BAND_HEIGHT 8 // height of each band, in lines
#define WATER_START 144 // line where the water starts (multiple of
↪ BAND_HEIGHT)
#define WAVE_SIZE 32 // number of entries in the wave table
// Precomputed horizontal offset table (a low-amplitude wave).
// The values are in pixels; they could be generated with sin() at design time,
// but are left as constants to avoid depending on floating-point calculations.
static const s16 waveTable[WAVE_SIZE] =
{
0, 6, 12, 17, 20, 22, 22, 20,
17, 12, 6, 0, -6,-12,-17,-20,
-22,-22,-20,-17,-12, -6, 0, 6,
12, 17, 20, 22, 22, 20, 17, 12
};
static u16 rasterLine; // screen line about to be drawn
static u16 waveFrame; // wave phase; advances one step per frame
// HInterrupt handler: runs once every BAND_HEIGHT lines.
// Must be as short as possible: no calls to heavy functions,
// no DMA, nothing that could take longer than the time available before the
// VDP starts drawing the next line.
HINTERRUPT_CALLBACK hintHandler(void)

{

↪ 1);

offset, offset, offset, offset };
VDP_setHorizontalScrollLine(BG_B, rasterLine, values, BAND_HEIGHT, CPU);
}

}
// Runs once per frame, during the vblank: resets the line counter
// for the frame that's starting and advances the wave phase.
void onVBlank(void)
{

}

A few of the example’s decisions deserve a separate explanation:
• Thelinecounter,rasterLine,isresetinthevblankcallback(onVBlank()),andnotatany
other point in the main loop, because the vblank is the only moment you can be sure

corresponds exactly to the start of a new frame. If it were reset in the middle of the

• The handler runs for every band on the screen, including the sky bands, but for those

• The transfer method used inside the handler is CPU, never DMA, DMA_QUEUE, nor
DMA_QUEUE_COPY. The next section explains why.
The visual result is what you’d expect from this kind of effect: the top sky strip stays fixed,
with no offset at all, while below the cutoff line each 8-pixel band moves with a horizontal
offset different from its neighbors, following the shape of the wave table. The progressive
difference between adjacent bands is what creates the sense of a rippling surface, rather
than blocks simply sliding each at its own speed with no relation to one another.
5. Cautions and limitations
The handler must be extremely fast. Between when an HInterrupt fires and when the
VDP starts drawing the next line, there’s very little margin: just the duration of the horizon-
tal blank, the interval between the end of one visible line and the start of the next. With
BAND_HEIGHT = 8,theexample’shandlerhasthewidthofeightfulllinesofmarginbeforethe
next trigger, which is more than enough to write eight words into the scroll table. An effect
configuredtofireoneveryline(VDP_setHIntCounter(0)),bycontrast,hasonlythemarginof
asingleline,andthehandlerhastobetrimmeddowntothebareminimum: noloops,nocalls
to functions beyond what’s strictly necessary, no calculations that aren’t already resolved in
a table.
Don’tuseDMAinsidethehandler. DMA,asexplainedinchapter44,hasitsownsetupcost
and blocks the CPU until it finishes; triggering it from inside an HInterrupt adds that cost at
exactlythemomentwiththeleastmarginavailable,andcanendupconsumingseveralwhole
linesinsteadofafractionofone. ThesameappliestoDMA_QUEUEandDMA_QUEUE_COPY:queuing
a transfer for “the next vblank” makes no sense inside a handler that runs in the middle of
active drawing, still far from the next vblank. The only reasonable transfer method inside an
HInterrupt is CPU, and in limited amounts: a few words, not a whole tileset.
Watchoutforreentrancy. Ifthehandler’sworktakeslonger,forwhateverreason,thanthe
configured interval between triggers, the next trigger’s moment can arrive before the previ-
ous one has finished. On the 68000, this doesn’t necessarily produce a second, overlapping
execution of the same handler, but it can cause the next trigger to be lost or delayed, with
the visible result of a band that “jumps” a position or looks misaligned for one frame. The
simplest way to avoid the problem isn’t to program the handler to tolerate reentrancy, but to
makesure,withmargintosparethroughcarefulmeasurement,thatitnevergetsclosetothe
available time limit.
AvoidleavingHInterruptsactiveinpartsofthegamethatdon’tneedthem. Whenthe
screen using the raster effect ends — a level transition, a pause screen, a menu — it’s best
to turn off the interrupt with VDP_setHInterrupt(FALSE) rather than leaving it active with a
handler that no longer makes sense for the current screen. Besides saving the CPU time it
consumes,thisavoidstheriskoftheoldhandleractingonaplaneorscrolltablethatthenew
screen has already reconfigured for another purpose.
Variablessharedbetweenthehandlerandtherestoftheprogramshouldstaysimple.
This chapter’s example shares only two variables (rasterLine, waveFrame) between the HIn-
438

=== PAGE 445 ===
terrupt handler, the vblank callback, and potentially the rest of the game. The more shared
variables there are, and the more complex the logic that updates them, the greater the risk
that an interrupt occurs right in the middle of a half-finished update from the main code.
Keeping that set of variables as small and simple as possible — integer counters, read-only
tables — is, in practice, the simplest way to avoid that kind of intermittent bug.

Chapter 64 — Saving Games -
SRAM and Flash Save
The cartridge’s battery-backed SRAM, the save declaration in the ROM header, SGDK’s

Upuntilnow,everytimeagameended—whetherbyturningofftheconsoleorresettingthe

thelevelreached, thescore, thestateofevery enemy. That’s exactlywhatyou’dexpect from
an ordinary variable, but it’s a real problem for any game that aspires to be played across
more than one session. This chapter tackles that concrete question: how to make a handful
ofbytessurvivetheconsolebeingturnedoff,usingthesamehardwaremechanismthatmade
cartridges like Phantasy Star IV or Sonic 3 famous, and the layer SGDK provides on top of it.
It’saself-containedtopic: itdoesn’tdependonthepreviouschapterofthisPartX(dedicated
to horizontal interrupts), but instead picks up ideas from further back in the manual, in par-
ticular the use of struct to group related data (Chapter 53) and the level catalog built as

Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have:
• Familiarity with C structs for grouping data, as presented in Chapter 53 (“C structs
applied to game entities”).
• Familiarity with the level catalog built as game data in Part IX (for example, an array or

1. What cartridge SRAM is, and why it exists
The 68000’s working memory (the system RAM) loses its contents as soon as power is cut:
it’s volatile memory, and there’s no way around that with the original Mega Drive hardware.
For a game to remember anything from one session to the next, it needs a different kind of
memory — one that keeps its contents even without external power.
Thesolutionadoptedbymanycartridgesoftheera—notallofthem,sinceitaddedmanufac-
turingcost—wastoincludeinsidethecartridgeitselfanSRAM(staticRAM)chipbackedby
a small lithium battery soldered to the board. While the console is powered on, that SRAM
is read and written just like any other mapped memory region; when the console is turned
440

=== PAGE 447 ===
off, the battery keeps the chip powered with minimal consumption, and its contents persist.
When the console is turned on again, the SRAM comes back with the same data it held the
last time it was written.
That battery is also the cause of a problem well known to anyone who has played original
cartridgesdecadesaftertheyweremanufactured: onceitrunsout,theSRAMstopsretaining
data, and saved games are lost as soon as power is cut. It’s a physical limitation of the
mechanism, not something software can work around, and it’s part of why section 6 of this
chapter covers a modern alternative that doesn’t depend on any battery.
CartridgeSRAMbelongstothecartridge,nottheconsole: everycartridgewithsave
supportbringsitsownchipanditsownbattery. Thatmattersbecauseitmeansthe
available space and its exact behavior depend on how the cartridge’s hardware is
built, not on the Mega Drive itself.
2. Declaring SRAM usage in the ROM header
The Mega Drive’s memory map reserves an entire region for a cartridge, if it has SRAM, to
expose it there. But nothing requires a cartridge to have it: that’s why the ROM includes,
withinitsheader(themetadataareaatthestartoftheROMalreadymentionedinpassingin
earlierchaptersforotherfields,suchasthevideoregion),aspecificblockdeclaringwhether
the game uses SRAM, in what address range, and of what type.
That declaration isn’t a cosmetic detail: it’s the information consulted both by real SRAM-
equipped cartridge hardware and by modern emulators and flash carts to decide whether
they should reserve persistent space for that particular game and at what address to expect
the accesses. Without a correct declaration in the header, a write to the SRAM region may
fail to persist, or may have no effect at all, even if the code correctly calls the save functions.
SGDKexposesthisconfigurationasaproject-leveldirective,withnoneedtohand-editheader
bytes. The usual approach is to define it in the project’s configuration file (or, in simpler
projects, with a macro at the top of main.c):
// Enables the SRAM block in the ROM header,
// declaring a 64 KB range of 8-bit SRAM.
#define SRAM_SIZE 0x10000
#define SRAM_TYPE 0 // 0 = normal SRAM (byte-wide), no automatic backup
Conceptually,whatmattersmorethantheexactmacronamearethetwopiecesofinformation
that declaration fixes: how much SRAM the cartridge has (up to 64 KB in the simplest
variant, addressed as bytes) and whether that SRAM is battery-backed or not. An emulator
that respects the header creates, the first time it runs that ROM, an associated save file
(typically with a .srm extension) that reproduces the behavior of that battery: it persists
between emulator runs just as the battery persists between power cycles on real hardware.
3. SGDK’s sram.h unit
WithSRAMalreadydeclaredintheheader,SGDKoffersadedicatedunit,sram.h,forreading
and writing it from game code without having to calculate memory addresses by hand or
worry about the exact mapping the hardware uses to expose it.
Before any access, it must be explicitly enabled:
void SRAM_enable(void);

WithSRAMenabled,thebasicreadandwritefunctionsworkoveranoffsetwithinthatregion,

“word”accessactuallyoccupiestwoaddresspositionswithonlyoneusefulbyteineach. This
is exactly the kind of detail that makes it worth relying on the sram.h functions instead of
computing offsets by hand: the unit already resolves it consistently.
4. Saving and loading a progress structure
The most common use case isn’t saving loose bytes, but a small structure holding the state a
game needs to remember. Picking up the level catalog from Part IX, a reasonable example is
saving the highest level reached and the highest score achieved:
typedef struct
{
u16 highestLevel; // index of the highest level reached, within the level
↪ catalog
u32 highScore; // highest score recorded
u8 checksum; // simple integrity check, computed on save
} GameProgress;
ThechecksumfieldisthemissingpiecebeforetrustinganydatareadbackfromSRAM.SRAM
with a battery that hasn’t run out is reliable, but a weak battery, SRAM that has never been
writtenbefore(filledwithanarbitraryfactoryvalue,notnecessarilyzeros),or,onaflashcart,
a corrupted save file, are all real scenarios. Before using the data read back to decide which
level to start on, it’s worth computing a simple checksum over the rest of the structure and
comparing it against the one saved alongside the data:
// Computes a simple checksum: the sum of every byte in progress,
// excluding the checksum field itself, truncated to 8 bits.
static u8 compute_checksum(const GameProgress *progress)
{
const u8 *bytes = (const u8 *) progress;
u16 sum = 0;

for (u16 i = 0; i < sizeof(GameProgress) - sizeof(progress->checksum); i++)

the whole structure to SRAM:
#define SAVE_OFFSET 0
void save_progress(u16 highestLevel, u32 highScore)
{

progress.highestLevel = highestLevel;
progress.highScore = highScore;
progress.checksum = 0; // filled in afterward, once the rest of the fields are
↪ set

SRAM_writeAll((const u8 *) &progress, SAVE_OFFSET, sizeof(GameProgress));
SRAM_disable();
}
Loading progress follows the reverse path, but it should never blindly trust what it reads: if

case, push the level catalog out of range:
bool load_progress(GameProgress *out)
{
GameProgress progress;
SRAM_enable();
SRAM_readAll((u8 *) &progress, SAVE_OFFSET, sizeof(GameProgress));
SRAM_disable();
u8 expected = compute_checksum(&progress);
if (progress.checksum != expected)
return FALSE; // missing or corrupted data: no valid saved game
*out = progress;
return TRUE;
}

In terms of memory, the cartridge ends up organized into two clearly separated regions: the
ROM, read-only, where the game’s code and data live, and the SRAM region, mapped sepa-
rately and backed by its battery. Within that SRAM region, GameProgress occupies a fixed
block starting at SAVE_OFFSET: the struct’s three fields (highestLevel, highScore, and check-
sum) sit one after another, in the same order in which they were defined, together occupying
sizeof(GameProgress) bytes.
5. Before reading: checking whether SRAM is available
Not every environment a ROM can run on has SRAM configured the same way: an emulator
that hasn’t yet initialized its associated .srm file, or factory-fresh SRAM that has never been
written, returns arbitrary bytes (often all 0xFF) instead of zeros. This is exactly the case the
checksum from the previous section is meant to catch: if nothing was ever saved, the initial
readwon’tmatchanyvalidchecksum,andload_progress()returnsFALSE,sendingthegame
down the “no saved game” path instead of interpreting factory bytes as if they were a real
level.
That’s why it’s worth resisting the temptation to skip the checksum check “since the SRAM
is already declared in the header”: the declaration in the ROM header guarantees that the
space exists and that an emulator or flash cart will persist it, but it guarantees absolutely
nothing about whether what’s there at any given moment is actually a valid GameProgress
written by this same game.
6. Flash save: the battery-free alternative
Everything above describes the historical mechanism, designed for a physical cartridge with
a soldered battery. For those developing today and testing mainly on modern flash carts
— devices like EverDrive, which load a ROM from an SD card and run it on real hardware
withoutneedingtomanufactureacartridgeforeveryversion—there’saconsiderablysimpler
alternative to work with from the development side: flash save.

Insteadofrelyingonabattery-backedSRAMchip,theseflashcartsoffertheirownpersistent
savemechanismbasedonflashmemory(thesametechnologyusedinSDcards),managedby
the flash cart itself rather than by a discrete chip on the cartridge board. From the point of
view of SGDK and game code, the practical difference is usually minimal or nonexistent: the
same sram.h unit, with the same size declaration in the ROM header, is the interface these
devicesalsoexpecttofind,sothesamesave_progress()/load_progress()codefromsection
4 works unchanged both on an emulator with simulated SRAM and on a flash cart with real
flash-based saving.
The advantage for modern development is twofold: there’s no need to manufacture or pro-
gramaphysicalbattery-backedcartridgetotestsavingonrealhardware,andthere’snorisk
of a battery running out between one testing session and the next. The downside is that
it remains, ultimately, a feature of the flash cart device used for testing, not of the Mega
Drive itself: a commercial cartridge actually manufactured for sale still needs, if it’s going
to offer persistent saving, to deal with the battery-backed SRAM mechanism (or some later
variant, such as the non-volatile memory chips that replaced the battery in later generations
of cartridges) from section 1 onward.

Chapter 65 — Multitasking and
Advanced SGDK 2.x Features
AbrieflookatrecentSGDKadditionsthatdon’tfitintoanyearlierchapter: cooperativetasks,
dynamic memory, and resource compression
The previous chapters of this part covered specific, well-delimited topics: horizontal inter-
ruptsandtheiruseforlineeffects, andSRAMhandlingforsavedgames. Thischaptercloses
Part X with something different: a set of features that SGDK gradually added throughout its
2.x series (from version 2.00 onward) and that, being either more general or more recent,
didn’t have a natural place in any earlier chapter of the manual. There isn’t a single unifying
theme, but there is a common denominator: these are tools that solve problems that only
show up once a project grows beyond a technical demo, and it’s worth knowing about them,
even just at an introductory level, before taking on a larger project of your own.
Prerequisites
• The main loop and SYS_doVBlankProcess(), introduced in Chapter 5.
• The concept of interrupts and the difference between code driven by hardware events
and code that runs inside the main loop, revisited in the previous chapter on horizontal
interrupts.
• A general sense of how SGDK organizes its resources in ROM (Chapter 39).
• SomefamiliaritywithpointersanddynamicmemoryinC(malloc/freeasaconcept,even
though SGDK doesn’t use exactly those functions).
1. The problem that motivates cooperative multitasking
A good part of the code in a Mega Drive game is naturally written as a state machine: a
variable indicates what state a character or sequence is in (walking, jumping, falling; or, in
a cutscene, “showing text,” “waiting for the player to press a button,” “moving the camera”),
andoneverypassthroughthemainloopafunctionchecksthatstateanddecideswhattodo.
It’s a pattern that works well and that has already been used implicitly in earlier chapters of
this manual, but it becomes awkward to write by hand when a sequence has many chained
steps that must happen one after another across several frames: a cutscene with dialogue,
cameramovements,andinterspersedwaits,forexample,endsupturningintoastatemachine
with dozens of cases, hard to read because the logical order of the sequence gets scattered
across a switch and several control variables.
What in a normal desktop program would be solved with a separate thread — writing the
sequence as a linear function, top to bottom, and letting the operating system handle split-
ting CPU time between that function and the rest of the program — isn’t available in the
446

=== PAGE 453 ===
same way on the Mega Drive: there’s no operating system with a thread scheduler, and the
68000executesasingleinstructionstreamatatime. Evenso,SGDK’s2.xseriesintroduceda
mechanismthatallowssomethingsimilarwithinthatconstraint: acooperative tasksystem,
designed for writing long sequences as linear code instead of as an explicit state machine.
2. What SGDK’s cooperative multitasking is (and isn’t)
It’sworthclarifyingupfrontwhatkindof“multitasking”thisis,becausethetermcanbemis-
leading. Thisisnotrealparallelexecution: theMegaDrivestillhasasingle68000executing
a single instruction at a time, just like in any other chapter of this manual. What SGDK of-
fers is a cooperative context-switching mechanism: each “task” is a function with its own
separately reserved stack, and SGDK’s internal scheduler takes turns handing the processor
to each task, saving and restoring the execution context (the 68000’s registers and the stack
pointer) when switching from one task to another. The difference from a hardware interrupt
— like the ones seen in the previous chapter — is that this task switch isn’t triggered by the
hardware at an arbitrary instant; rather, it’s decided by the task itself, voluntarily, by call-
ing a function that hands control back to the scheduler. It’s “cooperative” precisely for that
reason: a task that never yields control blocks all the others, including the main loop, just as
completely as an infinite loop without calls to SYS_doVBlankProcess() would.
This enables a coding style very different from the traditional state machine. A cutscene
sequence that used to require a state variable and a switch with one case per step can be
written, inside a task, as an ordinary function that proceeds from top to bottom, and that,
at the points where it needs to “wait” — for an animation to finish, for a certain number of
frames to pass, for the player to press a button — simply yields control and gets it back later,
at the exact point where it had left off, once the wait condition is met.
The usual skeleton of this pattern, regardless of the exact name of each function, looks like
this:
// Task that runs a multi-step intro sequence,
// written as linear code instead of as a state machine.
void introSequenceTask(void)
{
showText("Welcome to the adventure");
waitFrames(60); // yields control for 60 frames
moveCameraTo(200, 0);
waitCameraArrived(); // yields control until the camera arrives
showText("Press START to begin");
waitButtonPress(BUTTON_START);
}
Eachofthewaitingfunctions(waitFrames(),waitCameraArrived(),waitButtonPress()inthis
example)is,internally,aloopthatcheckstheconditionandyieldstheturnbacktothesched-
uler over and over while that condition isn’t met, in a way similar to how the game’s main
loopyieldsitsturntotheVDPbycallingSYS_doVBlankProcess(). Thedifferencefromwriting
that same logic directly in the main loop is that, while the intro task is “waiting,” the rest of
the game — including the main loop itself, which can keep calling other tasks or continuing
with its own logic — isn’t blocked: the scheduler distributes time among all active tasks on
every pass.
A task that performs a long computation without ever yielding control — for ex-
ample, a loop with thousands of iterations and no intermediate call to the yield
447

=== PAGE 454 ===
mechanism—behavesexactlyasbadlyasthatsamecomputationplaceddirectlyin
the main loop without calling SYS_doVBlankProcess(): it blocks everything else for
as long as it runs. Cooperative multitasking doesn’t automatically distribute CPU
time; it only offers an escape point that’s more convenient to use than a manual
state machine.
EachtaskalsoneedsitsownstackreservedinRAMinordertosaveitscontextwhenyielding
control, and that RAM is a scarce resource on the Mega Drive (barely 64 KB in total). That’s
why the stack size for each task is usually an explicit parameter when creating it, and it’s
worth sizing it carefully: too small, and a sequence with nested function calls can silently
overflow it and corrupt neighboring memory; too large, and several active tasks at once can
exhaust the RAM available for the rest of the game. In practice, this mechanism is best
reservedforsequencesthatgenuinelybenefitfrombeingwrittenaslinearcode—cutscenes,
dialoguescripts,longbossattackpatterns—ratherthanasageneralreplacementforframe-
by-framegameplaylogic,whichisstillbetterhandledwiththemainloopasusedthroughout
the rest of this manual.
3. Improvements in dynamic memory handling
AnotherareawhereSGDKadvancedthroughoutits2.xseries,withouthavinghadadedicated
chapter until now, is dynamic memory handling. SGDK has always offered MEM_alloc() and
MEM_free() as equivalents of standard C’s malloc()/free(), adapted to the Mega Drive’s lim-
ited RAM, and it’s the recommended way to allocate memory at runtime instead of using the
standard C library functions directly.
Recentversionsofthismemoryunitimprovedboththeallocator’sperformance(lessfragmen-
tation when reusing freed blocks of similar size) and the tools for diagnosing memory issues
during development: functions for finding out how much free memory remains available at a
given moment, and for inspecting the heap’s state, are particularly useful when debugging a
crash that only appears after playing for several minutes — a typical symptom of a memory
leak (code that allocates with MEM_alloc() and, along some code path, forgets to free it with
MEM_free()).
// Before loading a new level's resources, it's worth
// recording how much free memory remains, to detect leaks
// by comparing this value from one playthrough to the next.
u32 freeBefore = MEM_getFree();
loadLevelResources();
u32 freeAfter = MEM_getFree();
As a general rule of good practice, it’s best to allocate with MEM_alloc() as few times as
possible during active gameplay — ideally, all the dynamic memory a level needs is allocated
once when it loads, and freed all at once when leaving it — rather than constantly allocating
and freeing small blocks frame by frame, a pattern that fragments the heap over time even
with a well-optimized allocator.
4. Resource compression and the resource compiler
SGDK’s resource compiler, already introduced in Chapter 39 for converting images, tilesets,
and maps into data embedded in the ROM, gained compression support for several resource
types throughout the 2.x series. The underlying idea is simple: many graphics and sound
resources have considerable internal redundancy (repeated areas of a tileset, silences in an
audio track), and compressing them when building the ROM lets them take up less space on
448

=== PAGE 455 ===
the cartridge in exchange for a runtime decompression cost, which SGDK handles automati-
cally with decompression functions provided by the library itself.
Inpractice,thisisdeclaredasanadditionaloptionintheresourcefile(thesame.resformat
used since Chapter 39), specifying the desired compression method for a given resource in-
stead of leaving it uncompressed. SGDK’s own engine takes care of detecting, when loading
thatresourcefromROM,thatit’scompressed,andofinvokingthecorrespondingdecompres-
sion routine before using it, transparently to code that already knew how to draw an image
or play back a tileset without compression.
Thepracticalresultfortheprogrammeristhataprojectcangetmuchclosertoacartridge’s
space limit without having to manually reduce the quantity or quality of its graphics and
sound resources, as long as the CPU time budget spent on decompression — relevant above
allwhendecompressingalargeresourceduringtheloadingofanewlevel—fitswithinwhat
the game can afford at that moment, an analysis for which the same CPU load measurement
tools presented in Chapter 49 come in handy.

Chapter 66 — Raylib as an
Alternative for Porting Games to
PC
What Raylib is, how it differs conceptually from SGDK, and why it can be the bridge to PC
and other platforms
This chapter steps away from the Mega Drive, for once. The previous chapters taught how
to program directly for the console’s hardware, with all the particularities that implies: 16-
colorpalettes,8×8tiles,aquantityofVRAMmeasuredinahandfulofkilobytes. Thischapter
introducesRaylib,agamedevelopmentlibraryforPCandothermodernplatforms,meantfor
anyone who—after having programmed for the Mega Drive with SGDK—wants to port their
gametoamoreaccessibleplatform, orsimplyprogramwithouttheconstraintsoflate-1980s
hardware.
This is not an exhaustive technical chapter about Raylib: there’s no need to cover its en-
tire API to understand what it offers. The idea, rather, is to show the conceptual parallel
between programming for the Mega Drive’s fixed hardware and programming for a modern
cross-platform library, and to verify, with a concrete code example, how much of a game’s
logic—structs, enums, state machines, simple physics—is actually independent of the target
platform.
Prerequisites
Before continuing, it helps to have covered:
• AgoodpartofthismanualandareasonablefamiliaritywithSGDK,inordertoappreciate
the contrast this chapter presents.
• Chapter 30, “Palette Fades”: it is directly compared, later on, with the way Raylib
achieves an equivalent effect.
• Chapter 31, “D-pad Controls”: the example in this chapter replicates, with Raylib, the
same sprite movement via the joypad that was built there for the Mega Drive.
It is not necessary to install Raylib to read this chapter, though it is worth doing so to experi-
ment with the example: it can be downloaded for free from its official site (raylib.com), with
packages already prepared for Windows, Linux, and macOS.
1. Why consider a PC port
Almost anyone developing a new game for the Mega Drive, sooner or later, considers the
possibility of also bringing it to PC or some modern console, simply because that makes it
450

=== PAGE 457 ===
accessible to far more people than those who still own, or emulate, the original hardware.
Before settling on one, it’s worth reviewing the available options.
One option is general-purpose game engines, such as Unreal Engine or Unity: engines de-
signed for much more ambitious productions, whose power is disproportionate for a game in
thestyleoftheonesbuiltinthismanual—aplatformerwith16-bitaesthetics. Anotheroption,
closer in spirit to programming directly for hardware, is to interact at a low level with the
Windows API; it’s an interesting path, but considerably more arduous than working with a
library already designed for games. Raylib occupies a middle ground between those two ex-
tremes: itisnotagameengine,butratherwhatitsowndocumentationcallsa“development
library” (a simple and easy-to-use library to enjoy videogames programming), with a spirit
quite similar to that of SGDK.
2. What Raylib is, and how similar it is to SGDK
Raylibisafree, cross-platformgamedevelopmentlibrary, withitssourcecodepubliclyavail-
able. Although it supports several programming languages through various bindings, the
languagethatmostofitscommunitygathersaroundisC,thesameonealreadyusedthrough-
outthismanualwithSGDK.Anyonewhohasfollowedthepreviouschaptersthereforedoesn’t
need to learn a new language to experiment with Raylib, only a different library.
Raylib’s official website is one of its strongest points: it includes a large number of already-
solved examples—title screens, cameras, and many other common use cases—that can be
used directly as a starting point, along with a reference sheet (cheatsheet) listing all the
functions grouped by module, and a wiki with more extensive guides.
ThemostimportantconceptualdifferencebetweenRaylibandSGDKhastodowithhoweach
one treats graphics. SGDK forces you to distinguish, at all times, whether something is a
background or a sprite, because that distinction exists in the Mega Drive’s hardware itself:
a background is built from a tile map with its own VRAM and palette limits, and a sprite is a
completelydifferenthardwareentity,withitsownlimitsonsizeandonhowmanycanappear
on screen at once. Raylib makes no such distinction: both a background and a sprite are
loaded the same way, as a generic 2D texture.
// In Raylib there is no structural difference between loading
// a background or a sprite: both are simply textures.
Texture2D background = LoadTexture("background.png");
Texture2D player_sprite = LoadTexture("player.png");
Going deeper. A good example to illustrate this difference is the screen fade-in, already
coveredinchapter30. OntheMegaDrive,dimmingthescreentoblackmeansmanipulating,
colorbycolor,thevaluesstoredinCRAM—theconsole’spalettememory—asexplainedinthat
chapterviaPAL_fadeIn(). InRaylib,thesameeffectisachievedbydrawingablackrectangle
thesizeoftheentirescreen,ontopofeverythingelse,andgraduallyvaryingitstransparency
until it becomes invisible:
// alpha starts at 1.0f (screen completely black)
// and is reduced frame by frame until it reaches 0.0f
DrawRectangle(0, 0, GetScreenWidth(), GetScreenHeight(),
Fade(BLACK, alpha));
The visual result is equivalent to that of PAL_fadeIn(), but the path to achieve it is radically
different: one depends on understanding and manipulating a specific, limited hardware re-
source (sixteen colors per palette, four palettes in total, 64 color slots in play); the other
depends solely on a generic property—transparency, handled here through the Fade() func-
451

=== PAGE 458 ===
tion, which adjusts a color’s alpha channel—that any modern graphics engine offers out of
the box, with no hardware limits involved.
After programming for a good while for the Mega Drive’s limited hardware, working with
Raylib can feel, at first, almost like cheating. It’s worth not taking that feeling too literally,
though: Raylib’sfunctionsarealldifferentfromSGDK’s,sothereisalearningcurvejustlike
withanynewtool. JustaswithSGDK,Raylibdoesn’thandyouafinishedgameengineeither:
you still have to build your own, with your own game logic, your own systems, and your own
code organization. What it does eliminate is much of the repetitive, uninteresting work (the
boilerplate)thathastobewrittenbeforegettingtothatactualgamelogic: openingawindow,
creatingamainloopatastableframerate,loadinganimage,orplayingasoundareeach,in
Raylib, a single function call.
3. The same movement, two platforms
ThebestwaytoseetheparallelbetweenSGDKandRaylibistocomparehoweachonesolves
the same problem: moving a character on screen based on what the player presses. Chapter
31 solved this for the Mega Drive with JOY_readJoypad() and the BUTTON_* constants:
static void handle_input(void)
{
u16 value = JOY_readJoypad(JOY_1);
if (value & BUTTON_RIGHT)
player_x += 1;
else if (value & BUTTON_LEFT)
player_x -= 1;
if (value & BUTTON_UP)
player_y -= 1;
else if (value & BUTTON_DOWN)
player_y += 1;
SPR_setPosition(player, player_x, player_y);
SPR_update();
}
The equivalent version in Raylib needs no SGDK, ROM, or emulator: it’s a complete PC pro-
gram, compiled with any C compiler and run like any other executable on the operating sys-
tem.
#include "raylib.h"
int main(void)
{
const int screen_width = 320;
const int screen_height = 240;
InitWindow(screen_width, screen_height, "Movement example with Raylib");
SetTargetFPS(60);
// Player position, analogous to player_x/player_y in SGDK
Vector2 player_pos = { 100.0f, 50.0f };
Texture2D player_sprite = LoadTexture("player.png");
452

=== PAGE 459 ===
while (!WindowShouldClose())
{
// --- Logic: input reading, equivalent to handle_input() ---
if (IsKeyDown(KEY_RIGHT))
player_pos.x += 1.0f;
else if (IsKeyDown(KEY_LEFT))
player_pos.x -= 1.0f;
if (IsKeyDown(KEY_UP))
player_pos.y -= 1.0f;
else if (IsKeyDown(KEY_DOWN))
player_pos.y += 1.0f;
// --- Drawing: there is no separate SPR_update(), it is
// drawn directly every frame inside Begin/EndDrawing ---
BeginDrawing();
ClearBackground(BLACK);
DrawTextureV(player_sprite, player_pos, WHITE);
EndDrawing();
}
UnloadTexture(player_sprite);
CloseWindow();
return 0;
}
The overall structure is the same in both cases: a position value that gets updated based on
playerinput,andanif/else ifperaxistoallowdiagonalmovementwithoutneedingtochain
allfourdirectionstogether—exactlythesamereasoningasinchapter31. Whatchangesisthe
sourceoftheinput—JOY_readJoypad()againsttheBUTTON_*constantsinSGDK;IsKeyDown()
against the KEY_* constants in Raylib—and the way the result is applied on screen: SGDK
separatesSPR_setPosition()fromSPR_update(),whileRaylibhandlesallthedrawinginside
a BeginDrawing()/EndDrawing() block on every pass of the main loop, which also takes care
of clearing the previous frame with ClearBackground(). Raylib also supports gamepads via
IsGamepadButtonDown(), which brings the parallel with reading a Mega Drive joypad even
closer.
What’s interesting is to notice what didn’t change between one version and the other: the
position value itself, the idea of checking one direction at a time, the separation between
“read input” and “draw the result.” That part of the logic, the part that doesn’t depend on
anyhardwareregisteroranyplatform-specificfunction,isessentiallyportableas-isbetween
Mega Drive and PC. The same holds for more elaborate structures already seen in this man-
ual: a struct that groups an enemy’s position, velocity, and state (chapter 53), an enum that
identifies an enemy type or a game state (chapter 54 and chapter 57), or a function pointer
used to resolve an enemy’s AI (chapter 56) are written in standard C, with no dependency
on SGDK, and therefore compile just as well against Raylib. Porting a Mega Drive game to
PC with Raylib largely consists of reusing that code almost unchanged, and replacing only
the layer that interacts with the hardware—input reading, drawing, sound—with its Raylib
equivalent.

Chapter 67 — Scope Note - Sega

Why this manual limits itself to the base Mega Drive hardware, and what paths exist for
anyone who wants to continue on to those two peripherals
Everything developed throughout this manual — from the first program to the capstone
project in Part IX — runs on the base Mega Drive hardware: the Motorola 68000 proces-
sor, the Z80 as sound coprocessor, the VDP, and the YM2612 and PSG chips described in
PartI.Segaalsoreleasedtwoperipheralsthatsubstantiallyexpandthathardware: theSega

SH-2processorsanditsowngraphicsmodewithgreatercolordepth. Neitheroneiscovered

The reason is not that these are minor topics or of limited interest, but a matter of rigor:
writing with the same depth and technical reliability maintained throughout the previous
parts requires having reference material of the same caliber, verified with the same care as
theSGDK2.11changelogorthedma.hdocumentationcitedinPartVIII.NeithertheSegaCD

peripherals, where it exists in the homebrew development tooling ecosystem, comes from
separate kits and libraries, each with its own learning curve and its own set of hardware
quirks.
Including a superficial chapter on either peripheral, without sufficient verification, would go
against the standard upheld throughout this manual: when in doubt, it is better to flag a
featureaspendingverification—or,inthiscase,toleaveanentiretopicoutofscope—than
to offer information without the necessary reliability.
Anopendoor,notaclosedone. Whatyou’velearnedhereremainsthenecessary
foundation for taking the leap to the Sega CD or the 32X down the line: applied C
fundamentals, working with limited memory, organizing a project across multiple

homebrewdevelopmentscene,dedicateddevelopmentkitsandactivecommunities
ready to guide those first steps, in the same way this manual supported your first

The game is called BOINGMD, a clone of the classic Pong (1972) set in a simple aesthetic of

1. The game design in one sentence
Two vertical paddles, one at each end of the screen, move up and down; a ball bounces be-
tween them and off the ceiling and floor; each time the ball crosses one end without the

correspondingpaddleinterceptingit,theplayerontheoppositesidescoresapoint;whoever

height with a deliberate margin of error so the match remains winnable.
Reducing the design to a single sentence, before writing a single line of code, is a discipline

3. The game’s state machine
The entire lifecycle of a match is resolved with three states, following the same pattern that
already organized the level transitions in the Part IX project:

cpu_score = 0;

paddle_reset();
ball_reset();
current_state = STATE_PLAYING;

high_score = player_score;
save_high_score(high_score);

=== PAGE 467 ===
}
void game_update(void) {
switch (current_state) {
case STATE_MENU:
// Just waits for the Start button, handled in joyEvent()
break;
case STATE_PLAYING:
paddle_update();
ball_update();
if (player_score >= WINNING_SCORE || cpu_score >= WINNING_SCORE) {
end_match();
}
break;
case STATE_GAME_OVER:
// Just waits for the Start button, handled in joyEvent()
break;
}
}
void joyEvent(u16 joy, u16 changed, u16 state) {
if (changed & state & BUTTON_START) {
if (current_state == STATE_MENU || current_state == STATE_GAME_OVER) {
start_new_match();
}
}
}
With just three states and a simple win condition, this machine is enough to give the game
a sense of a complete match, with a clear beginning and end—something the Part IX project
deliberately left unresolved.
4. The paddles: sprites, human control, and an AI with a
margin of error
Each paddle is a vertical sprite with movement restricted to the Y axis, within a range that
keeps it from leaving the screen:

static void move_player(void) {
u16 joy_state = JOY_readJoypad(JOY_1);
if (joy_state & BUTTON_UP) player_y -= PADDLE_SPEED;
if (joy_state & BUTTON_DOWN) player_y += PADDLE_SPEED;
if (player_y < FIX32(PADDLE_MIN_Y)) player_y = FIX32(PADDLE_MIN_Y);
if (player_y > FIX32(PADDLE_MAX_Y)) player_y = FIX32(PADDLE_MAX_Y);
SPR_setPosition(player_paddle, 16, F32_toInt(player_y));
}
// Chases the ball's height with a deliberate margin of error,
// so the AI isn't impossible to beat
static void move_cpu(void) {
fix32 target_y = ball_get_y();
fix32 error_margin = FIX32(6);
if (cpu_y + error_margin < target_y) cpu_y += PADDLE_SPEED;
else if (cpu_y - error_margin > target_y) cpu_y -= PADDLE_SPEED;
if (cpu_y < FIX32(PADDLE_MIN_Y)) cpu_y = FIX32(PADDLE_MIN_Y);
if (cpu_y > FIX32(PADDLE_MAX_Y)) cpu_y = FIX32(PADDLE_MAX_Y);
462

=== PAGE 469 ===
SPR_setPosition(cpu_paddle, 296, F32_toInt(cpu_y));
}
void paddle_update(void) {
move_player();
move_cpu();
}
The AI’s margin of error (error_margin) is the most important piece of this section: without
it, an AI chasing the ball with perfect precision would, in practice, be unbeatable. Adjusting
that single value together with PADDLE_SPEED is the most direct way to calibrate the game’s
difficultywithouttouchinganyotherpartofthecode. Theunderlyingprinciplecanbereused
inanyprojectofyourown: isolatebalancevaluesinnamedconstants,ratherthanscattering
them as magic numbers throughout the logic.
5. The ball: movement, bouncing, and collision with the
paddles
The ball moves in a straight line until it hits something, at which point it reverses the cor-
responding component of its velocity, applying the same kind of AABB collision seen in Part
VII:
// src/ball.c
#include "ball.h"
#include "paddle.h"
#include "game.h"
#include "resources.h"
#include "sfx.h"
static Sprite *ball_sprite_obj;

static fix32 ball_vel_x, ball_vel_y;
void ball_reset(void) {
ball_x = FIX32(160);
ball_y = FIX32(112);
ball_vel_x = FIX32(1.5);
ball_vel_y = FIX32(1);
ball_sprite_obj = SPR_addSprite(&ball_sprite, F32_toInt(ball_x),
F32_toInt(ball_y), TILE_ATTR(PAL0, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE));
}
fix32 ball_get_y(void) {
return ball_y;
}
static bool check_paddle_collision(fix32 paddle_x, fix32 paddle_y) {
bool overlap_x = (ball_x + FIX32(8) > paddle_x) && (ball_x < paddle_x +
↪ FIX32(4));
bool overlap_y = (ball_y + FIX32(8) > paddle_y) && (ball_y < paddle_y +
↪ FIX32(32));

=== PAGE 470 ===
return overlap_x && overlap_y;
}
void ball_update(void) {
ball_x += ball_vel_x;
ball_y += ball_vel_y;
// Bounce off the ceiling and floor
if (ball_y <= FIX32(16) || ball_y >= FIX32(216)) {
ball_vel_y = -ball_vel_y;
SND_startPlay_PCM(&bounce_sfx, SOUND_PCM_CH_AUTO);
}
// Bounce off the player's paddle
if (ball_vel_x < 0 && check_paddle_collision(FIX32(16), player_y)) {
ball_vel_x = -ball_vel_x;
SND_startPlay_PCM(&bounce_sfx, SOUND_PCM_CH_AUTO);
}
// Bounce off the AI's paddle
if (ball_vel_x > 0 && check_paddle_collision(FIX32(296), cpu_y)) {
ball_vel_x = -ball_vel_x;
SND_startPlay_PCM(&bounce_sfx, SOUND_PCM_CH_AUTO);
}
// Point for the AI: the ball crossed the left edge
if (ball_x < FIX32(0)) {
cpu_score++;
SND_startPlay_PCM(&score_sfx, SOUND_PCM_CH_AUTO);
ball_reset();
}
// Point for the player: the ball crossed the right edge
if (ball_x > FIX32(320)) {
player_score++;
SND_startPlay_PCM(&score_sfx, SOUND_PCM_CH_AUTO);
ball_reset();
}
SPR_setPosition(ball_sprite_obj, F32_toInt(ball_x), F32_toInt(ball_y));
}
Every bounce—off the ceiling, the floor, or a paddle—triggers the same short sound
effect (bounce_sfx), played with SND_startPlay_PCM() on a free channel indicated with
SOUND_PCM_CH_AUTO, while scoring a point triggers a different effect (score_sfx), following
the rescomp mechanism for declaring both resources already covered in Part VI:
// res/resources.res
SPRITE paddle_sprite "sprites/paddle.png" 4 32 FAST
SPRITE ball_sprite "sprites/ball.png" 8 8 FAST
WAV bounce_sfx "sounds/bounce.wav" XGM
WAV score_sfx "sounds/score.wav" XGM

6. The HUD: on-screen score without additional sprites
With the player and the AI now scoring points, they still need to be shown on screen. Fol-
lowing the suggestion at the close of Part IX, this game’s HUD is resolved entirely with text
over a background plane, without any sprites of its own, thereby avoiding any conflict with
SPR_reset() or other sprite operations in the game:
// Inside game_update(), called once per frame during STATE_PLAYING
static void update_hud(void) {
char score_text[10];
sprintf(score_text, "%d - %d", player_score, cpu_score);
VDP_drawText(score_text, 18, 2);
}
Updating the HUD every frame, instead of only when the score changes, is needlessly costly
when viewed with the same criteria from Part VIII on profiling: update_hud() is best called
only inside ball_update(), right after incrementing player_score or cpu_score, and not on
every pass of the main loop.
7. Saving the high score
save.c isolates all interaction with SRAM behind two simple functions, directly applying the
save mechanism with integrity checking explained in the previous chapter:
// src/save.c
#include "save.h"
#define SAVE_MAGIC 0x42 // Control value to detect uninitialized SRAM
u16 load_high_score(void) {
SRAM_enable();
u8 magic = SRAM_readByte(0);
u16 score = 0;
if (magic == SAVE_MAGIC) {
score = SRAM_readWord(1);
}
SRAM_disable();
return score;
}
void save_high_score(u16 score) {
SRAM_enable();
SRAM_writeByte(0, SAVE_MAGIC);
SRAM_writeWord(1, score);
SRAM_disable();
}
If SRAM_readByte(0)doesnotreturntheexpectedcontrolvalue,load_high_score()assumes
theSRAMwasneverwrittenbythisgame—forexample,thefirsttimeitrunsonanewconsole
oranewemulator—andreturnsahighscoreofzeroinsteadofameaninglessvaluereadfrom
uninitialized memory.

8. main.c: bringing all the pieces together
// src/main.c
#include <genesis.h>
#include "game.h"
#include "paddle.h"
#include "ball.h"
int main(bool hard_reset) {
JOY_init();
JOY_setEventHandler(joyEvent);
SPR_init();
game_init();
while (TRUE) {
game_update();
SPR_update();
SYS_doVBlankProcess();
}
return 0;
}
Compared to what it would have been to write the entire game inside a single file without
the organization presented throughout this manual, main.c ends up being very short in this
finished project: each responsibility—game state, paddles, ball, saving—lives in its own pair
of files, and main.c is limited to initializing the hardware once and delegating the rest to the
functions exposed by each module.
9. What’s deliberately left out
BOINGMD is a playable game, but it does not aim to be an example of every technique in
this manual: it does not use queued DMA because its graphical resources are minimal and it
doesn’t need it, it has no multiple levels and doesn’t require the level catalog from Part IX,
and its AI is deliberately simple because a fixed margin of error is enough for a Pong design.
Each of these omissions is a design decision, not a technical limitation: the tools for solving
more complex problems—queued DMA, data catalogs, function pointers for more elaborate
AI—are already documented in earlier parts of this manual, ready to be applied the day a
project of your own needs them.
